The Type I part (n ≤ N) is handled by Cauchy and the Weyl bound; the Type II part (n > N) uses bilinear forms and the large sieve for cubic characters. Step 5 – Sieve. Apply the Harman sieve with dimension 3. The sifting limit yields an upper bound ≪ X/(log X)3/2 for numbers with at most two prime factors. The exponent 3/2 reflects the saving from the delta method compared with the linear sieve exponent 1.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for an upper bound via the delta method, first write the delta symbol with explicit Q. Then identify the degree of the polynomial and quote the appropriate Weyl or Deligne bound. Next, sketch the Type I/II split and indicate which sieve (Harman, Rosser–Iwaniec, or linear) is used. Finally, state the exponent in the bound. Memorise the standard exponents: for degree d, the delta method typically gives an exponent d/2 for almost primes with two prime factors. Keep a template: delta approximation → exponential sum → bilinear forms → sieve → exponent.

The Sieve for Almost Primes in Ternary Quadratic Forms

A ternary quadratic form Q(x,y,z) = ax² + by² + cz² + dxy + exz + fyz with integer coefficients and non‑zero discriminant represents integers subject to local congruence conditions. The Hardy–Littlewood circle method gives an asymptotic for the number of representations of a given integer, but detecting primes requires a sieve. Heath‑Brown (1996) combined the Selberg sieve with the circle method to show that any non‑degenerate ternary quadratic form satisfying the necessary local conditions represents infinitely many almost primes with at most three prime factors. The argument proceeds by writing the indicator of almost primes as a Selberg upper bound weight λ_d supported on d ≤ D = Xθ. The level of distribution θ is limited by the error term in the asymptotic formula for Σn≤X r_Q(n) where r_Q(n) counts representations of n by Q. Using the circle method, one obtains an asymptotic with error O(X1−δ) for δ > 0 provided the form is not a multiple of a binary form. This yields θ = 1/2 − ε, which is sufficient for the Selberg sieve to produce almost primes with three prime factors. The parity problem prevents reducing the number of prime factors to two without additional bilinear input. Later work by Browning and Heath‑Brown (2015) introduced a weighted sieve with a quadratic correction (the pretzel sieve) to improve the exponent for the number of prime factors to 2.5 on average, but the integer result remains three. In examinations, the key points are: (i) the circle method provides the level of distribution, (ii) the Selberg sieve weight is chosen with D = X1/2−ε, (iii) the fundamental lemma gives the main term multiplied by the singular series, (iv) the parity barrier explains why three prime factors is the current limit for unconditional results. A common examiner twist is to ask for the singular series expression and to verify its convergence for a specific form such as x² + y² + z².

The Sieve for Primes in Arithmetic Progressions with Moduli up to X2/3 and the Work of Fouvry and Iwaniec

The Bombieri–Vinogradov theorem gives a level of distribution 1/2 for primes in arithmetic progressions on average over moduli q ≤ Q. Fouvry and Iwaniec (1983) broke this barrier for a fixed residue class a by exploiting the structure of the modulus. They proved that for any fixed a coprime to q, the primes are well distributed in progressions modulo q up to Q = X2/3 / (log X)^A, provided q is restricted to be square‑free and composed of primes in a certain range. The proof uses the dispersion method: one writes the error term as a bilinear sum Σm,n α_m β_n (1mn≡a (mod q) − 1/φ(q)) and applies Cauchy–Schwarz to separate the variables. The resulting sums are estimated using the Weil bound for Kloosterman sums and the large sieve for Dirichlet characters. The critical innovation is the use of a smooth weight that localises the modulus q near X1/3, allowing the bilinear form to be of Type I/II with lengths M ≈ N ≈ X1/2. This yields a power saving over the trivial bound. The result was later extended by Bombieri, Friedlander and Iwaniec (1986) to moduli q ≤ X4/7 for a set of residue classes of density zero. In the context of sieve theory, this level of distribution feeds directly into the linear sieve to produce primes in sparse sequences such as {n²+1} or {a²+b⁴}. Students should be able to: (a) state the Fouvry–Iwaniec theorem precisely, including the condition on q, (b) outline the dispersion method steps: bilinear decomposition, Cauchy–Schwarz, application of the Weil bound, (c) explain why the exponent 2/3 appears (it comes from balancing M and N in the Type I/II split), and (d) describe how the result is used as an input for the linear sieve to obtain almost primes in polynomial sequences. A frequent trap is to confuse the Fouvry–Iwaniec level 2/3 with the Elliott–Halberstam conjecture (level 1) or with the Bombieri–Vinogradov level 1/2; the former is unconditional but for a restricted set of moduli, the latter is unconditional for all moduli on average.

The Sieve for Primes in Cubic Polynomial Values and the Work of Heath‑Brown

Heath‑Brown (2001) proved that the cubic form f(x,y) = x³ + 2y³ represents infinitely many primes. The proof combines the Selberg sieve with the circle method for cubic exponential sums. The sequence 𝒜 = {f(x,y) : |x|,|y| ≤ X1/3} has size ≈ X2/3. The sieve dimension is 3 because the polynomial is irreducible of degree 3. The linear sieve would give an upper bound of the correct order but cannot produce a lower bound for primes due to the parity problem. Heath‑Brown circumvents this by using a weighted sieve with a quadratic correction (the pretzel sieve) that exploits the fact that the number of representations of an integer by f is bounded on average. The circle method provides an asymptotic for Σn≤X r_f(n) with a power‑saving error term, where r_f(n) counts representations of n by f. This yields a level of distribution θ = 1/2 − ε for the sifted set. The pretzel weight is constructed as λ_d = μ(d) (log(D/d)/log D) for d ≤ D, plus a double sum over d₁,d₂ ≤ D1/2 with a logarithmic weight. The double sum corrects the overcount of integers with three prime factors and improves the upper bound exponent from 3/2 to approximately 1.9. The final step applies the lower bound sieve of Rosser–Iwaniec to show that the sifted set contains integers with at most two prime factors, and then a combinatorial argument (using the fact that f is a norm form in a cubic field) upgrades almost primes to primes. In examinations, the essential ingredients are: (i) the circle method for cubic forms gives the level of distribution, (ii) the pretzel sieve weight and its quadratic correction, (iii) the transition from almost primes to primes via the norm form property, (iv) the resulting exponent for the upper bound. A typical question asks to write the pretzel weight explicitly and to explain why the double sum is restricted to d₁,d₂ ≤ D1/2. The answer is that larger products would exceed the sifting limit and the logarithmic weight would not compensate.

  • Confusing the GL(3) large sieve level N ≤ Q3/2 with the GL(2) level N ≤ Q; the exponent differs because the conductor scales differently.
  • Misstating the delta method parameter Q; it must be X1/2−δ for degree 2, but X1/3 for degree 3, and the choice depends on the Weyl exponent.
  • Assuming the circle method for ternary quadratic forms gives level 1; it only gives 1/2−ε, which limits the Selberg sieve to three prime factors.
  • Attributing the Fouvry–Iwaniec 2/3 level to all moduli; it holds only for square‑free moduli with prime factors in a specific range.
  • Omitting the quadratic correction in the pretzel sieve for cubic forms and quoting the linear sieve exponent 3/2 instead of the improved 1.9.
  • Mixing the dispersion method with the delta method; the former uses bilinear forms and Cauchy–Schwarz, the latter uses a smooth delta symbol and exponential sums.
  • Forgetting that the singular series for a ternary quadratic form converges only when the form is isotropic over ℝ and ℚ_p for all p; a common exam trap is to ask for the condition on the coefficients.

Iwaniec's Linear Sieve for n²+1: The Half‑Dimensional Barrier and the Switching Principle

In 1978 Henryk Iwaniec proved that the polynomial f(n) = n²+1 assumes infinitely many values with at most two prime factors (P₂ numbers). This was the first result breaking the "half‑dimensional barrier" for a polynomial sequence of degree two. The sequence 𝒜 = {n²+1 : n ≤ X} has size X and sieve dimension κ = 1/2 because the congruence n² ≡ −1 (mod p) has either 0 or 2 solutions, giving an average density 1/p of admissible residue classes. The linear sieve with sifting parameter z = X1/2 yields an upper bound of the correct order X/(log X) but cannot produce a lower bound for primes due to the parity problem. Iwaniec's innovation was to combine the linear sieve upper bound with a switching principle that exploits the algebraic factorization n²+1 = (n+i)(n−i) in the Gaussian integers ℤ[i]. He constructs a lower bound sieve weight supported on integers with an even number of prime factors in ℤ[i], then switches to a weight supported on integers with an odd number of prime factors when the sifting level exceeds X1/2. The critical input is a level of distribution θ = 1/2 for the sequence 𝒜 in arithmetic progressions to moduli q ≤ X1/2/(log X)A, obtained via the Weil bound for Kloosterman sums and the large sieve for Dirichlet characters. The switching principle allows the lower bound sieve to reach sifting limit β(κ) = 2 for κ = 1/2, producing P₂ numbers. The final step uses Chen's theorem (or a simpler combinatorial argument) to show that the sifted set contains integers with at most two prime factors in ℤ. In examinations, students must: (a) compute the sieve dimension of n²+1 and explain why it is 1/2, (b) state the level of distribution required and how the Weil bound provides it, (c) describe the switching principle and why it overcomes the parity problem for almost primes but not for primes, (d) write the Rosser–Iwaniec linear sieve weights λd explicitly for upper and lower bounds. A common trap is to confuse the half‑dimensional sieve (dimension 1/2) with the linear sieve (dimension 1); the former applies to sequences where the average number of prime factors is 1/2 log log X, the latter to sequences with average log log X.

The Baker–Harman–Pintz Theorem: Primes in Short Intervals [x, x+x0.525]

In 2001 Roger Baker, Glyn Harman, and János Pintz proved that for all sufficiently large x the interval [x, x+x0.525] contains at least one prime. This remains the best unconditional result on primes in short intervals, improving on Huxley's 1972 exponent 7/12 ≈ 0.5833. The proof is a tour de force of the Harman sieve, a hybrid of the linear sieve and the dispersion method designed to handle Type I and Type II sums with unequal lengths. The interval is partitioned into subintervals of length H = x0.525. The characteristic function of primes is decomposed via the Heath‑Brown identity into a sum of bilinear forms Σm∼M Σn∼N ambn with MN ≈ x. The Harman sieve introduces a sifting parameter z = x1/3 and splits the bilinear forms into Type I (M ≤ z) and Type II (z < M ≤ N < x/z). The Type I sums are estimated using the large sieve and the Bombieri–Vinogradov theorem. The Type II sums require a more delicate treatment: Harman's "shifted convolution" method writes the sum as Σq≤Q Σa (mod q) |Σm∼M am e(am/q)|² and applies the Weil bound for Kloosterman sums after Cauchy–Schwarz. The critical innovation is the choice z = x1/3, which balances the Type I range (handled by Bombieri–Vinogradov up to Q = x1/2/(log x)A) against the Type II range (where the Weil bound gives a power saving for M, N ≥ x1/3). The exponent 0.525 arises from solving the optimisation problem: maximise θ such that the Type I/II decomposition covers all M, N with MN = x and the error terms are o(H/log x). The resulting condition is θ > 1/2 + 1/40 = 0.525. In examinations, the essential ingredients are: (i) the Heath‑Brown identity decomposition into Type I/II sums, (ii) the Harman sieve parameter z = x1/3 and its role in separating the ranges, (iii) the application of Bombieri–Vinogradov for Type I and the Weil bound for Type II, (iv) the optimisation yielding 0.525. A frequent trap is to state that the exponent comes from the Riemann Hypothesis; it is unconditional. Another is to confuse the Harman sieve with the linear sieve; the former is a combinatorial sieve with a flexible sifting limit adapted to bilinear forms, the latter has a fixed sifting limit β(κ).

Worked Example: Deriving the 0.525 Exponent
Show how the exponent 0.525 emerges from the Type I/II balance in the Harman sieve for primes in [x, x+xθ]. Assume Bombieri–Vinogradov gives level 1/2 for Type I (M ≤ x1/3) and the Weil bound gives power saving for Type II when M, N ≥ x1/3. Find the maximal θ.
The interval length is H = xθ. We need the sifted sum to exceed the error terms. The Heath‑Brown identity decomposes the von Mangoldt function into bilinear forms with M ≤ N, MN ≈ x. The Harman sieve splits at z = x1/3. Type I: M ≤ z = x1/3. Bombieri–Vinogradov handles moduli q ≤ x1/2/(log x)A. The Type I sum contributes error ≪ x/(log x)A provided M ≤ x1/2/(log x)A, which holds since M ≤ x1/3. Type II: z < M ≤ N < x/z = x2/3. The Weil bound for Kloosterman sums gives a power saving for the bilinear form when M, N ≥ x1/3 (the "diagonal" condition). The critical case is M ≈ N ≈ x1/2, which lies in the Type II range. The total error from Type II is ≪ x1−δ for some δ > 0. The main term is ≍ H/log x = xθ/log x. For the main term to dominate we need θ > 1/2. The precise optimisation comes from the "gap" between the Type I upper limit x1/3 and the Type II lower limit x1/3. The worst‑case bilinear form has M just above x1/3 and N just below x2/3. The Cauchy–Schwarz + Weil bound step introduces a factor (MN)1/2 = x1/2 in the error. Balancing x1/2 against H = xθ gives θ = 1/2 + ε. The extra 1/40 = 0.025 comes from the logarithmic losses in the large sieve and the need to cover all M, N with a single z. The exact calculation (Harman 2007, Ch. 10) shows that with z = x1/3 the method works for any θ > 0.525. Hence the maximal unconditional exponent is 0.525.
Exam Strategy: Short Interval Primes
When a question asks for the exponent in the Baker–Harman–Pintz theorem, write 0.525 and immediately note it comes from z = x1/3 balancing Type I (Bombieri–Vinogradov) and Type II (Weil bound). If asked to compare with Huxley (7/12 ≈ 0.583), state that Huxley used the classical large sieve and zero‑density estimates, while Harman's sieve exploits bilinear structure. Never claim the result assumes RH; it is unconditional. For "explain the role of the Heath‑Brown identity", list the decomposition Λ = Λ1 + Λ2 + Λ3 + Λ4 where Λ1 is Type I, Λ2, Λ3 are Type II, and Λ4 is negligible.

The Bombieri–Friedlander–Iwaniec Theorem: Level of Distribution 4/7 for Primes in Arithmetic Progressions

In 1986 Enrico Bombieri, John Friedlander, and Henryk Iwaniec proved that the primes have level of distribution θ = 4/7 for a set of moduli of density zero. Precisely, for any A > 0 there exists a set of moduli Q ⊂ [Q, 2Q] with |Q| ≪ Q/(log Q)A such that Σq∈Q max(a,q)=1 |π(x; q, a) − li(x)/φ(q)| ≪ x/(log x)A for Q ≤ x4/7/(log x)B. This goes beyond the Bombieri–Vinogradov level 1/2 (which holds for all moduli on average) and the Fouvry–Iwaniec level 2/3 (which holds for square‑free moduli with prime factors in a specific range). The proof uses the dispersion method combined with a bilinear forms decomposition of the von Mangoldt function via the Heath‑Brown identity. The critical innovation is the use of a smooth weight localising the modulus q near x1/3, which allows the bilinear form to be of Type I/II with lengths M ≈ N ≈ x1/2. The dispersion method writes the error term as Σq∼Q Σa (mod q) |Σm∼M am e(am/q)|², applies Cauchy–Schwarz, and then uses the Weil bound for Kloosterman sums to estimate the resulting character sums. The exponent 4/7 arises from balancing the length Q of the modulus against the lengths M, N of the bilinear form: the condition for the Weil bound to give a power saving is Q < MN/x1/2 = x1/2, but the smooth weight and the large sieve for Dirichlet characters allow Q up to x4/7. The set of moduli Q is restricted to those for which the associated Kloosterman sums satisfy a non‑degeneracy condition; this is the "density zero" restriction. In sieve applications, this level of distribution feeds directly into the linear sieve to produce almost primes in sparse sequences such as {n²+1} or {a²+b⁴}. Students must be able to: (a) state the theorem precisely including the density‑zero condition, (b) outline the dispersion method steps: bilinear decomposition, Cauchy–Schwarz, Weil bound, (c) explain why the exponent 4/7 appears (balancing Q against M, N in the Type I/II split with smooth weights), (d) describe how the result is used as input for the linear sieve. A frequent trap is to confuse the BFI level 4/7 with the Elliott–Halberstam conjecture (level 1) or with the Bombieri–Vinogradov level 1/2; the former is unconditional but for a restricted set of moduli, the latter is unconditional for all moduli on average.

Maynard's Sieve for Primes with Missing Digits

In 2016 James Maynard proved that for any base b ≥ 2 and any digit a ∈ {0, 1, …, b−1}, there are infinitely many primes whose base‑b expansion does not contain the digit a. This was the first result showing that primes can avoid a fixed digit in any base, and it introduced a new multidimensional sieve weight adapted to the fractal structure of digit‑restricted sets. The set of integers ≤ x missing a given digit has size ≈ xδ with δ = log(b−1)/log b < 1. For base 10 and missing digit 0, δ = log 9/log 10 ≈ 0.954. The sequence is extremely sparse and does not have a level of distribution in the classical sense. Maynard's insight was to construct a sieve weight supported on integers whose prime factors lie in a carefully chosen set of residue classes modulo powers of b. The weight is a multidimensional generalisation of the Selberg sieve: λd = Σr|d μ(r) f(log r/log R) where f is a smooth function on a simplex in ℝk and R = xθ with θ < δ/2. The key innovation is the use of correlation estimates for the von Mangoldt function twisted by additive characters modulo bk. Maynard proves that for any fixed k, the primes are well‑distributed in residue classes modulo bk that avoid the forbidden digit, with an error term that is a power saving in x. This is achieved by combining the circle method for exponential sums over digit‑restricted sets with the large sieve for Dirichlet characters. The multidimensional weight allows the sieve to "see" the fractal structure: the simplex is chosen so that the weight is large on integers with prime factors in the allowed residue classes and small elsewhere. The lower bound sieve then produces integers with at most k prime factors in the digit‑restricted set, and a combinatorial argument (using the fact that the set of integers missing a digit is multiplicatively structured) upgrades almost primes to primes for sufficiently large k. In examinations, the essential ingredients are: (i) the digit‑restricted set has size xδ with δ = log(b−1)/log b, (ii) the multidimensional Selberg weight on a simplex in ℝk, (iii) the correlation estimates for Λ twisted by additive characters modulo bk, (iv) the transition from almost primes to primes via the multiplicative structure. A typical question asks to write the multidimensional weight explicitly and explain why the simplex dimension k must exceed a threshold depending on δ. The answer is that the sieve dimension of the digit‑restricted set is κ = δ, and the linear sieve lower bound requires k > 2κ/(1−κ) to overcome the parity problem.

The Green–Tao–Ziegler Theorem on Polynomial Progressions in Primes

In 2008 Ben Green, Terence Tao, and Tamar Ziegler proved that the primes contain arbitrarily long polynomial progressions: for any polynomials P1, …, Pk ∈ ℤ[m] with Pi(0) = 0, there exist infinitely many x, m such that x+P1(m), …, x+Pk(m) are all prime. This generalises the Green–Tao theorem on arithmetic progressions (where Pi(m) = (i−1)m) to arbitrary polynomial configurations. The proof combines the Green–Tao transference principle with a polynomial exhaustion argument and a multidimensional sieve for the polynomial correlations. The transference principle embeds the primes into a pseudorandom measure ν (the "majorant") that is constructed using the Goldston–Yıldırım sieve weights. The key new ingredient is the polynomial forms condition: for any collection of linear forms L1, …, Lt in variables m, n1, …, nd, the average of Π ν(Li) over a box is 1+o(1). This is established by expanding the sieve weights and using the Weil bound for exponential sums over polynomial phases. The polynomial exhaustion argument reduces the problem to finding a single polynomial progression in a dense subset of a cyclic group ℤ/Nℤ, which is then lifted to the integers via the transference principle. The multidimensional sieve enters in the construction of the majorant ν: the Goldston–Yıldırım weights are generalised to a tensor product of Selberg sieve weights over the polynomial variables. The resulting weight is λd1,…,dk = Πi=1k μ(di) f(log di/log R) where f is a smooth function on a simplex in ℝk. The polynomial forms condition requires that the correlations of these weights along polynomial progressions are asymptotically 1. This is verified by a combination of the circle method (for the major arcs) and the Weil bound (for the minor arcs). In examinations, students must: (a) state the theorem precisely, including the condition Pi(0) = 0, (b) explain the role of the transference principle and the majorant ν, (c) describe the polynomial forms condition and how it is verified using the Weil bound, (d) outline the polynomial exhaustion argument. A common trap is to confuse polynomial progressions with arithmetic progressions; the former have Pi(m) of degree > 1, the latter are linear. Another is to assume the result gives a quantitative bound on the size of the progression; the proof is ineffective and gives no explicit bound. A third trap is to attribute the polynomial forms condition to the linear sieve; it requires the multidimensional Goldston–Yıldırım weights and the Weil bound for polynomial exponential sums.

  • Confusing the half‑dimensional sieve (dimension 1/2) with the linear sieve (dimension 1); the former applies to sequences like n²+1, the latter to sequences like n.
  • Stating that the Baker–Harman–Pintz exponent 0.525 assumes the Riemann Hypothesis; it is unconditional.
  • Attributing the Bombieri–Friedlander–Iwaniec level 4/7 to all moduli; it holds only for a set of moduli of density zero.
  • Omitting the density‑zero condition when stating the BFI theorem; the set of moduli must be explicitly restricted.
  • Confusing the Harman sieve with the linear sieve; the former uses a flexible sifting parameter z = x1/3 adapted to bilinear forms, the latter has a fixed sifting limit β(κ).
  • Assuming Maynard's missing‑digit result gives a positive proportion of primes; it only proves infinitude, not density.
  • Mixing up the Green–Tao theorem (arithmetic progressions) with the Green–Tao–Ziegler theorem (polynomial progressions); the latter requires the polynomial forms condition and the Weil bound for polynomial phases.

The Squarefree Sieve and Its Application to Polynomial Values

The squarefree sieve originated in Erdős’s 1951 paper on the distribution of squarefree values of polynomials. For a polynomial f ∈ ℤ[x] of degree d ≥ 1 with no fixed square factor (i.e. there is no prime p such that p² | f(n) for all integers n), the number of integers n ≤ x for which f(n) is squarefree satisfies

#{ n ≤ x : f(n) squarefree } = C_f x + O( x1 - δ )

where the constant C_f is the convergent product

C_f = ∏_p ( 1 - ρ(p²) / p² )

and ρ(p²) denotes the number of solutions of f(n) ≡ 0 (mod p²). The exponent δ > 0 depends on d and the height of f; for fixed d one can take δ = 1/(2d+2) by the classical argument of Ricci (1970). The proof combines the inclusion–exclusion principle up to a sifting level z = x1/2 with the fundamental lemma of the combinatorial sieve to control the remainder. The squarefree condition is a sifting problem of dimension κ = d because the congruence f(n) ≡ 0 (mod p) has at most d solutions modulo p. When the polynomial is irreducible and the Galois group is the full symmetric group, the product C_f can be expressed in terms of the discriminant and the splitting behaviour of primes. Granville (1998) refined the error term to O( x1 - 1/(d+1) (log x)O(1) ) under the abc conjecture, while unconditional results of Heath‑Brown (1984) give δ = 1/(2d+2) for all d. In examinations the key points are: (i) the definition of ρ(p²), (ii) the convergence of the product, (iii) the role of the fundamental lemma in truncating the inclusion–exclusion at z = x1/2, and (iv) the distinction between the squarefree sieve (which gives an asymptotic) and the Selberg upper bound sieve (which only gives an upper bound of the correct order).

The Sieve for Primes in Beatty Sequences and the Distribution of Fractional Parts

A Beatty sequence is the set B_α = { ⌊α n⌋ : n ∈ ℕ } for an irrational α > 1. Beatty’s theorem (1926) states that B_α and B_β partition the positive integers iff 1/α + 1/β = 1. The problem of primes in Beatty sequences asks whether B_α contains infinitely many primes. Banks and Shparlinski (2006) proved that for any irrational α with bounded partial quotients (i.e. α of finite type) the sequence B_α contains infinitely many primes. Their method uses Vaughan’s identity to decompose the von Mangoldt function, followed by the linear sieve of Rosser and Iwaniec applied to the sifted set { n ≤ x : ⌊α n⌋ has no small prime factor }. The crucial analytic input is an estimate for exponential sums of the form ∑n ≤ N e( β ⌊α n⌋ ), which reduces via the identity ⌊α n⌋ = α n - {α n} to sums over the fractional parts {α n}. Weyl’s equidistribution theorem guarantees that for irrational α the sequence {α n} is uniformly distributed modulo 1, and the discrepancy is bounded by O( N-1 log N ) when α has bounded continued‑fraction coefficients. This yields a level of distribution θ = 1/2 - ε for the sequence ⌊α n⌋, which is sufficient for the linear sieve to produce a lower bound of the correct order. Harman (1998) earlier obtained an asymptotic formula for primes in Beatty sequences with α of finite type using his sieve with a flexible sifting parameter z = x1/3. The sieve dimension for Beatty sequences is κ = 1 because the congruence ⌊α n⌋ ≡ 0 (mod p) has exactly one solution modulo p for each prime p not dividing the denominator of a rational approximation to α. In examinations students must: (a) state the definition of a Beatty sequence and Beatty’s theorem, (b) explain why the sieve dimension is 1, (c) describe how the equidistribution of {α n} enters the level of distribution, and (d) outline the transition from the linear sieve lower bound to the infinitude of primes.

Worked Example: Squarefree Density of a Quadratic Polynomial
Let f(n) = n² + 1. Compute the squarefree density C_f = ∏_p (1 - ρ(p²)/p²) and explain why the product converges.
For p = 2, f(n) ≡ n²+1 (mod 4). The squares modulo 4 are 0,1, so n²+1 ≡ 1,2 (mod 4). Hence ρ(4)=0. For odd p, the congruence n² ≡ -1 (mod p²) has solutions iff -1 is a quadratic residue modulo p, i.e. p ≡ 1 (mod 4). When p ≡ 1 (mod 4) there are exactly 2 solutions modulo p² (Hensel lifting), so ρ(p²)=2. When p ≡ 3 (mod 4) there are none, ρ(p²)=0. Therefore C_f = (1 - 0/4) ∏p≡1(4) (1 - 2/p²) ∏p≡3(4) (1 - 0/p²) = ∏p≡1(4) (1 - 2/p²). The product converges because ∑p≡1(4) 2/p² ≤ 2 ∑_p 1/p² < ∞. The density is a positive constant ≈ 0.686. The convergence argument uses the bound ρ(p²) ≤ deg f = 2, so ∑ ρ(p²)/p² ≤ 2 ∑ 1/p² < ∞.
Exam‑Day Strategy
Memorise the squarefree density product and the condition ρ(p²) ≤ deg f. For Beatty sequences, remember that the sieve dimension is 1 and the level of distribution 1/2−ε comes from equidistribution of {α n}. Write the linear sieve lower bound as π_Bα(x) ≫ x / log x when the sifting parameter satisfies z ≤ x1/2−ε.

The Sieve for Primes in the Sequence of Values of a Binary Form and the Geometry of Numbers

A binary form is a homogeneous polynomial F(x,y) = a_d x^d + ad-1 xd-1 y + … + a0 y^d with integer coefficients and degree d ≥ 2. The problem of representing primes by F asks for integer pairs (x,y) with |x|,|y| ≤ X such that F(x,y) is prime. Heath‑Brown (2001) proved that for any irreducible cubic binary form F there are infinitely many primes of the shape F(x,y), provided F is not a product of linear forms over ℚ. The proof uses the geometry of numbers to count lattice points in the region { (x,y) ∈ ℝ² : |x|,|y| ≤ X, F(x,y) > 0 }. The number of such points is asymptotic to c_F X² where c_F is the volume of the corresponding region in ℝ². One then applies the combinatorial sieve of dimension κ = d to the sequence a_n = F(x,y) indexed by the lattice points. The fundamental lemma of the combinatorial sieve (Diamond–Halberstam–Richert) gives an asymptotic for the sifted set when the sifting level z ≤ X2/(d+1). For d = 3 this allows z ≤ X1/2, which is exactly the range needed for the linear sieve lower bound. Browning and Heath‑Brown (2015) extended the result to binary forms of arbitrary degree d ≥ 3 under the condition that the projective hypersurface F = 0 is smooth. They use the determinant method to bound the number of rational points of bounded height on the singular locus, and the large sieve for algebraic varieties to handle the minor arcs. The singular series 𝔖(F) appears as the product over primes of local densities (1 - ω(p)/p) / (1 - 1/p) where ω(p) is the number of projective solutions of F ≡ 0 (mod p). In examinations the essential ingredients are: (i) the geometry‑of‑numbers count of lattice points giving the main term c_F X², (ii) the identification of the sieve dimension as the degree d, (iii) the application of the fundamental lemma with sifting level z = X2/(d+1), and (iv) the convergence of the singular series for smooth forms.

The Sieve for Primes in the Sequence of Values of a Polynomial with Restricted Prime Factors and the Fundamental Lemma

Let f ∈ ℤ[x] be a polynomial of degree k ≥ 1 with no fixed prime divisor. For a parameter z = x1/s we consider the sifted set S(x,z) = { n ≤ x : p | f(n) ⇒ p > z }. The fundamental lemma of the combinatorial sieve (Diamond, Halberstam, Richert, 1988) asserts that if s > 2k then

|S(x,z)| = X ∏p ≤ z ( 1 - ω(p)/p ) ( 1 + O( e-s log s ) )

where X = x and ω(p) is the number of solutions of f(n) ≡ 0 (mod p). The lemma provides both an upper and a lower bound of the same quality, which is rare for sieves of dimension k > 1. The proof constructs upper and lower bound sieve weights λ_d^± supported on squarefree d with d ≤ z that satisfy the Buchstab identity recursively. The weights are derived from the solution of a linear programming problem that minimises the quadratic form ∑d λ_d² / g(d) where g(d) = ∏p|d ω(p)/(p-ω(p)). The condition s > 2k ensures that the remainder terms in the Buchstab iteration are smaller than the main term by a factor e-s log s. When s ≤ 2k the fundamental lemma fails and one must use the Rosser–Iwaniec linear sieve (for k = 1) or the upper bound sieve of Selberg (for general k) which only give one‑sided bounds. The fundamental lemma is the engine behind many “almost‑prime” results: for example, taking f(n) = n(n+2) and z = x1/3 yields Chen’s theorem that there are infinitely many n such that n is prime and n+2 has at most two prime factors. In examinations students should be able to: (a) state the fundamental lemma with the precise range s > 2k, (b) explain why the sieve dimension equals the degree k, (c) describe the role of the Buchstab identity in constructing the weights, and (d) give an example where the lemma produces a lower bound for almost primes but the linear sieve cannot.

  • Trap 1: Confusing the squarefree sieve density product ∏(1−ρ(p²)/p²) with the singular series for primes; the former counts squarefree values, the latter counts prime values.
  • Trap 2: Assuming the level of distribution for Beatty sequences is 1 for all irrational α; it is 1/2−ε and requires bounded partial quotients.
  • Trap 3: Stating that the fundamental lemma works for any sifting level z ≤ x1/2; the correct condition is s > 2k where z = x1/s.
  • Trap 4: Using the linear sieve dimension κ = 1 for binary forms of degree d ≥ 3; the sieve dimension equals the degree d.
  • Trap 5: Claiming the singular series for a binary form always converges; convergence requires the projective hypersurface to be smooth (no singular points modulo p for large p).
  • Trap 6: Mixing the Rosser–Iwaniec linear sieve (dimension 1) with the fundamental lemma (dimension k) when the polynomial degree is > 1.
  • Trap 7: Forgetting that the squarefree sieve gives an asymptotic only when the polynomial has no fixed square factor; otherwise the density is zero.

The Sieve for Primes in the Sequence of Values of a Polynomial with Restricted Prime Factors and the Linear Sieve

The Rosser–Iwaniec linear sieve is the principal tool for obtaining both upper and lower bounds for sequences of sieve dimension one. When the sequence is given by the values of a polynomial f(n) with integer coefficients and no fixed prime divisor, the sieve dimension equals the degree of f only when f is linear; for higher degree the dimension is larger and the linear sieve does not apply directly. However, for linear polynomials f(n) = an + b with (a,b) = 1 the dimension is one and the linear sieve yields asymptotically optimal bounds. The sieve constructs weights λd± supported on squarefree d ≤ z that satisfy the Buchstab identity recursively. The upper bound weights minimise the quadratic form ∑ λd² / g(d) where g(d) = ∏p|d ω(p)/(p−ω(p)) and ω(p) is the number of roots of f modulo p. The lower bound weights are obtained by a similar variational problem with a sign change. The resulting sifted set S(x,z) = { n ≤ x : p | f(n) ⇒ p > z } satisfies |S(x,z)| = X ∏p≤z (1 − ω(p)/p) (1 + O(e−s log s)) for z = x1/s with s > 2. The error term is controlled by the beta function β(s) which arises from the differential‑difference system satisfied by the optimal weights. For s > 2 the linear sieve gives a lower bound of the correct order, and for s > 3 it even produces an asymptotic. The half‑dimensional barrier at s = 2 is the point where the parity problem prevents a lower bound; the switching principle of Iwaniec overcomes this for special sequences such as n²+1 by inserting a bilinear form that detects the parity of the number of prime factors. In examinations the key points are: (i) the linear sieve applies only when the sieve dimension κ = 1, (ii) the optimal weights are derived from the solution of a linear programming problem that reduces to the beta integral, (iii) the range s > 2 is necessary for a non‑trivial lower bound, and (iv) the switching principle is a separate technique that does not follow from the linear sieve alone.

The Sieve for Primes in the Sequence of Values of a Polynomial with Restricted Prime Factors and the Selberg Sieve

The Selberg sieve provides an upper bound for sequences of arbitrary sieve dimension κ. For a polynomial f of degree k ≥ 1 with no fixed prime divisor, the sieve dimension equals k. The Selberg weights are of the form λd = μ(d) g(d) ∑m≤z/d μ(m) g(m) F(log(z/dm)/log z) where F is a piecewise polynomial chosen to minimise the quadratic form ∑ λd² / g(d). The minimisation leads to a variational problem whose solution is expressed in terms of the Selberg integral J(κ) = ∫01 (1−t)κ−1 F(t)² dt. The optimal F is a polynomial of degree κ−1, and the resulting upper bound is |S(x,z)| ≤ X ∏p≤z (1 − ω(p)/p) (1 + O(e−s log s)) for z = x1/s with s > κ. The Selberg sieve does not give a lower bound; it is an upper‑bound sieve. However, by combining it with the Buchstab identity one can obtain lower bounds for almost‑prime values, leading to results such as Chen’s theorem (primes p such that p+2 has at most two prime factors). The fundamental lemma of the combinatorial sieve (Diamond–Halberstam–Richert) improves the range to s > 2κ and provides both upper and lower bounds of the same quality, but its proof is more intricate. In examinations students should be able to: (a) write down the Selberg quadratic form and explain the role of the multiplicative function g(d), (b) state the condition s > κ for the upper bound to be non‑trivial, (c) describe how the variational problem reduces to finding the optimal polynomial F, and (d) contrast the Selberg sieve with the linear sieve (dimension one) and the fundamental lemma (both bounds, wider range). A common trap is to apply the Selberg lower bound machinery to dimension > 1 without the fundamental lemma; the Selberg sieve alone never yields a lower bound.

Worked Example: Selberg Upper Bound for a Quadratic Polynomial
Let f(n) = n² + 1. Determine the sieve dimension, write the Selberg quadratic form, and state the range of s for which the Selberg sieve gives a non‑trivial upper bound for the number of n ≤ x with p | f(n) ⇒ p > x1/s.
The polynomial f(n) = n² + 1 has degree 2 and no fixed prime divisor (since f(0)=1). For each prime p, the congruence n² ≡ −1 (mod p) has either 0 or 2 solutions; on average ω(p) = 2 for p ≡ 1 (mod 4) and 0 otherwise. The sieve dimension κ is the average of ω(p), which equals 2. The Selberg weights are supported on squarefree d with d ≤ z = x1/s. The quadratic form to minimise is ∑d≤z λd² / g(d) where g(d) = ∏p|d ω(p)/(p−ω(p)). The Selberg sieve yields a non‑trivial upper bound provided s > κ = 2. Thus for any s > 2 the sifted set satisfies |S(x,x1/s)| ≪ X ∏p≤x1/s (1 − ω(p)/p). The implied constant depends only on κ.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the sieve dimension of a polynomial sequence, compute the degree if the polynomial is irreducible and has no fixed prime divisor; the dimension equals the degree. For the Selberg sieve, remember that it only gives an upper bound and the condition for a non‑trivial bound is s > κ. If the problem asks for a lower bound, you must invoke the fundamental lemma (which requires s > 2κ) or the linear sieve (only for κ = 1). Write the quadratic form explicitly and mention the variational principle; this shows you understand the mechanism, not just the statement.

The Sieve for Primes in the Sequence of Values of a Polynomial with Restricted Prime Factors and the Large Sieve

The large sieve inequality in its arithmetic form bounds the mean square of a sequence of complex numbers over reduced residue classes modulo many moduli. For a polynomial sequence an = 1f(n)∈A where A is a set of integers with certain congruence restrictions, the large sieve gives ∑q≤Q ∑a (mod q) |∑n≤N an e(an/q)|² ≤ (N + Q²) ∑n≤N |an|². When an is the indicator of f(n) having no small prime factors, the duality principle converts this into a bound for the number of n for which f(n) lies in a given set of residue classes. The large sieve is particularly powerful for establishing level of distribution results: one can show that the sequence f(n) is well‑distributed in arithmetic progressions on average up to moduli q ≤ xθ with θ = 1/2 for linear polynomials (Bombieri–Vinogradov) and θ < 1/2 for higher degree polynomials, depending on the geometry of the associated algebraic variety. For quadratic polynomials, the work of Fouvry and Iwaniec gives θ = 1/2 − ε under GRH, while unconditional results reach θ = 2/5. The large sieve also interacts with zero‑density estimates for Dirichlet L‑functions to produce primes in short intervals of the form f(n). In examinations the essential ingredients are: (i) the duality principle that turns a bound for exponential sums into a bound for the sifted set, (ii) the role of the level of distribution θ in determining the sifting range, (iii) the distinction between the large sieve for characters (which uses orthogonality of Dirichlet characters) and the large sieve for additive characters (which uses the Gallagher lemma), and (iv) the fact that the large sieve alone does not overcome the parity problem; it must be combined with a combinatorial sieve (e.g., the linear sieve or the Selberg sieve) to produce prime or almost‑prime results.

The Sieve for Primes in the Sequence of Values of a Polynomial with Restricted Prime Factors and the Combinatorial Sieve

The combinatorial sieve of Diamond, Halberstam, and Richert (the DHR sieve) is a general framework that produces both upper and lower bound sieves for sequences of any dimension κ. The construction proceeds by iterating the Buchstab identity S(A,z) = |A| − ∑p<z</sub> S(Ap,p) where Ap = { a ∈ A : p | a }. Truncating the iteration at a carefully chosen level yields sieve weights λd± supported on squarefree d with d ≤ z. The weights satisfy the linear programming constraints ∑d|n λd± ≥ 0 (for the upper bound) and ≤ 0 (for the lower bound) for all n composed of primes < z. The fundamental lemma states that if the sifting level z = x1/s with s > 2κ, then there exist weights such that |S(A,z)| = X ∏p<z</sub> (1 − ω(p)/p) (1 + O(e−s log s)), where X = ∑a∈A 1 and ω(p) is the number of residue classes modulo p occupied by A. The proof constructs the weights by solving a minimisation problem for the quadratic form ∑ λd² / g(d) with g(d) = ∏p|d ω(p)/(p−ω(p)), exactly as in the Selberg sieve, but the truncation is performed at a level that depends on the parity of the number of prime factors. The condition s > 2κ is sharp for the fundamental lemma; when s ≤ 2κ the remainder terms in the Buchstab iteration are no longer negligible and one must resort to the Rosser–Iwaniec linear sieve (κ = 1) or the Selberg upper bound sieve (κ > 1). For polynomial sequences f(n) of degree k, the dimension κ = k, so the fundamental lemma applies for s > 2k. This range is exactly what is needed to prove Chen’s theorem (take f(n) = n(n+2), κ = 2, s = 3). In examinations students should be able to: (a) write the Buchstab identity and explain how truncation leads to sieve weights, (b) state the fundamental lemma with the precise condition s > 2κ, (c) describe the role of the function g(d) in the quadratic form, and (d) give an example where the fundamental lemma yields a lower bound for almost primes while the Selberg sieve only gives an upper bound.

The Sieve for Primes in the Sequence of Values of a Polynomial with Restricted Prime Factors and the Switching Principle

The switching principle, introduced by Iwaniec, is a technique that allows one to bypass the parity barrier for certain sequences of sieve dimension 1/2 (half‑dimensional sieve). For a polynomial f(n) = n² + 1, the sequence of values has sieve dimension 1, but the associated sifting problem for primes is half‑dimensional because the condition p | n²+1 forces p ≡ 1 (mod 4), effectively halving the density of primes. The linear sieve gives an upper bound for the number of n ≤ x with n²+1 having no prime factor ≤ x1/s for s > 2, but it fails to give a lower bound at s = 2. The switching principle inserts a bilinear form ∑m,n αm βn amn where amn is the indicator of f(mn) having no small prime factors. By choosing the coefficients α, β to detect the parity of the number of prime factors of f(mn), one can obtain a lower bound for the number of n with f(n) prime or almost prime. The method relies on the asymptotic evaluation of the bilinear form using the large sieve and the Bombieri–Vinogradov theorem for the sequence f(n). The optimal weights for the half‑dimensional sieve are given by the beta function β(s) which satisfies a differential‑difference equation similar to the linear sieve but with a different initial condition. The switching principle has been extended to other polynomial sequences such as n² + k and to the affine sieve of Bourgain–Gamburd–Sarnak. In examinations the key points are: (i) the half‑dimensional sieve arises when the set of allowed primes has density 1/2 within all primes, (ii) the switching principle converts a lower bound problem into an upper bound problem for a bilinear form, (iii) the evaluation of the bilinear form requires a level of distribution result for the polynomial sequence, and (iv) the method does not produce a full asymptotic for primes but yields infinitely many almost primes of a specified type.

  • Trap 1: Confusing the sieve dimension of a polynomial sequence with its degree when the polynomial has a fixed prime divisor; the dimension is the average of ω(p), not the degree.
  • Trap 2: Applying the linear sieve (dimension 1) to a quadratic polynomial without reducing the problem to a half‑dimensional setting; the linear sieve only works for κ = 1.
  • Trap 3: Stating that the Selberg sieve gives a lower bound; it is an upper‑bound sieve only.
  • Trap 4: Using the fundamental lemma with s ≤ 2κ; the lemma requires s > 2κ for both upper and lower bounds of the same quality.
  • Trap 5: Assuming the large sieve alone can produce primes; it must be combined with a combinatorial sieve to overcome the parity problem.
  • Trap 6: Forgetting that the switching principle requires a level of distribution result for the specific polynomial sequence; without it the bilinear form cannot be evaluated.
  • Trap 7: Mixing the beta function of the linear sieve with the beta function of the half‑dimensional sieve; they satisfy different differential‑difference equations.

The Selberg–Delange Method for Polynomial Values with Restricted Prime Factors

The Selberg–Delange method extends the classical Selberg sieve by incorporating complex‑analytic information from Dirichlet series attached to the sifted set. For a polynomial f(n) of degree k with integer coefficients, one studies the generating series

∑n≤x zω(f(n)) = 1⁄2πi ∫c−i∞c+i∞ F(s) xs⁄s ds,

where ω(m) counts distinct prime factors of m and F(s) = ∑ an n−s with an = zω(f(n)). The method replaces the combinatorial truncation of the Selberg sieve by a contour shift that isolates the main term from the pole at s = 1 and estimates the remainder via zero‑free regions of the associated L‑functions. The key input is an asymptotic for the mean value of zω(f(n)) which, by the Selberg–Delange theorem, equals

C(z) x (log x)z−1 (1 + O((log x)−δ))

with an explicit constant C(z) depending on the singular series of f. When the prime factors are restricted to a set 𝒫 of density θ, the exponent becomes zθ and the constant acquires an Euler product over 𝒫. This refinement yields upper and lower bounds of the same quality for the number of n ≤ x such that f(n) has no prime factor outside 𝒫, provided the level of distribution of f in arithmetic progressions exceeds 1⁄2. The method is particularly effective for polynomials of degree ≥ 2 where the combinatorial sieve alone cannot reach the optimal sifting limit. In examinations candidates should be able to (a) write the Dirichlet series for zω(f(n)), (b) state the Selberg–Delange asymptotic with the precise dependence on z, (c) explain how the contour shift replaces the quadratic form minimisation of the Selberg sieve, and (d) give an example where the method produces a lower bound for almost‑prime values of n²+1 that the linear sieve cannot.

The Function Field Sieve and Its Application to Polynomial Sequences

The function field sieve transfers the large‑sieve machinery to the setting of polynomials over a finite field 𝔽q. Let A be a set of monic polynomials of degree ≤ N and let 𝒫 be a set of irreducible polynomials. The sifting problem asks for the number of f ∈ A having no irreducible factor from 𝒫 of degree ≤ Z. The analogue of the Bombieri–Vinogradov theorem in this context is the equidistribution of polynomial values in residue classes modulo irreducible polynomials, which follows from the Riemann hypothesis for curves over finite fields (Weil bounds). The large sieve inequality for function fields reads

∑deg Q ≤ Z ∑a mod Q |∑f∈A af e(Tr(a f / Q))|² ≤ (qN + qZ) ∑ |af|²,

where the additive character is built from the trace map 𝔽q[t] → 𝔽q. Using this inequality together with the duality principle one obtains an upper bound for the sifted set that matches the expected main term up to a factor 1 + O(q−cZ). The method also yields a lower bound via the Rosser–Iwaniec linear sieve adapted to the function field setting, where the sieve dimension equals the average number of irreducible factors of a random polynomial, namely 1. The crucial advantage is that the level of distribution can be taken as large as Z = N − o(N), far beyond the 1⁄2 barrier in the integer case. Consequently one can prove, for example, that a positive proportion of monic polynomials of degree N are irreducible, and more generally that the number of polynomials with exactly r irreducible factors follows a Poisson–Dirichlet law. In examinations the key points are: (i) the function field large sieve follows from Weil’s Riemann hypothesis, (ii) the level of distribution reaches N − o(N), (iii) the sieve dimension for polynomial sequences is 1, and (iv) the method gives both upper and lower bounds of the same quality for almost‑prime polynomials.

Worked Example: Applying the Function Field Large Sieve
Let A be the set of monic polynomials f ∈ 𝔽5[t] of degree ≤ 10. Let 𝒫 be the set of all irreducible polynomials of degree ≤ 3. Estimate the number of f ∈ A having no factor from 𝒫 using the function field large sieve.
The large sieve inequality gives ∑deg Q ≤ 3 ∑a mod Q |∑f∈A af e(Tr(a f / Q))|² ≤ (510 + 53) ∑ |af|². Choose af = 1 for f ∈ A and 0 otherwise. The left side counts the discrepancy of the distribution of A in residue classes modulo each Q. By Weil’s bound the discrepancy is O(5deg Q/2). Summing over all Q of degree ≤ 3 yields a total error O(510·5−3/2) = O(58.5). Hence the number of f with no small irreducible factor equals |A| ∏deg P ≤ 3 (1 − 1/5deg P) + O(58.5). The main term is 510·(1 − 1/5)(1 − 1/5²)(1 − 1/5³) ≈ 510·0.8·0.96·0.992 ≈ 510·0.764. The error is smaller by a factor 5−1.5, confirming the asymptotic.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for a sieve bound in a function field setting, first write the large‑sieve inequality with the correct parameters (q, N, Z). Then invoke the Weil bound to control character sums. Remember that the level of distribution can be taken as Z = N − o(N), so the sifting limit is essentially unrestricted. State the final asymptotic with the Euler product over the excluded irreducibles.

The Analytic Sieve: Complex Integration Techniques for Polynomial Prime Counting

The analytic sieve replaces the purely combinatorial truncation of the Selberg sieve by a contour integral representation of the sifted sum. For a set A of integers and a sifting parameter z, one writes

S(A, z) = ∑a∈A ∏p<z</sub> (1 − 1p|a) = 1⁄2πi ∫c−i∞c+i∞ F(s) xs⁄s ds,

where F(s) = ∑n≥1 an n−s with an = ∏p|n, p<z</sub> (1 − 1). The integrand is a product of the Dirichlet series of A and the Euler product over p < z. Shifting the contour to the left picks up the pole at s = 1, giving the main term X ∏p<z</sub> (1 − ω(p)/p), while the integral over the new line is bounded using zero‑free regions and mean‑value theorems for Dirichlet polynomials. The method is especially powerful when A is the set of values of a polynomial f(n) because the associated Dirichlet series can be expressed in terms of L‑functions of the number field generated by a root of f. The analytic sieve yields upper bounds of Selberg quality for any sieve dimension κ, and lower bounds of the same order when the level of distribution exceeds 1⁄2. It also provides a natural framework for incorporating bilinear forms (Type I/II sums) by inserting a smooth weight in the integral. In examinations students should be able to (a) set up the contour integral for S(A, z), (b) identify the main term from the pole at s = 1, (c) explain how the zero‑free region of ζ(s) or the relevant L‑function controls the error, and (d) compare the analytic sieve with the combinatorial Rosser–Iwaniec linear sieve for κ = 1.

The Spectral Large Sieve for GL(2) Automorphic Forms and Polynomial Values

The spectral large sieve bounds sums of Fourier coefficients of GL(2) automorphic forms over a family of moduli. Let {φj} be an orthonormal basis of Maass cusp forms for Γ0(q) with Laplace eigenvalues λj = 1⁄4 + tj². For a sequence a(n) supported on n ≤ N, the inequality reads

∑q≤Q ∑j |∑n≤N a(n) λj(n)|² ≤ (N + Q²) ∑ |a(n)|²,

where λj(n) are the Hecke eigenvalues. When a(n) is the indicator of polynomial values f(n) with f ∈ ℤ[x] of degree k, the sum over n becomes a sum over n ≤ N of λj(f(n)). The spectral large sieve then provides a level of distribution Q ≈ N1/2 for the sequence f(n) in the sense of the Bombieri–Vinogradov theorem. This is the key input for the switching principle in the half‑dimensional sieve for n²+1 and for the affine sieve of Bourgain–Gamburd–Sarnak. The proof uses the Kuznetsov trace formula to convert the sum over automorphic forms into a sum over Kloosterman sums, which are then bounded by Weil’s estimate. The resulting bound is uniform in the spectral parameter tj, allowing one to sum over a wide range of forms. In examinations the essential points are: (i) the spectral large sieve is a dual form of the classical large sieve, (ii) it gives a level of distribution N1/2 for polynomial sequences, (iii) the Kuznetsov formula and Weil bounds are the analytic engines, and (iv) the method is indispensable for overcoming the parity barrier in half‑dimensional problems.

The Harman Sieve for Primes in Short Intervals of Polynomial Sequences

The Harman sieve combines a combinatorial decomposition of the von Mangoldt function with a delicate treatment of Type I and Type II sums to detect primes in intervals of length xθ with θ < 1. For a polynomial f(n) of degree k, one considers the sum

∑x < f(n) ≤ x + xθ Λ(f(n)).

Using Heath‑Brown’s identity, Λ(f(n)) is expressed as a linear combination of convolutions of sequences supported on ranges determined by parameters U, V. The Type I sums involve a smooth coefficient α(m) and a sum over n of β(n) with m n = f(n). The Type II sums are bilinear forms ∑m∼M ∑n∼N α(m) β(n) 1f(mn)∈I. The large sieve and the Bombieri–Vinogradov theorem for the polynomial sequence give the necessary equidistribution in arithmetic progressions up to moduli Q ≈ x1/2−ε. By optimising the parameters one can take θ = 0.525 for linear polynomials (Baker–Harman–Pintz) and θ = 2⁄3 for quadratic polynomials under the Elliott–Halberstam conjecture. The Harman sieve also yields lower bounds for almost‑primes in short intervals, e.g. numbers with at most two prime factors. In examinations candidates should be able to (a) write Heath‑Brown’s identity for Λ(f(n)), (b) distinguish Type I and Type II ranges, (c) state the level of distribution required for each type, and (d) explain why the method fails to reach θ = 1⁄2 unconditionally for general polynomials.

  • Confusing the Selberg–Delange exponent zθ with the sieve dimension κ; the exponent is the product of the weight z and the density θ of the allowed primes.
  • Assuming the function field large sieve works with the same level of distribution as the integer large sieve; in function fields the level can be taken as N − o(N).
  • Neglecting the zero‑free region requirement when shifting the contour in the analytic sieve; the error term depends critically on the width of the zero‑free strip.
  • Mixing the spectral large sieve for GL(2) with the classical large sieve for Dirichlet characters; they bound different families and have different dual forms.
  • Applying the Harman sieve without verifying the Bombieri–Vinogradov theorem for the specific polynomial sequence; the level of distribution must be established before the Type I/II analysis.
  • Stating that the analytic sieve automatically gives lower bounds; it only yields lower bounds when the level of distribution exceeds 1⁄2.
  • Overlooking the role of the Kuznetsov trace formula in the spectral large sieve; it is the bridge between automorphic forms and Kloosterman sums.

The Spectral Large Sieve for Polynomial Sequences via the Kuznetsov Trace Formula

The spectral large sieve extends the classical large sieve by replacing Dirichlet characters with Fourier coefficients of automorphic forms. For a polynomial sequence f(n) of degree k ≥ 2, one considers the sum S = ∑q≤Q ∑φ |∑n≤N a(n) λ_φ(f(n))|² where φ runs over an orthonormal basis of Maass cusp forms for Γ₀(q) and λ_φ(m) are the Hecke eigenvalues. The Kuznetsov trace formula converts the double sum over forms and moduli into a sum over Kloosterman sums S(m,n;c) weighted by Bessel transforms. Weil’s bound |S(m,n;c)| ≤ τ(c) (m,n,c)1/2 c1/2 then yields the inequality S ≪ (N + Q²) ∑|a(n)|² uniformly in the spectral parameter. This provides a level of distribution Q ≈ N1/2 for the polynomial sequence, which is the critical input for the switching principle in half‑dimensional problems such as n²+1. The method also applies to the affine sieve of Bourgain–Gamburd–Sarnak, where one sieves orbits of thin groups. In examinations candidates should be able to (i) state the spectral large sieve inequality, (ii) outline the role of the Kuznetsov formula and Weil bounds, (iii) explain why the level N1/2 is optimal for general polynomials, and (iv) compare the spectral large sieve with the classical large sieve for Dirichlet characters.

The Selberg–Delange Method for Polynomial Values with a Fixed Number of Prime Factors

The Selberg–Delange method evaluates sums of the form ∑n≤x zΩ(f(n)) where Ω counts prime factors with multiplicity and f ∈ ℤ[x] is a polynomial without fixed prime divisors. One writes the Dirichlet series F(s) = ∑n≥1 zΩ(f(n)) n-s and expresses it as ζ(s)^z G(s) with G(s) analytic and non‑vanishing for Re(s) > 1−δ. By shifting the contour to the left of s = 1 and picking up the pole of order z at s = 1, one obtains an asymptotic ∑n≤x zΩ(f(n)) ∼ C_f(z) x (log x)z−1 where C_f(z) = G(1)/Γ(z) ∏p (1−1/p)^z (1 + z/p + z(z+1)/p² + …). For integer z = k the coefficient of z^k/k! gives the count of integers n ≤ x with Ω(f(n)) = k. The method requires a zero‑free region for ζ(s) and for the L‑functions attached to the polynomial, typically the classical zero‑free strip σ ≥ 1 − c/log t. The error term is O(x (log x)z−2) under the Riemann hypothesis, and O(x exp(−c√log x)) unconditionally. In examinations students must (a) derive the Euler product factorisation, (b) identify the singular expansion at s = 1, (c) explain how the zero‑free region controls the contour shift, and (d) apply the result to obtain the asymptotic for almost‑prime values of f(n) with a prescribed number of prime factors.

Worked Example: Applying the Selberg–Delange Method to f(n)=n²+1
Let f(n)=n²+1. Use the Selberg–Delange method to find the main term for the number of n ≤ x such that Ω(f(n)) = 2.
The Dirichlet series is F(s)=∑n≥1 zΩ(n²+1) n-s. For each prime p, the local factor is 1 + z·ρ(p)/p^s + z(z+1)·ρ(p²)/p2s+… where ρ(p^k) counts solutions of n²+1≡0 (mod p^k). For p≡1 (mod 4) there are two solutions modulo p, so ρ(p)=2; for p≡3 (mod 4) there are none, ρ(p)=0. The Euler product becomes ∏p≡1(4) (1−1/p^s)-2z ∏p≡3(4) (1−1/p^s)0 × G(s). Hence F(s)=ζ(s)2z·H(s) where H(s) is analytic and non‑zero for Re(s)>1/2. The pole at s=1 has order 2z. For z=1 (Ω=2) the residue gives C·x (log x)1 with C = H(1)/Γ(2) = H(1). The constant H(1)=∏p≡1(4) (1−1/p)2 (1+2/p+…). Thus the main term is C x log x. The error term follows from the zero‑free region of ζ(s).
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the asymptotic of integers with a fixed number of prime factors in a polynomial sequence, first write the Dirichlet series, factor out ζ(s)^z, and identify the local densities. Remember that the exponent of the pole equals z times the average number of roots of f modulo p. The constant involves a convergent Euler product over primes where f has roots. Always state the required zero‑free region explicitly; examiners award marks for citing the classical zero‑free strip or the Riemann hypothesis when needed.

The Sieve for Almost Primes in the Values of Binary Forms Using the Geometry of Numbers

Let F(x,y) be an irreducible binary form of degree d ≥ 3 with integer coefficients and non‑zero discriminant. One wishes to count pairs (x,y) with |x|,|y| ≤ B such that F(x,y) has at most r prime factors. The geometry of numbers enters via the lattice Λ = {(x,y) ∈ ℤ² : F(x,y) ≡ 0 (mod q)} for each modulus q. By applying the large sieve to the set of rational points on the projective line, one obtains a level of distribution Q ≈ B2/d−ε. The combinatorial sieve of Rosser–Iwaniec then yields an upper bound for the number of (x,y) with Ω(F(x,y)) ≤ r, provided r > d·κ where κ is the sieve dimension (here κ = 2/d). For r = d+1 the lower bound sieve of Chen gives a positive proportion of almost‑prime values. The key technical input is the estimate for the number of solutions of F(x,y) ≡ 0 (mod q) which follows from the Weil bounds for curves and the geometry of numbers bound |Λ| ≪ q1+ε. In examinations candidates should be able to (i) set up the sifting set A = {F(x,y) : |x|,|y| ≤ B}, (ii) compute the sieve dimension κ = 2/d, (iii) state the level of distribution obtained from the large sieve for binary forms, and (iv) explain why the parity barrier prevents reaching r = 1 (prime values) unconditionally.

The Sieve for Primes in Arithmetic Progressions with Moduli up to X3/4 and the Work of Fouvry–Iwaniec

Fouvry and Iwaniec proved a Bombieri–Vinogradov type theorem for primes in arithmetic progressions with moduli up to Q = x3/4−ε under the assumption of a suitable level of distribution for the ternary divisor function. Their argument combines the dispersion method with a bilinear form decomposition of the von Mangoldt function, exploiting the fact that the ternary divisor function d₃(n) has a level of distribution 2/3. By inserting a smooth weight and applying the large sieve for Dirichlet characters, they obtain ∑q≤Q max(a,q)=1 |π(x;q,a) − li(x)/φ(q)| ≪ x/(log x)^A for any A > 0. This result is a crucial ingredient in the proof of the existence of infinitely many primes of the form n²+1 with at most two prime factors, and it also feeds into the work of Baker–Harman–Pintz on primes in short intervals. In examinations students must (a) describe the dispersion method and the role of the ternary divisor function, (b) state the level of distribution 2/3 for d₃(n), (c) explain how the large sieve for characters yields the moduli range Q = x3/4−ε, and (d) discuss the limitations that prevent extending the exponent beyond 3/4 without new input such as the Elliott–Halberstam conjecture.

The Sieve for Primes in the Sequence of Values of a Polynomial with Restricted Prime Factors and the Spectral Large Sieve

Consider a polynomial f ∈ ℤ[x] of degree k ≥ 2 and a set of primes ℙ₀ of density θ. One sieves the sequence A = {f(n) : n ≤ N} by removing all prime factors outside ℙ₀. The spectral large sieve provides a level of distribution Q ≈ N1/2 for the sequence f(n) when the sifting set is defined by congruence conditions modulo q. By combining the spectral large sieve with the Selberg upper bound sieve, one obtains an upper bound S(A, z) ≪ X ∏p<z, p∉ℙ₀</sub> (1−ω(p)/p) where ω(p) is the number of roots of f modulo p. The lower bound requires a switching principle: one replaces the characteristic function of the sifted set by a bilinear form and applies the spectral large sieve to the dual sum. This yields a lower bound of the correct order when the sifting level z satisfies z ≤ N1/(2κ) with κ = θ·k. The method has been used to produce almost‑prime values of f(n) with a prescribed set of allowed prime factors, and it underlies recent results on primes in sparse polynomial sequences. In examinations candidates should be able to (i) formulate the sifting problem with restricted prime factors, (ii) state the spectral large sieve inequality for polynomial sequences, (iii) derive the upper bound via the Selberg sieve, and (iv) outline the switching principle that converts the upper bound into a lower bound for almost‑primes.

  • Confusing the spectral large sieve level N1/2 with the classical large sieve level N; the spectral version gains a square‑root saving only for automorphic forms.
  • Neglecting the zero‑free region when shifting the contour in the Selberg–Delange method; the error term depends critically on the width of the zero‑free strip.
  • Assuming the geometry‑of‑numbers bound for binary forms works for all degrees without the Weil estimates for curves.
  • Overstating the Fouvry–Iwaniec exponent 3/4 as unconditional for all arithmetic progressions; it requires the ternary divisor function level 2/3.
  • Applying the switching principle without verifying the bilinear form decomposition matches the spectral large sieve duality.
  • Remember to verify the level of distribution before applying any sieve to a polynomial sequence.

Higher‑Degree Polynomial Values: Selberg–Delange Method with Restricted Prime Factors

The Selberg–Delange method extends the classical Selberg sieve by incorporating complex‑analytic information from Dirichlet series attached to the sifted sequence. For a polynomial f ∈ ℤ[x] of degree d ≥ 3, one studies the set A = {f(n) : n ≤ N} after removing all prime factors outside a prescribed set ℙ₀ of natural density θ. The generating Dirichlet series F(s) = ∑n≤N, p|f(n)⇒p∈ℙ₀ n-s can be expressed as a product over p∈ℙ₀ of local factors (1 − ω(p)p-s)-1 multiplied by an Euler product over p∉ℙ₀ that is analytic for Re(s) > 1 − δ. By shifting the contour to the left of s = 1 and picking up the pole at s = 1, the main term emerges as C N (log N)θκ−1 where κ = d is the sieve dimension and C involves the singular series ∏p∈ℙ₀ (1 − ω(p)/p) (1 − 1/p)-θ. The error term depends critically on the zero‑free region of the associated L‑functions; under the Generalised Riemann Hypothesis one gains a power‑saving, while unconditionally the Hildebrand–Tenenbaum saddle‑point analysis yields an error of size N (log N)θκ−1−c for some c > 0.

A key technical point is the verification of the Siegel–Walfisz property for the sequence f(n) restricted to ℙ₀. This requires uniform estimates for ∑n≤N, f(n)≡0 (mod q) 1 with q up to (log N)^A, which follow from the Weil bounds for the projective hypersurface f(x) ≡ 0 (mod q) when q is prime and from the Chinese remainder theorem for composite moduli. The dimension κ = d enters the exponent of the logarithm, reflecting the fact that each irreducible factor of f contributes one to the sieve dimension. When ℙ₀ has density θ < 1, the effective dimension becomes θκ, and the fundamental lemma of the combinatorial sieve guarantees asymptotic formulae for sifting levels z ≤ N1/(θκ)−ε. The method also produces asymptotic counts for integers with a prescribed number of prime factors from ℙ₀, by extracting coefficients of the Selberg–Delange generating function via Cauchy’s integral formula.

In practice, the Selberg–Delange method is combined with the linear sieve of Rosser–Iwaniec to obtain upper and lower bounds of the correct order for the number of n ≤ N such that f(n) has at most r prime factors from ℙ₀. The optimal r is determined by the inequality r > θκ, which is the saturation threshold for the upper bound sieve. For r = ⌈θκ⌉ + 1 the lower bound sieve of Chen yields a positive proportion of almost‑prime values. The parity barrier manifests itself in the inability to reach r = 1 without additional bilinear input; the Selberg–Delange method alone cannot distinguish between integers with an even or odd number of prime factors from ℙ₀.

Examination questions often ask candidates to (i) write down the Dirichlet series for the sifted polynomial sequence, (ii) identify the pole at s = 1 and compute its residue in terms of the singular series, (iii) state the required zero‑free region for a power‑saving error term, and (iv) explain why the parity problem prevents a prime‑value result. A typical trap is to confuse the sieve dimension κ = d with the effective dimension θκ when the set of allowed primes has density θ < 1.

Spectral Large Sieve for Polynomial Sequences with Restricted Prime Factors

The spectral large sieve, developed by Deshouillers–Iwaniec and refined by Kowalski–Michel–VanderKam, provides a level of distribution Q ≈ N1/2 for sequences arising from Fourier coefficients of GL(2) automorphic forms. When the sifted set is A = {f(n) : n ≤ N} with f a polynomial of degree d, one can embed the sequence into the space of automorphic forms by considering the Hecke eigenvalues of a suitable cusp form whose Fourier coefficients encode the values f(n). The large sieve inequality then reads ∑q≤Q ∑a (mod q)^* |∑n≤N a_n e(an/q)|2 ≪ (N + Q2) ∑n≤N |a_n|2, where the asterisk denotes primitive characters. For polynomial sequences the coefficients a_n are taken as the indicator of the condition “all prime factors of f(n) lie in ℙ₀”. By applying the Selberg upper bound sieve to the dual sum, one obtains an upper bound S(A, z) ≪ X ∏p<z, p∉ℙ₀</sub> (1 − ω(p)/p) with X = N ∏p∈ℙ₀ (1 − ω(p)/p)-1. The level of distribution Q = N1/2−ε is essentially optimal for the spectral large sieve; any improvement would contradict known bounds for the Ramanujan–Petersson conjecture.

The lower bound requires a switching principle: one replaces the characteristic function of the sifted set by a bilinear form ∑m,n α_m β_n 1mn∈A and applies the spectral large sieve to the dual sum over automorphic forms. This technique, pioneered by Friedlander–Iwaniec for the polynomial n²+1, yields a lower bound of the correct order provided the sifting level satisfies z ≤ N1/(2θκ). The bilinear decomposition must be chosen so that the resulting sums factorise into products of sums over m and n that are amenable to the spectral large sieve. In the polynomial setting, a natural choice is to write f(n) = g(m) h(n) with m,n in suitable ranges, which is possible when f is reducible or when one uses a factorisation of the polynomial modulo many primes.

Applications of this method include the proof that there are infinitely many integers n such that n²+1 has at most two prime factors from a set of density 1/2, and the construction of almost‑prime values of binary forms F(x,y) with restricted prime factors. The spectral large sieve also feeds into the work of Bourgain–Gamburd–Sarnak on the affine sieve, where the sifted set consists of values of a polynomial map on a thin orbit of a Zariski‑dense subgroup of SL₂(ℤ). In that context the level of distribution is Q ≈ B2/d−ε for a binary form of degree d, and the combinatorial sieve of Rosser–Iwaniec yields upper bounds for Ω(F(x,y)) ≤ r with r > d·κ, κ = 2/d.

Candidates should be able to (i) state the spectral large sieve inequality for GL(2) automorphic forms, (ii) explain how the level of distribution Q = N1/2 is derived, (iii) outline the switching principle that converts the upper bound into a lower bound for almost‑primes, and (iv) discuss the limitations imposed by the Ramanujan–Petersson conjecture on further improvements. A common mistake is to confuse the spectral large sieve level N1/2 with the classical large sieve level N; the spectral version gains a square‑root saving only because the dual sum runs over an orthonormal basis of automorphic forms.

Worked Example: Upper Bound via Spectral Large Sieve
Let f(x) = x³ + 2 and ℙ₀ be the set of primes congruent to 1 modulo 3, which has density θ = 1/2. Using the spectral large sieve, derive an upper bound for the number of n ≤ N such that all prime factors of f(n) belong to ℙ₀, with sifting level z = N1/4.
The sequence a_n = 1p|f(n)⇒p∈ℙ₀ is supported on n ≤ N. The spectral large sieve gives a level of distribution Q = N1/2−ε. The sieve dimension for the full set of primes is κ = 3 (degree of f). Restricting to ℙ₀ reduces the effective dimension to θκ = 3/2. The Selberg upper bound sieve with sifting level z = N1/4 satisfies z ≤ N1/(2θκ) = N1/3, so the upper bound applies. The main term is X ∏p<z, p∉ℙ₀</sub> (1 − ω(p)/p) where X = N ∏p∈ℙ₀ (1 − ω(p)/p)-1. For p ≡ 2 (mod 3), ω(p) = 0 because x³ ≡ −2 (mod p) has no solution when 3 ∤ p−1. For p ≡ 1 (mod 3), ω(p) = 3 on average. The product over p∉ℙ₀ is therefore over p ≡ 2 (mod 3) and equals ∏p≡2 (3), p<z</sub> (1 − 0/p) = 1. Hence the upper bound simplifies to S(A, z) ≪ N ∏p≡1 (3) (1 − 3/p)-1 ≪ N (log N)3/2. The implied constant depends on the singular series for the polynomial. This matches the expected order of magnitude from the fundamental lemma.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for an upper bound via the spectral large sieve, first identify the automorphic form that encodes the polynomial sequence (often a Hecke eigenform of weight 0 or 1/2). Write down the large‑sieve inequality with the correct level Q = N1/2−ε. Then apply the Selberg sieve variational principle: the optimal weights are given by the solution of a quadratic minimisation problem whose answer is the singular series. Remember that the effective sieve dimension is θκ, not κ, when the allowed primes have density θ. Finally, check that the sifting level z satisfies z ≤ N1/(2θκ); otherwise the lower bound sieve cannot be invoked and only the upper bound is available.

Switching Principle for Polynomial Sequences with Restricted Prime Factors in Higher Dimensions

The switching principle is a versatile device that transforms an upper bound sieve problem into a lower bound problem by replacing the characteristic function of the sifted set with a carefully chosen bilinear form. For a polynomial map F : ℤ^k → ℤ of total degree d, one considers the set A = {F(x) : x ∈ ℤ^k, ‖x‖ ≤ B}. The goal is to show that many values of F have at most r prime factors from a prescribed set ℙ₀ of density θ. The upper bound sieve gives S(A, z) ≪ X ∏p<z, p∉ℙ₀</sub> (1 − ω(p)/p) with X = B^k ∏p∈ℙ₀ (1 − ω(p)/p)-1 provided the level of distribution is at least Bk/(θκ)−ε. To obtain a lower bound, one writes 1n∈A = ∑m,n α_m β_n 1mn = F(x) and applies the large sieve (classical or spectral) to the dual sum ∑q ∑a |∑m α_m e(am/q)|2. The coefficients α_m, β_n are chosen to approximate the indicator of the condition “all prime factors lie in ℙ₀” while keeping the bilinear form amenable to the large sieve.

In higher dimensions (k ≥ 2) the geometry of numbers enters: the number of solutions to F(x) ≡ 0 (mod q) with ‖x‖ ≤ B is bounded by O_ε (Bk−1+ε qε) for irreducible F, by a result of Heath‑Brown. This bound, together with the Weil estimates for the projective hypersurface F = 0, yields a level of distribution Q ≈ Bk/d−ε for the classical large sieve. The effective sieve dimension is κ = k/d, so the saturation threshold for the upper bound sieve is r > θκ. The switching principle then produces a lower bound for r = ⌈θκ⌉ + 1, provided the bilinear decomposition respects the factorisation of F modulo many primes. For binary forms (k = 2) this is the affine sieve of Bourgain–Gamburd–Sarnak; for general k it is the higher‑dimensional affine sieve developed by Salehi‑Golsefidy and Sarnak.

A concrete instance is the polynomial F(x,y,z) = x² + y² + z². The set of primes represented by this form has density 1/2 (those congruent to 1 mod 4). The sieve dimension is κ = 3/2, so θκ = 3/4. The upper bound sieve works for r > 3/4, i.e. r ≥ 2. The switching principle with a bilinear form supported on m,n ≤ B1/2 yields a lower bound for integers with at most two prime factors from ℙ₀. The key technical input is the estimate for the number of representations of an integer by the ternary quadratic form, which follows from the circle method and the theory of modular forms of half‑integral weight.

Examination questions may ask to (i) set up the bilinear form for a given polynomial map, (ii) state the required level of distribution and the resulting saturation threshold, (iii) explain how the geometry‑of‑numbers bound for solutions of F(x) ≡ 0 (mod q) feeds into the large sieve, and (iv) discuss why the parity barrier still prevents reaching r = 1. A frequent error is to assume that the switching principle works for any bilinear decomposition; the decomposition must be compatible with the large sieve duality, which forces the coefficients to be supported on intervals of length roughly Bk/2.

Fundamental Lemma for Polynomial Sequences with Restricted Prime Factors under Congruence Conditions

The fundamental lemma of the combinatorial sieve asserts that for a sifting problem of dimension κ, if the sifting level z satisfies z ≤ D1/κ where D is the level of distribution, then the sifted set S(A, z) satisfies S(A, z) = X ∏p<z</sub> (1 − ω(p)/p) (1 + O(e-s)) with s = log D / log z. When the sequence A consists of values of a polynomial f(n) with n ≤ N, and we restrict to prime factors in a set ℙ₀ of density θ, the effective dimension becomes κ_eff = θ·deg f. The level of distribution D is typically N1/2 for the classical large sieve, or N1/2 for the spectral large sieve when the polynomial sequence is embedded in an automorphic form. The fundamental lemma then gives an asymptotic formula for the number of n ≤ N such that f(n) has no prime factor outside ℙ₀ up to z, provided z ≤ N1/(2θκ)−ε.

Congruence conditions on n (e.g., n ≡ a (mod q)) modify the local densities ω(p). For each prime p, the number of solutions to f(n) ≡ 0 (mod p) with n in the prescribed congruence class is either 0 or the same as the unrestricted count, depending on whether the congruence class intersects the solution set. This changes the singular series by a factor that is a product over p|q of local correction terms. The fundamental lemma remains valid with the modified singular series, provided the level of distribution is not degraded by the congruence condition. In practice, one uses the Chinese remainder theorem to combine the polynomial congruence f(n) ≡ 0 (mod p) with the fixed congruence n ≡ a (mod q), and the large sieve for Dirichlet characters supplies the necessary level of distribution uniformly in q up to (log N)^A.

An important application is the proof of Chen’s theorem on Goldbach’s problem: every sufficiently large even integer is a sum of a prime and an almost‑prime with at most two prime factors. The sifted set is A = {n ≤ N : n ≡ a (mod q)} where q is the product of small primes, and the polynomial is f(n) = n(N−n). The fundamental lemma with congruence conditions yields the required upper and lower bounds for the number of representations with restricted prime factors. The parity barrier appears as the inability to separate the contributions of integers with an even versus odd number of prime factors; the fundamental lemma alone cannot overcome this, and one must introduce a bilinear form (the switching principle) to obtain a lower bound for almost‑primes.

Candidates should be able to (i) state the fundamental lemma with explicit dependence on the sifting parameter s, (ii) compute the effective sieve dimension θκ for a polynomial sequence with restricted prime factors, (iii) explain how congruence conditions alter the local factors ω(p) and the singular series, and (iv) describe the role of the large sieve in providing the level of distribution D. A typical trap is to forget that the fundamental lemma requires z ≤ D1/κ_eff; using a larger z invalidates the asymptotic formula and only the upper bound sieve remains applicable.

  • Confusing the effective sieve dimension θκ with the polynomial degree κ when the allowed prime set has density θ < 1.
