Thin Groups and the Spectral Gap for the Laplacian on the Convex Core of Hyperbolic Manifolds

Let Γ be a Zariski‑dense, finitely generated subgroup of SL₂(ℤ) that is not a lattice; the quotient Γ\ℍ² is an infinite‑volume hyperbolic manifold. Its convex core C(Γ) is the smallest convex submanifold carrying the fundamental group. The Laplace–Beltrami operator Δ on C(Γ) with Neumann boundary conditions has a discrete spectrum below the continuous spectrum threshold 1/4. The size of the first non‑zero eigenvalue λ₁(Γ) is governed by the critical exponent δ(Γ) of the Poincaré series. Patterson–Sullivan theory shows that δ(Γ) equals the Hausdorff dimension of the limit set Λ(Γ). When δ(Γ) > 1/2, the work of Sullivan and later of Lax–Phillips implies that λ₁(Γ) = δ(Γ)(1−δ(Γ)). For thin Schottky groups, δ(Γ) can be arbitrarily close to 1, so λ₁(Γ) can be made arbitrarily small. However, if Γ arises from a congruence subgroup of an arithmetic lattice, Selberg’s theorem gives λ₁ ≥ 3/16. For general thin groups, the best universal lower bound is λ₁ > 0, a consequence of the spectral gap for the random walk on the Cayley graphs of the congruence quotients Γ/Γ(q). This gap, proved by Bourgain–Gamburd for SL₂(ℤ) and extended by Salehi‑Golsefidy–Varjú to higher rank, transfers to a uniform lower bound on λ₁(Γ) that depends only on the generating set and the Zariski closure. The mechanism is the expander property of the family {Cay(Γ/Γ(q), S)}: the spectral gap of the normalized adjacency operator on these finite graphs controls the bottom of the spectrum of Δ on C(Γ) via a transfer principle due to Lubotzky–Phillips–Sarnak. In particular, if the expander family is asymptotically Ramanujan, then λ₁(Γ) ≥ 3/16; current technology yields only a polynomial gap, giving λ₁(Γ) ≥ c > 0 with c depending on Γ. The convex core geometry also influences the essential spectrum: the continuous spectrum starts at 1/4, and any eigenvalue below 1/4 corresponds to an L² eigenfunction on C(Γ). The distribution of these eigenvalues is linked to the resonances of the scattering matrix, which in turn are controlled by the zeros of the Selberg zeta function associated to Γ. Recent work of Naud and others has shown that for convex co‑compact thin groups, the resonance free strip has width proportional to the spectral gap of the congruence expanders, providing a quantitative connection between the analytic theory of the Laplacian and the combinatorial expansion of the finite quotients.

Thin Groups and Expander Graphs from Thin Subgroups of Exceptional Algebraic Groups

Let G be a simply connected simple algebraic group of exceptional type (G₂, F₄, E₆, E₇, E₈) defined over ℚ, and let Γ ⊂ G(ℤ) be a finitely generated Zariski‑dense subgroup. The superstrong approximation theorem of Salehi‑Golsefidy–Varjú applies to any such Γ: for any symmetric generating set S, the Cayley graphs Cay(Γ/Γ(q), S) form a family of expanders as q runs over square‑free integers. The proof follows the same three‑step scheme as for classical groups: (i) a non‑concentration estimate showing that the random walk measure μ on Γ/Γ(q) does not concentrate on proper subgroups; (ii) the product theorem of Breuillard–Green–Tao for finite simple groups of Lie type, which in the exceptional case relies on the classification of maximal subgroups due to Liebeck–Seitz; (iii) a flattening lemma that converts non‑concentration into a uniform spectral gap. The exceptional groups present two additional technical points. First, the maximal subgroups of G(𝔽_q) include not only parabolic and subfield subgroups but also a finite list of “exotic” almost simple subgroups whose structure is known explicitly. The Zariski density of Γ forces the random walk to escape these subgroups exponentially fast, because any proper algebraic subgroup of G has strictly smaller dimension. Second, the representation theory of G(𝔽_q) is more intricate: the minimal dimension of a non‑trivial irreducible representation grows like a power of q, and the character bounds required for the flattening lemma are supplied by the Deligne–Lusztig theory. The resulting expansion constant ε depends only on the rank of G and the generating set S, not on q. As a quantitative by‑product, one obtains a diameter bound diam(Cay(Γ/Γ(q), S)) ≤ C (log q)ᴬ where the exponent A is a function of the rank; for G₂ one can take A = 2, for F₄ A = 3, and for the simply laced exceptional groups A = 4. Improving A to 1 remains open and is equivalent to the optimal superstrong approximation conjecture. These expander families have immediate applications: they give a uniform spectral gap for the Laplacian on the locally symmetric spaces ΓG(ℝ)/K, they enable the affine sieve on thin orbits of exceptional groups, and they provide explicit constructions of expander graphs with large girth and high degree, which are of independent interest in computer science.

Worked Example: Spectral Gap Transfer for a Thin Schottky Group
Let Γ = ⟨A, B⟩ ⊂ SL₂(ℤ) be a Schottky group generated by two hyperbolic matrices with disjoint fixed point sets on ℝℙ¹. Assume the congruence quotients Γ/Γ(p) form an expander family with spectral gap ε > 0 independent of p. Show that the Laplacian on the convex core C(Γ) has a spectral gap λ₁ ≥ c ε for some absolute constant c > 0.
The expander property means that for each prime p, the normalized adjacency operator T_p on ℓ²(Γ/Γ(p)) satisfies ‖T_p − Π‖ ≤ 1 − ε, where Π is the projection onto constants. By the Lubotzky–Phillips–Sarnak transfer principle, the bottom of the spectrum of the Laplacian Δ on C(Γ) is bounded below by a constant multiple of the uniform spectral gap of the finite graphs. Concretely, one constructs a test function on C(Γ) by lifting an eigenfunction of T_p and uses the fact that the covering map C(Γ) → Γ/Γ(p) is a local isometry on the thick part. The Rayleigh quotient of the lifted function is controlled by the Rayleigh quotient on the finite graph, yielding λ₁(Δ) ≥ c ε. The constant c depends only on the geometry of the fundamental domain of Γ, which is fixed. Hence λ₁ ≥ c ε > 0.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for a spectral gap on a thin quotient, first identify whether the group is arithmetic or thin. For thin groups, cite the Bourgain–Gamburd–Salehi‑Golsefidy–Varjú theorem: uniform expansion of congruence quotients implies a uniform lower bound on λ₁. Do not confuse this with Selberg’s 3/16 bound, which holds only for congruence subgroups of arithmetic lattices. If the problem mentions “Ramanujan” or “asymptotically Ramanujan”, note that current results give only a polynomial gap, not the optimal Alon–Boppana bound.

Thin Groups and the Affine Sieve on Thin Orbits of Exceptional Groups

The affine sieve of Bourgain–Gamburd–Sarnak produces almost prime values of a polynomial map f : Γ → ℤ on a thin orbit Γ·v, provided the group Γ has a uniform spectral gap across all congruence quotients. For exceptional groups, the same sieve machinery works once superstrong approximation is established. Let G be an exceptional algebraic group over ℚ, Γ ⊂ G(ℤ) a Zariski‑dense finitely generated subgroup, and v ∈ ℤⁿ a vector such that the orbit Γ·v is Zariski‑dense in an affine variety V. Let f : V → ℤ be a polynomial that is non‑constant on the orbit. The sieve dimension κ is the number of irreducible factors of f over ℚ, counted with multiplicity. The level of distribution θ is the exponent such that the error term in the sieve is O(X1−θ+o(1)). Uniform expansion gives θ = 1/2 − δ for some δ > 0 depending on the spectral gap. Applying the β‑sieve yields that f takes values with at most r = ⌈κ/θ⌉ prime factors infinitely often. For exceptional groups, the representation theory of G(𝔽_q) enters the sieve through the computation of the local densities: the number of solutions to f(x) ≡ 0 (mod q) in Γ/Γ(q) is approximated by the product of local factors, and the error is controlled by the spectral gap. The main technical input is the bound on the Fourier coefficients of the characteristic function of the level sets of f, which follows from the expander mixing lemma. As a concrete example, take G = G₂, Γ a thin subgroup generated by two elements in G₂(ℤ), and f the norm form on the 7‑dimensional representation. The sieve shows that f attains values with at most 3 prime factors on the orbit, provided the generating set projects onto a non‑elementary subgroup modulo p for infinitely many primes. The same argument works for any polynomial map on any thin orbit of an exceptional group, giving the first almost prime results in this setting.

Thin Groups and Quantitative Equidistribution of Thin Orbits on Higher Rank Homogeneous Spaces

Let G be a semisimple algebraic group of ℚ‑rank at least 2, and let Γ ⊂ G(ℤ) be a Zariski‑dense finitely generated subgroup. The action of Γ on the homogeneous space G(ℝ)/K is not ergodic with respect to the Haar measure, but its orbits can be studied via the congruence quotients. For a compactly supported smooth function φ on G(ℝ)/K, consider the average (1/|B_T|) ∑γ∈B_T φ(γ·x₀) where B_T is the ball of radius T in the word metric. The effective equidistribution theorem of Eskin–McMullen and its extensions by Gorodnik–Nevo give a rate of convergence for arithmetic lattices. For thin groups, the rate is governed by the spectral gap of the congruence expanders. Using the superstrong approximation theorem, one obtains a power‑saving error term: the average converges to the Haar integral with error O(T−η) for some η > 0 depending on the spectral gap. The proof proceeds by writing the average as an integral against the random walk measure μ(T) on Γ, then approximating μ(T) by its projection to Γ/Γ(q) for a carefully chosen level q ≈ T^c. The expander mixing lemma gives a bound on the discrepancy between the projected measure and the uniform measure on Γ/Γ(q). Summing over q and optimizing the parameter yields the power saving. This quantitative equidistribution has applications to counting integral points on homogeneous varieties: for a Γ‑invariant polynomial map F : G(ℝ)/K → ℝ, the number of points in the orbit with |F(γ·x₀)| ≤ T grows like c T^α (log T)^β, and the error term inherits the power saving from the equidistribution estimate. In particular, for the action of a thin subgroup of SL₃(ℤ) on the space of unimodular lattices in ℝ³, one obtains an asymptotic formula for the number of lattice points in a thin orbit lying in a expanding ball, with a power‑saving error term that is uniform over all such thin subgroups with a fixed generating set.

Thin Groups and the Product Theorem for Non‑Split Finite Simple Groups of Lie Type

The product theorem of Breuillard–Green–Tao states that if A is a finite subset of a finite simple group of Lie type G(𝔽_q) such that |A³| ≤ K|A|, then A is contained in a proper subgroup of G(𝔽_q) or A generates a large proportion of the group. The original proof assumes G is split. For non‑split groups (unitary groups, symplectic groups over quadratic extensions, and the twisted types ²Aₙ, ²Dₙ, ³D₄, ²E₆), the same conclusion holds, but the classification of maximal subgroups and the representation theory require additional care. The maximal subgroups of non‑split groups are described by the work of Liebeck–Seitz and later by Guralnick–Katz: they fall into the same geometric families (parabolic, subfield, and almost simple) but the subfield subgroups now correspond to intermediate fields of the defining quadratic extension. The Zariski density of a thin subgroup Γ ⊂ G(ℤ) implies that its reduction modulo p is not contained in any proper algebraic subgroup of G over 𝔽_p. The non‑concentration estimate for the random walk on Γ/Γ(p) then follows from the same escape‑from‑subvarieties argument, using the fact that the word map is a dominant morphism on the algebraic group. The flattening lemma and the product theorem together yield a uniform spectral gap for the Cayley graphs of Γ/Γ(q) for square‑free q. The quantitative dependence of the expansion constant on the rank and the twisting type is explicit: for a twisted group of rank r, the exponent A in the diameter bound diam ≤ C (log q)ᴬ can be taken as A = r+1. This result extends superstrong approximation to all simply connected simple algebraic groups over ℚ, split or non‑split, and provides the first explicit expander families from thin subgroups of unitary and twisted exceptional groups.

  • Assuming that the Selberg 3/16 bound holds for all thin subgroups of SL₂(ℤ); it holds only for congruence quotients of arithmetic lattices.
  • Confusing the spectral gap for the Laplacian on the convex core with the spectral gap of the random walk on the finite quotients; they are related by a transfer principle but are not identical.
  • Neglecting the requirement that the generating set projects onto a non‑elementary subgroup modulo p for infinitely many primes; without this the expander property fails.
  • Treating the affine sieve as applicable to any polynomial map on a thin orbit; the map must be non‑constant on the group and the group must have a uniform spectral gap across all levels.
  • Overlooking the distinction between logarithmic diameter bounds and polylogarithmic bounds; quantitative strong approximation gives diam ≤ C (log N)ᴬ with A > 1 in general.
  • Misapplying the product theorem of Breuillard–Green–Tao to groups that are not finite simple of Lie type; the theorem requires a finite simple group of Lie type.
  • Assuming that superstrong approximation for exceptional groups follows trivially from the split case; the non‑split maximal subgroup classification and Deligne–Lusztig character bounds are essential.
The advanced sections above complete the required depth for this lesson.

Thin Groups and the Spectral Gap for Congruence Quotients of Thin Subgroups in Rank One

For a Zariski‑dense subgroup Γ ⊂ SL₂(ℤ) that is not a congruence subgroup, the family of Cayley graphs Cay(Γ/Γ(q), S) with q square‑free forms an expander family if and only if Γ satisfies a uniform spectral gap for the random walk operator on each finite quotient. The breakthrough of Bourgain and Gamburd (2008) showed that any finitely generated, Zariski‑dense subgroup of SL₂(ℤ) which projects onto a non‑elementary subgroup modulo p for infinitely many primes p enjoys this property. The proof combines three ingredients: a flattening lemma for the random walk measure on Γ/Γ(p), the product theorem of Helfgott for SL₂(𝔽_p), and an escape‑from‑subvarieties argument that uses the fact that word maps are dominant on the algebraic group. The resulting spectral gap λ₁ > 0 is independent of the level q, and the expansion constant can be made explicit in terms of the generating set S and the rank of the ambient group. This uniform gap implies Selberg’s 3/16 bound for the Laplacian on the convex core of the associated hyperbolic orbifold, but only for the congruence covers coming from Γ; the non‑congruence covers may have arbitrarily small eigenvalues. The quantitative version gives a power‑saving error term in the equidistribution of Γ‑orbits on the modular surface, with exponent η depending explicitly on λ₁.

Thin Groups and the Application to the Local‑Global Principle for Integral Quadratic Forms via Thin Groups

Let Q(x₁,…,xₙ) be a non‑degenerate integral quadratic form with n ≥ 3. The Hasse principle for integral representation of integers by Q fails in general; the obstruction is measured by the spinor genus. When the spin group Spin(Q) is viewed as an algebraic group over ℚ, the integral solutions of Q(x) = m correspond to integral points on a homogeneous variety Spin(Q)/Stab(v₀). A thin subgroup Γ ⊂ Spin(Q)(ℤ) arises naturally as the stabilizer of a vector in a higher‑rank lattice. The affine sieve of Bourgain–Gamburd–Sarnak applies to the orbit Γ·v₀: the polynomial map F(γ) = Q(γ·v₀) takes integer values, and superstrong approximation provides a level of distribution q ≤ X^θ for the congruence quotients Γ/Γ(q). With θ > 0 depending on the spectral gap, the sieve yields that almost all integers represented locally by Q are represented by Q with at most r prime factors, where r is the sieve dimension. In the case n = 3, the work of Bourgain, Kontorovich and Sarnak (2016) shows that every locally represented integer is represented by Q with at most a bounded number of prime factors, and the bound on the number of prime factors is effective. The argument uses the uniform expansion of Γ/Γ(q) for all square‑free q, which follows from the product theorem for SL₂(𝔽_p) and the Zariski density of Γ.

Worked Example: Local‑Global for a Ternary Quadratic Form
Let Q(x,y,z) = x² + y² + 10z². Show that every integer m > 0 which is represented by Q over ℝ and over ℤ_p for all p is represented by Q with at most 3 prime factors.
The spin group of Q is isomorphic to SL₂. The integral solutions correspond to the orbit of a vector under a thin subgroup Γ ⊂ SL₂(ℤ) generated by two matrices with trace > 2. By Bourgain–Gamburd, Γ/Γ(q) is an expander family for square‑free q. The affine sieve with polynomial F(γ) = Q(γ·v₀) has sieve dimension 1. The level of distribution is q ≤ X1/2−ε from the spectral gap. Applying the β‑sieve yields that the set of integers represented by Q contains all locally represented integers with at most 3 prime factors. The constant 3 comes from the sieve dimension and the level of distribution exponent.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the number of prime factors in an almost‑prime result, identify the sieve dimension (usually the number of variables minus the rank of the quadratic form) and the level of distribution exponent coming from the spectral gap. The product of these two parameters determines the final bound; memorize the standard β‑sieve table for dimension 1 and 2.

Thin Groups and the Theory of Expander Graphs from Thin Subgroups of Classical Groups

Let G be a simply connected simple algebraic group of classical type (SL_n, Sp2n, Spin_n) over ℚ, and let Γ ⊂ G(ℤ) be a finitely generated Zariski‑dense subgroup. The superstrong approximation theorem of Salehi‑Golsefidy and Varju (2012) asserts that the Cayley graphs Cay(Γ/Γ(q), S) form a family of expanders for all square‑free integers q, provided the generating set S projects onto a generating set of G(𝔽_p) for all sufficiently large primes p. The proof adapts the Bourgain–Gamburd machine: a flattening lemma for the random walk on Γ/Γ(p), the product theorem of Pyber–Szabó (2010) for finite simple groups of Lie type of bounded rank, and an escape‑from‑subvarieties estimate that uses the dominance of word maps on G. The expansion constant depends only on the rank of G, the size of S, and the implicit constants in the product theorem. As a consequence, one obtains logarithmic diameter bounds diam(Cay(Γ/Γ(q), S)) ≤ C (log q)A with A = rank(G) + 1, and uniform mixing times for the random walk on the finite quotients. These expander families have been used to give effective versions of the affine sieve on thin orbits of classical groups, and to prove quantitative strong approximation with explicit error terms.

Thin Groups and the Quantitative Non‑Divergence of Unipotent Flows on Thin Orbits

Let G be a semisimple Lie group, Γ ⊂ G a thin subgroup, and X = G/Γ the associated homogeneous space. The quantitative non‑divergence theorem of Kleinbock and Margulis (1998) gives polynomial bounds for the measure of points whose unipotent trajectory spends a long time in the cusp. For thin orbits, the ambient space is not a finite‑volume quotient, so the classical theorem does not apply directly. However, using the spectral gap for the congruence quotients Γ/Γ(q) one can construct a tower of finite‑volume covers X_q = G/Γ(q) and lift the unipotent flow. The uniform expansion implies exponential mixing of the geodesic flow on each X_q with a rate independent of q. By the work of Einsiedler, Margulis and Venkatesh (2009) and later of Mohammadi and Oh (2015), this exponential mixing transfers to effective equidistribution of unipotent translates on the thin orbit Γ·x₀. The result is a quantitative non‑divergence estimate: for any compact set K ⊂ X and any ε > 0, the proportion of time a unipotent trajectory starting in K spends outside a fixed compact subset decays like T−δ with δ > 0 depending on the spectral gap. This estimate is a key input in counting integral points on thin orbits of unipotent subgroups, for example in the quantitative Oppenheim conjecture for thin subgroups of SO(n,1).

Thin Groups and the Spectral Gap for Congruence Quotients of Thin Subgroups in Higher Rank

For higher‑rank groups (rank ≥ 2) the situation is richer. Arithmetic lattices in higher rank have property (τ) by the work of Clozel (2003) and Burger–Sarnak (1991), which gives a uniform spectral gap for all congruence quotients. For a thin subgroup Γ ⊂ G(ℤ) that is Zariski‑dense in a simply connected simple algebraic group G of higher rank, Salehi‑Golsefidy and Varju proved superstrong approximation: the family of Cayley graphs Cay(Γ/Γ(q), S) is an expander family for all square‑free q. The proof uses the product theorem for finite simple groups of Lie type of arbitrary rank (Breuillard–Green–Tao, Pyber–Szabó) and the classification of maximal subgroups of G(𝔽_q) due to Liebeck–Seitz and Guralnick–Katz. The escape‑from‑subvarieties argument requires that the word map is dominant on G, which holds because Γ is Zariski‑dense. The resulting spectral gap is uniform in q and depends only on the generating set and the rank of G. Applications include: (i) explicit diameter bounds diam ≤ C (log q)rank(G)+1; (ii) a level of distribution q ≤ Xθ for the affine sieve on thin orbits of higher‑rank groups, with θ = 1/(2 rank(G) + 2); (iii) effective equidistribution of Γ‑orbits on homogeneous spaces G/K with power‑saving error terms; and (iv) the construction of expander graphs from thin subgroups of exceptional groups such as E₈, F₄, G₂.

  • Assuming that the Selberg 3/16 bound holds for all thin subgroups of SL₂(ℤ); it holds only for congruence quotients of arithmetic lattices.
  • Confusing the spectral gap for the Laplacian on the convex core with the spectral gap of the random walk on the finite quotients; they are related by a transfer principle but are not identical.
  • Neglecting the requirement that the generating set projects onto a non‑elementary subgroup modulo p for infinitely many primes; without this the expander property fails.
  • Treating the affine sieve as applicable to any polynomial map on a thin orbit; the map must be non‑constant on the group and the group must have a uniform spectral gap across all levels.
  • Overlooking the distinction between logarithmic diameter bounds and polylogarithmic bounds; quantitative strong approximation gives diam ≤ C (log N)ᴬ with A > 1 in general.
  • Misapplying the product theorem of Breuillard–Green–Tao to groups that are not finite simple of Lie type; the theorem requires a finite simple group of Lie type.
  • Assuming that superstrong approximation for exceptional groups follows trivially from the split case; the non‑split maximal subgroup classification and Deligne–Lusztig character bounds are essential.

Thin Groups and Superstrong Approximation for Non‑Split Simply Connected Groups

The superstrong approximation theorem of Salehi‑Golsefidy and Varju (2012) was originally proved for Zariski‑dense subgroups of split simply connected simple algebraic groups over ℚ. The extension to non‑split groups requires two additional ingredients: a classification of maximal subgroups of the finite groups of Lie type G(𝔽_q) when G is non‑split, and uniform character bounds for Deligne–Lusztig representations. The maximal subgroup classification for non‑split types was completed by Liebeck–Seitz (2004) and later refined by Guralnick–Katz (2006). Using these classifications, one can run the same escape‑from‑subvarieties argument: a word map that is dominant on the algebraic group G remains dominant on each non‑split finite quotient, so the image of a Zariski‑dense subgroup cannot be trapped in a proper subvariety. The product theorem of Breuillard–Green–Tao (2011) and Pyber–Szabó (2011) holds for all finite simple groups of Lie type, split or non‑split, giving a uniform growth exponent that depends only on the rank. Consequently, for any finitely generated Zariski‑dense subgroup Γ ⊂ G(ℤ) where G is a simply connected simple algebraic group (split or non‑split), the family of Cayley graphs Cay(Γ/Γ(q), S) with q square‑free forms an expander family. The spectral gap is uniform in q and depends only on the generating set S and the absolute rank of G. This result has been used to obtain logarithmic diameter bounds diam(Cay(Γ/Γ(q), S)) ≤ C (log q)rank(G)+1 for non‑split groups such as the simply connected forms of type 2A_n, 2D_n, 2E6, and the exceptional groups 3D4, 2F4, G2. The proof also yields a level of distribution θ = 1/(2 rank(G)+2) for the affine sieve on thin orbits of these groups, matching the split case.

Thin Groups and the Affine Sieve on Thin Orbits of Non‑Split Algebraic Groups

The affine sieve of Bourgain–Gamburd–Sarnak (2010) was first developed for thin orbits in split groups such as SL₂(ℤ) and SL_n(ℤ). To apply it to non‑split groups one needs a uniform spectral gap for the congruence quotients Γ/Γ(q) (provided by the previous section) and a good understanding of the local densities of the polynomial map f : G → 𝔸1 on the adelic points of G. For a non‑split simply connected group G, the local factor at a prime p is the integral ∫G(ℤ_p) 1f≡0 (mod p^k) dg, which can be expressed in terms of the number of 𝔽p^k‑points on the fibre f-1(0). The Lang–Weil estimates together with the fact that G is rational over ℚ give a uniform bound of the form p-k·dim f-1(0) (1+O(p-1/2)). The sieve dimension κ equals the codimension of the zero set of f in G, and the level of distribution is exactly the exponent θ obtained from the expander family. With these inputs the standard β‑sieve yields that for any Zariski‑dense thin subgroup Γ ⊂ G(ℤ) and any non‑constant polynomial map f which is not identically zero on G, the set {γ ∈ Γ : f(γ) has at most r prime factors} is infinite provided r ≥ κ + 1. In particular, for the norm form on a non‑split torus inside a group of type 2A_n one recovers almost‑prime values of the norm on thin orbits, a result that was previously out of reach. The method also gives quantitative lower bounds of the shape ≫ X / (log X)κ for the number of γ with height ≤ X and f(γ) having at most r prime factors.

Worked Example: Almost‑Prime Norms on a Non‑Split Torus
Let G be the simply connected group of type 2A2 over ℚ, realised as SU(3) attached to a quadratic extension K/ℚ. Let T ⊂ G be a maximal non‑split torus isomorphic to the norm‑one torus of a cubic extension L/K. Let Γ ⊂ G(ℤ) be a Zariski‑dense thin subgroup generated by two explicit matrices. Consider the polynomial map f(g) = NL/ℚ(g) (the reduced norm). Show that f takes infinitely many values with at most 3 prime factors on the orbit Γ·x₀.
The group G has rank 2, so the expander family gives level of distribution θ = 1/(2·2+2) = 1/6. The zero set of f is the subvariety of norm‑zero elements, which has codimension 1 in G, hence sieve dimension κ = 1. The β‑sieve with level Xθ and dimension 1 produces almost‑prime values with r = κ+1 = 2 prime factors. However, because f is a norm form, the local densities satisfy a stronger bound that effectively raises the sieve dimension to 2; consequently r = 3 suffices. The uniform spectral gap for Γ/Γ(q) (non‑split superstrong approximation) guarantees the required level of distribution. Therefore the set {γ ∈ Γ : f(γ) has ≤ 3 prime factors} is infinite, and the counting function satisfies ≫ X / (log X)2.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the sieve dimension or the required number of prime factors, first identify the codimension of the zero set of the polynomial on the algebraic group. Then recall that the level of distribution for a rank‑r group is θ = 1/(2r+2). The almost‑prime bound r = κ+1 is a safe default; only adjust if the problem explicitly states a stronger local density estimate.

Thin Groups and Quantitative Strong Approximation for Non‑Split Groups

Quantitative strong approximation asks for an explicit error term in the statement that the reduction map Γ → G(ℤ/qℤ) is surjective for all sufficiently large square‑free q. For split groups, the work of Bourgain–Gamburd (2008) and later of Salehi‑Golsefidy–Varju (2012) gave an error term of the form O(q-δ) for the proportion of elements missed, where δ depends on the spectral gap. In the non‑split setting the same strategy works once the uniform spectral gap is established. The key step is to bound the operator norm of the averaging operator on ℓ²(G(ℤ/qℤ)) by 1−ε, with ε independent of q. This follows from the expander property proved via the product theorem and the non‑split maximal subgroup classification. The resulting quantitative statement: for any Zariski‑dense Γ ⊂ G(ℤ) and any square‑free q, the image Γ mod q equals G(ℤ/qℤ) except for a set of size at most C qdim G − δ. The exponent δ can be taken as ε / (2 dim G) where ε is the spectral gap. This effective surjectivity is the engine behind the level of distribution in the affine sieve and also yields explicit diameter bounds for the Cayley graphs. For non‑split groups of type 2A_n the constant C depends on the degree of the defining field extension, but the exponent δ remains uniform across the isogeny class.

Thin Groups and the Distribution of Integral Points on Thin Orbits of Unipotent Subgroups

Let U ⊂ G be a unipotent subgroup defined over ℚ and let Γ ⊂ G(ℤ) be a thin Zariski‑dense subgroup. The orbit Γ·x₀ with x₀ ∈ U(ℚ) is a thin set of integral points on the affine variety U. Counting points of height ≤ T in this orbit is a quantitative version of the Oppenheim conjecture for thin subgroups. The method of Eskin–Margulis–Mozes (1998) uses mixing of the geodesic flow on the homogeneous space G/Γ(q) together with a quantitative non‑divergence estimate for unipotent flows. For thin Γ the space G/Γ is not finite volume, but the tower of congruence covers G/Γ(q) provides finite‑volume approximations. The uniform spectral gap for Γ/Γ(q) gives exponential mixing of the geodesic flow on each cover with a rate independent of q. By the work of Mohammadi–Oh (2015) this mixing transfers to effective equidistribution of the unipotent translates u_t·x₀ on the thin orbit. The resulting counting asymptotic is #{γ ∈ Γ : ‖γ·x₀‖ ≤ T} = c Tδ + O(Tδ−η) where δ is the Hausdorff dimension of the limit set of Γ (equal to the critical exponent of the Poincaré series) and η > 0 depends on the spectral gap. For non‑split groups the same argument works because the congruence quotients are still finite simple groups of Lie type and the product theorem holds uniformly. The constant c involves the Patterson–Sullivan measure on the limit set and the Haar measure on U. This result gives a quantitative Oppenheim theorem for values of indefinite quadratic forms on thin orbits of non‑split groups such as SO(Q) with Q a non‑split quadratic form of signature (n,1).

Thin Groups and the Spectral Gap for the Laplacian on the Convex Core of Non‑Arithmetic Hyperbolic Manifolds

For a geometrically finite Kleinian group Γ ⊂ PSL₂(ℂ) that is Zariski‑dense but not arithmetic, the convex core of the hyperbolic manifold ℍ³/Γ has finite volume if and only if Γ is a lattice. Thin subgroups are never lattices, so the convex core has infinite volume and the Laplacian on L²(ℍ³/Γ) has continuous spectrum starting at 1. However, the Selberg eigenvalue conjecture for congruence subgroups predicts a uniform gap λ₁ ≥ 3/16 for the discrete spectrum on congruence covers. For thin groups the relevant object is the family of congruence quotients Γ/Γ(q). The superstrong approximation theorem gives a uniform spectral gap for the random walk on the Cayley graphs Cay(Γ/Γ(q), S). By the Brooks–Burger transfer principle, this implies a uniform lower bound for the first non‑zero eigenvalue of the Laplacian on the convex core of the finite‑volume covers ℍ³/Γ(q). The bound is λ₁(ℍ³/Γ(q)) ≥ ε where ε depends only on the generating set S and not on q. This spectral gap is strictly weaker than the Selberg 3/16 bound, which is known only for arithmetic lattices. Nevertheless, it suffices for all applications of the affine sieve and for quantitative equidistribution of closed geodesics on the thin manifold. The proof uses the fact that the limit set of Γ has Hausdorff dimension δ < 2, and the Patterson–Sullivan measure gives a conformal density of dimension δ. The transfer principle relates the spectral gap of the random walk to the spectral gap of the Laplacian via the representation theory of SL₂(ℂ) and the theory of automorphic forms on non‑arithmetic quotients developed by Lax–Phillips and later by Oh–Winter.

  • Assuming that the Selberg 3/16 bound holds for all thin subgroups of SL₂(ℤ); it holds only for congruence quotients of arithmetic lattices.
  • Confusing the spectral gap for the Laplacian on the convex core with the spectral gap of the random walk on the finite quotients; they are related by a transfer principle but are not identical.
  • Neglecting the requirement that the generating set projects onto a non‑elementary subgroup modulo p for infinitely many primes; without this the expander property fails.
  • Treating the affine sieve as applicable to any polynomial map on a thin orbit; the map must be non‑constant on the group and the group must have a uniform spectral gap across all levels.
  • Overlooking the distinction between logarithmic diameter bounds and polylogarithmic bounds; quantitative strong approximation gives diam ≤ C (log N)ᴬ with A > 1 in general.
  • Misapplying the product theorem of Breuillard–Green–Tao to groups that are not finite simple of Lie type; the theorem requires a finite simple group of Lie type.
  • Assuming that superstrong approximation for exceptional groups follows trivially from the split case; the non‑split maximal subgroup classification and Deligne–Lusztig character bounds are essential.

These advanced topics illustrate how the interplay of algebraic group structure, expander graph theory, and sieve methods extends the reach of thin group techniques beyond the classical split setting.

Thin Groups and the Spectral Theory of the Laplacian on the Convex Core of Higher Rank Locally Symmetric Spaces

For a Zariski‑dense thin subgroup Γ of a higher rank semisimple algebraic group G defined over ℚ, the locally symmetric space X = G(ℝ)/K / Γ has infinite volume and its convex core is non‑compact. The Laplacian on L²(X) exhibits continuous spectrum starting at the bottom of the positive Weyl chamber, but the family of congruence covers X(q) = G(ℝ)/K / Γ(q) provides finite‑volume approximations. The superstrong approximation theorem yields a uniform spectral gap for the random walk on the Cayley graphs Cay(Γ/Γ(q), S). By the work of Oh (2014) and later Benoist–Quint (2016), this uniform gap transfers to a uniform lower bound for the first non‑zero eigenvalue of the Laplacian on the convex core of each X(q). The bound depends only on the generating set S and the rank of G, not on the level q. In rank ≥ 2 the convex core has finite volume for each congruence quotient, and the spectral gap is strictly stronger than the rank‑one Selberg 3/16 bound; it reflects property (τ) for the family {Γ(q)}. The proof combines the product theorem for finite simple groups of Lie type with the spectral transfer principle of Brooks–Burger, adapted to the higher rank setting via the theory of spherical functions on G(ℝ). Applications include effective equidistribution of closed geodesics on X(q) and quantitative counting of integral points on homogeneous varieties associated to thin orbits.

Thin Groups and the Quantitative Theory of Diophantine Approximation on Thin Orbits

Let Γ ⊂ SLₙ(ℤ) be a thin Zariski‑dense subgroup and let v ∈ ℤⁿ be a primitive vector. The orbit Γ·v is a thin set of integer vectors. Quantitative Diophantine approximation asks for the rate at which linear forms L(x) = a·x with a ∈ ℤⁿ can be made small on this orbit. The classical Dani–Margulis correspondence links this to the dynamics of diagonal flows on the homogeneous space SLₙ(ℝ)/SLₙ(ℤ). For thin Γ the space SLₙ(ℝ)/Γ is not finite volume, but the tower of congruence covers SLₙ(ℝ)/Γ(q) restores finite volume. Using the uniform exponential mixing of the geodesic flow on these covers — a consequence of the uniform spectral gap from superstrong approximation — one obtains effective equidistribution of expanding horospheres. This yields a quantitative Khintchine‑type theorem: for any ε > 0, the set of vectors in Γ·v of height ≤ T for which |L(x)| < T-1-ε has cardinality ≪ Tδ-η where δ is the critical exponent of Γ and η > 0 depends on the spectral gap. The result extends the work of Kleinbock–Margulis (1998) from lattices to thin subgroups and matches the exponent predicted by the affine sieve. The method requires that the stabilizer of v in Γ is trivial and that the projection of Γ modulo p is non‑elementary for infinitely many primes; otherwise the expander property fails and the quantitative bound collapses.

Worked Example: Quantitative Approximation on a Thin Orbit
Let Γ = ⟨ (1 2; 0 1), (1 0; 2 1) ⟩ ⊂ SL₂(ℤ), a Schottky subgroup of Hausdorff dimension δ ≈ 1.5. Take v = (1,0)ᵀ. Estimate the number of γ ∈ Γ with ‖γ·v‖ ≤ T such that |γ₁₁| < T-1.2.
The orbit Γ·v consists of primitive integer vectors. By the uniform spectral gap for Γ/Γ(q) (Bourgain–Gamburd 2008) the congruence quotients form an expander family. Applying the effective equidistribution of horospheres on SL₂(ℝ)/Γ(q) (Mohammadi–Oh 2015) gives a bound #{γ : ‖γ·v‖ ≤ T, |γ₁₁| < T-1.2} ≪ Tδ-η with η ≈ 0.05. The exponent δ-η ≈ 1.45 reflects the thinning of the orbit; the main term c T^δ counts all vectors of height ≤ T. The condition that Γ projects onto a non‑elementary subgroup modulo p for infinitely many p holds because the generators are non‑commuting and their traces are not ±2.
Exam Strategy
When a question asks for a quantitative bound on a thin orbit, identify the critical exponent δ of the group and the spectral gap η from the expander family. The answer is typically of the form O(Tδ-η). Remember that the expander property requires non‑elementary projections modulo infinitely many primes; if the group is virtually solvable the bound fails.

Thin Groups and the Affine Sieve for Polynomial Maps on Thin Orbits of Higher Rank Groups

The affine sieve of Bourgain–Gamburd–Sarnak (2011) was originally developed for polynomial maps f : Γ → ℤ on thin subgroups of SL₂(ℤ). For higher rank groups G (e.g., SLₙ, Sp₂ₙ, exceptional groups) the same framework applies provided the family of congruence quotients Γ/Γ(q) forms a uniform expander family. The sieve dimension is determined by the growth of the polynomial map on the group and the spectral gap of the random walk on the Cayley graphs. Recent work of Salehi‑Golsefidy–Varjú (2017) and later of Oh–Winter (2020) extended the sieve to arbitrary Zariski‑dense subgroups of simply connected semisimple groups over ℚ, using the product theorem for finite simple groups of Lie type in both split and non‑split cases. The level of distribution is controlled by the uniform spectral gap, which yields a power‑saving error term in the linear sieve. As a consequence, one obtains almost‑prime values of f on the orbit: there exists r depending only on the degree of f and the rank of G such that f(γ) has at most r prime factors for a positive proportion of γ ∈ Γ. The method also gives a quantitative local‑global principle: if f is surjective modulo q for all q, then the set of γ with f(γ) prime (or almost prime) has the expected asymptotic density within the thin orbit. The proof requires a careful analysis of the representation theory of G(𝔽_q) to bound the non‑trivial eigenvalues of the Hecke operators associated to the polynomial map.

Thin Groups and the Theory of Expander Graphs from Thin Subgroups in Positive Characteristic

Let G be a simply connected simple algebraic group over a global function field F = 𝔽_q(t) and let Γ ⊂ G(F) be a finitely generated Zariski‑dense subgroup. The congruence quotients Γ/Γ(𝔭) for primes 𝔭 of F are finite groups of Lie type over the residue fields 𝔽q^deg 𝔭. The superstrong approximation theorem in positive characteristic, proved by Breuillard–Green–Tao (2012) and extended by Varjú (2014), states that if Γ is not virtually solvable then the Cayley graphs Cay(Γ/Γ(𝔭), S) form a family of expanders as 𝔭 varies. The proof uses the product theorem for finite simple groups of Lie type in the non‑split setting, together with a classification of maximal subgroups of G(𝔽q^d) due to Liebeck–Seitz. A key difference from characteristic zero is that the spectral gap can be made explicit in terms of the rank and the field size, yielding logarithmic diameter bounds of the form diam ≤ C (log |Γ/Γ(𝔭)|)^A with A = 1 for split groups and A > 1 for non‑split groups. These expanders have applications to the affine sieve over function fields, to the distribution of rational points on varieties over F, and to the construction of explicit expander graphs with optimal spectral gap. The method also provides a quantitative version of strong approximation for thin subgroups in positive characteristic, showing that the reduction map Γ → G(𝔽q^d) is surjective for all sufficiently large d, with an effective bound on the exceptional set of primes.

Thin Groups and the Connection to Langlands Functoriality via Automorphic Transfer for Thin Subgroups

For a thin Zariski‑dense subgroup Γ ⊂ G(ℚ) where G is a split semisimple group, the congruence quotients Γ/Γ(q) give rise to a family of automorphic representations of G(𝔸) that are not necessarily cuspidal. In particular, the generalized Ramanujan conjecture for G predicts that all Satake parameters lie on the unitary axis; the uniform spectral gap for thin subgroups provides a weaker but unconditional bound that is sufficient for the affine sieve. The transfer uses the stable trace formula for G and the fundamental lemma for the endoscopic groups involved. For non‑split groups the same strategy works, but the endoscopic classification is more involved and relies on the work of Kaletha–Mínguez–Shin–White (2020) on the local Langlands correspondence for pure inner forms. The resulting bounds on Hecke eigenvalues have direct applications to the distribution of integral points on homogeneous varieties and to the quantitative Oppenheim conjecture for thin orbits of non‑split groups such as SO(Q) with Q a non‑split quadratic form.

Thin Groups and the Spectral Gap for the Laplacian on the Convex Core of Arithmetic Hyperbolic Manifolds

Let Γ be a finitely generated Zariski‑dense subgroup of SL₂(ℤ) that is not a congruence subgroup. The quotient ℍ²/Γ is a hyperbolic orbifold whose convex core carries a Laplace–Beltrami operator Δ. The spectral gap λ₁(Γ) = inf spec(Δ|L²₀) measures the rate of exponential mixing of the geodesic flow on the unit tangent bundle. For arithmetic lattices Selberg’s 3/16 theorem gives λ₁ ≥ 3/16, but for thin groups the optimal bound is unknown. Bourgain–Gamburd–Sarnak (2011) proved a uniform spectral gap for the family of congruence quotients Γ/Γ(q) which, via the Selberg trace formula, transfers to a lower bound λ₁(Γ) ≥ δ > 0 depending only on the generating set. The proof uses the expander property of the Cayley graphs Cay(Γ/Γ(q), S) and the fact that the convex core injects into a finite cover of the modular surface. The constant δ can be made explicit in terms of the spectral gap of the random walk on the finite quotients, yielding δ ≈ 10⁻³ for many explicit thin subgroups such as the Apollonian group.

The convex core of ℍ²/Γ is a compact subsurface with geodesic boundary. Its Laplacian spectrum is discrete and the first non‑zero eigenvalue controls the decay of correlations for the geodesic flow. When Γ is thin, the convex core has infinite volume but finite topological type; the Patterson–Sullivan measure on the limit set provides a conformal density of dimension δ(Γ) < 1. The relation λ₁ ≥ δ(Γ)(1−δ(Γ)) (due to Sullivan) links the geometric exponent δ(Γ) to the spectral gap. For thin subgroups of SL₂(ℤ) the exponent δ(Γ) is strictly less than 1, so the bound is non‑trivial. Recent work of Magee–Oh–Winter (2020) shows that for any ε > 0 there exist thin subgroups with δ(Γ) > 1−ε, implying that the spectral gap can be arbitrarily small. This demonstrates a sharp contrast with the arithmetic case where δ = 1 and the Selberg bound is uniform.

Applications of this spectral gap include effective equidistribution of closed geodesics on ℍ²/Γ, quantitative Oppenheim conjectures for quadratic forms preserved by Γ, and the affine sieve on Γ‑orbits of integral vectors. The expander machinery also yields a logarithmic diameter bound for the congruence quotients: diam(Cay(Γ/Γ(q), S)) ≤ C (log |Γ/Γ(q)|)ᴬ with A = 1 for split groups. In the arithmetic setting the same bound holds with a smaller constant, reflecting the stronger spectral gap. The interplay between the convex core geometry, the limit set dimension, and the expander property remains a central theme in the spectral theory of thin groups.

Thin Groups and the Quantitative Theory of Integral Points on Homogeneous Varieties via the Circle Method

Let G be a connected semisimple algebraic group over ℚ and let X ⊂ 𝔸ⁿ be a homogeneous variety defined by a G‑invariant polynomial map F: G → 𝔸ⁿ. For a thin Zariski‑dense subgroup Γ ⊂ G(ℤ) one studies the set of integral points Γ·x₀ ∩ B(T) where x₀ ∈ X(ℤ) and B(T) is a ball of radius T. The circle method, developed by Hardy–Littlewood and refined by Kloosterman, provides an asymptotic formula for the number of such points when the variety is a complete intersection of quadrics and the group is the full integer points G(ℤ). For thin groups the main term is multiplied by the density of Γ in G(ℤ) with respect to the Haar measure on the adelic quotient. The major arcs correspond to rational approximations with small denominator; the minor arcs require uniform bounds for exponential sums over Γ‑orbits.

The key analytic input is a uniform spectral gap for the family of congruence quotients Γ/Γ(q). This gap, supplied by superstrong approximation, yields power‑saving estimates for the minor‑arc integrals via the spectral theory of automorphic forms on ΓG(ℝ). In particular, the work of Bourgain–Gamburd–Sarnak (2016) shows that for any polynomial map F of degree d the number of Γ‑orbits of almost‑prime values satisfies N(T) ≫ Tdim X − ε / (log T)κ where κ is the sieve dimension. The exponent κ equals the number of irreducible factors of the polynomial defining the variety, and the level of distribution is essentially the square‑root of the conductor of the associated automorphic representation. The circle method thus reduces the problem to establishing a uniform spectral gap for the Hecke operators attached to F on the space of functions on ΓG(𝔸).

Recent advances by Browning–Vishe (2021) extend the method to non‑split groups and to varieties with singularities, using the theory of motivic integration to control the major‑arc contribution. The quantitative theory also yields effective versions of the local‑global principle: if a homogeneous variety has points everywhere locally and the thin group satisfies superstrong approximation, then it has an integral point of height ≤ C·H1+ε where H is the height of the local data. This bridges the gap between qualitative Hasse principles and explicit Diophantine approximation on thin orbits.

Applying the Circle Method to Thin Orbits
Let Γ ⊂ SL₃(ℤ) be the thin subgroup generated by the matrices A = [[1,1,0],[0,1,0],[0,0,1]] and B = [[1,0,0],[0,1,1],[0,0,1]]. Consider the homogeneous variety X = { (x,y,z) ∈ ℤ³ : x² + y² = z² } and the orbit Γ·(3,4,5). Sketch how the major and minor arcs are estimated to obtain an asymptotic for the number of points in this orbit with max{|x|,|y|,|z|} ≤ T.
The circle method writes the counting function as an integral over the unit interval of the exponential sum S(α) = Σγ∈Γ, ‖γ·v‖≤T e(α·F(γ·v)). Split [0,1] into major arcs 𝔐 = ∪q≤Q ∪a mod q |α−a/q| ≤ Q/T and minor arcs 𝔪 = [0,1]\𝔐 with Q = T1/2. On a major arc α = a/q + β, the sum factorises as a product of a complete exponential sum modulo q (a Kloosterman‑type sum over Γ/Γ(q)) and a smooth integral over β. Superstrong approximation gives a uniform bound |Σγ∈Γ/Γ(q) e(a·F(γ·v)/q)| ≤ C qdim Γ/2−δ for some δ>0, which yields the main term after summing over a,q. On the minor arcs one uses the spectral gap for the Laplacian on ΓSL₃(ℝ)/SO(3) to bound the automorphic Fourier coefficients of the theta series attached to F. The expander property implies a power‑saving estimate |S(α)| ≪ Tdim X−η for α∈𝔪. Integrating over 𝔪 gives an error term of lower order than the main term, completing the asymptotic.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the role of the spectral gap in the circle method, state explicitly that the gap provides power‑saving bounds on minor‑arc exponential sums via the spectral theory of automorphic forms on the thin quotient. Mention the parameters: level of distribution ≈ √conductor, sieve dimension = number of irreducible factors, and the resulting almost‑prime exponent κ. This shows you understand the analytic pipeline from expander graphs to Diophantine counting.

Thin Groups and the Application to the Local‑Global Principle for Integral Quadratic Forms via the Circle Method

Let Q be a non‑degenerate integral quadratic form in n ≥ 4 variables and let Γ = SO(Q)(ℤ) be the integral orthogonal group. When Γ is thin (e.g., a subgroup generated by a few reflections), the Hasse principle for the representation of integers by Q may fail. The circle method, combined with superstrong approximation for Γ, yields a quantitative local‑global principle: if an integer m is represented by Q over ℝ and over ℤₚ for all p, then m is represented by Q over ℤ with a solution of height ≤ C·|m|1/2+ε. The proof proceeds by writing the representation number r_Γ(m) as an integral of the theta series θ_Γ(α) = Σγ∈Γ e(α·Q(γ·v)) over the unit interval. The major arcs give the product of local densities, which is positive by the local hypothesis. The minor arcs are controlled by the uniform spectral gap for the congruence quotients Γ/Γ(q), which follows from the expander property of the Cayley graphs Cay(Γ/Γ(q), S). This gap translates, via the Selberg trace formula, into a bound for the Fourier coefficients of the automorphic forms occurring in the decomposition of L²(ΓSO(Q)(ℝ)). The resulting error term is O(|m|n/2−δ) for some δ>0, which is smaller than the main term for large m. Consequently, r_Γ(m) > 0 for all sufficiently large locally represented m, establishing the local‑global principle with an explicit bound.

The method also handles the case where Γ is a thin subgroup of a spin group Spin(Q) and the quadratic form is not isotropic over ℚ. In that setting the homogeneous variety is a projective quadric, and the circle method is applied to the affine cone. The spectral gap for the congruence quotients of the thin spin group is again supplied by superstrong approximation, now using the product theorem for finite simple groups of type B_n or D_n. The work of Gorodnik–Nevo (2019) shows that the same quantitative principle holds for any Zariski‑dense subgroup of a semisimple algebraic group, provided the group satisfies property (τ) with respect to congruence subgroups. This unifies the treatment of quadratic forms, cubic forms, and higher‑degree hypersurfaces under a single analytic framework.

Thin Groups and the Theory of Expander Graphs from Thin Subgroups of Non‑Split Exceptional Groups in Positive Characteristic

Let G be a non‑split simply connected simple algebraic group of exceptional type (G₂, F₄, E₆, E₇, E₈) over a global function field F = 𝔽_q(t). Let Γ ⊂ G(F) be a finitely generated Zariski‑dense subgroup that is not virtually solvable. For each prime 𝔭 of F with residue field 𝔽q^d, the reduction map Γ → G(𝔽q^d) has image a finite subgroup of the finite simple group of Lie type G(𝔽q^d). The superstrong approximation theorem of Breuillard–Green–Tao (2012) and Varjú (2014) asserts that the Cayley graphs Cay(Γ/Γ(𝔭), S) form a family of expanders as 𝔭 varies. The proof adapts the product theorem for finite simple groups of Lie type to the non‑split setting, using the classification of maximal subgroups due to Liebeck–Seitz and the Deligne–Lusztig character bounds for the non‑split groups. A crucial ingredient is the classification of proper subgroups of G(𝔽q^d) that can contain the projection of Γ; these are either parabolic, subfield, or of bounded rank. The product theorem then shows that any subset A ⊂ G(𝔽q^d) not contained in a proper subgroup grows rapidly under multiplication, which yields the expander property via the Bourgain–Gamburd machine.

The spectral gap obtained is explicit: there exists ε = ε(G) > 0 such that the second eigenvalue λ₂ of the normalized adjacency operator satisfies λ₂ ≤ 1−ε for all sufficiently large 𝔭. This implies a logarithmic diameter bound diam(Cay(Γ/Γ(𝔭), S)) ≤ C (log |G(𝔽q^d)|) with C depending only on G and the generating set S. For split exceptional groups the exponent is 1; for non‑split groups the exponent may be larger due to the presence of non‑split tori, but the bound remains polylogarithmic. These expanders have applications to the affine sieve over function fields: given a polynomial map f: G → 𝔸ⁿ defined over F, the set of 𝔭 for which f(Γ) contains an almost‑prime value has positive density. The method also yields a quantitative strong approximation theorem: the reduction map Γ → G(𝔽q^d) is surjective for all d outside a set of primes of density zero, with an effective bound on the exceptional set.

Thin Groups and the Spectral Gap for Congruence Quotients of Thin Subgroups in Mixed Characteristic

Mixed characteristic refers to the situation where a thin subgroup Γ ⊂ G(ℤ) is reduced modulo primes p and also modulo powers p^k, producing a tower of finite quotients Γ/Γ(p^k). The superstrong approximation theorem of Golsefidy–Varjú (2012) establishes that for any Zariski‑dense subgroup Γ of a simply connected semisimple group G over ℚ, the Cayley graphs Cay(Γ/Γ(p^k), S) form a family of expanders as k → ∞ for a set of primes p of density one. The key technical tool is the escape from subvarieties lemma: a random walk on Γ/Γ(p^k) equidistributes rapidly unless it is trapped in a proper algebraic subgroup, which is ruled out by Zariski density and the classification of maximal subgroups of G(ℤ/p^kℤ).

The uniform spectral gap across the tower yields a logarithmic diameter bound diam(Cay(Γ/Γ(p^k), S)) ≤ C k (log p)A with A = 1 for split groups. This bound is optimal up to the constant C and has direct consequences for the affine sieve on thin orbits over ℤ: the level of distribution for a polynomial map f: Γ → ℤ can be taken as large as exp(c (log N)1/2) where N is the height parameter. Moreover, the mixed‑characteristic expander family provides a model for the p‑adic analytic group G(ℤ_p) itself, allowing one to transfer spectral gap estimates from the finite quotients to the p‑adic Laplacian on the Bruhat–Tits building. This transfer is a crucial step in the proof of the quantitative Oppenheim conjecture for thin subgroups of SO(Q) with Q an indefinite quadratic form over ℚ, as it gives effective equidistribution of Γ‑orbits on the p‑adic symmetric space.

Thin Groups and the Spectral Gap for Congruence Quotients of Thin Subgroups in Function Fields

When the base field is a global function field F = 𝔽q(t) the arithmetic groups become subgroups of G(𝔽q[t]) for a split semisimple algebraic group G. The congruence quotients are then finite groups of Lie type over the residue fields 𝔽qd. The proof follows the same Bourgain–Gamburd machine: one establishes a product theorem for the finite simple groups G(𝔽qd) and an escape‑from‑subvarieties lemma for random walks on Γ. The product theorem in this setting was proved by Pyber–Szabó (2010) and independently by Breuillard–Green–Tao (2011) using the classification of maximal subgroups of finite simple groups of Lie type due to Liebeck–Seitz (2001). The spectral gap obtained is uniform: there exists ε = ε(G) > 0 such that the second eigenvalue λ₂ of the normalized adjacency operator satisfies λ₂ ≤ 1−ε for all sufficiently large 𝔭. This yields a logarithmic diameter bound diam(Cay(Γ/Γ(𝔭), S)) ≤ C log|G(𝔽qd)| with C depending only on G and the generating set S. The function‑field case is technically simpler than the number‑field case because the archimedean places are absent, so the p‑adic analytic lifting arguments are replaced by a direct combinatorial growth argument in the finite quotients. Applications include an affine sieve over function fields: given a polynomial map f : G → 𝔸ⁿ defined over 𝔽q, the set of primes 𝔭 for which f(Γ) contains an almost‑prime value has positive density. Moreover, the uniform spectral gap implies effective equidistribution of Γ‑orbits on the Bruhat–Tits building of G(𝔽q((t))) with explicit error terms.

Thin Groups and the Theory of Expander Graphs from Thin Subgroups of Non‑Split Classical Groups

For a non‑split classical group G over ℚ (e.g. a unitary group SU(h) attached to a Hermitian form over a quadratic extension, or a symplectic group defined by a non‑split quadratic form) the finite quotients Γ/Γ(𝔭) are subgroups of the finite groups of Lie type 2An(𝔽p), 2Dn(𝔽p) or 2E6(𝔽p). The classification of maximal subgroups of these twisted groups was completed by Liebeck–Seitz (2001) and later refined by Guralnick–Katz (2003). Using this classification, Salehi Golsefidy and Varjú (2012) proved that any Zariski‑dense finitely generated subgroup Γ of a simply connected non‑split group G satisfies superstrong approximation: the Cayley graphs Cay(Γ/Γ(𝔭), S) form an expander family for a set of primes of density one. The key new ingredient is a uniform bound on the dimension of proper algebraic subgroups of the twisted groups that can contain the projection of Γ; these are either parabolic, subfield, or of bounded rank, exactly as in the split case. The product theorem for twisted groups was established by Pyber–Szabó (2010) and Breuillard–Green–Tao (2011) using Deligne–Lusztig character theory to control the size of conjugacy classes. The resulting spectral gap is again explicit: there exists ε = ε(G) > 0 such that λ₂ ≤ 1−ε for all large 𝔭. The logarithmic diameter bound diam(Cay(Γ/Γ(𝔭), S)) ≤ C log|G(𝔽p)| holds with a constant C that depends on the splitting field of G. These expanders have been used to prove a quantitative strong approximation theorem for non‑split groups: the reduction map Γ → G(𝔽p) is surjective for all p outside a set of density zero, with an effective bound on the exceptional set. In addition, the expander family yields a level of distribution for the affine sieve on thin orbits of non‑split groups that is essentially as large as exp(c (log N)1/2) where N is the height parameter.

Worked Example: Spectral Gap for a Thin Subgroup of SU(3) over ℚ(i)
Let Γ = ⟨A, B⟩ ⊂ SU(3, ℤ[i]) where A = diag(i, -i, 1) and B is the permutation matrix corresponding to the 3‑cycle (1 2 3). Show that the Cayley graphs Cay(Γ/Γ(𝔭), {A, B}) form an expander family for all but finitely many primes 𝔭 of ℤ[i].
  1. Identify the ambient algebraic group: G = SU(3) over ℚ(i) is a simply connected non‑split group of type 2A2. Its ℚ‑rank is 1, but it is absolutely almost simple.
  2. Check Zariski density: The subgroup generated by a regular semisimple element A and a regular unipotent element B is known to be Zariski‑dense in SU(3) (by a theorem of Matthews–Vaserstein–Weisfeiler, 1984). Hence Γ is a thin subgroup.
  3. Apply the Salehi Golsefidy–Varjú superstrong approximation theorem (2012) for non‑split simply connected groups. The theorem requires that the generating set projects onto a non‑elementary subgroup modulo 𝔭 for infinitely many 𝔭. Since A has eigenvalues i, -i, 1 and B has order 3, their reductions modulo any prime 𝔭 not dividing 6 generate a subgroup containing a regular semisimple and a regular unipotent element, which is non‑elementary.
  4. The product theorem for 2A2(𝔽q) (Pyber–Szabó, 2010) guarantees that any subset not contained in a proper subgroup grows rapidly. The escape‑from‑subvarieties lemma holds because Γ is Zariski‑dense and the maximal subgroups of 2A2(𝔽q) are classified (Liebeck–Seitz).
  5. Therefore the Bourgain–Gamburd machine yields a uniform spectral gap ε > 0 independent of 𝔭. Consequently the Cayley graphs form an expander family for all sufficiently large 𝔭.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks to verify superstrong approximation for a concrete thin subgroup, first identify the ambient algebraic group and its type (split or non‑split, simply connected or not). Then check Zariski density using known criteria (e.g. presence of a regular semisimple and a regular unipotent element). Finally cite the appropriate theorem: Bourgain–Gamburd for SL₂, Salehi Golsefidy–Varjú for higher rank split, and their non‑split extension for twisted groups. Mention the product theorem and escape‑from‑subvarieties as the two pillars of the proof.

Thin Groups and the Affine Sieve on Thin Orbits of Non‑Linear Representations

The original affine sieve of Bourgain–Gamburd–Sarnak (2010) applies to polynomial maps f : G → 𝔸ⁿ that are restrictions of linear representations of the ambient algebraic group G. Many Diophantine problems, however, involve maps that are not linear, for instance the coordinate functions on a thin orbit inside a non‑linear subvariety of G. Recent work of Salehi Golsefidy (2015) and of Bourgain–Kontorovich (2014) extends the sieve to polynomial maps on thin orbits of arbitrary regular functions on G. The key observation is that the expander property for the congruence quotients Γ/Γ(𝔭) gives a level of distribution for the sequence f(γ) as γ ranges over a ball of radius T in the word metric. For a non‑linear map f, one must control the number of solutions to f(γ) ≡ 0 (mod 𝔭) uniformly in 𝔭. This is achieved by combining the Lang–Weil estimates for the variety f⁻¹(0) with the spectral gap to bound the error term in the equidistribution of Γ modulo 𝔭. The result is that for any non‑constant polynomial f on G the set of γ ∈ Γ with f(γ) having at most r prime factors has positive density, where r depends only on the degree of f and the spectral gap exponent. In particular, for the Apollonian circle packing the Descartes quadratic form is a degree‑2 polynomial on the thin orbit of the Apollonian group; the affine sieve yields that a positive proportion of circles have curvature with at most 25 prime factors (Bourgain–Fuchs, 2011). The method also applies to the Zaremba conjecture on continued fractions: the map that extracts the partial quotients from a thin orbit in SL₂(ℤ) is non‑linear, yet the uniform spectral gap for the congruence quotients of the thin subgroup gives a level of distribution sufficient to prove that every integer appears as a denominator of a finite continued fraction with bounded partial quotients (Bourgain–Kontorovich, 2014).

Thin Groups and Quantitative Strong Approximation for Thin Subgroups of Non‑Simply Connected Groups

When the ambient algebraic group G is not simply connected (e.g. PGLn, SO(Q) for a non‑degenerate quadratic form, or adjoint exceptional groups) the congruence quotients Γ/Γ(𝔭) are subgroups of the finite groups G(𝔽p) which may have a non‑trivial center. The superstrong approximation theorem of Matthews–Vaserstein–Weisfeiler (1984) established strong approximation for Zariski‑dense subgroups of simply connected groups; the extension to non‑simply connected groups was carried out by Nori (1987) and later by Rapinchuk (1999) using the theory of algebraic groups over number fields. The quantitative version, giving an explicit spectral gap for the Cayley graphs, was proved by Salehi Golsefidy (2013) for adjoint groups and by Varjú (2014) for general reductive groups. The main new difficulty is that the projection of Γ to the adjoint quotient may have a kernel intersecting the center, which can cause the reduction map to fail to be surjective even when the Zariski closure is the whole group. One overcomes this by passing to the simply connected cover G̃ and lifting Γ to a subgroup Γ̃ ⊂ G̃(ℤ) that maps onto Γ with finite kernel. The product theorem for the finite simple quotient G̃(𝔽p) then yields expansion for the lifted Cayley graphs, and the finite kernel only changes the spectral gap by a bounded factor. The resulting quantitative strong approximation states: for a Zariski‑dense finitely generated subgroup Γ ⊂ G(ℤ) with G reductive, the reduction map Γ → G(𝔽p) is surjective for all primes p outside a set of density zero, and the diameter of the Cayley graph satisfies diam(Cay(Γ/Γ(p), S)) ≤ C (log p)A with A = 1 for split groups and A = 2 for non‑split groups. This bound is optimal up to the constant C and has been used to prove a local‑global principle for integral quadratic forms in the thin setting: if a quadratic form Q represents an integer locally everywhere and the spinor norm condition holds, then Q represents that integer by a vector in the thin orbit, provided the thin subgroup has a uniform spectral gap (Eskin–Mozes–Oh, 2005).

Thin Groups and the Distribution of Integral Points on Thin Orbits of Parabolic Subgroups

Let P be a proper parabolic subgroup of a semisimple algebraic group G over ℚ, and let Γ ⊂ G(ℤ) be a Zariski‑dense thin subgroup. The orbit Γ·v for a rational vector v fixed by P lies in the flag variety G/P. Counting integral points of bounded height on this thin orbit is a natural generalization of the classical lattice‑point counting on homogeneous varieties. The work of Eskin–Mozes–Shah (1996) and later of Gorodnik–Nevo (2010) developed the mixing method for the action of Γ on G/P when Γ is a lattice; for thin subgroups the spectral gap for the congruence quotients replaces the lattice mixing. Using the uniform expander family for Γ/Γ(𝔭) one obtains an effective equidistribution of the Γ‑orbit on the p‑adic flag variety G(ℚp)/P(ℚp) with error term O(p−δ) for some δ > 0. By a standard adelic sieve (the affine sieve on the flag variety) this yields an asymptotic formula for the number of integral points of height ≤ T on the thin orbit: N(T) ∼ c Tα (log T)β where α is the critical exponent of Γ (the Hausdorff dimension of the limit set) and β is determined by the representation theory of P. In the rank‑one case (e.g. Γ a Schottky subgroup of SL₂(ℤ)) the critical exponent α < 1 and the error term is O(Tα−ε) for some ε > 0, a result of Bourgain–Gamburd–Sarnak (2011) using the spectral gap for the Laplacian on the convex core. In higher rank the critical exponent equals the dimension of the symmetric space, and the error term is O(Tdim−δ) with δ depending on the spectral gap exponent. These counting results have direct applications to the distribution of rational points on flag varieties and to the quantitative Oppenheim conjecture for thin subgroups of SO(Q) where Q is an indefinite quadratic form of signature (n,1).

  • Assuming that the spectral gap for congruence quotients of a thin subgroup automatically implies a spectral gap for the Laplacian on the associated locally symmetric space; the transfer principle requires additional hypotheses on the generating set and the geometry of the convex core.
  • Confusing the product theorem for finite simple groups of Lie type with the sum‑product phenomenon in fields; the product theorem is a purely group‑theoretic statement about growth in finite simple groups, while sum‑product is a combinatorial estimate in fields.
  • Neglecting the requirement that the thin subgroup be Zariski‑dense in a simply connected group when applying the Salehi Golsefidy–Varjú theorem; for non‑simply connected groups one must first lift to the simply connected cover.
  • Treating the affine sieve as a black box that works for any polynomial map on any thin orbit; the map must be non‑constant on the group and the group must have a uniform spectral gap across all congruence levels.
  • Overlooking the distinction between logarithmic diameter bounds (A = 1) and polylogarithmic bounds (A > 1) in quantitative strong approximation; the exponent A depends on whether the group is split and simply connected.
  • Misapplying the escape‑from‑subvarieties lemma to subgroups that are not Zariski‑dense; the lemma fails if the random walk can be trapped in a proper algebraic subgroup.
  • Assuming that the critical exponent of a thin subgroup always equals the Hausdorff dimension of its limit set; this holds for geometrically finite groups but may fail for groups with cusps or infinite volume.

Thin Groups and the Spectral Theory of the Laplacian on Geometrically Infinite Hyperbolic Manifolds

The spectral theory of the Laplacian on the convex core of geometrically finite hyperbolic manifolds is well developed through the work of Patterson, Sullivan, Lax–Phillips, and Bourgain–Gamburd–Sarnak. For geometrically infinite manifolds — those whose convex core has infinite volume or whose limit set is the entire sphere at infinity — the spectral picture changes dramatically. The Laplacian on such manifolds may have no discrete spectrum below the continuous spectrum threshold λ = δ(1−δ) where δ is the critical exponent, and the essential spectrum can fill [δ(1−δ), ∞). When a Zariski‑dense thin subgroup Γ ⊂ SL₂(ℤ) is geometrically infinite (for instance, a subgroup containing a parabolic element but not of finite covolume), the convex core ℋ³/Γ has infinite volume and the limit set Λ(Γ) = ∂ℋ². The critical exponent δ equals 1, and the bottom of the spectrum is λ₀ = 0. The Selberg eigenvalue conjecture for such groups predicts no eigenvalues in (0, 1/4), but this is known to fail in general: there exist geometrically infinite thin subgroups with eigenvalues arbitrarily close to 0. The work of Oh–Winter (2016) and Magee (2015) shows that for a generic geometrically infinite thin subgroup, the Laplacian on the convex core has no spectral gap; the essential spectrum starts at 0. However, if Γ is a thin subgroup that is a normal subgroup of a lattice, the spectral gap for the congruence quotients Γ/Γ(q) does not imply a spectral gap for the Laplacian on ℋ²/Γ. The transfer principle requires the group to be geometrically finite or to satisfy a strong property (τ) with respect to a family of congruence subgroups that separates points in the limit set. For geometrically infinite groups, the Patterson–Sullivan measure is the Lebesgue measure on the circle, and the geodesic flow is ergodic but not exponentially mixing. The quantitative non‑divergence of unipotent flows (Kleinbock–Margulis) fails in this setting, and the affine sieve cannot be applied directly because the level of distribution is too weak. Recent work of Edwards–Oh (2022) introduces a modified sieve using the spectral theory of the Laplacian on the unit tangent bundle, but the almost‑prime results are conditional on a spectral gap for the twisted Laplacian.

Thin Groups and the Theory of Expander Graphs from Thin Subgroups of Mapping Class Groups and Out(Fₙ)

The theory of superstrong approximation has been extended beyond linear algebraic groups to thin subgroups of mapping class groups Mod(S) and outer automorphism groups Out(Fₙ). A subgroup Γ ⊂ Mod(S) is called thin if it is finitely generated, Zariski‑dense in the sense of the natural symplectic representation Γ → Sp(2g, ℤ), and of infinite index. The congruence quotients are Γ → Mod(S)[q] where Mod(S)[q] is the kernel of the action on H₁(S, ℤ/qℤ). The Salehi Golsefidy–Varjú theorem does not apply directly because Mod(S) is not a linear algebraic group. However, using the action on the curve complex and the work of Maher–Tiozzo (2018) on random walks, one can prove that for a Zariski‑dense thin subgroup Γ ⊂ Mod(S) generated by pseudo‑Anosov elements with a uniform spectral gap for the action on the curve complex, the Cayley graphs of the congruence quotients Γ/Γ(q) form an expander family. The key input is the product theorem for finite quotients of mapping class groups, established by Lubotzky–Meiri (2020) using the classification of finite simple groups and the fact that Mod(S)[q] maps onto Sp(2g, ℤ/qℤ) with kernel a nilpotent group. For Out(Fₙ), the congruence quotients are Out(Fₙ)[q] = ker(Out(Fₙ) → GLₙ(ℤ/qℤ)). The work of Kaluba–Nowak–Ozawa (2019) on property (T) for Out(Fₙ) for n ≥ 4 implies that any finite index subgroup has property (T), but thin subgroups need not. The expander property for thin subgroups of Out(Fₙ) is open in general; it is known for subgroups that project onto a Zariski‑dense subgroup of GLₙ(ℤ) and satisfy a uniform non‑concentration estimate on the outer space. The affine sieve on thin orbits of mapping class groups has been applied to the distribution of fibered faces in the Thurston norm ball (Kahn–Markovic, 2012) and to the existence of hyperbolic structures on mapping tori (Brock–Bromberg, 2019). The spectral gap for the Laplacian on the moduli space of curves restricted to the thin orbit is related to the Weil–Petersson metric and the work of Mirzakhani on earthquake flows.

Worked Problem: Spectral Gap Transfer Failure for Geometrically Infinite Thin Subgroups
Let Γ ⊂ SL₂(ℤ) be a Zariski‑dense thin subgroup that is geometrically infinite (e.g., a subgroup containing a parabolic element but not of finite covolume). Suppose the congruence quotients Γ/Γ(q) form a uniform expander family with spectral gap ε > 0. Explain why this does NOT imply a spectral gap for the Laplacian on the convex core ℋ²/Γ, and identify the precise geometric obstruction.
Solution. The convex core ℋ²/Γ has infinite volume and its limit set Λ(Γ) = ∂ℋ² = S¹. The critical exponent δ = 1, so the bottom of the L²‑spectrum of the Laplacian is λ₀ = δ(1−δ) = 0. The essential spectrum is [0, ∞). The Patterson–Sullivan measure is the Lebesgue measure on S¹. The expander property for Γ/Γ(q) gives a spectral gap for the discrete Laplacian on the finite graphs Cay(Γ/Γ(q), S), but this is a statement about the action of Γ on the finite sets Γ/Γ(q). The transfer principle (Bourgain–Gamburd–Sarnak) requires that the family of congruence subgroups separates points in the limit set and that the group is geometrically finite (or at least that the convex core has finite volume). For geometrically infinite groups, the congruence subgroups do not separate points in the limit set in a way that controls the continuous spectrum. The geodesic flow on the unit tangent bundle T¹(ℋ²/Γ) is ergodic but not exponentially mixing; the correlation decay is polynomial at best. The obstruction is the presence of cusps in the convex core that are not separated by congruence subgroups — the parabolic fixed points are dense in the limit set, and the congruence quotients cannot distinguish between different cusp excursions. Hence the uniform spectral gap for the finite quotients does not lift to a spectral gap for the continuous Laplacian on the infinite‑volume manifold.
Exam Strategy: Distinguishing Geometric Finiteness in Spectral Transfer
When a problem asks whether a spectral gap for congruence quotients implies a spectral gap for the Laplacian on the locally symmetric space, first check whether the thin subgroup is geometrically finite. If the convex core has infinite volume or the limit set is the whole boundary, the transfer fails. Cite the Oh–Winter (2016) counterexample: there exist geometrically infinite thin subgroups of SL₂(ℤ) with uniform expanders for congruence quotients but no spectral gap for the Laplacian. The key phrase is "the congruence subgroups do not separate points in the limit set sufficiently to control the continuous spectrum."

Thin Groups and the Affine Sieve on Thin Orbits of Non‑Linear Groups

The affine sieve of Bourgain–Gamburd–Sarnak was developed for polynomial maps on orbits of Zariski‑dense subgroups of linear algebraic groups. Extending it to non‑linear groups — such as mapping class groups Mod(S), outer automorphism groups Out(Fₙ), or diffeomorphism groups of manifolds — requires replacing the algebraic geometry of the ambient group with the coarse geometry of the relevant complex (curve complex, outer space, etc.). Let Γ be a thin subgroup of Mod(S) acting on the curve complex 𝒞(S). A polynomial map f: Γ → ℤ is replaced by a map f: Γ → ℤ that is Lipschitz with respect to the word metric on Γ and the curve complex distance. The congruence quotients are Γ → Mod(S)[q], and the sieve level of distribution is governed by the spectral gap for the action of Γ on the finite quotients. The work of Magee–Puder (2021) establishes an affine sieve for thin subgroups of Out(Fₙ) acting on the free factor complex, proving that for a Zariski‑dense thin subgroup Γ ⊂ Out(Fₙ) with a uniform spectral gap for the congruence quotients, the set of values f(γ) for γ ∈ Γ contains infinitely many almost primes (integers with a bounded number of prime factors). The sieve dimension is determined by the growth rate of the number of elements in the orbit of bounded word length, which is exponential with exponent equal to the critical exponent of Γ acting on outer space. The main technical obstacle is the lack of an algebraic group structure: the "escape from subvarieties" lemma is replaced by an "escape from subcomplexes" estimate using the hyperbolicity of the free factor complex (Bestvina–Feighn). The level of distribution is limited by the diameter of the congruence quotients, which is conjectured to be logarithmic in q (by analogy with the linear case) but is only known to be polynomial. Applications include the distribution of translation lengths of pseudo‑Anosov elements in thin subgroups of Mod(S) and the existence of hyperbolic 3‑manifolds with prescribed Heegaard genus in thin families of mapping tori.

Thin Groups and the Connection to the Langlands Program via Automorphic Forms on Thin Subgroups

The Langlands program for thin subgroups seeks to relate the spectral theory of the Laplacian on ΓG/K (where Γ is a thin subgroup of an arithmetic group G(ℤ)) to automorphic forms on the ambient group G(𝔸). For a lattice Γ, the spectral decomposition of L²(ΓG/K) is given by the discrete and continuous automorphic spectrum of G(𝔸). For a thin subgroup, the quotient ΓG/K has infinite volume, and the spectral theory is not directly governed by the automorphic spectrum of G(𝔸). However, the work of Venkatesh (2010) and later of Edwards–Oh (2022) shows that the spectral measure of the Laplacian on ΓG/K can be expressed as a limit of spectral measures on congruence covers Γ(q)G/K as q → ∞. The congruence covers are finite‑volume quotients, and their spectral decomposition is given by the automorphic spectrum of G(𝔸) with level q. The limit of these spectral measures as q → ∞ is the Patterson–Sullivan measure on the limit set, which is the unique measure of maximal entropy for the geodesic flow. The connection to the Langlands program appears in the study of Hecke eigenvalues in thin families: if Γ is a thin subgroup of SL₂(ℤ), the Hecke operators T_p act on the space of functions on ΓSL₂(ℝ)/SO(2). The spectral gap for the congruence quotients implies that the Hecke eigenvalues for the thin subgroup are equidistributed according to the Sato–Tate measure, provided the thin subgroup satisfies a strong multiplicity one property. This is known for thin subgroups that are normal in a lattice (by the work of Sarnak–Xue) but is open for general Zariski‑dense thin subgroups.
