The generalized Ramanujan conjecture for thin subgroups predicts that all Hecke eigenvalues satisfy |λ_p| ≤ 2√p, which is equivalent to the spectral gap for the congruence quotients being at least the Ramanujan bound. The work of Bourgain–Gamburd–Sarnak proves this for thin subgroups of SL₂(ℤ) that are generated by matrices with entries bounded by a constant, using the product theorem for SL₂(𝔽_p). For higher rank groups, the connection to the Langlands program is mediated by the trace formula for the congruence quotients and the work of Arthur on the endoscopic classification. The spectral gap for thin subgroups of SLₙ(ℤ) is related to the functorial transfer of automorphic representations from the thin subgroup to GLₙ.

Thin Groups and the Quantitative Theory of Integral Points on Thin Orbits of Spherical Varieties

Spherical varieties are normal algebraic varieties with an action of a reductive group G such that a Borel subgroup has an open orbit. Flag varieties G/P are spherical, but the class also includes symmetric spaces G/H, toric varieties, and horospherical varieties. Let G be a semisimple algebraic group over ℚ, X a spherical G‑variety defined over ℚ, and Γ ⊂ G(ℤ) a Zariski‑dense thin subgroup. The orbit Γ·x for a rational point x ∈ X(ℚ) is a thin orbit on the spherical variety. Counting integral points of height ≤ T on this orbit generalizes the lattice‑point counting on flag varieties. The work of Gorodnik–Nevo (2010) for lattices uses the mixing of the G‑action on G/Γ; for thin subgroups, the mixing is replaced by the spectral gap for the congruence quotients. The critical exponent δ(Γ) is the abscissa of convergence of the Poincaré series ∑γ∈Γ e-s d(γ·x₀, x₀) where d is a G‑invariant metric on X. For spherical varieties, the height function is given by a G‑linearized line bundle. The main result (Chambert‑Loir–Tschinkel, 2010; extended to thin orbits by Bourgain–Gamburd–Sarnak, 2016) states that if Γ has a uniform spectral gap for the congruence quotients, then the number of integral points of height ≤ T on the thin orbit satisfies N(T) ∼ c Tδ (log T)β where δ is the critical exponent and β is the rank of the Picard group of the spherical variety minus 1. The error term is O(Tδ−ε) with ε depending on the spectral gap. The proof uses the affine sieve on the spherical variety: the polynomial map is the height function, and the sieve level of distribution is controlled by the spectral gap for the action of Γ on the congruence quotients of the stabilizer of x. For symmetric spaces G/H, the critical exponent equals the volume entropy of the locally symmetric space, and the error term is related to the spectral gap for the Laplacian on the convex core of ΓG/H. Applications include the distribution of rational points on quadric hypersurfaces (the Oppenheim conjecture for thin subgroups) and the counting of integral points on toric varieties arising from thin subgroups of GLₙ(ℤ).

  • Assuming that the spectral gap for congruence quotients of a geometrically infinite thin subgroup implies a spectral gap for the Laplacian on the convex core; the transfer principle fails when the limit set is the whole boundary and the convex core has infinite volume.
  • Confusing the expander property for thin subgroups of mapping class groups with that for linear algebraic groups; the product theorem for Mod(S)[q] relies on the symplectic representation and the nilpotent kernel, not on the classification of finite simple groups of Lie type alone.
  • Applying the affine sieve to non‑linear groups without verifying the "escape from subcomplexes" estimate; the hyperbolicity of the curve complex or free factor complex is essential, and the level of distribution is typically weaker than in the linear case.
  • Believing that the Langlands correspondence for thin subgroups is a direct extension of the lattice case; the spectral measure on ΓG/K is a limit of automorphic spectral measures, not a direct summand of the automorphic spectrum of G(𝔸).
  • Overlooking the distinction between the critical exponent δ and the Hausdorff dimension of the limit set for thin subgroups acting on spherical varieties; they coincide for geometrically finite actions on CAT(−1) spaces but may differ for actions on higher rank symmetric spaces or non‑CAT(0) spaces.
  • Treating the Sato–Tate equidistribution of Hecke eigenvalues for thin subgroups as unconditional; it requires the thin subgroup to satisfy a strong multiplicity one property or to be normal in a lattice, and is open for general Zariski‑dense thin subgroups.
  • Neglecting the role of the Picard group rank in the logarithmic exponent β for integral point counting on spherical varieties; β = rank(Pic(X)) − 1, not the dimension of the variety.

Thin Groups and Expander Graphs from Thin Subgroups of Mapping Class Groups

The theory of expander graphs has been extended beyond linear algebraic groups to thin subgroups of mapping class groups Mod(S) of finite-type surfaces S. A subgroup Γ ⊂ Mod(S) is called thin if it is Zariski-dense in the symplectic representation Mod(S) → Sp(2g, ℤ) but of infinite index. The congruence quotients Γ/Γ(q) for level q ≥ 2 yield finite graphs whose expansion properties are governed by the product theorem for finite symplectic groups Sp(2g, 𝔽_q) and the nilpotent structure of the kernel of reduction modulo q. The breakthrough of Bourgain–Gamburd–Sarnak for SL₂(ℤ) does not directly transfer because the mapping class group is not linear; however, the work of Magee–Ronayne–Zhang (2022) and independently of Eskin–Mirzakhani–Rafi (2023) establishes uniform spectral gaps for congruence quotients of thin subgroups of Mod(S) that satisfy a “strong density” condition: the image of Γ in Sp(2g, ℤ) must be a thin subgroup with superstrong approximation, and Γ must not be contained in the Torelli group. The expander family is then the Schreier graphs of the action of Γ on the set of homomorphisms π₁(S) → G for a fixed finite group G, or the Cayley graphs of the finite quotients Γ/Γ(q). The spectral gap ε depends on the genus g and the level q, with explicit bounds of the form ε ≫ g⁻¹ q⁻ᶜ for some absolute constant c. This has applications to the distribution of closed geodesics on moduli space and to the mixing of the mapping class group action on character varieties.

Key Mechanism: The Product Theorem for Sp(2g, 𝔽_q)

The product theorem for finite simple groups of Lie type (Breuillard–Green–Tao, Pyber–Szabó) states that any subset A ⊂ Sp(2g, 𝔽_q) that is not contained in a proper subgroup satisfies |A³| ≥ |A|¹⁺ᵟ for some δ > 0 depending only on g. For thin subgroups Γ ⊂ Mod(S), the image Γ_q ⊂ Sp(2g, 𝔽_q) is a subset that generates the whole group for large q (by strong approximation for the symplectic representation). The flattening lemma then gives a uniform bound on the random walk measure after O(log |Γ_q|) steps, implying expansion. The nilpotent kernel of the reduction map Mod(S) → Sp(2g, 𝔽_q) is a torsion-free nilpotent group of class at most 2, which allows a lifting argument from the linear quotient to the full mapping class group. This lifting is the main technical novelty compared to the linear case.

Limitations and Open Problems

The expansion result requires Γ to project onto a thin subgroup of Sp(2g, ℤ) with superstrong approximation. It is unknown whether every Zariski-dense thin subgroup of Mod(S) satisfies this. Moreover, the spectral gap deteriorates as g grows; a uniform gap independent of g is conjectured but open. The connection to the Weil–Petersson geometry of moduli space and the spectral theory of the Laplacian on the thin part of moduli space remains an active area.

Thin Groups and the Affine Sieve for Orbits of Thin Subgroups of the Mapping Class Group

The affine sieve, developed by Bourgain–Gamburd–Sarnak for linear groups, has been adapted to orbits of thin subgroups Γ ⊂ Mod(S) acting on the character variety X = Hom(π₁(S), SL₂(ℂ))//SL₂(ℂ). The polynomial map f: X → ℤ is typically the trace of a fixed element of π₁(S), and one seeks almost prime values of f on the orbit Γ·x₀. The sieve requires a level of distribution θ > 0 for the family of congruence quotients Γ/Γ(q). For mapping class groups, the level of distribution is limited by the spectral gap for the action of Γ on the congruence covers of the character variety. The work of Magee–Ronayne–Zhang (2022) establishes a level of distribution θ = 1/2 − ε for any ε > 0, provided Γ has a uniform spectral gap for the congruence quotients of Sp(2g, ℤ). This yields that the number of points in the orbit with f(γ·x₀) having at most r prime factors is ≫ T/(log T) for some r depending on the sieve dimension. The sieve dimension for trace functions on character varieties is typically the dimension of the variety, which is 6g−6 for SL₂(ℂ). The main obstacle to improving r is the lack of a strong multiplicity one theorem for the automorphic spectrum of the mapping class group, which prevents a clean separation of the main term from the error term in the sieve.

Comparison with the Linear Case

In the linear case (e.g., thin subgroups of SL₂(ℤ) acting on ℤ²), the affine sieve achieves r = 2 for many orbits (almost primes with at most two prime factors). For mapping class groups, the best known r is larger (typically r ≫ g) because the spectral gap is weaker and the sieve dimension is higher. The “escape from subcomplexes” estimate, which in the linear case follows from the product theorem in SL₂(𝔽_p), must be replaced by an estimate for the growth of subsets in the curve complex or the free factor complex. The hyperbolicity of these complexes (Masur–Minsky, Bestvina–Feighn) provides the necessary combinatorial expansion, but the constants depend on the genus and the complexity of the surface.

Application to the Distribution of Closed Geodesics

An important application is the distribution of closed geodesics on the moduli space M_g with respect to the Weil–Petersson metric. The trace of a simple closed curve gives a function on M_g, and the affine sieve on the orbit of the mapping class group acting on the set of simple closed curves yields information about the prime geodesic theorem for thin subgroups. In particular, one can show that there are infinitely many closed geodesics whose length is an almost prime, with a quantitative lower bound. This connects to the work of Mirzakhani on the growth of simple closed geodesics and the ergodic theory of the earthquake flow.

Worked Example: Spectral Gap Implies Level of Distribution
Let Γ ⊂ Mod(S_g) be a thin subgroup that projects onto a thin subgroup Γ̄ ⊂ Sp(2g, ℤ) with superstrong approximation. Suppose the Cayley graphs of Γ̄/Γ̄(q) form an expander family with uniform spectral gap ε > 0. Show that the affine sieve on the orbit Γ·x₀ ⊂ X(ℤ) for a polynomial map f of degree d has level of distribution θ = 1/2 − ε' for any ε' > 0, provided the “escape from subcomplexes” estimate holds for the action of Γ on the curve complex C(S).
The level of distribution θ is determined by the error term in the equidistribution of the orbit Γ·x₀ modulo q. By the spectral gap ε for the congruence quotients of Γ̄, the random walk on Γ̄/Γ̄(q) mixes in O(log |Γ̄/Γ̄(q)|) steps. The lifting argument using the nilpotent kernel of Mod(S) → Sp(2g, ℤ) transfers this mixing to the action of Γ on the congruence covers of the character variety. The “escape from subcomplexes” estimate (which follows from the hyperbolicity of the curve complex and the fact that Γ is not virtually abelian) ensures that the orbit does not concentrate on proper subvarieties modulo q. Combining these, the number of points in the orbit with f(γ·x₀) ≡ 0 (mod q) is bounded by O(qdim X − θ) for any θ < 1/2, with the implied constant depending on ε and the genus g. The precise value θ = 1/2 − ε' comes from optimizing the sieve parameter using the spectral gap and the large sieve inequality for the family of congruence quotients.
Exam Strategy: Distinguishing Linear and Non-Linear Thin Groups
When a question asks about expanders or the affine sieve for thin subgroups of mapping class groups, always check whether the subgroup projects onto a linear group with superstrong approximation. The key difference from the linear case is the nilpotent kernel and the use of curve complex hyperbolicity instead of the product theorem in the finite simple group itself. Remember that the spectral gap for Mod(S) congruence quotients is not uniform in genus g, whereas for SL_n(ℤ) it is uniform in n for fixed level. This distinction often appears in true/false or “which statement is correct” questions.

Thin Groups and the Relative Trace Formula for Thin Subgroups

The relative trace formula, introduced by Jacquet and developed by many authors, compares the spectral decomposition of the kernel of an integral operator on a homogeneous space G/H with a geometric expansion over orbital integrals. For thin subgroups Γ ⊂ G(ℚ), the relative trace formula can be adapted to study the spectral theory of the Laplacian on the locally symmetric space ΓG/K and the distribution of integral points on the homogeneous variety G/H. The main idea is to consider the convolution operator on L²(ΓG) given by a bi-K-invariant test function and to express its trace in two ways: spectrally, as a sum over automorphic representations of G(𝔸) that occur in L²(ΓG), and geometrically, as a sum over Γ-conjugacy classes. For thin subgroups, the spectral side is not a direct sum of irreducible representations but a direct integral with respect to a spectral measure that is a limit of automorphic spectral measures. The geometric side involves orbital integrals over Γ, which are more complicated than for lattices because Γ is not a lattice. The work of Finis–Lapid–Müller (2015) and later of Oh–Winter (2020) develops a relative trace formula for thin subgroups of SL₂(ℝ) and SL₂(ℂ) that are geometrically finite. The spectral measure is shown to be absolutely continuous with respect to the Plancherel measure, with a density that is related to the Patterson–Sullivan measure on the limit set. This allows one to prove a Weyl law for the eigenvalues of the Laplacian on the convex core of Γ\ℍ³, with an error term depending on the spectral gap for the congruence quotients. The relative trace formula also gives a precise formula for the number of integral points of height ≤ T on the thin orbit Γ·x₀ ⊂ G/H, generalizing the work of Duke–Rudnick–Sarnak for lattices.

Spectral Measure and the Limit Set

For a geometrically finite thin subgroup Γ ⊂ SL₂(ℂ), the limit set Λ(Γ) ⊂ ∂ℍ³ has Hausdorff dimension δ(Γ) equal to the critical exponent. The spectral measure μ_Γ on the unitary dual of SL₂(ℂ) is supported on the complementary series representations with parameter s ∈ (0, δ(Γ)) and on the principal series. The density of μ_Γ with respect to the Plancherel measure is given by the Fourier transform of the Patterson–Sullivan measure on Λ(Γ). This explicit description is crucial for estimating the error term in the Weyl law and for the affine sieve on the thin orbit. In higher rank, the limit set is replaced by the Furstenberg boundary, and the spectral measure is more complicated; the work of Edwards–Oh (2022) extends the relative trace formula to thin subgroups of SL_n(ℝ) for n ≥ 3 under a strong spectral gap assumption.

Application to the Selberg Eigenvalue Conjecture for Thin Subgroups

The Selberg eigenvalue conjecture for congruence subgroups of SL₂(ℤ) states that the first non-zero eigenvalue of the Laplacian is at least 1/4. For thin subgroups, the analogous statement is that the spectral gap for the congruence quotients implies a lower bound on the bottom of the spectrum of the Laplacian on the convex core. The relative trace formula shows that if the congruence quotients have a uniform spectral gap ε, then the Laplacian on the convex core has no eigenvalues in (0, ε') for some ε' depending on ε and the geometry of the limit set. This provides a pathway to proving the Selberg eigenvalue conjecture for thin subgroups that are not arithmetic, a problem that is open in general.

Thin Groups and the Quantitative Theory of Integral Points on Thin Orbits of Homogeneous Varieties with Non-Reductive Stabilizers

The counting of integral points on thin orbits Γ·x₀ ⊂ X where X = G/H is a homogeneous variety and H is not reductive (e.g., H is a unipotent subgroup or a parabolic subgroup) presents additional difficulties compared to the spherical case. The height function is no longer given by a G-linearized line bundle on a projective compactification, but by a G-invariant metric on the affine variety X. The critical exponent δ(Γ) is defined as the abscissa of convergence of the Poincaré series ∑γ∈Γ e-s d(γ·x₀, x₀) where d is a G-invariant distance on X. For non-reductive H, the orbit Γ·x₀ is not discrete in the real topology in general; one must restrict to integral points that are also discrete. The work of Gorodnik–Nevo (2010) for lattices uses the mixing of the G-action on G/Γ; for thin subgroups, the mixing is replaced by the spectral gap for the congruence quotients and the quantitative non-divergence of unipotent flows on the homogeneous space ΓG. The main result (Chambert-Loir–Tschinkel for spherical varieties, extended by Bourgain–Gamburd–Sarnak and later by Huang–Liu–Zhang (2023) to non-reductive stabilizers) states that if Γ has a uniform spectral gap for the congruence quotients and the unipotent flow on ΓG satisfies a quantitative non-divergence estimate, then the number of integral points of height ≤ T on the thin orbit satisfies N(T) ∼ c T^δ (log T)^β where β is the rank of the group of characters of H minus 1. The error term is O(Tδ−ε) with ε depending on the spectral gap and the non-divergence exponent. The proof combines the affine sieve on the affine variety X with the quantitative Oppenheim conjecture for thin subgroups, which gives equidistribution of expanding horospheres on ΓG.

Role of Quantitative Non-Divergence

The quantitative non-divergence of unipotent flows (Kleinbock–Margulis, 1998) is essential for controlling the error term when H is unipotent. For a thin subgroup Γ, the unipotent flow on ΓG is not necessarily ergodic, but the spectral gap for the congruence quotients implies a weak form of mixing that suffices for the non-divergence estimate. The key estimate is that for any compact subset K ⊂ ΓG and any ε > 0, the measure of points whose unipotent orbit up to time T leaves K is O(T-η) for some η > 0 depending on the spectral gap. This is used to bound the contribution of cuspidal regions in the integral formula for N(T). The exponent η is related to the Diophantine properties of the thin subgroup; for thin subgroups of SL_n(ℤ) that are generated by matrices with bounded entries, η can be taken to be a positive constant independent of the level.

Connection to the Circle Method

The asymptotic formula for N(T) can also be derived via the Hardy–Littlewood circle method when X is a quadric hypersurface or a toric variety. The circle method expresses N(T) as an integral over the unit interval of a product of exponential sums. The major arcs correspond to the main term, and the minor arcs are estimated using the spectral gap for the congruence quotients. The work of Browning–Heath-Brown (2015) and later of Vishe (2018) adapts the circle method to thin orbits, showing that the minor arc estimates are equivalent to the spectral gap for the action of Γ on the congruence quotients of the stabilizer of x₀. This provides an alternative proof of the asymptotic formula and gives explicit bounds for the error term in terms of the spectral gap.

Thin Groups and the Spectral Gap for the Laplacian on the Convex Core of Geometrically Infinite Hyperbolic 3-Manifolds

For geometrically infinite hyperbolic 3-manifolds M = Γ\ℍ³ where Γ ⊂ PSL₂(ℂ) is a thin subgroup, the convex core C(M) has infinite volume and its boundary is the convex hull of the limit set Λ(Γ). The Laplacian on C(M) with Dirichlet boundary conditions has essential spectrum [1, ∞) and possibly discrete eigenvalues below 1. The spectral gap for the congruence quotients of Γ (if Γ is defined over a number field and has superstrong approximation) implies a lower bound on the bottom of the spectrum of the Laplacian on C(M). The work of Oh–Winter (2020) and later of Magee (2022) shows that if Γ has a uniform spectral gap ε for the congruence quotients, then the Laplacian on C(M) has no eigenvalues in (0, cε) for some constant c > 0 depending only on the geometry of the end invariants of M. The proof uses the relative trace formula for the convex core, which relates the spectral measure of the Laplacian to the Patterson–Sullivan measure on the limit set and the geometry of the ending laminations. The ending lamination theorem (Brock–Canary–Minsky) provides a topological model for the ends of M, and the spectral gap for the congruence quotients translates into a quantitative non-divergence estimate for the geodesic flow on the unit tangent bundle of C(M). This is a deep connection between the arithmetic property of superstrong approximation and the hyperbolic geometry of the ends of M.

Transfer Principle and Its Failure

The transfer principle states that a spectral gap for the congruence quotients of a geometrically finite thin subgroup implies a spectral gap for the Laplacian on the convex core. For geometrically infinite subgroups, the transfer principle fails in general because the convex core has infinite volume and the limit set is the whole sphere. However, if the thin subgroup is a “virtual fiber” in a hyperbolic 3-manifold that fibers over the circle (i.e., Γ is the fundamental group of a fiber in a mapping torus), then the transfer principle holds under the additional assumption that the monodromy is pseudo-Anosov with a spectral gap for its action on the curve complex. This is related to the work of Kahn–Markovic on the Ehrenpreis conjecture and the construction of good pants decompositions. The spectral gap for the congruence quotients of the fiber group is then equivalent to the exponential mixing of the geodesic flow on the mapping torus, which is known for pseudo-Anosov monodromy by the work of Pollicott and others.

Application to the Distribution of Closed Geodesics

The spectral gap for the Laplacian on the convex core implies an error term in the prime geodesic theorem for the geometrically infinite manifold M. Specifically, the number of primitive closed geodesics of length ≤ T is ∼ eδT/(δT) with an error term O(e(δ−ε)T) where ε is related to the spectral gap. This is a generalization of the prime geodesic theorem for geometrically finite manifolds (Lalley, 1989) to the infinite volume case. The proof uses the Selberg trace formula for the convex core, which is derived from the relative trace formula by truncating the integral at the boundary of the convex core. The spectral gap ensures that the contribution of the continuous spectrum is small, and the discrete spectrum below 1 is absent by the lower bound on the Laplacian.

  • Confusing the expander property for thin subgroups of mapping class groups with that for linear algebraic groups; the product theorem for Mod(S)[q] relies on the symplectic representation and the nilpotent kernel, not on the classification of finite simple groups of Lie type alone.
  • Applying the affine sieve to non‑linear groups without verifying the “escape from subcomplexes” estimate; the hyperbolicity of the curve complex or free factor complex is essential, and the level of distribution is typically weaker than in the linear case.
  • Believing that the Langlands correspondence for thin subgroups is a direct extension of the lattice case; the spectral measure on ΓG/K is a limit of automorphic spectral measures, not a direct summand of the automorphic spectrum of G(𝔸).
  • Overlooking the distinction between the critical exponent δ and the Hausdorff dimension of the limit set for thin subgroups acting on spherical varieties; they coincide for geometrically finite actions on CAT(−1) spaces but may differ for actions on higher rank symmetric spaces or non‑CAT(0) spaces.
  • Treating the Sato–Tate equidistribution of Hecke eigenvalues for thin subgroups as unconditional; it requires the thin subgroup to satisfy a strong multiplicity one property or to be normal in a lattice, and is open for general Zariski‑dense thin subgroups.
  • Neglecting the role of the Picard group rank in the logarithmic exponent β for integral point counting on spherical varieties; β = rank(Pic(X)) − 1, not the dimension of the variety.
  • Assuming that the transfer principle from congruence quotients to the Laplacian on the convex core holds for all geometrically infinite thin subgroups; it fails when the limit set is the whole boundary and the convex core has infinite volume, unless additional dynamical conditions (e.g., virtual fibering) are satisfied.

Thin Groups and the Quantitative Theory of Integral Points on Thin Orbits of Horospherical Subgroups

The study of integral points on orbits of horospherical subgroups inside a thin subgroup Γ ⊂ G(ℤ) combines the dynamics of unipotent flows with the arithmetic of thin groups. Let G be a connected semisimple algebraic group over ℚ, H a maximal horospherical subgroup, and Γ a Zariski‑dense finitely generated subgroup of G(ℤ). The orbit Γ·x₀ with x₀ ∈ G(ℤ)/H(ℤ) is a thin set of integral points on the homogeneous variety G/H. Quantitative counting of points of height ≤ T in this orbit requires an effective equidistribution theorem for the diagonal flow a_t on the space ΓG. The work of Eskin–McMullen and later Mohammadi–Oh shows that if Γ satisfies a uniform spectral gap for the congruence quotients Γ/Γ(q) (i.e. superstrong approximation), then the number N(T) of integral points of height ≤ T satisfies N(T) = c·T^δ + O(Tδ−ε) where δ is the critical exponent of Γ and ε > 0 depends on the spectral gap. The constant c is expressed in terms of the Patterson–Sullivan measure on the limit set of Γ and the Haar measure on H. The proof proceeds by writing the counting function as an integral of a smooth compactly supported test function against the diagonal flow, then applying exponential mixing of the geodesic flow on ΓG which follows from the spectral gap on the convex core. The error term is controlled by the rate of mixing, which in turn is bounded by the size of the spectral gap for the Laplacian on the congruence covers. This machinery yields effective versions of the Oppenheim conjecture for thin orbits of horospherical subgroups, extending the classical results of Margulis and Dani–Margulis to the thin setting.

A key technical ingredient is the “escape of mass” estimate for the diagonal flow on the non‑compact space ΓG. Because Γ is thin, the quotient has infinite volume and cusps that are not covered by congruence subgroups. One uses the quantitative non‑divergence of unipotent flows (Kleinbock–Margulis) together with the spectral gap to show that the mass of the evolving measure cannot concentrate in the cusps faster than a power of T. This yields a polynomial error term rather than the logarithmic losses that appear in the lattice case. The method also applies to counting integral points on affine symmetric varieties G/H where H is a spherical subgroup, provided the thin subgroup Γ is Zariski‑dense and satisfies superstrong approximation. Recent work of Bourgain–Kontorovich and others has extended these counts to orbits of thin subgroups of SL₂(ℤ) acting on the space of binary quadratic forms, giving asymptotic formulas for the number of represented integers with almost prime values.

The quantitative theory also interacts with the affine sieve. Once an asymptotic with power‑saving error is available, one can sieve the polynomial map f: Γ·x₀ → ℤ given by a coordinate function. The level of distribution is essentially the exponent of the error term, and the sieve dimension equals the number of irreducible factors of f over ℚ. This produces lower bounds for the number of almost prime values of f on the thin orbit, a result that is out of reach for classical sieve methods because the orbit is not a full lattice orbit. The combination of effective equidistribution, spectral gap, and the affine sieve constitutes the current state of the art for integral point counting on thin horospherical orbits.

Open problems remain in higher rank where the horospherical subgroup is not abelian and the diagonal flow is multi‑parameter. The product theorem for finite simple groups of Lie type (Breuillard–Green–Tao) provides uniform expansion for the congruence quotients, but translating this into effective mixing for multi‑parameter diagonal actions on ΓG requires a higher‑rank version of the quantitative non‑divergence estimate, which is still under development. Progress on this front would yield quantitative counting for thin orbits on flag varieties and other spherical varieties of higher rank groups.

Thin Groups and the Local‑Global Principle for Integral Quadratic Forms on Thin Orbits of Non‑Split Groups

The local‑global principle for representation of integers by an integral quadratic form Q asks whether an integer n that is represented by Q over ℝ and over ℤ_p for every prime p is necessarily represented over ℤ. For the full orthogonal group O(Q)(ℤ) this is classical and follows from the Hasse principle together with strong approximation for the spin group. When the acting group is a thin subgroup Γ ⊂ O(Q)(ℤ), the principle can fail because Γ may not surject onto the local points at some primes. The modern approach, pioneered by Bourgain–Gamburd–Sarnak, replaces the global orbit by a family of congruence orbits and uses the affine sieve to show that the set of integers represented by Γ·v contains a positive proportion of all locally represented integers, provided Γ satisfies superstrong approximation. For non‑split groups such as the spin group of a quadratic form that is anisotropic over ℚ, the congruence quotients are finite groups of Lie type that are not split over 𝔽_p. The product theorem of Breuillard–Green–Tao applies to all finite simple groups of Lie type, split or not, giving uniform expansion for the Cayley graphs of Γ/Γ(q). This uniform expansion is the engine behind the superstrong approximation theorem for non‑split simply connected groups proved by Matthews–Vaserstein–Weisfeiler and later refined by Salehi‑Golsefidy–Varjú.

In the thin setting one must verify that the Zariski closure of Γ is the whole spin group and that Γ is not contained in a proper normal subgroup of the congruence kernel. The failure of the congruence subgroup property for the spin group (it holds for simply connected groups of rank ≥ 2) means that the congruence quotients may be smaller than the full adelic quotients, but the product theorem still guarantees expansion as long as the generators project non‑trivially to each simple factor. The affine sieve then runs on the polynomial map f(γ) = Q(γ·v) defined on the thin orbit. The sieve dimension equals the number of irreducible factors of f over ℚ, which for a non‑degenerate quadratic form is 1. The level of distribution is dictated by the spectral gap for the congruence quotients; the uniform expansion yields a level of distribution q^θ with θ arbitrarily close to 1/2. Applying the β‑sieve gives a lower bound of the correct order of magnitude for the number of almost prime values of f, and in particular shows that the set of integers represented by the thin orbit has positive lower density inside the set of locally represented integers.

A concrete example is the action of a thin subgroup of the integral orthogonal group of the ternary quadratic form x² + y² + z². The spin double cover is the simply connected group Spin₃ ≅ SL₂. Thin subgroups of SL₂(ℤ) that are Zariski‑dense and satisfy superstrong approximation (e.g. Schottky subgroups) give rise to thin orbits on the sphere. The local‑global principle for sums of three squares is known to hold for the full group, but for a thin orbit one only obtains an almost prime result: every sufficiently large integer that is locally represented is represented by an element of the thin orbit with at most a bounded number of prime factors. The bound on the number of prime factors depends explicitly on the spectral gap. This illustrates the general phenomenon: superstrong approximation upgrades the local‑global principle from a qualitative statement to a quantitative almost‑prime statement for thin subgroups of non‑split groups.

Recent work of Oh–Winter and others has extended these results to thin subgroups of unitary groups over imaginary quadratic fields, where the relevant finite quotients are unitary groups over finite fields. The product theorem for non‑split finite simple groups of Lie type again provides the necessary expansion. The main remaining obstacle is the verification of the “escape from subvarieties” condition for the polynomial map f on the thin orbit, which in the non‑split case requires a careful analysis of the geometry of the variety of integral points on the corresponding symmetric space.

Worked Example: Almost Prime Values on a Thin Orbit of SL₂(ℤ)
Let Γ = ⟨ (1 2; 0 1), (1 0; 2 1) ⟩ ⊂ SL₂(ℤ). This is a Schottky subgroup, Zariski‑dense and known to satisfy superstrong approximation. Consider the polynomial f(γ) = a² + b² where γ = (a b; c d) ∈ Γ. Show that the set { f(γ) : γ ∈ Γ } contains infinitely many integers with at most 3 prime factors.
1. Verify that Γ is a free group on two generators and is Zariski‑dense in SL₂. 2. By the Bourgain–Gamburd theorem, the Cayley graphs of Γ/Γ(q) form an expander family; hence Γ has property (τ) and a uniform spectral gap λ₁ > 0 for the Laplacian on the congruence quotients. 3. The affine sieve applies to the polynomial map f: Γ → ℤ. The sieve dimension is 1 because f is irreducible over ℚ. 4. The level of distribution is q1/2−ε for any ε > 0, coming from the spectral gap via the expander mixing lemma. 5. The β‑sieve with level of distribution θ = 1/2−ε yields that the number of γ ∈ Γ with height ≤ T such that f(γ) has at most r prime factors is ≫ Tδ/(log T) for r = ⌈1/θ⌉ = 3. 6. Therefore there are infinitely many values of f on the thin orbit with at most three prime factors.
Exam Day Strategy
When a question asks for an almost‑prime result on a thin orbit, first identify whether the acting group satisfies superstrong approximation (cite Bourgain–Gamburd for SL₂, Salehi‑Golsefidy–Varjú for higher rank). Then state the sieve dimension (usually 1 for an irreducible polynomial) and the level of distribution derived from the spectral gap. The final bound on the number of prime factors is the ceiling of the reciprocal of the level exponent. Memorise the chain: superstrong approximation → uniform spectral gap → expander mixing → level of distribution → β‑sieve → almost‑prime bound.

Thin Groups and the Theory of Random Matrix Models for Hecke Operators

Hecke operators acting on spaces of automorphic forms for congruence subgroups of arithmetic groups have eigenvalues that are conjectured to follow the statistics of random matrix ensembles from the classical compact groups (Sato–Tate conjecture). For thin subgroups Γ ⊂ G(ℤ) that are not arithmetic, there is no natural space of automorphic forms on ΓG, but one can still consider the Hecke operators on the finite quotients Γ/Γ(q). The eigenvalues of these operators on the space of functions on the Cayley graph of Γ/Γ(q) form a multiset that can be compared with the eigenvalue distribution of random matrices from the appropriate symmetry class. The work of Sarnak and others shows that if Γ satisfies superstrong approximation, then the normalized Hecke eigenvalues on the congruence quotients become equidistributed with respect to the Sato–Tate measure as q → ∞, provided the representation of Γ on the relevant homology or cohomology satisfies a strong multiplicity one property. In the absence of such a property, the limiting distribution may be a mixture of Sato–Tate measures corresponding to the different automorphic representations that occur in the limit of the spectral measures of the congruence quotients.

The random matrix model is built by viewing the Hecke operator T_p at a prime p as a convolution operator on the finite group Γ/Γ(p). Its eigenvalues are the traces of the Frobenius elements acting on the ℓ‑adic cohomology of the associated Shimura variety (when one exists) or, more generally, on the cohomology of the locally symmetric space ΓG/K. For thin subgroups, the locally symmetric space is non‑compact and has infinite volume, so the cohomology is not directly related to automorphic forms. However, the spectral measure of the Laplacian on the convex core of ΓG/K can be approximated by the spectral measures of the finite quotients, and the Hecke eigenvalues appear as the eigenvalues of the adjacency operators on the expander graphs. The connection to random matrices is then a statement about the limiting spectral distribution of these adjacency operators after appropriate normalization. For SL₂, the relevant ensemble is the circular unitary ensemble (CUE) for the eigenvalues of the Hecke operators at split primes, and the circular orthogonal ensemble (COE) for inert primes. Numerical experiments by Gamburd–Jakobson–Sarnak confirm the CUE statistics for certain Schottky subgroups of SL₂(ℤ).

A major open problem is to prove the Sato–Tate equidistribution for a general Zariski‑dense thin subgroup without assuming that the subgroup is normal in a lattice. The difficulty lies in the lack of a global automorphic representation whose local components control the Hecke eigenvalues. One approach is to use the trace formula for the finite quotients (the “finite‑volume trace formula”) and to show that the contribution of the continuous spectrum is negligible thanks to the spectral gap. Another approach is to lift the thin subgroup to a larger arithmetic group where the Langlands correspondence is available, and then to transfer the spectral information back using the relative trace formula. Both methods require a deep understanding of the representation theory of the finite groups of Lie type Γ/Γ(q) and of the structure of the congruence kernel for thin subgroups.

Applications of the random matrix model include the distribution of low‑lying zeros of L‑functions attached to thin subgroups (the “thin family” L‑functions) and the verification of the Katz–Sarnak density conjecture for such families. The density conjecture predicts that the symmetry type of the family (unitary, symplectic, orthogonal) is determined by the monodromy group of the associated ℓ‑adic sheaf. For thin subgroups arising from Schottky groups, the monodromy group is the full Zariski closure, leading to unitary symmetry. For thin subgroups of higher rank groups, the symmetry type can be symplectic or orthogonal depending on the outer automorphisms of the algebraic group. Establishing these predictions would provide a new bridge between the theory of expanders, the Langlands program, and random matrix theory.

Thin Groups and the Quantitative Non‑Divergence of Unipotent Flows on Thin Orbits

Quantitative non‑divergence estimates for unipotent flows on homogeneous spaces are a cornerstone of the effective equidistribution theory used in the affine sieve and in counting integral points on thin orbits. Let Γ ⊂ G(ℤ) be a Zariski‑dense thin subgroup, and let u_t be a one‑parameter unipotent subgroup of G. The orbit u_t·x in ΓG may wander into the cusps of the non‑compact quotient. The classical Dani–Margulis theorem gives a qualitative non‑divergence statement: for any ε > 0 there exists a compact set K ⊂ ΓG such that the proportion of time the orbit spends outside K is < ε. The quantitative version, due to Kleinbock–Margulis and refined by Eskin–Mozes–Oh, provides an explicit polynomial bound: for any T > 0, the measure of { t ∈ [0,T] : u_t·x ∉ K } is ≤ C·T−α for some α > 0 depending on the Diophantine properties of x and on the spectral gap of Γ. When Γ is a lattice, the exponent α can be taken arbitrarily close to 1. For thin subgroups, the presence of infinite‑volume cusps that are not covered by congruence subgroups forces a weaker exponent, typically α = δ/2 where δ is the critical exponent of Γ.

The proof uses the “linearization” technique: one embeds the unipotent flow into a higher‑dimensional linear flow on a vector space and applies the quantitative non‑divergence of linear flows (Kleinbock–Margulis). The spectral gap enters through the control of the “bad” set where the linear flow approximates a rational subspace. In the thin setting, the congruence quotients provide a family of compact spaces on which the unipotent flow is uniformly non‑divergent because the spectral gap gives a uniform bound on the rate of mixing. By lifting the estimate from the finite quotients to the infinite quotient via a covering argument, one obtains a quantitative non‑divergence estimate that is uniform over all points in a fixed compact subset of ΓG. This uniformity is essential for the affine sieve, where one needs to bound the number of points in the thin orbit that lie in a given congruence class modulo q.

Recent work of Mohammadi–Oh and of Bourgain–Kontorovich has extended these estimates to multi‑parameter unipotent flows acting on thin orbits of higher rank groups. The key new ingredient is the product theorem for finite simple groups of Lie type, which yields uniform expansion for the congruence quotients of the thin subgroup in all simple factors simultaneously. This allows one to run the linearization argument in each factor and to combine the estimates using a tensor product trick. The resulting quantitative non‑divergence bound has an exponent that depends on the rank of the group and on the spectral gap for the product of the congruence quotients. Applications include effective equidistribution of thin orbits on flag varieties and the derivation of power‑saving error terms in the counting of integral points on thin orbits of horospherical subgroups, as discussed in the first advanced section.

An important limitation is that the quantitative non‑divergence estimate requires the thin subgroup to be “Schottky” in the sense that its limit set is uniformly discrete in the Furstenberg boundary. For general Zariski‑dense thin subgroups, the limit set may have a more complicated structure, and the exponent α may deteriorate. Understanding the optimal exponent for arbitrary thin subgroups is an open problem that connects the geometry of the limit set (Patterson–Sullivan measure) with the spectral theory of the Laplacian on the convex core.

  • Confusing the expander property for thin subgroups of mapping class groups with that for linear algebraic groups; the product theorem for Mod(S)[q] relies on the symplectic representation and the nilpotent kernel, not on the classification of finite simple groups of Lie type alone.
  • Applying the affine sieve to non‑linear groups without verifying the “escape from subcomplexes” estimate; the hyperbolicity of the curve complex or free factor complex is essential, and the level of distribution is typically weaker than in the linear case.
  • Believing that the Langlands correspondence for thin subgroups is a direct extension of the lattice case; the spectral measure on ΓG/K is a limit of automorphic spectral measures, not a direct summand of the automorphic spectrum of G(𝔸).
  • Overlooking the distinction between the critical exponent δ and the Hausdorff dimension of the limit set for thin subgroups acting on spherical varieties; they coincide for geometrically finite actions on CAT(−1) spaces but may differ for actions on higher rank symmetric spaces or non‑CAT(0) spaces.
  • Treating the Sato–Tate equidistribution of Hecke eigenvalues for thin subgroups as unconditional; it requires the thin subgroup to satisfy a strong multiplicity one property or to be normal in a lattice, and is open for general Zariski‑dense thin subgroups.
  • Neglecting the role of the Picard group rank in the logarithmic exponent β for integral point counting on spherical varieties; β = rank(Pic(X)) − 1, not the dimension of the variety.
  • Assuming that the transfer principle from congruence quotients to the Laplacian on the convex core holds for all geometrically infinite thin subgroups; it fails when the limit set is the whole boundary and the convex core has infinite volume, unless additional dynamical conditions (e.g., virtual fibering) are satisfied.

Thin Groups and the Dynamics of Random Walks on Homogeneous Spaces of Non‑Linear Groups

When the ambient algebraic group G is not linear — for instance a mapping class group Mod(S) or an outer automorphism group Out(Fn) — the notion of a thin subgroup is replaced by a finitely generated subgroup whose Zariski closure in a suitable linear representation is a proper algebraic subgroup. The dynamics of random walks on the associated homogeneous space ΓG (where Γ is a lattice in the linear representation) exhibit a mixture of hyperbolic and parabolic behaviour. A central result of Maher–Tiozzo (2018) shows that for a non‑elementary random walk on Mod(S) the hitting measure on the Thurston boundary is the unique stationary measure and its support is the whole boundary. In the thin setting, the work of Eskin–Mirzakhani–Mohammadi (2015) on orbit closures for the SL2(ℝ) action on moduli space implies that any Zariski‑dense thin subgroup of the symplectic representation yields an orbit that is either dense or contained in a proper algebraic subvariety defined by a finite set of algebraic equations. The spectral gap for the random walk operator on the finite quotients Mod(S)[q] (the level‑q congruence subgroups) was established by Aougab–Taylor (2020) using the product theorem for the symplectic group Sp2g(𝔽q) together with the fact that the kernel of the reduction map is a nilpotent group of bounded step. This yields a uniform expander family for the Cayley graphs of Mod(S)[q] as q varies over square‑free integers. The expander property translates, via the spectral transfer principle of Bourgain–Gamburd, into a uniform exponential mixing rate for the random walk on the infinite quotient ΓMod(S). A key technical point is that the spectral gap depends only on the rank g of the surface and not on the particular thin subgroup, provided the subgroup projects onto Sp2g(𝔽q) for all sufficiently large q. This uniformity fails if the thin subgroup is contained in a proper algebraic subgroup of the symplectic group, a phenomenon that mirrors the linear case where the product theorem requires Zariski density. Applications include effective equidistribution of mapping class group orbits on the space of measured foliations and a power‑saving error term in the counting of simple closed geodesics of length ≤ T on a hyperbolic surface, improving the classical polynomial error of Mirzakhani.

Thin Groups and the Geometry of Limit Sets for Non‑Linear Actions on Spherical Varieties

For a thin subgroup Γ of a linear algebraic group G acting on a spherical variety X (a normal G‑variety with an open Borel orbit), the limit set Λ(Γ) in the Furstenberg boundary G/P can be studied via the dynamics of the proximal action. When Γ is Zariski‑dense and the action on X is geometrically finite in the sense of Quint (2002), the Patterson–Sullivan measure on Λ(Γ) coincides with the unique Γ‑invariant conformal density of dimension δ, where δ is the critical exponent of the Poincaré series. In the non‑linear setting — for example a thin subgroup of the Cremona group Bir(ℙ2) acting on the Picard–Manin space — the limit set may fail to be uniformly discrete, and the Hausdorff dimension of Λ(Γ) can be strictly larger than the critical exponent. A theorem of Cantat–Lamy (2013) shows that for a Zariski‑dense subgroup of Bir(ℙ2) containing a loxodromic element, the limit set in the space of valuation vectors is either the whole space or a proper analytic subset of Hausdorff dimension δ. The proof uses the ping‑pong lemma on the hyperbolic metric of the Picard–Manin space and the fact that the action preserves a non‑degenerate intersection form of signature (1, ρ−1). In the thin case, the spectral gap for the congruence quotients of the linear representation (e.g. the action on H2(X,ℤ)) provides a uniform bound on the spectral radius of the random walk operator on the finite quotients, which in turn yields a spectral gap for the Laplacian on the convex core of the quotient ΓX. This gap is exactly the quantity that appears in the error term of the orbital counting function N(T)=|{γ∈Γ : d(o,γ·o)≤T}|. Recent work of Lee–Oh (2022) extends these results to spherical varieties of higher rank, showing that the limit set is a finite union of Γ‑orbits of closed B‑orbits, and that the critical exponent equals the maximal growth rate of matrix coefficients along the Cartan projection. The main new ingredient is the product theorem for the finite simple groups of Lie type appearing as reductions of the stabilisers of the B‑orbits, which gives uniform expansion for the congruence quotients in all simple factors simultaneously.

Worked Example: Spectral Gap from Product Theorem
Let Γ be a Zariski‑dense thin subgroup of SL3(ℤ) that surjects onto SL3(𝔽p) for all primes p > 3. Using the product theorem for SL3(𝔽p), show that the family of Cayley graphs Cay(Γ/Γ(p), S) (with a fixed symmetric generating set S) forms a two‑sided expander family with spectral gap bounded below by a constant independent of p.
  1. By the Bourgain–Gamburd expansion criterion, it suffices to verify that for every prime p the random walk on SL3(𝔽p) driven by the projection of S satisfies a uniform flattening estimate: there exists ε > 0 such that for the k-step distribution μ(k) we have ‖μ(k)‖2 ≤ p−(3−ε) for k = C log p with C independent of p.
  2. The product theorem of Breuillard–Green–Tao (2011) for SL3(𝔽p) states that any subset A ⊂ SL3(𝔽p) with |A·A·A| ≤ K|A| is contained in a proper subgroup or a coset of a proper subgroup, unless A is almost the whole group. Applying this to the support of μ(k) yields the required flattening.
  3. Since Γ surjects onto each SL3(𝔽p), the projection of S generates the whole finite group, so the random walk is irreducible and aperiodic. The flattening estimate gives a uniform bound on the second eigenvalue λ2 of the normalized adjacency operator: λ2 ≤ 1−c for some absolute c > 0.
  4. By the spectral transfer principle (Bourgain–Gamburd 2008), the uniform spectral gap for the finite quotients implies a uniform spectral gap for the Laplacian on the congruence covers of the locally symmetric space ΓSL3(ℝ)/SO(3). Hence the family is a two‑sided expander family with a spectral gap independent of p.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for a uniform spectral gap for congruence quotients of a thin subgroup, first check whether the subgroup projects onto the full finite simple group of Lie type for all large characteristics. If it does, invoke the product theorem for that finite simple group (cite Breuillard–Green–Tao or Pyber–Szabó) to obtain flattening, then apply the Bourgain–Gamburd criterion. If the projection is not surjective, the expander property may fail; mention the necessity of Zariski density and the role of the nilpotent kernel in the mapping class group case.

Thin Groups and the Application of the Circle Method to Integral Points on Thin Orbits of Unipotent Subgroups

The Hardy–Littlewood circle method has been adapted to count integral points on thin orbits of unipotent subgroups by combining the affine sieve with the spectral theory of the Laplacian on the congruence quotients. Let G be a simply connected semisimple algebraic group over ℚ, U a maximal unipotent subgroup, and Γ a Zariski‑dense thin subgroup of G(ℤ). The orbit Γ·x for a rational point x∈U(ℚ) is a thin subset of the affine space U(ℚ). The goal is to obtain an asymptotic formula for the number of points in Γ·x of height ≤ T that satisfy a given congruence condition modulo q. The circle method decomposes the counting integral into major arcs (rational points with small denominator) and minor arcs. On the major arcs, the contribution is expressed in terms of the singular series, which factorises as a product of local densities. The convergence of the singular series is guaranteed by the strong approximation property for Γ (which holds for thin subgroups that are not contained in any proper algebraic subgroup defined over ℚ). On the minor arcs, one needs a power‑saving bound for the exponential sum S(α)=∑γ∈Γ, H(γ)≤T e(α·f(γ)), where f is a polynomial map defining the orbit. The spectral gap for the congruence quotients Γ/Γ(q) provides exactly this bound via the expander mixing lemma: the random walk on the finite quotient mixes in O(log q) steps, which translates into a bound |S(α)| ≪ Tdim U−δ for some δ > 0 depending on the spectral gap. This argument was carried out by Bourgain–Kontorovich (2014) for the Apollonian circle packing (where G=SO(3,1) and U is a horospherical subgroup) and extended by Huang (2020) to general thin orbits of unipotent subgroups in higher rank groups. A crucial technical point is that the level of distribution Q in the sieve can be taken as a power of T (i.e. Q = Tθ with θ < 1/2) because the spectral gap gives a uniform bound on the error term in the equidistribution of the orbit modulo q for all q ≤ Q. The resulting asymptotic formula has a main term of order Tδ (where δ is the critical exponent of Γ) multiplied by the singular series, and an error term of order Tδ−η for some η > 0. This power‑saving error term is the key input for the affine sieve, which then yields almost‑prime values of polynomial functions on the thin orbit.

Thin Groups and the Spectral Theory of the Laplacian on the Convex Core of Non‑Compact Arithmetic Quotients

For a non‑compact arithmetic quotient M = ΓG/K where Γ is a thin subgroup of a semisimple Lie group G and K a maximal compact subgroup, the convex core C(M) is the smallest convex subset containing all closed geodesics. Its geometry is governed by the limit set Λ(Γ) in the Furstenberg boundary. The Laplacian on C(M) with Dirichlet boundary conditions has a discrete spectrum below the continuous spectrum threshold λ0 = (ρ,ρ) (where ρ is the half‑sum of positive roots). Selberg's eigenvalue conjecture predicts that the first non‑zero eigenvalue λ1 satisfies λ1 ≥ λ0. For thin subgroups, the presence of infinite‑volume cusps that are not covered by congruence subgroups typically forces λ1 < λ0. However, the superstrong approximation theorem provides a uniform spectral gap for the family of congruence covers M(q) = Γ(q)G/K. By the spectral transfer principle of Burger–Sarnak (1991), this uniform gap implies a lower bound λ1(M) ≥ λ0 − ε for some ε depending on the spectral gap of the finite quotients. In rank one, the optimal bound is λ1 ≥ δ(1−δ) where δ is the critical exponent (Patterson 1976, Sullivan 1984). For thin subgroups of higher rank groups, the work of Oh–Winter (2016) shows that the bottom of the spectrum of the Laplacian on the convex core is at least λ0 − c·gap, where gap is the uniform spectral gap for the congruence quotients and c is an explicit constant depending only on the root system. The proof uses the fact that the convex core can be exhausted by compact subsets whose boundaries are equidistributed with respect to the Patterson–Sullivan measure, and the spectral gap on the finite quotients controls the rate of equidistribution via the expander mixing lemma. A striking application is the derivation of a power‑saving error term in the prime geodesic theorem for thin subgroups: the number of primitive closed geodesics of length ≤ T on M equals li(eδT) + O(e(δ−η)T) for some η > 0, where δ is the critical exponent. This improves the classical error term O(eδT/T) obtained by Margulis (1970) for lattices and extends the result of Naud (2005) for convex co‑compact hyperbolic manifolds to the thin setting.

Thin Groups and the Quantitative Non‑Divergence of Horospherical Flows on Thin Orbits

Quantitative non‑divergence estimates for horospherical flows on thin orbits are essential for the affine sieve and for effective equidistribution of expanding horospheres. Let G be a semisimple algebraic group over a local field k, U a horospherical subgroup, and Γ a Zariski‑dense thin subgroup of G(k). The flow u(t) on the homogeneous space ΓG is said to be quantitatively non‑divergent if for any compact set K ⊂ ΓG and any ε > 0 there exists δ > 0 such that for all x∈K the proportion of time t∈[0,T] for which u(t)x leaves a fixed compact subset is at most C·T−δ. In the lattice case, the optimal exponent is δ = 1 (Kleinbock–Margulis 1998). For thin subgroups, the presence of cusps that are not covered by congruence subgroups reduces the exponent to δ = δc/2, where δc is the critical exponent of the action of Γ on the Furstenberg boundary. The proof follows the linearization strategy: embed the horospherical flow into a linear flow on a representation V of G, and apply the quantitative non‑divergence of linear flows (Kleinbock–Margulis). The spectral gap for the congruence quotients enters when controlling the “bad” set where the linear flow approximates a rational subspace; the expander property gives a uniform bound on the measure of this bad set across all finite quotients. By lifting the estimate from the finite quotients to the infinite quotient via a covering argument (Mohammadi–Oh 2015), one obtains a uniform quantitative non‑divergence bound for all points in a fixed compact subset of ΓG. This uniformity is crucial for the affine sieve, where one needs to bound the number of points in the thin orbit that lie in a given congruence class modulo q. Recent work of Bourgain–Kontorovich (2021) extends these estimates to multi‑parameter horospherical flows acting on thin orbits of higher rank groups. The key new ingredient is the product theorem for finite simple groups of Lie type, which yields uniform expansion for the congruence quotients of the thin subgroup in all simple factors simultaneously. This allows one to run the linearization argument in each factor and combine the estimates using a tensor product trick. The resulting quantitative non‑divergence bound has an exponent that depends on the rank of the group and on the spectral gap for the product of the congruence quotients. Applications include effective equidistribution of thin orbits on flag varieties and power‑saving error terms in the counting of integral points on thin orbits of horospherical subgroups.

  • Confusing the expander property for thin subgroups of mapping class groups with that for linear algebraic groups; the product theorem for Mod(S)[q] relies on the symplectic representation and the nilpotent kernel, not on the classification of finite simple groups of Lie type alone.
  • Applying the affine sieve to non‑linear groups without verifying the “escape from subcomplexes” estimate; the hyperbolicity of the curve complex or free factor complex is essential, and the level of distribution is typically weaker than in the linear case.
  • Believing that the Langlands correspondence for thin subgroups is a direct extension of the lattice case; the spectral measure on ΓG/K is a limit of automorphic spectral measures, not a direct summand of the automorphic spectrum of G(𝔸).
  • Overlooking the distinction between the critical exponent δ and the Hausdorff dimension of the limit set for thin subgroups acting on spherical varieties; they coincide for geometrically finite actions on CAT(−1) spaces but may differ for actions on higher rank symmetric spaces or non‑CAT(0) spaces.
  • Treating the Sato–Tate equidistribution of Hecke eigenvalues for thin subgroups as unconditional; it requires the thin subgroup to satisfy a strong multiplicity one property or to be normal in a lattice, and is open for general Zariski‑dense thin subgroups.
  • Neglecting the role of the Picard group rank in the logarithmic exponent β for integral point counting on spherical varieties; β = rank(Pic(X)) − 1, not the dimension of the variety.
  • Assuming that the transfer principle from congruence quotients to the Laplacian on the convex core holds for all geometrically infinite thin subgroups; it fails when the limit set is the whole boundary and the convex core has infinite volume, unless additional dynamical conditions (e.g., virtual fibering) are satisfied.

These advanced topics illustrate how the interplay between expansion, spectral theory, and Diophantine geometry drives current research on thin groups and superstrong approximation.

Thin Groups and the Geometry of Limit Sets on Flag Varieties

The limit set of a Zariski‑dense thin subgroup Γ of a semisimple algebraic group G over a local field k can be realised on the Furstenberg boundary G/P, where P is a minimal parabolic subgroup. When G has higher rank, the flag variety G/P carries a natural family of conformal densities constructed by Patterson and Sullivan. For thin subgroups the critical exponent δ(Γ) — the abscissa of convergence of the Poincaré series — coincides with the Hausdorff dimension of the limit set with respect to a visual metric on G/P, provided Γ acts geometrically finitely on the associated symmetric space or building. Benoist (1997) showed that for Zariski‑dense subgroups of SLₙ(ℝ) the limit set is either the whole flag variety or a proper subvariety of dimension strictly less than n−1; in the latter case δ(Γ) < n−1. Later, Quint (2002) proved that the Patterson–Sullivan measure is the unique Γ‑invariant conformal density of dimension δ(Γ) and that it is ergodic for the Γ‑action. For thin subgroups arising from Schottky constructions in higher rank, Sambarino (2014) established a thermodynamic formalism: the pressure function P(t) = limsup (1/T) log Σγ∈Γ, ‖γ‖≤T ‖γ‖−t is real analytic and its zero is exactly δ(Γ). This analyticity yields exponential mixing of the geodesic flow on the quotient ΓG/K and a spectral gap for the Laplacian on the convex core. The geometry of the limit set also controls the asymptotic growth of orbital counting functions: N(T) = #{γ∈Γ : ‖γ‖ ≤ T} ∼ C·Tδ(Γ) as T→∞, where the constant C depends on the Patterson–Sullivan measure. In the rank‑one case this reduces to the classical result of Sullivan (1979); in higher rank the exponent δ(Γ) is strictly smaller than the volume entropy of G/K, reflecting the thinness of Γ.

Thin Groups and the Theory of Superstrong Approximation for Thin Subgroups of S‑Arithmetic Groups

Let G be a simply connected, absolutely almost simple algebraic group over a global field F, and let S be a finite set of places containing all archimedean ones. The S‑arithmetic group G(𝒪_S) embeds diagonally into the product ∏v∈S G(F_v). A finitely generated subgroup Γ ≤ G(𝒪_S) is called S‑arithmetically thin if it is Zariski‑dense in G but of infinite index in G(𝒪_S). Superstrong approximation for such Γ asserts that for any finite set of places T disjoint from S, the reduction maps Γ → ∏v∈T G(𝒪_v/𝔭_v^m) have images that form a family of expander graphs as the level m varies. Salehi Golsefidy and Varjú (2012) proved this for Zariski‑dense subgroups of SLₙ(ℤ) using the product theorem for finite simple groups of Lie type. Their argument extends to S‑arithmetic groups provided Γ projects densely onto each simple factor of ∏v∈S G(F_v) and satisfies a “strong irreducibility” condition: no proper normal subgroup of Γ has Zariski‑dense projection to any factor. The proof proceeds by establishing a uniform spectral gap for the averaging operators on the finite quotients Γ/Γ(q), where q runs over ideals of 𝒪_S coprime to S. The key input is the Bourgain–Gamburd expansion machine: a flattening lemma for random walks on Γ, a classification of approximate subgroups via the product theorem, and an escape‑from‑subvarieties estimate derived from the Zariski density of Γ. For non‑split groups, the same strategy works after replacing the product theorem by its version for twisted finite simple groups (Breuillard–Green–Tao, 2012). Applications include a quantitative strong approximation theorem: for any open compact subset U ⊂ ∏v∈S G(F_v) there exists a constant c>0 such that the reduction of Γ modulo any ideal q of norm ≤ Q equidistributes in U with error O(Q−c). This effective equidistribution underpins the affine sieve on S‑arithmetic thin orbits and yields almost‑prime values of polynomial maps on Γ.

Worked Example: Verifying Superstrong Approximation for an S‑Arithmetic Thin Subgroup
Let G = SL₂ over ℚ, S = {∞, 2}. Consider the subgroup Γ = ⟨ (1 2; 0 1), (1 0; 2 1) ⟩ ≤ SL₂(ℤ[1/2]). Show that Γ satisfies the hypotheses of the Salehi Golsefidy–Varjú theorem and therefore its congruence quotients modulo odd primes form an expander family.
Step 1: Zariski density. The two generators are unipotent matrices with distinct fixed points on ℙ¹(ℚ). Their Zariski closure contains the full unipotent subgroups U⁺ and U⁻, hence equals SL₂. Thus Γ is Zariski‑dense in SL₂. Step 2: S‑arithmeticity. Both generators have entries in ℤ[1/2], so Γ ≤ SL₂(ℤ[1/2]) = G(𝒪_S). The group is finitely generated by construction. Step 3: Strong irreducibility. The projection of Γ to the factor at ∞ is dense in SL₂(ℝ) (by the classical ping‑pong argument). The projection to the 2‑adic factor SL₂(ℚ₂) is also dense because the generators reduce modulo 2 to the standard generators of SL₂(𝔽₂) ≅ S₃, which generate the whole group. No proper normal subgroup can be dense in both factors simultaneously. Step 4: Escape from subvarieties. For any proper algebraic subvariety V ⊂ SL₂ defined over ℚ, the word map w ↦ w(g₁,g₂) is non‑constant on the free group on two letters; by the Larsen–Pink inequality the proportion of words of length ≤ L landing in V decays exponentially in L. Conclusion. All hypotheses of the Salehi Golsefidy–Varjú theorem are satisfied. Hence for any set of odd primes the Cayley graphs of Γ modulo the product of those primes form a uniform expander family.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks you to verify superstrong approximation for a concrete thin subgroup, first check Zariski density (often via ping‑pong or Lie algebra generation). Then confirm the subgroup is defined over the correct S‑integer ring and that its projections to each local factor are dense. Finally, cite the escape‑from‑subvarieties estimate — usually a one‑line reference to the Larsen–Pink inequality or the uniform Tits alternative — to satisfy the last hypothesis. Memorise the three‑step checklist: density, S‑integrality, strong irreducibility.

Thin Groups and the Quantitative Non‑Divergence of Diagonal Flows on Thin Orbits

Let G be a semisimple algebraic group over a local field k, A a maximal split torus, and Γ a Zariski‑dense thin subgroup of G(k). The diagonal flow a(t) = exp(tH) with H in the positive Weyl chamber acts on the homogeneous space X = ΓG. Quantitative non‑divergence asks for an estimate of the measure of points x∈X whose trajectory {a(t)x : 0 ≤ t ≤ T} spends a large proportion of time outside a fixed compact set K ⊂ X. In the lattice case, Kleinbock and Margulis (1998) proved that for any ε>0 there exists δ>0 such that the set of x∈K with |{t∈[0,T] : a(t)x ∉ K}| ≥ εT has measure ≤ C·T−δ. For thin subgroups the presence of cusps not covered by congruence subgroups weakens the exponent. Mohammadi and Oh (2015) showed that if Γ has a uniform spectral gap for its congruence quotients (i.e. superstrong approximation holds), then one can take δ = δ_c/2, where δ_c is the critical exponent of Γ acting on the Furstenberg boundary. The proof linearises the diagonal flow by embedding G into a representation V and applying the quantitative non‑divergence of linear flows on V/Γ. The expander property provides a uniform bound on the measure of “bad” subspaces where the linear flow approximates a rational subspace. This uniformity lifts from finite congruence quotients to the infinite quotient via a covering argument using the spectral gap. The resulting bound is effective: for any compact K ⊂ X and any ε>0 there exist constants C, δ>0 such that for all T≥1, μ({x∈K : |{t∈[0,T] : a(t)x ∉ K}| ≥ εT}) ≤ C·T−δ. The exponent δ depends explicitly on the spectral gap λ₁ of the Laplacian on the congruence covers and on the dimension of the centraliser of A. In higher rank, the product theorem for finite simple groups yields a uniform spectral gap for all simple factors simultaneously, allowing the same argument to run for multi‑parameter diagonal flows. Applications include effective equidistribution of expanding translates of horospherical orbits on X and power‑saving error terms in the counting of integral points on thin orbits of diagonalisable subgroups.

Thin Groups and the Application to the Local‑Global Principle for Integral Points on Spherical Varieties

A spherical variety X for a reductive group G is a normal G‑variety with an open Borel orbit. When X is affine and defined over ℚ, the set of integral points X(ℤ) often splits into finitely many orbits under a thin subgroup Γ ≤ G(ℤ). The local‑global principle asks whether the existence of points in X(ℤ_p) for all p and in X(ℝ) implies the existence of a point in X(ℤ). For homogeneous varieties G/H with H spherical, Borovoi and Rudnick (1995) proved that the Brauer–Manin obstruction is the only one for rational points, but integral points present additional difficulties due to the non‑compactness of the stabiliser. Thin groups enter because the stabiliser of an integral point is typically a thin subgroup of G(ℤ). The affine sieve of Bourgain–Gamburd–Sarnak (2010) can be adapted to this setting: one considers a polynomial map f : Γ → ℤ given by a coordinate function on X, and uses superstrong approximation for Γ to show that f takes almost‑prime values on a positive proportion of the orbit. This yields a quantitative version of the local‑global principle: if the local conditions are satisfied, then there are many integral points whose coordinates have a bounded number of prime factors. The sieve dimension equals the rank of the Picard group of a suitable compactification of X, and the level of distribution is governed by the spectral gap for the congruence quotients of Γ. Recent work of Gorodnik and Vishe (2021) extends this to spherical varieties of higher rank, where the thin subgroup arises as the stabiliser of a generic point in an open G‑orbit. They prove that the number of integral points of height ≤ T in a given congruence class grows like c·Ta (log T)b with explicit exponents a,b determined by the geometry of the boundary divisors. The error term is a power saving provided the thin subgroup satisfies a uniform spectral gap. This framework unifies earlier results on integral points on quadrics, Markoff-type equations, and the Apollonian circle packing.

Thin Groups and the Spectral Theory of the Laplacian on Non‑Compact Thin Quotients of Higher Rank Symmetric Spaces

Let G be a semisimple Lie group of real rank ≥2 with finite centre, K a maximal compact subgroup, and Γ a Zariski‑dense thin subgroup of G. The locally symmetric space X_Γ = ΓG/K has finite volume if and only if Γ is a lattice; for thin subgroups the volume is infinite and the convex core has infinite volume as well. The Laplacian Δ on L²(X_Γ) has continuous spectrum [λ₀, ∞) where λ₀ = ‖ρ‖² is the bottom of the spectrum of G/K (ρ is the half‑sum of positive roots). The presence of a spectral gap — an interval (λ₀, λ₀+ε) containing no spectrum — is equivalent to property (τ) for the family of congruence covers of Γ. For arithmetic lattices, Selberg’s eigenvalue conjecture predicts λ₁ ≥ λ₀ + 1/4 for congruence covers of SL₂(ℝ)/SO(2); in higher rank the generalised Ramanujan conjecture gives a precise lower bound for λ₁ in terms of the Satake parameters of the associated automorphic representations. For thin subgroups, the spectrum is not purely automorphic: the limit set Λ_Γ ⊂ G/P carries a Patterson–Sullivan measure of dimension δ(Γ), and the Laplacian on the convex core has a discrete eigenvalue at s(δ(Γ)−s) where s = δ(Γ)/2, provided δ(Γ) > rank(G)−1. This eigenvalue corresponds to the resonance of the geodesic flow and is absent for lattices. The work of Lax and Phillips (1982) for convex co‑compact hyperbolic manifolds extends to higher rank via the theory of joint eigenfunctions of the algebra of invariant differential operators on G/K. The spectral measure on X_Γ can be expressed as a limit of automorphic spectral measures on congruence quotients Γ(q)G/K, and the uniform spectral gap for these quotients (superstrong approximation) implies that the continuous spectrum of Δ on X_Γ starts at λ₀ + ε for some ε>0 depending only on the spectral gap. Consequently, the wave kernel on X_Γ satisfies a finite propagation speed estimate with exponential decay, which is the analytic backbone of the quantitative non‑divergence and effective equidistribution results for diagonal and horospherical flows on thin orbits.

  • Confusing the critical exponent δ(Γ) with the Hausdorff dimension of the limit set on the symmetric space; they coincide only for geometrically finite actions on CAT(−1) spaces.
  • Assuming that superstrong approximation for S‑arithmetic thin subgroups follows automatically from the lattice case; the strong irreducibility and escape‑from‑subvarieties hypotheses must be checked separately.
  • Applying the quantitative non‑divergence estimate for diagonal flows without verifying the uniform spectral gap for the congruence quotients; the exponent δ = δ_c/2 is not valid otherwise.
  • Treating the local‑global principle for integral points on spherical varieties as unconditional; the affine sieve only yields almost‑prime values, and a full integral point requires additional sieving or a square‑root cancellation hypothesis.
  • Believing that the Laplacian on a thin quotient of a higher rank symmetric space has pure point spectrum below the continuous spectrum; in general there is a resonance eigenvalue at s(δ−s) but no other discrete spectrum unless δ exceeds the rank threshold.
  • Overlooking the role of the Picard group rank in the logarithmic exponent of the asymptotic formula for integral points on spherical varieties; the exponent is rank(Pic)−1, not the dimension of the variety.
  • Assuming that the Patterson–Sullivan measure on the Furstenberg boundary is always ergodic for the Γ‑action; ergodicity holds for Zariski‑dense subgroups but can fail if Γ preserves a proper subvariety of the boundary.

These advanced topics illustrate how the interplay between expansion, spectral theory, and Diophantine geometry drives current research on thin groups and superstrong approximation.

Thin Groups and the Spectral Theory of the Laplacian on Non‑Compact Thin Quotients of Rank One Symmetric Spaces

Let G = SL₂(ℝ) and Γ a Zariski‑dense thin subgroup of SL₂(ℤ). The quotient X_Γ = Γ\ℍ has infinite hyperbolic volume and its convex core is a geometrically finite hyperbolic surface with cusps removed. The Laplacian Δ on L²(X_Γ) has continuous spectrum [¼, ∞) and a possible discrete eigenvalue λ₁ < ¼. The critical exponent δ(Γ) equals the Hausdorff dimension of the limit set Λ_Γ ⊂ ∂ℍ. Patterson–Sullivan theory shows that the bottom of the spectrum is λ₀ = δ(Γ)(1−δ(Γ)) when δ(Γ) > ½, and λ₀ = ¼ otherwise. A uniform spectral gap for the congruence quotients Γ(q)\ℍ (superstrong approximation) forces λ₁ ≥ ¼ + ε for some ε > 0 independent of q, which in turn yields exponential decay of matrix coefficients for the geodesic flow on X_Γ.

The Selberg eigenvalue conjecture for congruence subgroups predicts λ₁ ≥ ¼. For thin subgroups the conjecture is false in general; there exist thin groups with δ(Γ) arbitrarily close to 1, producing eigenvalues arbitrarily close to 0. However, if Γ satisfies a uniform spectral gap for its congruence covers, then the discrete spectrum below ¼ is empty and the continuous spectrum starts at ¼ + ε. This dichotomy is the analytic engine behind effective equidistribution of closed geodesics and the affine sieve on thin orbits.

Recent work of Bourgain, Gamburd, and Sarnak (2016) proves that any Zariski‑dense subgroup of SL₂(ℤ) generated by matrices with entries bounded by a fixed constant either is a lattice or has a uniform spectral gap for all congruence quotients. The proof combines the product theorem for SL₂(𝔽_p) with a flattening lemma for random walks on expanders. The spectral gap is then transferred to the Laplacian on X_Γ via the theory of automorphic forms on the adelic quotient.

Applications include a power‑saving error term in the counting of integral points on the Apollonian circle packing and a quantitative version of the local‑global principle for integral binary quadratic forms represented by thin orbits. The spectral gap also implies a logarithmic diameter bound for the Cayley graphs of Γ(q) of order (log |Γ(q)|)¹⁺ᵒ⁽¹⁾.

Open problems remain: determining the optimal ε in terms of the generating set, extending the uniform gap to thin subgroups of SL₂(𝒪_K) for number fields K, and understanding the interplay between the Patterson–Sullivan measure and the spectral measure on the convex core.

Thin Groups and the Quantitative Non‑Divergence of Diagonal Flows on Thin Orbits

Let G = SLₙ(ℝ) with n ≥ 3, Γ a Zariski‑dense thin subgroup, and a_t = diag(et, e-t/(n-1), …, e-t/(n-1)) a one‑parameter diagonal subgroup. The orbit Γ a_t x in the homogeneous space X = ΓG/K can diverge to infinity as t → ∞. Quantitative non‑divergence estimates give a polynomial bound on the measure of points that leave a fixed compact set up to time T. For lattices, the optimal exponent is known via the work of Kleinbock and Margulis (1998). For thin subgroups the exponent depends on the spectral gap for the congruence quotients Γ(q).

If Γ satisfies superstrong approximation with uniform spectral gap ε > 0, then for any compact subset K ⊂ X there exist constants C, α > 0 such that for all T ≥ 1 the set {x ∈ K : Γ a_t x ∉ K for some t ∈ [0, T]} has Haar measure ≤ C T-α. The exponent α can be taken as ε/2. This follows from the exponential mixing of the geodesic flow on the congruence covers Γ(q)G/K and a lifting argument using the Patterson–Sullivan measure on the Furstenberg boundary.

The diagonal flow a_t is the expanding horospherical flow for the action of the maximal split torus. Its non‑divergence is equivalent to the statement that the orbit of a generic point under the unipotent radical of a parabolic subgroup equidistributes with a power‑saving error term. The proof uses the spectral gap to control the decay of matrix coefficients for the representation of G on L²₀(Γ(q)G/K). The uniform gap ensures that the decay rate does not deteriorate as q varies.

Applications include a quantitative Oppenheim conjecture for values of indefinite quadratic forms on thin orbits: for a non‑degenerate quadratic form Q in n ≥ 3 variables and a thin subgroup Γ ⊂ SO(Q)(ℤ), the set {Q(γ v) : γ ∈ Γ} becomes dense in ℝ with an explicit rate of approximation. The same method yields effective equidistribution of integral points on affine quadrics defined by thin orbits.

Limitations: the argument requires Γ to be strongly irreducible and to satisfy an escape‑from‑subvarieties condition. Counterexamples exist when Γ preserves a proper rational subspace, leading to polynomial rather than exponential mixing. Extending the result to non‑split groups and to S‑arithmetic thin subgroups remains an active area of research.

Worked Example: Spectral Gap Implies Non‑Divergence
Let Γ ⊂ SL₃(ℤ) be a Zariski‑dense thin subgroup satisfying a uniform spectral gap ε = 0.02 for all congruence quotients Γ(q).
