Let a_t = diag(et, e-t/2, e-t/2) and K a fixed compact subset of X = ΓSL₃(ℝ)/SO(3). Estimate the measure of points in K that leave K under the flow a_t for some t ∈ [0, T] with T = 10⁶.
The quantitative non‑divergence theorem gives a bound C T-α with α = ε/2 = 0.01. Taking C = 1 for simplicity, the measure is ≤ (10⁶)-0.01 = 10-0.06 ≈ 0.87. This crude bound shows that a positive proportion of points may still diverge; sharper constants from the explicit spectral gap improve the estimate to a power saving of order T-0.01. The key step is the transfer of the uniform spectral gap on congruence covers to exponential mixing of the diagonal flow on X, which yields the polynomial non‑divergence exponent α = ε/2.
Exam Strategy
When a question asks for the exponent in a quantitative non‑divergence estimate, identify the uniform spectral gap ε first. The exponent is always ε/2 for diagonal flows and ε for unipotent flows. Write the relation explicitly and state the required hypotheses (strong irreducibility, escape from subvarieties). This avoids the common mistake of quoting the lattice exponent without checking the thin‑group hypotheses.

Thin Groups and the Application to the Local‑Global Principle for Integral Points on Spherical Varieties

Let G be a connected semisimple algebraic group over ℚ, H a spherical subgroup, and X = G/H the associated spherical variety. Assume X has a ℚ‑point and consider the set of integral points X(ℤ) inside a fixed G(ℤ)‑orbit. The local‑global principle asks whether the existence of points in X(ℝ) and X(ℤ_p) for all p implies the existence of an integral point. For thin subgroups Γ ⊂ G(ℤ) arising as stabilisers of generic points, the affine sieve provides almost‑prime values of the coordinate functions on the orbit Γ·x₀.

Bourgain–Gamburd–Sarnak (2016) proved that if Γ satisfies superstrong approximation, then the orbit Γ·x₀ contains points whose coordinates have at most R prime factors, where R depends only on the dimension of X and the sieve dimension. The sieve dimension equals the rank of the Picard group of a smooth compactification of X. For quadrics and Markoff‑type surfaces the rank is 1, giving R = 2 (almost primes). For higher‑rank spherical varieties the rank can be larger, leading to a larger R.

The proof combines the uniform spectral gap for Γ(q) with the combinatorial sieve of Iwaniec. The level of distribution is controlled by the expansion property of the Cayley graphs of Γ(q). The error term in the asymptotic formula for the number of integral points of height ≤ T is a power saving T-δ provided the spectral gap is uniform. Recent work of Gorodnik and Vishe (2021) extends this to arbitrary spherical varieties, giving explicit exponents a, b in the asymptotic c·Ta(log T)b.

A full local‑global principle (R = 1) would require square‑root cancellation in the error term, which is equivalent to the Generalised Ramanujan Conjecture for the automorphic representations generated by the thin orbit. This is currently out of reach. However, the almost‑prime result is sufficient for many Diophantine applications, such as proving that a given integral quadratic form represents infinitely many integers with a bounded number of prime factors.

Open questions include determining the optimal R for each spherical variety, extending the sieve to non‑split groups, and understanding the role of the Brauer–Manin obstruction in the thin‑group setting.

Thin Groups and the Geometry of Limit Sets in Rank One Hyperbolic Manifolds

For a Zariski‑dense thin subgroup Γ ⊂ SL₂(ℝ) the limit set Λ_Γ ⊂ ∂ℍ is a Cantor‑type set of Hausdorff dimension δ(Γ) ∈ (0,1). The Patterson–Sullivan measure μ_Γ on Λ_Γ is the unique (up to scaling) Γ‑invariant conformal density of dimension δ(Γ). The convex core C(Γ) = hull(Λ_Γ)/Γ is a geometrically finite hyperbolic surface with infinite area. Its ends correspond to cusps of the quotient and to funnels bounded by closed geodesics.

The critical exponent δ(Γ) governs the growth of the orbit: #{γ ∈ Γ : d(i, γ i) ≤ T} ∼ c eδ(Γ) T. It also determines the bottom of the spectrum of the Laplacian on C(Γ): λ₀ = δ(Γ)(1−δ(Γ)) if δ(Γ) > ½, otherwise λ₀ = ¼. When δ(Γ) > ½ there is a discrete eigenvalue at λ₀, corresponding to the resonance of the geodesic flow. This eigenvalue is absent for lattices (where δ = 1).

The Hausdorff dimension of Λ_Γ can be computed via the thermodynamic formalism: δ(Γ) is the unique zero of the pressure function P(s) = limT→∞ (1/T) log Σγ: d(i,γ i)≤T e-s d(i,γ i). For Schottky groups the pressure reduces to the topological entropy of a subshift of finite type, allowing numerical approximation of δ(Γ). The work of McMullen (1998) gives an algorithm to compute δ(Γ) to any desired precision for classical Schottky groups.

Superstrong approximation for Γ implies a uniform spectral gap for the congruence quotients Γ(q). This gap translates into exponential mixing of the geodesic flow on the convex core and a power‑saving error term in the orbit counting problem. The mixing rate is directly related to the distance of the first non‑trivial eigenvalue of the Laplacian on Γ(q)\ℍ from ¼.

Recent advances: the work of Oh and Winter (2017) shows that for any ε > 0 there exists a thin subgroup with δ(Γ) > 1−ε and a uniform spectral gap. This demonstrates that the critical exponent and the spectral gap are independent parameters. The geometry of the limit set, in particular its porosity and the structure of the Patterson–Sullivan measure, continues to be a central tool in the analysis of thin groups.

Thin Groups and the Connection to the Langlands Correspondence via Functoriality for Thin Subgroups

The Langlands program predicts a correspondence between automorphic representations of a reductive group G and Galois representations into the L‑group ^L G. For arithmetic lattices this correspondence is realised via the trace formula and the theory of automorphic forms. For thin subgroups Γ ⊂ G(ℤ) the space L²(ΓG/K) is not purely automorphic; it contains a continuous spectrum coming from the limit set and possibly discrete eigenvalues not attached to automorphic representations of G.

Nevertheless, the congruence quotients Γ(q)G/K are finite‑volume orbifolds, and their automorphic spectra are governed by the Langlands correspondence for G. Superstrong approximation provides a uniform spectral gap for the family {Γ(q)}. This uniform gap implies that the automorphic representations occurring in L²(Γ(q)G/K) satisfy a uniform Ramanujan bound at the unramified places. By the work of Clozel (1990) and subsequent refinements, this uniform bound transfers to a bound on the Satake parameters of the associated Galois representations.

Functoriality predicts that for any homomorphism ^L H → ^L G of L‑groups, automorphic representations of H lift to automorphic representations of G. For thin subgroups, one can consider the restriction of automorphic representations of G to the subgroup Γ. The uniform spectral gap ensures that the lifted representations retain a spectral gap, which can be used to prove expansion properties for the Cayley graphs of the images of Γ in finite quotients of H.

Applications include the construction of expander graphs from thin subgroups of exceptional groups via the functorial lift from G₂ to SO₇, and the proof of a uniform spectral gap for thin subgroups of Spin groups using the lift from Spin to SL. The method also yields new cases of the Generalised Ramanujan Conjecture for automorphic forms on thin orbits.

Open problems: establishing functoriality for non‑split groups in the thin‑group setting, understanding the contribution of the continuous spectrum from the limit set to the trace formula, and proving a uniform bound for the Satake parameters of the residual spectrum on Γ(q)G/K.

  • Confusing the critical exponent δ(Γ) with the Hausdorff dimension of the limit set on the symmetric space; they coincide only for geometrically finite actions on CAT(−1) spaces.
  • Assuming that superstrong approximation for S‑arithmetic thin subgroups follows automatically from the lattice case; the strong irreducibility and escape‑from‑subvarieties hypotheses must be checked separately.
  • Applying the quantitative non‑divergence estimate for diagonal flows without verifying the uniform spectral gap for the congruence quotients; the exponent α = ε/2 is not valid otherwise.
  • Treating the local‑global principle for integral points on spherical varieties as unconditional; the affine sieve only yields almost‑prime values, and a full integral point requires additional sieving or a square‑root cancellation hypothesis.
  • Believing that the Laplacian on a thin quotient of a higher rank symmetric space has pure point spectrum below the continuous spectrum; in general there is a resonance eigenvalue at s(δ−s) but no other discrete spectrum unless δ exceeds the rank threshold.
  • Overlooking the role of the Picard group rank in the logarithmic exponent of the asymptotic formula for integral points on spherical varieties; the exponent is rank(Pic)−1, not the dimension of the variety.
  • Assuming that the Patterson–Sullivan measure on the Furstenberg boundary is always ergodic for the Γ‑action; ergodicity holds for Zariski‑dense subgroups but can fail if Γ preserves a proper subvariety of the boundary.

Thin Groups and the Quantitative Theory of Integral Points on Spherical Varieties

Spherical varieties are normal algebraic varieties equipped with an action of a reductive group G such that a Borel subgroup has an open dense orbit. When a thin subgroup Γ ⊂ G(ℤ) acts on a spherical variety X defined over ℚ, the set of integral points X(ℤ) ∩ Γ·x₀ inherits a rich arithmetic structure. The main quantitative problem is to obtain an asymptotic formula for the number of points of height ≤ T in a thin orbit, together with a power‑saving error term. Recent work of Gorodnik–Nevo and of Oh–Shah shows that if Γ is Zariski‑dense and satisfies a uniform spectral gap for its congruence quotients, then the orbit counting function N(T) = #{γ ∈ Γ : H(γ·x₀) ≤ T} satisfies N(T) = c·T^δ (log T)r−1 + O(Tδ−η) where δ is the critical exponent of Γ, r = rank(Pic(X)) and η > 0 depends on the spectral gap. The constant c is expressed via the Patterson–Sullivan measure on the Furstenberg boundary and the volume of a suitable fundamental domain. The proof combines the affine sieve on thin orbits with the spectral theory of the Laplacian on the locally symmetric space ΓG/K, using the fact that spherical varieties admit a wonderful compactification whose boundary divisors correspond to the colors of the spherical system.

The exponent r−1 reflects the number of independent boundary divisors in the wonderful compactification; it is not the dimension of X but the rank of the Picard group. This distinction is a frequent source of error in examinations. The power‑saving η is directly linked to the distance of the first non‑trivial eigenvalue of the congruence Laplacian from the bottom of the continuous spectrum. When Γ is a lattice, the classical Duke–Rudnick–Sarnak theorem gives η = 1/2 under the Generalised Ramanujan Conjecture; for thin groups the best unconditional η comes from the uniform spectral gap proved by Bourgain–Gamburd–Sarnak for SL₂ and by Salehi‑Golsefidy–Varjú for higher rank. The method also yields equidistribution of the integral points on the boundary of the wonderful compactification, which is essential for applications to local‑global principles for integral quadratic forms on spherical varieties.

A concrete illustration is the action of a thin subgroup of SL₃(ℤ) on the space of binary cubic forms, which is a spherical variety for SL₂ × SL₃. The integral orbits correspond to isomorphism classes of cubic rings. The asymptotic formula for the number of such rings of bounded discriminant with a prescribed splitting type was obtained by Bhargava–Shankar–Tsimerman using the geometry of numbers; the thin‑group approach recovers the same main term and provides a power‑saving error term under the spectral gap hypothesis. This demonstrates how the abstract theory of spherical varieties translates into concrete counting problems in arithmetic statistics.

One must also verify the strong irreducibility and escape‑from‑subvarieties conditions for the Zariski‑dense subgroup Γ acting on the spherical variety. These hypotheses guarantee that the random walk on Γ equidistributes on the Furstenberg boundary and that the affine sieve can be applied with a level of distribution that is a power of the height. Failure of either condition leads to a thinner set of integral points for which the asymptotic formula may have a different main term or may even fail to hold. The verification of these conditions is often the most delicate part of a proof and requires a case‑by‑case analysis of the representation of Γ on the coordinate ring of X.

In summary, the quantitative theory of integral points on spherical varieties for thin groups unifies the affine sieve, spectral gap estimates, and the geometry of wonderful compactifications. The resulting asymptotic formulas have the shape predicted by the Manin–Peyre conjectures, with the logarithmic exponent given by the Picard rank, and the error term controlled by the uniform spectral gap of the congruence quotients.

Thin Groups and the Spectral Gap for Congruence Quotients of Thin Subgroups in Rank Two

For a Zariski‑dense subgroup Γ of a split simply connected algebraic group G of rank two (for example G = SL₃ or Sp₄), the congruence quotients Γ(q) = Γ mod q form a family of finite groups. Superstrong approximation asserts that the Cayley graphs of Γ(q) with respect to a fixed symmetric generating set form a family of expanders. The spectral gap λ₁(Γ(q)) is the difference between the trivial eigenvalue 1 and the second largest eigenvalue of the normalized adjacency operator. A uniform lower bound λ₁(Γ(q)) ≥ ε > 0 independent of q is equivalent to property (τ) for the family {Γ(q)}. In rank two the proof of a uniform spectral gap combines the product theorem for finite simple groups of Lie type (Breuillard–Green–Tao, Pyber–Szabó) with the Bourgain–Gamburd expansion machine. The key input is that Γ is not contained in any proper algebraic subgroup of G and that the random walk on Γ escapes from subvarieties at an exponential rate.

The product theorem states that for any finite simple group of Lie type of bounded rank, any subset A which is not too small and not too large satisfies |A³| ≥ |A|1+δ for some absolute δ > 0. When applied to the images of Γ in G(𝔽_p), this yields a growth statement that feeds into the flattening lemma of Bourgain–Gamburd. The flattening lemma shows that the ℓ²‑norm of the k‑step random walk measure decays exponentially in k, provided the measure is not concentrated on a proper subgroup. The escape‑from‑subvarieties hypothesis guarantees that the walk does not concentrate on any proper algebraic subgroup of G(𝔽_p). Together these ingredients give a uniform spectral gap for all square‑free moduli q, and by a standard lifting argument for prime powers the gap extends to all q.

The uniform spectral gap has several immediate consequences. First, it implies exponential mixing of the geodesic flow on the locally symmetric space ΓG/K with a rate that is independent of the congruence level. Second, it yields a power‑saving error term in the orbit counting problem for Γ acting on the symmetric space, with exponent directly related to the size of the gap. Third, it provides the level of distribution needed for the affine sieve on thin orbits in rank two, allowing one to produce almost‑prime values of polynomial maps on Γ·x₀. The work of Salehi‑Golsefidy and Varjú (2012) established the uniform spectral gap for all Zariski‑dense subgroups of simply connected groups of arbitrary rank, assuming only the product theorem and the escape condition. For rank two the product theorem is known unconditionally, so the result is unconditional for any thin subgroup satisfying the escape hypothesis.

A subtle point is that the escape‑from‑subvarieties condition must be checked for the specific thin subgroup. For Schottky subgroups generated by sufficiently high powers of a fixed set of elements, the condition holds by a ping‑pong argument on the Furstenberg boundary. For subgroups arising from monodromy of hypergeometric equations, the condition follows from the Zariski density of the monodromy group and the fact that the representation is strongly irreducible. In examinations, a common mistake is to assume that Zariski density alone implies escape; one must also exclude the possibility that the random walk stays close to a proper subvariety for a long time, which is a quantitative statement.

The rank‑two case is the first where the product theorem for non‑split groups (e.g. SU(3) over a quadratic extension) is required. The proof for non‑split groups uses the same strategy but relies on the classification of approximate subgroups in finite simple groups of Lie type, which was completed by Breuillard–Green–Tao for all types. Consequently, the uniform spectral gap holds for thin subgroups of any simply connected absolutely almost simple algebraic group of rank two, split or non‑split, provided the escape condition is verified.

Worked Example: Verifying Escape for a Schottky Subgroup of SL₃(ℤ)
Let Γ be the subgroup of SL₃(ℤ) generated by the matrices A = diag(2,2,1/4) and B = diag(1/4,2,2) (interpreted as integer matrices after clearing denominators). Show that the random walk on Γ escapes from any proper algebraic subvariety of SL₃ at an exponential rate.
The matrices A and B are diagonal with eigenvalues (2,2,1/4) and (1/4,2,2) respectively. Their logarithms lie in a two‑dimensional subspace of the Cartan subalgebra and generate a free semigroup because the ratios of eigenvalues are not roots of unity. By the ping‑pong lemma on the flag variety ℙ² × (ℙ²)*, one can find disjoint open sets U_A, U_B such that Aⁿ(U_B) ⊂ U_A and Bⁿ(U_A) ⊂ U_B for all n ≥ 1. This implies that any reduced word in A,B of length n maps a fixed base point into a set of diameter ≤ C·λ⁻ⁿ for some λ > 1. Consequently, the probability that the n‑step random walk lies in a given proper algebraic subvariety V is bounded by the proportion of words whose image falls in V, which decays exponentially in n. Hence the escape‑from‑subvarieties condition holds with an explicit exponent.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the spectral gap of congruence quotients of a thin subgroup, first identify the rank of the ambient algebraic group. For rank one, cite Bourgain–Gamburd–Sarnak; for rank ≥ 2, cite Salehi‑Golsefidy–Varjú and note the two hypotheses: Zariski density and escape from subvarieties. If the problem gives explicit generators, check whether a ping‑pong argument on the Furstenberg boundary can be set up; this is the standard way to verify escape in examinations.

Thin Groups and the Dynamics of Unipotent Flows on Thin Orbits

Let G be a semisimple algebraic group over ℚ and Γ ⊂ G(ℤ) a Zariski‑dense thin subgroup. Consider a one‑parameter unipotent subgroup {u(t)} ⊂ G(ℝ) and its action on the homogeneous space ΓG(ℝ). The orbit of a point x = Γg under the unipotent flow is the set {Γg u(t) : t ∈ ℝ}. When Γ is a lattice, Ratner's theorems guarantee that the closure of any such orbit is a homogeneous submanifold and that the flow equidistributes on its closure. For thin subgroups the space ΓG(ℝ) has infinite volume, so Ratner's measure classification does not apply directly. Nevertheless, recent work of Einsiedler–Lindenstrauss–Michel–Venkatesh and of Mohammadi–Oh shows that if Γ satisfies a uniform spectral gap for its congruence quotients, then the unipotent flow on any compact subset of the convex core of ΓG(ℝ) satisfies a quantitative non‑divergence estimate: for any ε > 0 there exists δ > 0 such that the proportion of time the orbit spends outside a fixed compact set is ≤ C·T-δ. This estimate is proved by combining the spectral gap with the Dani–Margulis linearisation technique and the theory of polynomial‑like maps.

The quantitative non‑divergence estimate is the key input for the affine sieve on thin orbits of unipotent flows. It provides a level of distribution for the family of polynomial maps t ↦ f(Γg u(t)) where f is a polynomial function on G. With this level of distribution, the sieve of Bourgain–Gamburd–Sarnak yields almost‑prime values of f along the unipotent orbit. In particular, one obtains infinitely many points on the orbit where the value of f has at most r prime factors, with r depending on the sieve dimension and the spectral gap exponent. This method has been applied to produce almost‑prime values of the discriminant polynomial on the space of binary cubic forms under the action of a thin subgroup of SL₃(ℤ), giving a new proof of the existence of infinitely many cubic fields with almost‑prime discriminant.

A crucial technical point is that the uniform spectral gap must hold for the congruence quotients of Γ intersected with the centraliser of the unipotent subgroup. In rank one this is automatic from the work of Bourgain–Gamburd; in higher rank one needs the product theorem for the relevant finite simple groups. The escape‑from‑subvarieties condition for the random walk on Γ ensures that the spectral gap is uniform across all congruence levels, which in turn gives a uniform non‑divergence exponent δ that does not depend on the starting point x as long as x stays in a fixed compact subset of the convex core.

Another application of the quantitative non‑divergence estimate is to the equidistribution of expanding horospheres in thin quotients. For a diagonalisable element a ∈ G(ℝ) and a unipotent subgroup U normalised by a, the translates aⁿU x equidistribute on the convex core with a power‑saving error term. This result, due to Oh–Winter, uses the spectral gap to control the decay of matrix coefficients for the representation of G on L²(ΓG). The error term is of the form O(e-η n) where η is proportional to the spectral gap. Such effective equidistribution statements are essential for counting problems on thin orbits, for example for counting integral points on affine symmetric varieties.

In examinations, a typical question may ask to state the quantitative non‑divergence theorem for unipotent flows on thin orbits and to explain how the spectral gap enters the proof. The answer should mention the Dani–Margulis linearisation, the reduction to a bound on the measure of a neighbourhood of a proper subvariety, and the use of the spectral gap to obtain a power‑saving bound via the theory of polynomial‑like maps. It is also important to note that the theorem holds only on compact subsets of the convex core; outside the convex core the flow may diverge to the cusps, and the estimate fails.

Thin Groups and the Geometry of Limit Sets in Higher Rank Symmetric Spaces

For a Zariski‑dense discrete subgroup Γ of a higher rank semisimple Lie group G (real rank ≥ 2), the limit set Λ(Γ) is defined as the set of accumulation points in the Furstenberg boundary G/P of a Γ‑orbit in the symmetric space G/K. Unlike the rank‑one case, where the limit set is a subset of the visual boundary of a CAT(−1) space, in higher rank the Furstenberg boundary is a flag manifold and the limit set carries a natural structure of a closed Γ‑invariant subset. The critical exponent δ(Γ) is defined as the abscissa of convergence of the Poincaré series Σγ∈Γ e-s d(o,γ·o). For higher rank groups, δ(Γ) is related to the growth of Γ with respect to a chosen norm on the Cartan projection. The work of Quint and of Benoist–Quint shows that if Γ is Anosov (in particular, if it is a Schottky subgroup in higher rank), then the limit set is the image of a Hölder continuous embedding of the Gromov boundary of Γ into G/P, and the Patterson–Sullivan measure on Λ(Γ) is the unique measure of maximal dimension.

The Hausdorff dimension of the limit set with respect to a visual metric on G/P equals δ(Γ) divided by the minimal root of the restricted root system. This formula generalises the rank‑one equality dim_H Λ = δ. However, for general Zariski‑dense subgroups that are not Anosov, the limit set may be the whole Furstenberg boundary, and the Patterson–Sullivan measure may not be ergodic for the Γ‑action. Ergodicity holds if Γ is strongly irreducible and proximal, which is guaranteed for Anosov subgroups but can fail for thin subgroups that preserve a proper subvariety of the boundary. In examinations, a common trap is to assume that the Patterson–Sullivan measure is always ergodic; one must check the strong irreducibility and proximality hypotheses.

The geometry of the limit set also controls the spectral theory of the Laplacian on the locally symmetric space ΓG/K. For Anosov subgroups, the convex core is a compact manifold with boundary, and the Laplacian on the convex core has a discrete spectrum below the bottom of the continuous spectrum. The first non‑zero eigenvalue λ₁ is related to the critical exponent by the inequality λ₁ ≥ δ(Γ)(rank−δ(Γ)) (a higher‑rank analogue of the Selberg eigenvalue conjecture). This inequality follows from the work of Lafforgue on the spectral gap for congruence quotients and the transfer of the gap to the convex core via the Patterson–Sullivan measure. The equality case corresponds to the existence of a complementary series representation, which is known not to occur for Anosov subgroups of higher rank groups.

Another important aspect is the porosity of the limit set. In rank one, the limit set of a Schottky group is uniformly porous, which implies that its Hausdorff dimension is strictly less than the dimension of the boundary. In higher rank, the limit set of an Anosov subgroup is also porous in the sense of metric spaces, but the quantitative porosity constant depends on the Anosov constants. This porosity is used in the proof of the uniform spectral gap for congruence quotients of Anosov subgroups, because it allows one to apply the Bourgain–Gamburd expansion machine on the finite quotients G(𝔽_p) by showing that the random walk does not concentrate on proper subvarieties of the flag variety.

Finally, the limit set geometry enters the counting of integral points on thin orbits via the Patterson–Sullivan measure. The asymptotic formula for the number of orbit points of height ≤ T involves the measure of a certain subset of the limit set, and the error term is controlled by the spectral gap on the convex core. This circle of ideas — limit set geometry, Patterson–Sullivan measure, spectral gap, and orbit counting — forms the backbone of the modern theory of thin groups in higher rank.

Thin Groups and the Quantitative Non‑Divergence of Diagonal Flows on Thin Orbits

Let G be a semisimple algebraic group over ℚ, Γ ⊂ G(ℤ) a Zariski‑dense thin subgroup, and A = {a(t)} a one‑parameter diagonalisable subgroup of G(ℝ). The diagonal flow acts on the homogeneous space ΓG(ℝ) by right multiplication. For a lattice Γ, the quantitative non‑divergence of diagonal flows was established by Kleinbock–Margulis using the theory of polynomial‑like maps and the Mahler compactness criterion. For thin subgroups the space has infinite volume, but the convex core C(Γ) = ΓG(ℝ) ∩ {points with injectivity radius ≥ ε} is a compact subset with boundary. The work of Einsiedler–Katok–Lindenstrauss and of Mohammadi–Oh shows that if Γ satisfies a uniform spectral gap for its congruence quotients, then for any compact subset K ⊂ C(Γ) there exist constants C, α > 0 such that for all T ≥ 1, the proportion of time the diagonal flow starting in K spends outside K is ≤ C·T-α. The exponent α can be taken as ε/2 where ε is the spectral gap exponent from the congruence quotients.

The proof follows the same linearisation strategy as in the lattice case: one reduces the problem to estimating the measure of the set of points in a parameter domain where a polynomial map takes values in a small neighbourhood of a proper subvariety. The uniform spectral gap provides a power‑saving bound for the number of solutions to congruence conditions modulo q, which translates via the affine sieve into a bound for the measure of the bad set. The key difference from the lattice case is that the spectral gap must be uniform across all congruence levels, which is exactly the superstrong approximation property. Without superstrong approximation, the level of distribution would be too weak to obtain a power‑saving exponent.

An important application is to Diophantine approximation on thin orbits. Let x ∈ G(ℝ) and consider the orbit Γx under the diagonal flow a(t). The quantitative non‑divergence estimate implies that for any ε > 0, the set of t ∈ [0,T] for which a(t)x lies in a fixed compact subset of the convex core has measure at least (1−C·T-α)T. This yields a quantitative version of the Dani correspondence: the set of badly approximable vectors on the thin orbit has full Hausdorff dimension. Moreover, the exponent α gives a rate of approximation for the convergence of the diagonal flow to the boundary of the convex core, which is directly related to the quality of rational approximations to points on the orbit.

In the context of the Oppenheim conjecture for thin subgroups, the quantitative non‑divergence of diagonal flows is used to prove that the values of an indefinite quadratic form Q on a thin orbit Γ·v are dense in ℝ, with a quantitative rate. The proof uses the fact that the diagonal flow on the space of lattices corresponds to the action of the diagonal subgroup on the values of Q. The spectral gap for the congruence quotients of the stabiliser of Q in Γ gives the required non‑divergence exponent. This method, developed by Gorodnik–Nevo and by Oh–Shah, provides the first effective density results for values of quadratic forms on thin orbits.

Examination questions often ask to state the quantitative non‑divergence theorem for diagonal flows on thin orbits and to explain the role of the spectral gap. The answer should include: (1) the definition of the convex core and the compact subset K; (2) the statement that the measure of {t ∈ [0,T] : a(t)x ∉ K} is O(T1−α); (3) the dependence α = ε/2 where ε is the spectral gap exponent; (4) the requirement that Γ satisfies superstrong approximation (uniform spectral gap for all congruence quotients); (5) the application to Diophantine approximation or to the Oppenheim conjecture. A common mistake is to omit the hypothesis that the starting point x lies in the convex core; outside the convex core the flow can diverge to cusps and the estimate fails.

  • Confusing the critical exponent δ(Γ) with the Hausdorff dimension of the limit set on the symmetric space; they coincide only for geometrically finite actions on CAT(−1) spaces.
  • Assuming that superstrong approximation for S‑arithmetic thin subgroups follows automatically from the lattice case; the strong irreducibility and escape‑from‑subvarieties hypotheses must be checked separately.
  • Applying the quantitative non‑divergence estimate for diagonal flows without verifying the uniform spectral gap for the congruence quotients; the exponent α = ε/2 is not valid otherwise.
  • Treating the local‑global principle for integral points on spherical varieties as unconditional; the affine sieve only yields almost‑prime values, and a full integral point requires additional sieving or a square‑root cancellation hypothesis.
  • Believing that the Laplacian on a thin quotient of a higher rank symmetric space has pure point spectrum below the continuous spectrum; in general there is a resonance eigenvalue at s(δ−s) but no other discrete spectrum unless δ exceeds the rank threshold.
  • Overlooking the role of the Picard group rank in the logarithmic exponent of the asymptotic formula for integral points on spherical varieties; the exponent is rank(Pic)−1, not the dimension of the variety.
  • Assuming that the Patterson–Sullivan measure on the Furstenberg boundary is always ergodic for the Γ‑action; ergodicity holds for Zariski‑dense subgroups but can fail if Γ preserves a proper subvariety of the boundary.

Thin Groups and the Geometry of Limit Sets on Buildings

When a Zariski‑dense subgroup Γ of a simple algebraic group G over a non‑archimedean local field acts on the associated Bruhat–Tits building X, the orbit Γ·x accumulates on a compact subset of the spherical building at infinity ∂X. This accumulation set is called the limit set Λ(Γ). For lattices the limit set coincides with the whole boundary, but for thin subgroups it is a proper fractal subset whose Hausdorff dimension δ(Γ) equals the critical exponent of the Poincaré series Σγ∈Γ e-s·d(x,γx). The Patterson–Sullivan construction yields a Γ‑invariant conformal density of dimension δ(Γ) supported on Λ(Γ). In the building setting the visual metric on ∂X is ultrametric, so the limit set inherits a Cantor‑like structure. Recent work shows that if Γ satisfies a uniform spectral gap for its congruence quotients (superstrong approximation), then δ(Γ) is strictly smaller than the topological dimension of ∂X and the Patterson–Sullivan measure is exact‑dimensional. Moreover, the geometry of Λ(Γ) controls the asymptotic growth of orbital counting functions N(T)=|{γ∈Γ : d(x,γx)≤T}|, which satisfies N(T)∼C·Tδ(Γ) for a constant C>0. The exponent δ(Γ) also governs the rate of equidistribution of expanding horospheres in the convex core of ΓX.

Key structural facts:

  • The limit set Λ(Γ) is the unique minimal non‑empty closed Γ‑invariant subset of ∂X.
  • If Γ is geometrically finite (in the sense of Borel–Harpe), then Λ(Γ) is the union of the radial limit set and a countable set of parabolic fixed points.
  • The critical exponent δ(Γ) satisfies 0<δ(Γ)
  • For Schottky subgroups generated by sufficiently separated hyperbolic elements, Λ(Γ) is a Cantor set and δ(Γ) can be computed via the pressure function of a symbolic coding.

These geometric properties are the starting point for transferring analytic techniques from the classical hyperbolic setting to buildings, enabling the study of spectral gaps, expander graphs, and the affine sieve on thin orbits in this broader context.

Thin Groups and the Theory of Random Walks on Buildings

Let μ be a symmetric probability measure on Γ with finite first moment and whose support generates Γ. The random walk driven by μ on the building X projects to a Markov chain on the vertices of X. When Γ has a uniform spectral gap for its congruence quotients, the projected walk on the finite quotients X/Γ(q) (where Γ(q) is the principal congruence subgroup of level q) mixes rapidly: the total variation distance to the uniform distribution decays like exp(−c·t) for some c>0 independent of q. This uniform exponential mixing is equivalent to the family of Cayley graphs Cay(Γ/Γ(q), supp μ) forming an expander family. The proof uses the flattening lemma of Bourgain–Gamburd: one shows that the L²‑norm of the n‑step convolution μ*n on Γ/Γ(q) drops by a factor q-ε after O(log q) steps, provided the walk does not concentrate on proper subvarieties. The escape‑from‑subvarieties condition is verified using the product theorem for finite simple groups of Lie type, which holds uniformly for all characteristics. Consequently, the spectral gap ε depends only on the rank of G and the generating set, not on the level q. This uniform gap yields quantitative equidistribution of the random walk on the building modulo q, with error term O(q-ε/2). Applications include diameter bounds of order (log q)^C for the congruence quotients and the affine sieve on thin orbits in the building, producing almost‑prime values of polynomial maps with a level of distribution that is a power of q.

Important technical points:

  • The flattening lemma requires a non‑concentration estimate: for any proper algebraic subvariety V⊂G, μ*n(V) ≤ q-δ for n≈C·log q.
  • The product theorem (Breuillard–Green–Tao) provides the necessary growth in finite simple groups of Lie type, including those arising from non‑split forms.
  • Uniformity across all levels q is exactly the superstrong approximation property; without it the exponent ε would deteriorate with q.
  • The same argument works for S‑arithmetic thin subgroups acting on products of buildings, giving expanders for the combined congruence quotients.
Worked Example: Spectral Gap from Flattening
Let Γ⊂SL₃(ℤ[1/p]) be a Zariski‑dense subgroup generated by a symmetric set S. Assume Γ satisfies the escape‑from‑subvarieties condition with exponent δ>0. Show that the Cayley graphs Cay(Γ/Γ(q), S) form an expander family with spectral gap ε depending only on δ and the rank.
  1. Consider the random walk on Γ/Γ(q) driven by the uniform measure μ on S. The goal is to bound the second eigenvalue λ₂ of the averaging operator T_μ f(g)=½ Σs∈S f(gs).
  2. By the flattening lemma (Bourgain–Gamburd), if for some n≈C·log q we have ‖μ*n‖₂ ≤ q-ε, then λ₂ ≤ 1−c·ε for a constant c depending only on |S|.
  3. The escape‑from‑subvarieties hypothesis gives μ*n(V) ≤ q-δ for any proper subvariety V. Using the product theorem for SL₃(𝔽_q), any subset A⊂SL₃(𝔽_q) with |A|≥q3−η either grows under multiplication or is contained in a proper subvariety. Iterating this alternative yields the required L²‑flattening after O(log q) steps.
  4. The exponent ε obtained is a function of δ and the constants in the product theorem; it does not depend on q. Hence the family is a uniform expander family.
Exam Strategy
When a question asks for the mechanism behind uniform expansion in thin subgroups, structure the answer in three layers: (1) state the flattening lemma and its L²‑norm conclusion; (2) explain how escape‑from‑subvarieties and the product theorem feed into the lemma; (3) conclude that the resulting spectral gap is independent of the congruence level. Examiners reward explicit mention of the product theorem and the non‑concentration hypothesis.

Thin Groups and Superstrong Approximation for Groups Acting on Buildings

Superstrong approximation asserts that for a Zariski‑dense subgroup Γ of a simply connected simple algebraic group G over a global field, the congruence quotients Γ/Γ(𝔮) approximate the full adelic group G(𝔸_f) in the sense that the closure of Γ in the profinite completion is open. When G is defined over a function field and acts on a product of Bruhat–Tits buildings, the same statement holds provided Γ satisfies strong irreducibility and the escape‑from‑subvarieties condition uniformly across all places. The proof adapts the Bourgain–Gamburd–Sarnak strategy: one first establishes a uniform spectral gap for the action of Γ on the finite quotients of the building at a single place using the product theorem for the corresponding finite simple group of Lie type. Then a lifting argument (the “strong approximation” step) shows that the gap persists for the product of quotients at several places, because the projections to each factor are surjective and the factors are independent. The key new ingredient in the building setting is the use of the Bruhat–Tits fixed point theorem to control the geometry of the action on the building and to verify that the congruence subgroups Γ(𝔮) act freely on the vertices for sufficiently large 𝔮. This freeness guarantees that the Cayley graphs of the quotients are genuine expanders without loops or multiple edges. As a consequence, the family of Schreier graphs of Γ acting on the coset spaces G(𝔬/𝔮)/Γ(𝔮) forms an expander family with a spectral gap bounded below by a constant depending only on the rank of G and the generating set.

Consequences for thin orbits:

  • Quantitative strong approximation: the number of Γ‑orbits on the reduction modulo 𝔮 of a given integral variety grows like |𝔮|dim V with a power‑saving error term.
  • Affine sieve on the building: polynomial maps on thin orbits attain almost‑prime values with a level of distribution that is a power of the norm of 𝔮.
  • Effective equidistribution of expanding horospheres in the convex core of ΓX, with error term controlled by the uniform spectral gap.

Thin Groups and the Affine Sieve on Thin Orbits in Buildings

The affine sieve of Bourgain–Gamburd–Sarnak transfers the uniform spectral gap for congruence quotients into a level of distribution for polynomial maps on thin orbits. In the building context, let Γ⊂G(K) be a thin subgroup acting on the Bruhat–Tits building X of a simple algebraic group G over a global field K. Let f: G→𝔸¹ be a non‑constant polynomial map defined over the ring of integers 𝔬_K. For a prime ideal 𝔭 of 𝔬_K, consider the reduction f_𝔭: G(𝔬_K/𝔭)→𝔬_K/𝔭. The superstrong approximation property implies that the pushforward of the uniform measure on the Γ‑orbit of a point x∈G(𝔬_K) equidistributes in G(𝔬_K/𝔭) with error O(N(𝔭)-ε). Applying the combinatorial sieve (e.g., the β‑sieve) yields that the set of γ∈Γ with ‖γ‖≤T for which f(γ·x) has at most r prime factors has cardinality ≫ Tδ(Γ)/(log T)^κ, where δ(Γ) is the critical exponent and κ is the sieve dimension (typically the degree of f). The exponent r can be taken as r = κ+1 under the uniform spectral gap hypothesis; without it the level of distribution would be too weak to beat the parity barrier. Recent extensions to higher rank buildings show that the same argument works for polynomial maps taking values in affine spaces of higher dimension, provided the map is not constant on any Γ‑orbit. The main technical obstacle is verifying the escape‑from‑subvarieties condition for the polynomial map on the building, which reduces to a statement about the growth of the image of Γ under f in the finite quotients G(𝔬_K/𝔭). This growth is guaranteed by the product theorem for the finite simple groups of Lie type arising as G(𝔬_K/𝔭).

Key parameters in the sieve:

  • Sieve dimension κ = deg f (for a single polynomial) or the sum of degrees for a system.
  • Level of distribution D = Tθ with θ = ε/(2·dim G) coming from the uniform spectral gap ε.
  • Almost‑prime bound r = κ+1 (or κ+2 in the presence of local obstructions).
  • The implied constant depends on the height of the polynomial and the generating set of Γ.

Thin Groups and Quantitative Non‑Divergence of Diagonal Flows on Buildings

Thin Groups and the Geometry of Limit Sets on Higher Rank Buildings

The limit set of a Zariski‑dense thin subgroup Γ acting on a higher rank building X is a compact subset of the spherical building at infinity. Unlike the rank‑one case where the limit set coincides with the radial limit set and carries a Patterson–Sullivan measure of dimension δ(Γ), in higher rank the limit set decomposes into a finite union of faces of the spherical building. The work of Quint (2002) and later of Leuzinger (2004) shows that the Hausdorff dimension of the limit set equals the critical exponent δ(Γ) only when Γ is a lattice; for thin subgroups the dimension is strictly smaller and is governed by the growth of Γ in the Weyl chambers. The limit set carries a natural Γ‑invariant measure class obtained as a weak‑* limit of orbital measures on the building. This measure is ergodic for the Γ‑action and its dimension can be expressed in terms of the Lyapunov spectrum of the random walk on Γ driven by a symmetric generating set. In particular, if the random walk satisfies a spectral gap on the Furstenberg boundary, the limit set has full dimension in the corresponding face. The geometry of the limit set controls the asymptotic distribution of Γ‑orbits on X: the number of orbit points in a ball of radius R grows like eδ(Γ)R up to a polynomial factor, and the error term is dictated by the spectral gap of the Laplacian on the convex core of ΓX. These results rely on the product theorem for finite simple groups of Lie type (Breuillard–Green–Tao, Pyber–Szabó) to obtain uniform expansion in the congruence quotients of Γ, which in turn yields the required equidistribution on the building.

Worked Example: Quantitative Non‑Divergence on a Rank‑Two Building
Let Γ = ⟨ (1 2; 0 1), (1 0; 2 1) ⟩ ⊂ SL₂(ℤ[1/2]) acting on the product of the 2‑adic tree and the real hyperbolic plane. Take a(t) = diag(e^t, e−t) in the real factor. Assuming Γ has uniform spectral gap ε = 0.1 for all congruence quotients, estimate the measure of times t ∈ [0, T] for which a(t)x leaves a fixed compact set C in the convex core.
The quantitative non‑divergence theorem gives α = ε/2 = 0.05. Hence the measure of the exceptional set is O(T1−0.05) = O(T0.95). In particular, for large T the proportion of time spent outside C decays like T−0.05. This power‑saving bound follows from the affine sieve on the horospherical orbit, which uses the uniform spectral gap to obtain a level of distribution D = Tθ with θ = ε/(2·dim G) = 0.1/(2·3) ≈ 0.0167, sufficient to control the polynomial congruences arising from the linearisation.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the exponent in a quantitative non‑divergence estimate, first identify the uniform spectral gap ε for the relevant congruence quotients. The exponent is always ε/2 for diagonal flows and ε for unipotent flows. Check whether the subgroup is thin and whether superstrong approximation is known; if not, the estimate may fail or require a weaker exponent.

Thin Groups and the Local‑Global Principle for Integral Points on Spherical Varieties

A spherical variety Y over ℚ is a normal G‑variety with an open dense orbit of a Borel subgroup. The set of integral points Y(ℤ) is often studied via the affine sieve on thin orbits. Let Γ ⊂ G(ℤ) be a thin subgroup acting on Y with a Zariski‑dense orbit O = Γ·y₀. The local‑global principle asks whether the existence of points in Y(ℤ_p) for all p and in Y(ℝ) implies the existence of an integral point in O. For thin subgroups the principle can fail due to Brauer–Manin obstructions, but the affine sieve of Bourgain–Gamburd–Sarnak shows that almost‑prime points (points whose coordinates have at most r prime factors) are abundant. The sieve dimension κ equals the rank of the Picard group of a smooth compactification of Y, and the level of distribution D = Tθ comes from the uniform spectral gap ε via θ = ε/(2·dim G). The almost‑prime bound is r = κ+1 (or κ+2 if local obstructions persist). Recent work of Gorodnik–Vishe (2020) and of Browning–Heath‑Brown (2022) extends this to non‑split spherical varieties and to thin subgroups of exceptional groups, using the product theorem for finite simple groups of Lie type to verify the escape‑from‑subvarieties condition. The method also yields quantitative asymptotics: the number of almost‑prime points of height ≤ T in O is ≍ Tδ(Γ) (log T)κ−1 up to a constant depending on the height of the defining polynomials and the generating set of Γ.

The method also yields effective equidistribution of Γ‑orbits on the associated symmetric space and on the building at finite places.
