Examiners test the distinction between the unstable A¹-homotopy category H(k) (where the motivic sphere is not invertible) and the stable motivic homotopy category SH(k) (where the Tate sphere 𝔾_m becomes invertible). The Tate sphere S1,1 = 𝔾_m is the motivic analogue of the circle; its suspension gives the Tate twist. The motivic Hopf map η: S2,1 → S1,0 is the first non-trivial stable motivic homotopy group, and its étale realization is the Kummer map.

The Theory of Diamonds and v-Stacks: Scholze's New Foundations

Scholze's theory of diamonds and v-stacks (2017–present) provides a new geometric framework for p-adic geometry that unifies perfectoid spaces, adic spaces, and the étale cohomology of p-adic varieties. A diamond is a sheaf on the category of perfectoid spaces over a perfectoid field, equipped with the v-topology (the topology generated by covers that are universally open and quasi-compact). The category of diamonds contains the category of perfectoid spaces as a full subcategory and is closed under quotients by pro-étale equivalence relations. The v-site of a perfectoid space X is the category of perfectoid spaces over X with the v-topology; the v-cohomology of a v-sheaf F on X is the étale cohomology of the associated diamond. The key theorem is the comparison isomorphism: for a smooth proper rigid analytic variety X over a p-adic field C, the v-cohomology of the constant sheaf ℤ_ℓ on X^♢ (the diamond associated to X) computes the ℓ-adic étale cohomology of X: H^i_v(X^♢, ℤ_ℓ) ≅ H^i_et(X, ℤ_ℓ). This extends the perfectoid comparison theorems to non-proper and non-smooth varieties.

The pro-étale site Xproét of a scheme X (or adic space) has covers that are pro-étale maps (inverse limits of étale maps with finite étale transition maps). The condensed cohomology of Scholze replaces the derived category of sheaves of abelian groups with the derived category of condensed abelian groups, which behaves better with respect to limits and colimits. The v-stack is a sheaf of groupoids on the v-site; the moduli stack of local systems LocSys_G(X) for a curve X over a p-adic field is a v-stack. The geometric Langlands correspondence in the p-adic setting is formulated as an equivalence between the category of D-modules on Bun_G(X) and the category of quasi-coherent sheaves on LocSys_G(X), both interpreted as categories of sheaves on v-stacks. The Fargues–Fontaine curve XFF is a complete curve over a p-adic field whose étale cohomology realizes the p-adic Langlands correspondence for GL_n. The diamond associated to the Fargues–Fontaine curve is the quotient of the perfectoid open unit disk by the action of the Frobenius; its v-cohomology computes the cohomology of the curve.

The six operations formalism for étale sheaves on diamonds (developed by Scholze, Hansen, and others) provides functors f_*, f_!, f^*, f^!, ⊗, Hom for morphisms of diamonds, satisfying the usual adjunctions and base change. The proper base change and smooth base change theorems hold in this setting. The perverse t-structure on the derived category of ℓ-adic sheaves on a diamond is defined using the dimension function on the underlying topological space. The decomposition theorem for proper maps of diamonds is open in general but known for the Hitchin fibration on the moduli stack of Higgs bundles (as a map of v-stacks). The weight theory for ℓ-adic sheaves on diamonds extends Deligne's Weil II: a sheaf is pure of weight w if its stalks have Frobenius eigenvalues of weight w. The trace formula for diamonds expresses the trace of Frobenius on the compactly supported cohomology of a diamond in terms of fixed points. The local Langlands correspondence for GL_n is realized geometrically via the cohomology of the Rapoport–Zink spaces (which are diamonds) and the Lubin–Tate tower. The moduli stack of shtukas Sht_G is a v-stack whose ℓ-adic cohomology realizes the global Langlands correspondence over function fields. The geometric Satake equivalence for the affine Grassmannian Gr_G is formulated as an equivalence between the category of perverse sheaves on Gr_G (as a v-stack) and the category of representations of the Langlands dual group ^L G. Examiners test the distinction between the étale site (covers are étale maps), the pro-étale site (covers are pro-étale), and the v-site (covers are v-covers, which include pro-étale covers and also "almost finite" covers). The v-topology is strictly finer than the pro-étale topology; a v-cover is a map that is universally open and quasi-compact. The diamond X^♢ of a perfectoid space X is the sheaf on Perf/X represented by X; it is a v-sheaf. The tilting equivalence X ↦ X^♭ identifies perfectoid spaces in characteristic 0 with those in characteristic p, and this equivalence extends to diamonds.

The Langlands–Kottwitz Method for the Étale Cohomology of Shimura Varieties

The Langlands–Kottwitz method computes the ℓ-adic cohomology of Shimura varieties Sh_K(G, X) as a module under the action of the Hecke algebra at finite level and the Galois group Gal(E/E) (where E is the reflex field). The method expresses the alternating sum of the ℓ-adic cohomology groups with compact support, ∑_i (-1)^i H^i_c(Sh_K(G, X)E, ℚ_ℓ), as a virtual representation of G(𝔸_f) × Gal(E/E) in terms of automorphic representations of G and their Langlands parameters. The key formula is the Kottwitz fixed point formula: for a Hecke correspondence T_g and a Frobenius element Frob_π at a prime of good reduction, the trace of T_g × Frob_π on the cohomology equals a sum over elliptic endoscopic data (H, s, η) of stable orbital integrals on H times the trace of the Langlands parameter on the cohomology of the Shimura variety for H. This is the geometric side of the Arthur–Selberg trace formula specialized to Shimura varieties.

The Shimura variety Sh_K(G, X) is a projective system of varieties over the reflex field E, indexed by compact open subgroups K ⊂ G(𝔸_f). Its ℓ-adic cohomology carries an action of G(𝔸_f) (via Hecke correspondences) and Gal(E/E). The Langlands–Kottwitz conjecture (proved by Kottwitz for PEL-type Shimura varieties, and by Shin, Caraiani–Scholze, and others in general) states that the cohomology decomposes as a direct sum over automorphic representations π of G(𝔸_f) of π ⊗ r_π(σ), where r_π is the Langlands parameter of π (a representation of the Weil–Deligne group of E) and σ is the Galois action. The Kottwitz fixed point formula computes the trace of a Hecke operator T_g and a Frobenius element Frob_π on the cohomology by counting fixed points of the correspondence on the special fiber of the Shimura variety at a prime of good reduction. The fixed points are parametrized by isogeny classes of abelian varieties with additional structure, which are in bijection with Langlands parameters (conjugacy classes of homomorphisms from the Weil group to the L-group ^L G). The formula involves orbital integrals on G and stable orbital integrals on endoscopic groups H, linked by the fundamental lemma (proved by Ngô). The stabilization of the trace formula for Shimura varieties expresses the geometric side (fixed point counts) in terms of stable distributions on endoscopic groups, which are then matched to the spectral side (automorphic representations).

The local Langlands correspondence for G(F) (F a p-adic field) enters via the local Shimura varieties (Rapoport–Zink spaces) and the Kottwitz set B(G, μ) of σ-conjugacy classes in G(F) with a given Hodge cocharacter μ. The Newton stratification of the special fiber of a Shimura variety is indexed by B(G, μ), and the cohomology of the strata is related to the local Langlands correspondence via the Harris–Taylor method (for GL_n) and the Fargues–Scholze geometrization (for general G). The Fargues–Fontaine curve XFF provides a geometric realization of the local Langlands correspondence: the category of vector bundles on XFF is equivalent to the category of isocrystals with G-structure, and the moduli stack of G-bundles on XFF is a diamond whose cohomology realizes the local Langlands correspondence. The Kottwitz conjecture for the cohomology of Rapoport–Zink spaces predicts that the alternating sum of the cohomology groups is the virtual representation corresponding to the local Langlands parameter. This is known for GL_n (Harris–Taylor, Boyer) and for some other groups (Shin, Hansen). The weight spectral sequence for the cohomology of the special fiber of a Shimura variety degenerates at E₂ (by Rapoport–Zink, Faltings), and the graded pieces are described by the cohomology of the Igusa varieties and the central leaves. The Igusa variety parametrizes trivializations of the p-divisible group up to isogeny; its cohomology computes the local factors of the automorphic representation. Examiners test the distinction between the global Langlands–Kottwitz method (cohomology of Shimura varieties over number fields) and the local Langlands–Kottwitz method (cohomology of Rapoport–Zink spaces over p-adic fields). The global method uses the Arthur–Selberg trace formula and the fundamental lemma; the local method uses the geometry of the Fargues–Fontaine curve and the classification of G-bundles on it. The Kottwitz fixed point formula is the bridge: it expresses the trace of Frobenius on the cohomology of the Shimura variety in terms of orbital integrals, which are then stabilized using the fundamental lemma.

  • Confusing the section conjecture (rational points sections of π₁^ét sequence) with the birational anabelian conjecture (isomorphism class of variety π₁^ét as profinite group with Galois action). The former is about points; the latter is about the variety itself.
  • Stating that Ngô's proof of the fundamental lemma works directly on the local field F. The proof is global: it uses the Hitchin fibration over a curve X/𝔽_q and the decomposition theorem for R h_* ℚ_ℓ. The local statement is deduced via the "transfer of orbital integrals" and the stabilization of the trace formula.
  • Treating the motivic t-structure on DM(k) and the perverse t-structure on D^b_c(k, ℚ_ℓ) as the same. They live on different categories; the étale realization functor is only right t-exact for the motivic t-structure, not left t-exact, and does not preserve perversity.
  • Believing the v-topology on perfectoid spaces is the same as the pro-étale topology. The v-topology is strictly finer: v-covers include pro-étale covers but also "almost finite" covers that are not pro-étale. A diamond is a v-sheaf, not necessarily a pro-étale sheaf.
  • Assuming the Langlands–Kottwitz method computes the individual cohomology groups H^i(Sh_K, ℚ_ℓ). It computes the alternating sum ∑ (-1)^i H^i_c as a virtual representation; the individual groups are not determined by the trace formula alone (the "multiplicity problem").
  • Identifying the étale cohomology of the Fargues–Fontaine curve with the cohomology of the perfectoid disk. The curve is the quotient of the disk by the Frobenius; its cohomology is the group cohomology of the Frobenius acting on the disk's cohomology, not the disk's cohomology itself.
  • Neglecting the role of the transfer factor Δ(γ, δ) in the fundamental lemma. It is not a normalization constant; it arises from the comparison of the Weil group actions on the cohomology of the Hitchin fibers and is essential for the matching of orbital integrals.

Étale Cohomology and the Poitou–Tate Exact Sequence

The Poitou–Tate exact sequence is the global duality theorem for Galois cohomology of a number field, and it is most naturally expressed in the language of étale cohomology of the arithmetic scheme Spec 𝒪K,S, where 𝒪K,S is the ring of S‑integers in a number field K. For a finite Galois module M (or more generally a constructible ℓ‑adic sheaf) the sequence reads

0 → H⁰(GK,S, M) → ⊕v∈S H⁰(Kv, M) → H²(GK,S, M*)* → H¹(GK,S, M) → ⊕v∈S H¹(Kv, M) → H¹(GK,S, M*)* → H²(GK,S, M) → ⊕v∈S H²(Kv, M) → H⁰(GK,S, M*)* → 0

where M* = Hom(M, μ) is the Tate dual, GK,S is the Galois group of the maximal extension of K unramified outside S, and the asterisk denotes Pontryagin dual. The exactness is a consequence of the étale cohomological duality theorems of Artin–Verdier and the local Tate duality for each completion Kv. The sequence connects global cohomology groups (which are the étale cohomology of Spec 𝒪K,S) with the direct sum of local cohomology groups, and the dual global groups appear as the kernels and cokernels of the localisation maps.

Key applications include the definition of Selmer groups for abelian varieties: the Selmer group Sel(A/K) sits in the middle of the Poitou–Tate sequence for M = A[ℓⁿ] and its dual, and the Shafarevich–Tate group Ш(A/K) appears as the quotient of the Selmer group by the image of the Mordell–Weil group. The sequence also underlies the proof of the finiteness of Ш for elliptic curves with complex multiplication (Rubin) and the control theorems in Iwasawa theory. Examiners often test the distinction between the compactly supported cohomology Hc¹(Spec 𝒪K,S, M) and the usual H¹, and the role of the Euler characteristic formula χ(Spec 𝒪K,S, M) = 0 for self‑dual modules.

Étale Cohomology and the Cassels–Tate Pairing

The Cassels–Tate pairing is a bilinear, alternating pairing on the Shafarevich–Tate group Ш(A/K) of an abelian variety A over a number field K. It is constructed by interpreting elements of Ш as classes in H¹(GK,S, A) that are locally trivial, and then using the cup product in étale cohomology together with the Weil pairing on A. Concretely, for x, y ∈ Ш(A/K) one chooses representatives in H¹(GK,S, A) and H¹(GK,S, A*) (where A* is the dual abelian variety), takes the cup product in H²(GK,S, A ⊗ A*), and evaluates via the Weil pairing A ⊗ A* → 𝔾m followed by the invariant map H²(GK,S, 𝔾m) → ℚ/ℤ. The resulting pairing is independent of choices and satisfies ⟨x, y⟩ = −⟨y, x⟩.

A fundamental theorem of Cassels (for elliptic curves) and Tate (for general abelian varieties) states that the pairing is non‑degenerate modulo the maximal divisible subgroup of Ш. In particular, if Ш is finite then the pairing is a perfect alternating form, forcing the order of Ш to be a perfect square. This result is a cornerstone of the Birch and Swinnerton‑Dyer conjecture: the conjectural formula for the leading coefficient of L(A/K, s) at s = 1 contains the order of Ш as a square factor. The Cassels–Tate pairing also appears in the Poitou–Tate exact sequence as the connecting homomorphism between the local and global duality pairings. Examiners frequently ask for the definition of the pairing in terms of the cup product and the Weil pairing, and for the proof that it is alternating (using the symmetry of the cup product and the skew‑symmetry of the Weil pairing).

Worked Example: Computing the Cassels–Tate Pairing on a 2‑Torsion Subgroup
Let E/ℚ be the elliptic curve y² = x³ − x, which has full rational 2‑torsion E[2] ≅ (ℤ/2ℤ)². The Shafarevich–Tate group Ш(E/ℚ)[2] is known to be trivial. Show that the Cassels–Tate pairing on Ш(E/ℚ)[2] is the zero pairing.
Since Ш(E/ℚ)[2] = 0, the pairing is vacuously zero. For a non‑trivial example, one would represent classes by 2‑cocycles in H¹(Gℚ,S, E[2]), lift them to H¹(Gℚ,S, E) via the Kummer sequence, take the cup product with the dual class in H¹(Gℚ,S, E*), and evaluate using the Weil pairing E[2] × E[2] → μ₂. The alternating property forces ⟨x, x⟩ = 0 for all x, and bilinearity then gives ⟨x, y⟩ = −⟨y, x⟩. In this specific curve the 2‑Selmer group has rank 0, so Ш[2] = 0 and the pairing is identically zero.
Exam Strategy
When a question asks for the Cassels–Tate pairing, write down the three ingredients: (1) the Kummer exact sequence for A, (2) the cup product in étale cohomology, (3) the Weil pairing A × A* → 𝔾m and the invariant map H² → ℚ/ℤ. Mention that the pairing is defined on the quotient of the Selmer group by the image of A(K), i.e. on Ш. State the non‑degeneracy modulo divisible subgroups and the consequence that a finite Ш has square order. This structure earns full marks even if the explicit computation is not required.

Étale Cohomology and the Bloch–Kato Conjecture on Special Values of L‑functions

The Bloch–Kato conjecture (also known as the Tamagawa number conjecture for motives) predicts a precise formula for the leading term of the L‑function L(M, s) of a pure motive M over a number field at its critical integer points. In the étale cohomological setting, the conjecture relates the value L*(M, r) (the leading coefficient at s = r) to the order of the étale cohomology groups H¹f(K, M*(1−r)) and H⁰(K, M*(1−r)), where H¹f denotes the Bloch–Kato Selmer group defined by local conditions at all places. The conjecture states

L*(M, r) ∼ (∏v cv(M, r)) · |H⁰(K, M*(1−r))| / |H¹f(K, M*(1−r))| · Reg(M, r)

where cv are the local Tamagawa factors (defined via the Bloch–Kato exponential map for v ∤ p and via Fontaine’s rings for v | p), and Reg(M, r) is the determinant of the Bloch–Kato exponential map on the de Rham comparison isomorphism. The conjecture generalises the Birch and Swinnerton‑Dyer conjecture (M = h¹(E)(1)) and the analytic class number formula (M = ℚ(0)). Kato proved the conjecture for modular forms of weight ≥ 2 (hence for elliptic curves over ℚ) up to a power of 2, using his Euler system in the étale cohomology of modular curves. The Bloch–Kato exponential map is constructed from the p‑adic Hodge theory comparison isomorphism H¹ét(Kv, ℚp(r)) ≅ DdR(ℚp(r)) and plays the role of the regulator. Examiners test the definition of the Selmer group H¹f, the distinction between the finite and singular parts at p, and the role of the Tamagawa factors at bad primes.

Étale Cohomology and the Euler System Method

An Euler system is a collection of cohomology classes cn ∈ H¹(Kn, T) for a tower of number fields Kn/K (typically the cyclotomic ℤp-extension or an anticyclotomic extension) satisfying norm‑compatibility relations that mimic the Euler factors of an L‑function. The method, pioneered by Kolyvagin for Heegner points and extended by Rubin, Perrin‑Riou, and Kato, uses these classes to bound Selmer groups. In the étale cohomological framework, Kato’s Euler system lives in H¹ét(Y₁(N), ℤp(1)) for the modular curve Y₁(N); the classes are obtained from the Siegel units (or more generally from the Beilinson–Kato elements in motivic cohomology, realised étale‑ly). The key property is the Euler system relation

corKn/Kn−1(cn) = Pℓ(Frobℓ⁻¹) · cn−1

where Pℓ is the Euler polynomial of the associated Galois representation. By applying the machinery of Kolyvagin derivatives (or the more general “Euler system argument” of Rubin), one deduces that the characteristic ideal of the Pontryagin dual of the Selmer group divides the ideal generated by the p‑adic L‑function. This yields one divisibility in the Iwasawa main conjecture. The method also gives explicit bounds on the Mordell–Weil rank and the order of Ш. Examiners often ask for the definition of an Euler system, the norm relation, and the deduction of the divisibility “char(Sel) | (Lp)”. They also test the distinction between the “Euler system bound” and the “Kolyvagin system” formalism of Mazur–Rubin.

Étale Cohomology and the Iwasawa Main Conjecture

The Iwasawa main conjecture for an elliptic curve E/ℚ (or more generally a p‑adic Galois representation V) asserts an equality of ideals in the Iwasawa algebra Λ = ℤp[[Γ]] (where Γ = Gal(K∞/K) ≅ ℤp) between the characteristic ideal of the Pontryagin dual of the Selmer group Selp∞(E/K∞) and the ideal generated by the p‑adic L‑function Lp(E, s). In the étale cohomological formulation, the Selmer group is defined as the kernel of the localisation map

H¹(GK,S, V) → ⊕v∈S H¹(Kv, V) / H¹f(Kv, V)

where H¹f is the Bloch–Kato finite subspace. The p‑adic L‑function is constructed by interpolating the critical values L(E, χ, 1) for finite‑order characters χ of Γ, using the étale cohomology of the modular curve and the Perrin‑Riou exponential map. The main conjecture was proved for elliptic curves with good ordinary reduction at p by Skinner–Urban (using the Eisenstein congruence and the Euler system of Kato) and for the multiplicative case by Kato (using his Euler system and the explicit reciprocity law). The “±‑main conjecture” for supersingular primes was formulated by Kobayashi and proved by Pollack–Weston and Sprung using signed Selmer groups. Examiners test the statement of the main conjecture, the definition of the Selmer group as an étale cohomology group with local conditions, the construction of the p‑adic L‑function via modular symbols or overconvergent modular forms, and the role of the Euler system in proving one divisibility. They also ask for the distinction between the classical Iwasawa module X = Gal(M∞/K∞) and the Selmer group, and the control theorem relating Selmer groups over finite layers to the Iwasawa module.

  • Confusing the Poitou–Tate exact sequence with the local Tate duality sequence; the former is global and involves a sum over places, the latter is a single place.
  • Stating that the Cassels–Tate pairing is always non‑degenerate; it is only non‑degenerate modulo the maximal divisible subgroup of Ш.
  • Mixing up the Bloch–Kato Selmer group H¹f (defined by crystalline conditions at p) with the Greenberg Selmer group (defined by ordinary conditions); they coincide in the ordinary case but differ in general.
  • Believing that Kato’s Euler system directly proves the full Iwasawa main conjecture; it proves one divisibility, the other requires an Eisenstein congruence or a level‑raising argument.
  • Assuming the p‑adic L‑function is an element of the Iwasawa algebra for all primes; for supersingular primes one needs signed p‑adic L‑functions (Kobayashi) and the main conjecture is formulated for the ±‑Selmer groups.
  • Neglecting the role of the Tamagawa factors cv in the Bloch–Kato conjecture; they are not all 1 at bad primes and must be computed via the component group of the Néron model.
  • Treating the étale cohomology of Spec 𝒪K,S as the same as the Galois cohomology of GK,S without mentioning the equivalence of categories between constructible sheaves on the étale site and continuous GK,S-modules.

Étale Cohomology and the Étale Cohomology of Logarithmic Schemes

Logarithmic geometry, introduced by Kato and developed by Illusie, Olsson, and others, equips a scheme with a sheaf of monoids encoding degeneracy data such as normal‑crossing divisors. The étale site of a logarithmic scheme (X, M) is defined by taking étale morphisms of the underlying schemes together with compatible charts of the log structures. A constructible sheaf of ℓ‑adic modules on this site yields a logarithmic étale cohomology theory Hⁱₑₜ((X, M), ℚₗ) which satisfies the usual formalism: proper base change, smooth base change, and a logarithmic version of the purity theorem. The key new feature is the presence of a weight filtration on the cohomology of the boundary strata, governed by the combinatorics of the associated fan. For a log smooth morphism f: (X, M) → (Y, N) of relative dimension d, the relative logarithmic étale cohomology sheaves Rⁱfₑₜ*ℚₗ carry a natural monodromy operator N coming from the action of the inertia groups at the boundary. The logarithmic weight spectral sequence, due to Nakayama, degenerates at E₂ and computes the graded pieces of the weight filtration in terms of the cohomology of the toroidal strata. In particular, for a proper log smooth variety over a finite field, the Frobenius eigenvalues on Hⁱₑₜ((X, M), ℚₗ) are algebraic numbers whose absolute values are qi/2 after accounting for the weight shift coming from the log structure. This theory underlies the proof of the Weil conjectures for open varieties with normal‑crossing compactifications and provides the geometric input for the p‑adic comparison isomorphisms of logarithmic crystalline cohomology.

Étale Cohomology and the Étale Cohomology of Formal Schemes and the Rigid Analytic Comparison

Let 𝔛 be a formal scheme topologically of finite type over the ring of integers O_K of a p‑adic field K. The étale site of 𝔛 is defined by taking adic étale morphisms of formal schemes; its cohomology with ℓ‑adic coefficients (ℓ ≠ p) is denoted Hⁱₑₜ(𝔛, ℚₗ). When 𝔛 is the formal completion of a proper scheme X along a closed subscheme, the proper base change theorem identifies Hⁱₑₜ(𝔛, ℚₗ) with the ℓ‑adic cohomology of the generic fibre X_K as a Galois representation. For ℓ = p one must use the pro‑étale site or the theory of prismatic cohomology to obtain a p‑adic cohomology theory that compares with rigid analytic étale cohomology. Scholze’s comparison theorem states that for a smooth proper rigid analytic variety Y over K, the étale cohomology Hⁱₑₜ(Y, ℚₚ) is naturally isomorphic to the prismatic cohomology of a formal model after inverting p and completing. The proof proceeds by constructing a perfectoid cover of Y, using the tilting equivalence to reduce to characteristic p, and then applying the almost purity theorem. The resulting Galois representation is de Rham, and its Hodge–Tate weights are read off from the Hodge filtration on the prismatic complex. This comparison is the cornerstone of p‑adic Hodge theory for rigid spaces and feeds into the construction of the p‑adic local Langlands correspondence for GL₂(ℚₚ) via the cohomology of the Lubin–Tate tower.

Worked Example: Logarithmic Purity
Let (X, M) be a log smooth scheme over a finite field 𝔽_q with a normal‑crossing divisor D defined by the log structure. Show that the Frobenius eigenvalues on Hⁱₑₜ((X, M), ℚₗ) have absolute value qi/2.
The logarithmic weight spectral sequence of Nakayama expresses Hⁱₑₜ((X, M), ℚₗ) as an iterated extension of the cohomology groups Hi‑j(D(j), ℚₗ(‑j)) where D(j) are the j‑fold intersections of the components of D. Each D(j) is smooth and proper over 𝔽_q, so by the Weil conjectures the eigenvalues of Frobenius on Hi‑j(D(j), ℚₗ) have absolute value q(i‑j)/2. The Tate twist (‑j) multiplies eigenvalues by q^j, giving absolute value q(i‑j)/2 + j = qi/2. Since the spectral sequence degenerates at E₂ and respects the Frobenius action, the same bound holds on the abutment Hⁱₑₜ((X, M), ℚₗ).
Exam Strategy
When a question asks for the weight of Frobenius on logarithmic étale cohomology, recall the Nakayama spectral sequence and the effect of Tate twists on the boundary strata. Write down the E₁ page explicitly; the weight shift is always i/2 regardless of the log structure.

Étale Cohomology and the Étale Cohomology of the Moduli Stack of Higgs Bundles on Higher Dimensional Varieties

For a smooth projective variety X of dimension ≥ 2 over an algebraically closed field k of characteristic ℓ ≠ p, the moduli stack ℳHiggs(X, G) of semistable G‑Higgs bundles (with fixed topological type) is an Artin stack locally of finite type. Its ℓ‑adic étale cohomology Hⁱₑₜ(ℳHiggs, ℚₗ) carries a natural action of the motivic Galois group and, via the non‑abelian Hodge correspondence of Simpson (extended to higher dimensions by Hausel–Thaddeus and others), is expected to match the cohomology of the character stack ℳBetti(X, G) of representations of π₁(X) into G. The decomposition theorem for the Hitchin fibration h: ℳHiggs → 𝒜 (where 𝒜 is the Hitchin base) yields a direct sum decomposition of Rhₑₜ*ℚₗ into shifted perverse sheaves. The support of these perverse sheaves is controlled by the singularities of the spectral curves in the total space of the canonical bundle K_X. When X is a surface, the generic fibre of h is an abelian variety of dimension (g‑1)dim G, and the perverse Leray filtration coincides with the weight filtration coming from the mixed Hodge structure on the Betti side. Recent work of Maulik–Shen and of Mellit uses the ℓ‑adic cohomology of ℳHiggs to prove the P = W conjecture for certain surfaces, identifying the perverse filtration with the weight filtration on the character variety. The cohomology also carries a natural action of the spherical Hecke algebra via the geometric Satake equivalence, linking it to the Langlands dual group ^L G.

Étale Cohomology and the Étale Cohomology of the Moduli Stack of Parabolic Bundles on Surfaces

Let S be a smooth projective surface over an algebraically closed field k, and let D ⊂ S be a simple normal‑crossing divisor. A parabolic bundle on (S, D) is a vector bundle E on S together with a filtration of the restriction E|_D by subbundles and a system of weights in [0,1). The moduli stack ℳpar(S, D, r, c₁, c₂) of semistable parabolic bundles of rank r and fixed Chern classes is a proper Artin stack. Its ℓ‑adic étale cohomology Hⁱₑₜ(ℳpar, ℚₗ) can be studied via the parabolic Hitchin fibration, which maps a parabolic Higgs bundle to its characteristic polynomial with prescribed residues along D. The generic fibre is a Prym variety associated to a spectral cover of S ramified along D. The decomposition theorem for this fibration, proved by Yun and by Chen–Zhu using the Ngô support theorem, expresses the pushforward of the constant sheaf as a sum of intersection cohomology complexes of the Hitchin base with coefficients in local systems coming from the cohomology of the Prym varieties. The resulting perverse filtration on Hⁱₑₜ(ℳpar, ℚₗ) is conjectured to match the weight filtration on the cohomology of the corresponding parabolic character variety under the non‑abelian Hodge correspondence in positive characteristic (work of Lan–Sheng–Zuo). The ℓ‑adic cohomology also carries an action of the parabolic Hecke operators, which are defined by modifying the parabolic structure at points of D; these operators generate a commutative algebra isomorphic to the spherical Hecke algebra of the Langlands dual group with prescribed ramification.

Étale Cohomology and the Étale Cohomology of the Moduli Stack of Coherent Sheaves on Fano Threefolds

Let Y be a smooth Fano threefold over an algebraically closed field k of characteristic zero (or large enough). The moduli stack ℳsh(Y, v) of semistable coherent sheaves with fixed Chern character v is an Artin stack of finite type. Its ℓ‑adic étale cohomology Hⁱₑₜ(ℳsh, ℚₗ) is expected to categorify the Donaldson–Thomas invariants of Y. The virtual fundamental class of ℳsh is constructed using the obstruction theory of Thomas, and the associated Behrend function ν: ℳsh → ℤ yields the weighted Euler characteristic χ(ℳsh, ν) = DT(v). In the ℓ‑adic setting, the cohomology carries a natural mixed Hodge structure (via the comparison with complex cohomology) and a weight filtration whose graded pieces are pure of weight i. The cohomological Hall algebra (CoHA) of Kontsevich–Soibelman acts on the direct sum ⊕_v Hⁱₑₜ(ℳsh(Y, v), ℚₗ), providing a geometric realization of the quantum torus algebra associated to the numerical Grothendieck group of Y. For the quintic threefold, the CoHA action has been used by Davison–Meinhardt to prove the integrality conjecture for DT invariants. The ℓ‑adic cohomology also admits a perverse filtration induced by the natural map to the stack of objects in the derived category, and the P = W conjecture predicts that this filtration coincides with the weight filtration after passing to the associated graded of the motivic DT invariants.

Common Traps

  • Confusing the logarithmic weight spectral sequence with the usual weight spectral sequence; the former includes Tate twists from the boundary strata.
  • Assuming the rigid analytic comparison theorem holds for ℓ = p without invoking prismatic or pro‑étale cohomology.
  • Neglecting the role of the parabolic weights in the definition of the Hitchin base for parabolic bundles on surfaces.
  • Treating the CoHA action on the cohomology of the moduli of sheaves on a Fano threefold as commutative; it is generally non‑commutative and only becomes commutative after passing to the associated graded of the perverse filtration.
  • Overlooking the necessity of a properness hypothesis for the decomposition theorem on the Hitchin fibration; the fibration is proper only after restricting to the semistable locus.
  • Mixing up the perverse Leray filtration with the weight filtration on the Betti side; they coincide only under the P = W conjecture, which is a theorem in limited cases.
  • Forgetting that the logarithmic purity theorem requires the log structure to be fine and saturated; non‑fine log structures can introduce extra monodromy weights.

Étale Cohomology and the Categorical Geometric Langlands Program

The categorical geometric Langlands program seeks an equivalence of ∞‑categories between the derived category of D‑modules on the moduli stack BunG of G‑bundles on a smooth projective curve X over a field k and the derived category of quasi‑coherent sheaves on the moduli stack LocSys^L G of ^L G‑local systems, where ^L G is the Langlands dual group. In the ℓ‑adic setting, D‑modules are replaced by constructible ℓ‑adic sheaves and the six operations formalism provides the necessary functors. The Hecke category, defined via the correspondence HeckeG ← BunG × X → BunG, acts on D‑mod(BunG) and on QCoh(LocSys^L G) via the spectral action constructed by Gaitsgory and Lurie. The categorical equivalence is expected to intertwine these actions and to send the Whittaker category on the automorphic side to the category of sheaves on the spectral side with prescribed singular support. For GLn, the work of Drinfeld, Laumon, and later Arinkin–Gaitsgory established the equivalence for generic parameters using the geometric Satake equivalence and the theory of perverse sheaves on the affine Grassmannian. The ℓ‑adic realization of this equivalence, due to Varshavsky and others, uses the étale cohomology of the moduli stack of shtukas to construct the spectral action and to prove the compatibility with the classical Langlands correspondence via the function–sheaf dictionary. Key technical inputs include the decomposition theorem for the Hitchin fibration, the Ngô support theorem, and the theory of weights for mixed ℓ‑adic sheaves, which guarantee that the relevant complexes are pure of the expected weight. The categorical formulation also predicts a compatibility with the Arthur–Selberg trace formula: the trace of Frobenius on the ℓ‑adic cohomology of the moduli stack of shtukas recovers the spectral side of the trace formula. Recent advances by Gaitsgory–Raskin and by Chen–Zhu–Yun have extended the equivalence to non‑simply connected groups and to the parabolic setting, where the Hecke category is replaced by a parabolic Hecke category and the spectral side involves local systems with prescribed ramification. For examiners, the central points are the role of the six operations in defining the Hecke functors, the use of the perverse t‑structure to control the cohomological amplitude, and the fact that the categorical equivalence is a theorem only for GLn and in the generic setting; for general reductive groups it remains a conjecture.

Étale Cohomology and the Theory of ℓ-adic Sheaves on Derived Stacks

Derived algebraic geometry replaces classical schemes by derived stacks, i.e. functors from the ∞‑category of simplicial commutative rings to spaces that satisfy étale descent. The étale site of a derived stack X is defined by taking the ∞‑category of derived schemes étale over X; its ∞‑topos of étale sheaves admits a stable ∞‑category of ℓ‑adic sheaves Dét(X, ℚℓ) constructed by Lurie and by Bhatt–Scholze. The six operations formalism (f*, f!, f*, f!, ⊗, Hom) extends to this setting and satisfies the usual adjunctions and base‑change formulas, provided one works with the pro‑étale topology or with the condensed formalism of Scholze to handle infinite‑dimensional fibres. A key result is that for a derived Artin stack locally of finite presentation over a field, the étale cohomology of a constructible ℓ‑adic sheaf agrees with the classical étale cohomology of its truncation, so derived nilpotent thickenings do not affect ℓ‑adic cohomology. However, the derived structure is essential for the correct formulation of the cotangent complex, which controls the obstruction theory for moduli problems such as the derived moduli stack of local systems LocSysGder. The derived Hitchin fibration, introduced by Arinkin and Gaitsgory, is a morphism from the derived moduli stack of Higgs bundles to an affine space; its fibres are derived Prym varieties. The decomposition theorem for this derived fibration, proved using the perverse t‑structure on derived stacks developed by Bhatt–Lurie, expresses the pushforward of the constant sheaf as a sum of shifted intersection cohomology complexes of the base with coefficients in local systems coming from the cohomology of the derived Prym. This derived decomposition theorem underlies the categorical geometric Langlands equivalence for GLn because it identifies the Hecke category with the category of singular support conditions on the spectral side. Another application is the derived version of the geometric Satake equivalence, where the affine Grassmannian is replaced by its derived enhancement; the convolution product on the derived category of ℓ‑adic sheaves on the derived affine Grassmannian recovers the tensor category of representations of the Langlands dual group. For exam purposes, the essential facts are: (1) the étale topos of a derived stack is equivalent to the étale topos of its classical truncation, so ℓ‑adic cohomology is invariant under derived nilpotent thickenings; (2) the six operations exist and satisfy the usual formalism on derived Artin stacks locally of finite presentation; (3) the perverse t‑structure on derived stacks is defined via the classical perverse t‑structure on truncations, and the decomposition theorem holds for proper morphisms of derived stacks that are representable by algebraic spaces.

Identifying the correct categorical equivalence in a geometric Langlands question
A question asks: "Which of the following statements correctly describes the categorical geometric Langlands equivalence for GL2 over a function field?" Options: (A) It is an equivalence between the derived category of ℓ‑adic sheaves on BunGL2 and the derived category of quasi‑coherent sheaves on LocSysGL2 that intertwines the Hecke action with the spectral action. (B) It is an equivalence between the category of D‑modules on BunGL2 and the category of constructible sheaves on LocSysGL2 that sends the Whittaker category to the category of skyscraper sheaves. (C) It is an equivalence between the derived category of ℓ‑adic sheaves on the moduli stack of shtukas and the derived category of representations of the Galois group. (D) It is an equivalence between the category of perverse sheaves on the affine Grassmannian and the category of representations of the dual group.
The correct answer is (A). The categorical geometric Langlands equivalence for GLn (proved by Arinkin–Gaitsgory in the ℓ‑adic setting) is precisely an equivalence of stable ∞‑categories Dét(BunG) ≃ QCoh(LocSys^L G) that intertwines the Hecke category action on the automorphic side with the spectral action on the spectral side. Option (B) incorrectly mixes D‑modules and constructible sheaves and misstates the image of the Whittaker category. Option (C) describes the classical Langlands correspondence via the function–sheaf dictionary, not the categorical equivalence. Option (D) describes the geometric Satake equivalence, which is a component of the categorical Langlands program but not the full equivalence.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question mentions "categorical geometric Langlands", look for the pair (automorphic side, spectral side) and the requirement that the equivalence intertwines Hecke and spectral actions. The automorphic side is always a category of sheaves (ℓ‑adic or D‑modules) on BunG; the spectral side is a category of quasi‑coherent sheaves on LocSys^L G. The Whittaker category maps to the category of sheaves with nilpotent singular support, not to skyscrapers. The geometric Satake equivalence is a separate theorem about the affine Grassmannian. Memorise the precise formulation for GLn as a theorem; for general G it remains conjectural.

Étale Cohomology and the Motivic t-Structure and the Étale Realization

The motivic stable homotopy category SH(k) over a field k, constructed by Morel and Voevodsky, is the universal home for cohomology theories on smooth schemes. A central conjecture, due to Morel, predicts the existence of a motivic t‑structure on SH(k) whose heart is the abelian category of mixed motives MM(k). The étale realization functor Reét : SH(k) → Dét(k, ℚℓ) sends a motivic spectrum to its ℓ‑adic étale cohomology. Ayoub and Cisinski–Déglise proved that Reét is conservative and that it sends the motivic t‑structure (when it exists) to the perverse t‑structure on the derived category of ℓ‑adic sheaves over the absolute Galois group of k. In particular, the weight filtration on mixed motives corresponds under Reét to the weight filtration on mixed ℓ‑adic sheaves defined by Deligne. The slice filtration on SH(k), constructed by Voevodsky, provides a candidate for the motivic t‑structure; its layers are the motivic Eilenberg–MacLane spectra representing motivic cohomology. The Beilinson–Soulé vanishing conjecture predicts that the motivic t‑structure is non‑positively graded, which would imply that the étale realization of a motivic spectrum is concentrated in non‑positive perverse degrees. Recent work of Bachmann and Hoyois established the existence of the motivic t‑structure over perfect fields of characteristic zero and over finite fields, using the conservativity of the étale realization and the theory of weights. The étale realization also provides a bridge to the Bloch–Kato conjecture (now a theorem of Voevodsky–Rost): the norm residue isomorphism identifies the Galois cohomology of k with the motivic cohomology of k, and the étale realization of the motivic Hopf map η yields the Kummer map in Galois cohomology. For examiners, the key points are: (1) the motivic t‑structure is a conjectural t‑structure on SH(k) whose heart is mixed motives; (2) the étale realization is a symmetric monoidal functor that is t‑exact for the motivic t‑structure and the perverse t‑structure; (3) the weight filtration on motives matches the weight filtration on ℓ‑adic sheaves; (4) the Bloch–Kato theorem is equivalent to the statement that the étale realization of the motivic sphere spectrum computes Galois cohomology.

Étale Cohomology and the Geometric Langlands Correspondence for Non-Connected Reductive Groups

When the reductive group G is not connected, the moduli stack BunG decomposes as a disjoint union of components indexed by the group of connected components π0(G). The Hecke correspondences preserve this decomposition, and the Hecke category becomes a π0(G)‑graded monoidal category. On the spectral side, the Langlands dual group ^L G is also non‑connected, and the moduli stack LocSys^L G of ^L G‑local systems similarly splits according to the component of the monodromy at a chosen base point. The categorical geometric Langlands equivalence for non‑connected groups, formulated by Yun and by Chen–Zhu, predicts an equivalence of ∞‑categories between the derived category of ℓ‑adic sheaves on BunG and the derived category of quasi‑coherent sheaves on LocSys^L G that respects the component grading and intertwines the graded Hecke action with the graded spectral action. A crucial technical tool is the decomposition theorem for the Hitchin fibration for non‑connected groups, proved by Ngô using the theory of endoscopic groups and the fundamental lemma for non‑connected groups. The Hitchin base is unchanged, but the fibres are now disjoint unions of Prym varieties associated to the various components of the spectral curve. The pushforward of the constant sheaf decomposes into a sum of intersection cohomology complexes on the base with coefficients in local systems that carry an action of the component group. This decomposition yields a perverse filtration on the ℓ‑adic cohomology of BunG that matches the weight filtration on the cohomology of the corresponding character variety under the non‑abelian Hodge correspondence in positive characteristic (work of Lan–Sheng–Zuo). The Whittaker category for non‑connected groups is defined using a non‑degenerate character of the unipotent radical of a Borel subgroup of the identity component G0, extended trivially across components. The categorical equivalence sends this Whittaker category to the category of sheaves on LocSys^L G with singular support contained in the global nilpotent cone, a condition that is again graded by π0(^L G). For exam purposes, the essential facts are: (1) BunG and LocSys^L G split according to π0(G) and π0(^L G); (2) the Hecke category and the spectral action are graded by these component groups; (3) the decomposition theorem for the Hitchin fibration holds for non‑connected groups and provides the perverse filtration; (4) the categorical equivalence is a theorem for GLn (which is connected) but remains conjectural for general non‑connected groups, with partial results for groups with abelian component group.

Étale Cohomology and the Étale Cohomology of the Moduli Stack of Higgs Bundles on Surfaces

Let S be a smooth projective surface over an algebraically closed field k of characteristic zero (or sufficiently large). A Higgs bundle on S is a pair (E, φ) where E is a vector bundle and φ : E → E ⊗ ΩS is an 𝒪S‑linear map satisfying φ ∧ φ = 0. The moduli stack ℳHiggs(S, r, c1, c2) of semistable Higgs bundles of fixed rank and Chern classes is an Artin stack of finite type, but it is not proper; its properness fails because Higgs fields can degenerate. The ℓ‑adic étale cohomology Hiét(ℳHiggs, ℚℓ) carries a mixed Hodge structure (via comparison with complex cohomology) and a weight filtration whose graded pieces are pure of weight i. The Hitchin fibration for surfaces maps a Higgs bundle to the coefficients of the characteristic polynomial of φ, which are sections of Symj ΩS. The generic fibre is a compactified Prym variety associated to a spectral cover of S ramified along the discriminant divisor. The decomposition theorem for this fibration, proved by Maulik and Shen using the Ngô support theorem adapted to surfaces, expresses the pushforward of the constant sheaf as a sum of intersection cohomology complexes of the Hitchin base with coefficients in local systems coming from the cohomology of the Prym varieties. This yields a perverse filtration on Hiét(ℳHiggs, ℚℓ) that is conjectured to coincide with the weight filtration on the cohomology of the corresponding character variety under the non‑abelian Hodge correspondence for surfaces (work of Simpson, and in positive characteristic by Lan–Sheng–Zuo). The ℓ‑adic cohomology also carries an action of the Hecke operators defined by modifying the Higgs bundle at points of S; these operators generate a commutative algebra isomorphic to the spherical Hecke algebra of the Langlands dual group GLr. The cohomological Hall algebra (CoHA) of Kontsevich–Soibelman acts on the direct sum ⊕v Hiét(ℳHiggs(S, v), ℚℓ), providing a geometric realization of the quantum torus algebra associated to the numerical Grothendieck group of S. For K3 surfaces, the CoHA action has been used by Davison–Meinhardt to prove the integrality conjecture for Donaldson–Thomas invariants of the surface. Key points for examiners: (1) the moduli stack of Higgs bundles on a surface is not proper, so the decomposition theorem requires a proper morphism after restricting to the semistable locus; (2) the Hitchin base is the space of spectral curves, and the generic fibre is a Prym variety; (3) the perverse filtration from the Hitchin fibration is expected to match the weight filtration (P = W conjecture for surfaces); (4) the CoHA action is non‑commutative in general and becomes commutative only after passing to the associated graded of the perverse filtration.

  • Confusing the categorical geometric Langlands equivalence (an equivalence of ∞‑categories) with the classical geometric Langlands correspondence (a bijection of irreducible objects).
  • Assuming the étale topos of a derived stack differs from that of its classical truncation; ℓ‑adic cohomology is invariant under derived nilpotent thickenings.
  • Misidentifying the motivic t‑structure as the slice filtration; the slice filtration provides a candidate but the motivic t‑structure is a separate conjectural t‑structure whose heart is mixed motives.
  • Overlooking the grading by π0(G) in the non‑connected geometric Langlands correspondence; both automorphic and spectral sides split, and the equivalence must respect this grading.
  • Treating the moduli stack of Higgs bundles on a surface as proper; it is not proper, and the decomposition theorem applies only after restricting to the semistable locus or using a proper compactification.
  • Assuming the CoHA action on the cohomology of the moduli of Higgs bundles on a surface is commutative; it is generally non‑commutative and only becomes commutative on the associated graded of the perverse filtration.
  • Mixing up the perverse filtration from the Hitchin fibration with the weight filtration on the Betti side; they coincide only under the P = W conjecture, which is a theorem in limited cases (e.g., GLn on curves).

Étale Cohomology and the Theory of ℓ-adic Sheaves on the Moduli Stack of Abelian Varieties

The moduli stack Ag of principally polarized abelian varieties of dimension g over a separably closed field carries a natural ℓ-adic sheaf theory that intertwines the geometry of the Siegel modular variety with the representation theory of GSp(2g). The ℓ-adic cohomology groups Hiét(Ag, ℚℓ) admit a weight filtration whose graded pieces are pure of weight i, a consequence of the proper smooth base change theorem applied to the universal abelian scheme over the open locus of good reduction. The boundary strata in the toroidal compactifications constructed by Faltings and Chai contribute Eisenstein cohomology classes that are accounted for by the weight spectral sequence of Rapoport–Zink. The interior cohomology, defined as the image of compactly supported cohomology in ordinary cohomology, is conjectured by Harder to be generated by cuspidal automorphic representations of GSp(2g) that satisfy the Ramanujan–Petersson bounds; this has been proved for g ≤ 2 by work of Weissauer and for higher genus under the endoscopic classification of Arthur. The Hecke operators acting on the cohomology arise from correspondences given by isogenies of abelian varieties and generate a commutative algebra isomorphic to the spherical Hecke algebra of the Langlands dual group GSpin(2g+1). The comparison isomorphism with Betti cohomology over ℂ identifies the ℓ-adic realization of the Hodge structure on the cohomology of the Siegel modular variety, and the Eichler–Shimura isomorphism for g=1 extends to a description of the (p, q)-components of the interior cohomology in terms of Siegel cusp forms of weight (p+q, …). The ℓ-adic monodromy representation on the Tate module of the universal abelian variety factors through the ℓ-adic Galois representation attached to the standard representation of GSp(2g), providing a geometric incarnation of the local Langlands correspondence for symplectic groups.

When a level structure of type Γ(N) with N ≥ 3 is imposed, the stack becomes a smooth Deligne–Mumford stack and the ℓ-adic cohomology carries an action of the finite group GSp(2g, ℤ/Nℤ). The resulting equivariant cohomology groups are the ℓ-adic realizations of the motives attached to Siegel modular forms, and the trace formula of Arthur–Kottwitz expresses the alternating sum of traces of Frobenius on these groups in terms of orbital integrals on GSp(2g). The weight monodromy conjecture for the boundary of the minimal (Baily–Borel) compactification predicts that the monodromy logarithm on the nearby cycles is nilpotent of index at most the codimension of the stratum; this has been verified for the Siegel threefold by Lan and Suh using the theory of toroidal compactifications and the Clemens–Schmid exact sequence. The ℓ-adic cohomology of the universal abelian scheme over Ag also encodes the ℓ-adic realization of the polylogarithm sheaves constructed by Kings and Levin, which interpolate special values of L-functions of Siegel modular forms.

Étale Cohomology and the Theory of ℓ-adic Sheaves on the Moduli Stack of Enriques Surfaces

The moduli stack ℰ of Enriques surfaces over an algebraically closed field of characteristic different from 2 is a smooth Deligne–Mumford stack of dimension 10. Its coarse moduli space is the quotient of a 10‑dimensional type IV Hermitian symmetric domain D by the arithmetic group O+(U ⊕ E8(−1) ⊕ U, ℤ), where U denotes the hyperbolic plane and E8(−1) the negative definite E8 lattice. The ℓ-adic cohomology Hiét(ℰ, ℚℓ) inherits a pure Hodge structure of weight i via the comparison isomorphism with the Betti cohomology of the complex analytic quotient. The global Torelli theorem for Enriques surfaces, proved by Barth and Peters, identifies the period map as an open immersion onto the complement of a Heegner divisor in D/Γ, so the cohomology of the stack coincides with the group cohomology of Γ with coefficients in the ℓ-adic local systems arising from the standard representation of the orthogonal group. The weight filtration on the cohomology of the Baily–Borel compactification is described by the Zucker conjecture (proved by Looijenga and by Saper–Stern), which identifies the intersection cohomology of the compactification with the L2-cohomology of the locally symmetric space. The boundary components correspond to degenerations of Enriques surfaces to unions of rational surfaces; their contributions are computed by the Clemens–Schmid sequence applied to the Kulikov models of type II and III degenerations. The ℓ-adic monodromy representation on the second cohomology of the universal Enriques surface factors through the orthogonal group of the Enriques lattice U ⊕ E8(−1), and the associated Galois representation is known to be crystalline at primes of good reduction by the work of Nygaard and Ogus on the crystalline Torelli theorem. The double cover of an Enriques surface by a K3 surface induces a finite étale morphism of moduli stacks, and the resulting push‑forward of the constant sheaf splits into a direct sum of the constant sheaf and a rank‑one local system corresponding to the non‑trivial torsion line bundle; this decomposition is reflected in the ℓ-adic cohomology as a splitting of the weight‑graded pieces.

Worked Example: Weight Filtration on the Moduli of Enriques Surfaces
Let ℰ be the moduli stack of Enriques surfaces over ℂ and let j : ℰ → ℰ* be the inclusion into its Baily–Borel compactification. Describe the weight filtration on H2ét(ℰ, ℚℓ) and identify the graded pieces in terms of automorphic forms.
The weight filtration W• on H2ét(ℰ, ℚℓ) has three non‑zero steps: W0=0, W1=0, W2=H2. The graded piece GrW2 is pure of weight 2 and is isomorphic to the space of cuspidal automorphic forms on O+(U ⊕ E8(−1) ⊕ U) of weight (1,1) that are orthogonal to the Heegner divisor. The boundary contributes no classes in degree 2 because the boundary strata have codimension ≥ 2 in the Baily–Borel compactification, so the Zucker isomorphism identifies IH2(ℰ*) with the L2-cohomology, which coincides with the cuspidal cohomology. Hence H2ét(ℰ, ℚℓ) ≅ H2cusp(Γ, ℚℓ) as Galois representations.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the weight filtration on the cohomology of a Shimura‑type moduli stack, first identify the compactification (Baily–Borel or toroidal), then recall the Zucker conjecture (now theorem) which equates intersection cohomology with L2-cohomology. The graded pieces are then expressed in terms of cuspidal, Eisenstein, and boundary cohomology. Write down the relevant arithmetic group and the symmetric domain; the weight of each piece equals the degree of cohomology for interior classes and is shifted by the codimension of the boundary stratum for Eisenstein classes.

Étale Cohomology and the Theory of ℓ-adic Sheaves on the Moduli Stack of Hyperkähler Varieties

The moduli stack ℳHK of polarized hyperkähler varieties of a fixed deformation type (for example, Hilbert schemes of n points on a K3 surface or generalized Kummer varieties) is a smooth Artin stack of finite type over ℤ[1/2]. The period map sends a hyperkähler variety to its Beauville–Bogomolov–Fujiki quadratic form on H2 and takes values in a type IV domain D associated to the lattice Λ of the deformation type. The global Torelli theorem, proved by Huybrechts and by Markman, shows that the period map is an open immersion onto the complement of a countable union of Heegner divisors in D/Γ, where Γ is the monodromy group (a finite index subgroup of O+(Λ)). The ℓ-adic cohomology Hiét(ℳHK, ℚℓ) therefore carries a pure Hodge structure of weight i and a continuous action of the absolute Galois group of the field of definition. The monodromy representation on the second ℓ-adic cohomology of the universal hyperkähler variety factors through the ℓ-adic realization of the standard representation of the orthogonal group of Λ. The decomposition theorem for the Lagrangian fibration on a hyperkähler variety (when it exists) was established by de Cataldo and Migliorini using the perverse Leray filtration; the resulting perverse filtration on the cohomology of the total space is conjectured to coincide with the weight filtration on the cohomology of the corresponding character variety under the non‑abelian Hodge correspondence (the P = W conjecture for hyperkähler varieties, proved in the case of Hilbert schemes of K3 surfaces by Maulik and Shen). The ℓ-adic cohomology of the moduli stack with level structure admits an action of the Hecke operators defined by modifying the polarization at a point; these operators generate a commutative algebra isomorphic to the spherical Hecke algebra of the Langlands dual group SO(Λ ⊗ ℚℓ). The comparison with the cohomology of the moduli of K3 surfaces via the Beauville–Mukai isomorphism identifies the ℓ-adic realization of the Mukai lattice inside the cohomology of the Hilbert scheme.

Étale Cohomology and the Theory of ℓ-adic Sheaves on the Moduli Stack of Fano Varieties

The moduli stack ℳFano of K‑stable Fano varieties of a fixed dimension n and volume V has been constructed as a good moduli space in the sense of Alper by the work of Xu, Zhuang, and collaborators using the minimal model program and the theory of K‑stability. The resulting moduli space is a proper Artin stack with finite automorphism groups, and its ℓ-adic cohomology Hiét(ℳFano, ℚℓ) carries a mixed Hodge structure whose weight filtration reflects the stratification by the singularity type of the Fano varieties. The smooth locus of the moduli stack parametrizes smooth Fano varieties; its cohomology is pure of weight i and can be related to the cohomology of the corresponding period domains when the Fano varieties are of Picard rank one (e.g., cubic threefolds, del Pezzo surfaces). For del Pezzo surfaces of degree d ≤ 6, the moduli stack is a quotient of a rational variety by a finite group, and its ℓ-adic cohomology has been computed explicitly by Cheltsov, Park, and Won using the geometry of the Cremona group. The boundary of the moduli stack consists of K‑semistable Fano varieties with non‑trivial automorphisms; the nearby cycles complex on the boundary encodes the weight monodromy filtration, and the weight monodromy conjecture predicts that the monodromy logarithm is nilpotent of index at most the codimension of the stratum. The ℓ-adic cohomology of the universal family over the smooth locus admits a relative Lefschetz decomposition with respect to the anticanonical polarization, and the primitive part is expected to be generated by algebraic cycles via the Bloch–Beilinson conjectures. The comparison with the moduli of stable maps to Fano varieties, studied by Abramovich and Chen, shows that the virtual fundamental class of the moduli of stable maps pushes forward to a class in the ℓ-adic cohomology of ℳFano that coincides with the Gromov–Witten invariants of the Fano variety.

Étale Cohomology and the Theory of ℓ-adic Sheaves on the Moduli Stack of Stable Quotients

The moduli stack ℳSQ(X, β, r) of stable quotients of a fixed coherent sheaf F on a smooth projective variety X with numerical class β and rank r was introduced by Marian, Oprea, and Pandharipande as a compactification of the moduli of stable maps that behaves well in families. The stack is a proper Deligne–Mumford stack with a perfect obstruction theory of virtual dimension given by the Riemann–Roch formula. The ℓ-adic cohomology Hiét(ℳSQ, ℚℓ) carries a mixed Hodge structure whose weight filtration is governed by the stratification according to the splitting type of the quotient sheaf. The virtual fundamental class in ℓ-adic homology, constructed by Ciocan‑Fontanine, Kim, and Maulik using the intrinsic normal cone, yields a cycle class in the ℓ-adic cohomology of the stack that defines the stable quotient invariants. These invariants satisfy the same gluing axioms as Gromov–Witten invariants and are related to them by a wall‑crossing formula involving the ℓ-adic cohomology of the nested Hilbert schemes of points on X. The universal stable quotient over ℳSQ gives rise to a tautological bundle whose Chern classes generate a subring of the ℓ-adic cohomology; the action of the Heisenberg algebra on the direct sum of cohomology groups of the Hilbert schemes of points, discovered by Nakajima, extends to an action on the cohomology of ℳSQ via the correspondence given by adding a point to the support of the quotient. The weight filtration on the cohomology of the moduli stack of stable quotients of a curve coincides with the perverse filtration coming from the Hitchin fibration on the moduli of Higgs bundles, providing a geometric realization of the P = W phenomenon in this setting. The ℓ-adic realization of the motivic Donaldson–Thomas invariants of the category of coherent sheaves on X factors through the cohomology of ℳSQ, and the integrality conjecture for these invariants has been proved by Davison and Meinhardt using the cohomological Hall algebra action on the ℓ-adic cohomology of the stack of objects in the derived category.

  • Confusing the weight filtration on the cohomology of a Shimura‑type moduli stack with the perverse filtration from a Lagrangian fibration; they coincide only under the P = W conjecture, which is a theorem in limited cases.
  • Assuming that the ℓ-adic cohomology of the Baily–Borel compactification computes the interior cohomology; one must pass to intersection cohomology or use the Zucker isomorphism to L2-cohomology.
  • Overlooking the contribution of Eisenstein cohomology classes coming from the boundary strata of toroidal compactifications; these classes are not cuspidal and have different Galois representations.
  • Treating the monodromy representation on the universal family as unramified at all primes; it is only crystalline at primes of good reduction and may have non‑trivial Swan conductor at bad primes.
  • Identifying the Hecke algebra acting on the cohomology of the moduli stack of abelian varieties with the spherical Hecke algebra of the dual group without specifying the level structure; the isomorphism holds only for sufficiently deep level.
  • Neglecting the distinction between the moduli stack and its coarse moduli space when computing ℓ-adic cohomology; the stack cohomology includes contributions from the inertia groups at points with non‑trivial automorphisms.
  • Assuming the weight monodromy conjecture is known for all degenerations of Fano varieties; it is proved only for semistable degenerations of certain types (e.g., K3 surfaces, abelian varieties) and remains open in general.

The advanced topics above illustrate how ℓ-adic étale cohomology serves as a bridge between the geometry of moduli stacks and the arithmetic of automorphic forms.

The Sato-Tate Conjecture: Statistical Distribution of Frobenius Angles

While the Weil Conjectures provide fundamental bounds on the eigenvalues of the Frobenius endomorphism acting on ℓ-adic cohomology groups, the Sato-Tate conjecture delves deeper into the *statistical distribution* of these eigenvalues. For an elliptic curve E defined over the rational numbers ℚ, or more generally, over a number field, the Frobenius eigenvalues at a prime p of good reduction are complex conjugates αp, βp with |αp| = |βp| = √p. We can write αp = √p eiθp for some angle θp ∈ [0, π]. The Sato-Tate conjecture, initially formulated for elliptic curves without complex multiplication, posits that these angles θp are equidistributed with respect to the measure (2/π) sin²(θ) dθ on [0, π]. This means that as one considers more and more primes, the proportion of primes for which θp falls into a given interval approaches the integral of this measure over that interval.

The conjecture was extended by Lang and Tate to abelian varieties of higher dimension and later generalized by Serre to arbitrary motives. For a general motive M over a number field, the Frobenius eigenvalues at good primes p are complex numbers whose absolute values are determined by the weights of the motive (as per the Weil Conjectures). The Sato-Tate conjecture predicts the distribution of the arguments of these eigenvalues. Its profound significance lies in connecting the arithmetic properties of varieties (via Frobenius eigenvalues) to deep statistical patterns, often linked to random matrix theory. For elliptic curves with complex multiplication, the distribution is different, being uniform on [0, π/2] or [0, π] depending on the specific CM field, reflecting the additional algebraic structure.

The proof of the Sato-Tate conjecture for elliptic curves over ℚ was a monumental achievement, completed by Richard Taylor and his collaborators (Laurent Clozel, Michael Harris, Nicholas Shepherd-Barron) in the early 2000s, building upon the modularity theorem for elliptic curves (Wiles, Taylor-Wiles, et al.). The key idea involves relating the ℓ-adic Galois representations associated with elliptic curves to automorphic forms and then using the trace formula and properties of automorphic L-functions. Specifically, the distribution of Frobenius eigenvalues is linked to the distribution of Hecke eigenvalues for certain automorphic forms on GL(2) or higher rank groups. The general Sato-Tate conjecture for motives remains a major open problem, though significant progress has been made for specific classes of motives, often relying on the existence of automorphic realizations and deep results from the Langlands program.

Understanding the Sato-Tate conjecture requires a firm grasp of the properties of ℓ-adic representations, their Frobenius eigenvalues, and the interplay between arithmetic geometry and the theory of automorphic forms. It moves beyond simply counting points or establishing bounds, towards predicting the fine-grained statistical behavior of these fundamental arithmetic invariants. The conjecture has implications for understanding the average behavior of arithmetic functions and the distribution of prime numbers in various contexts.

Grothendieck's Motivic Vision: The Category of Motives and Standard Conjectures

Grothendieck's theory of motives represents a profound attempt to unify all cohomology theories for algebraic varieties into a single, universal framework. The core idea is that the cohomology groups of an algebraic variety X (whether de Rham, Betti, crystalline, or ℓ-adic étale) should be "realizations" of a more fundamental, abstract object called a "motive" associated with X. This vision posits the existence of a universal category, the category of motives, whose objects are built from algebraic varieties and whose morphisms are given by algebraic cycles. If such a category existed with desirable properties, it would provide a powerful tool for understanding the structure of algebraic varieties and their cohomology.

The construction of the category of motives proceeds by taking algebraic varieties and formally inverting projectors (correspondences that are idempotent). Different choices for the equivalence relation on algebraic cycles lead to different categories of motives:

  1. Numerical Equivalence: Two cycles are numerically equivalent if their intersection numbers with all other cycles of complementary dimension are equal. This leads to the category of numerical motives (Num(k)).
  2. Homological Equivalence: Two cycles are homologically equivalent if their images in a chosen cohomology theory (e.g., ℓ-adic, Betti) are equal. This defines the category of homological motives (Hom(k)).
  3. Algebraic Equivalence: Two cycles are algebraically equivalent if they lie in the same family of cycles parameterized by an algebraic curve. This gives the category of algebraic motives (Alg(k)).
The relations are nested: algebraic equivalence implies homological equivalence, which implies numerical equivalence. The fundamental open problem is whether these equivalences coincide, particularly whether numerical equivalence implies homological equivalence (the Tate Conjecture for algebraic cycles is a specific instance of this). If they did, the category of motives would be semi-simple, simplifying its structure considerably.

Central to Grothendieck's motivic program are the Standard Conjectures, a set of unproven hypotheses that would endow the category of motives with the properties necessary for a robust theory. These conjectures include:

  • The Lefschetz Standard Conjecture (B(X)): This states that the Lefschetz operator (multiplication by the class of a hyperplane section) has an inverse in the ring of algebraic cycles modulo homological equivalence. It implies the hard Lefschetz theorem for algebraic cycles.
  • The Hodge Standard Conjecture (C(X)): This asserts that the projector onto the primitive part of the cohomology, defined by the Lefschetz decomposition, is given by an algebraic cycle. This is crucial for relating algebraic cycles to the Hodge decomposition.
  • The Künneth Standard Conjecture (D(X)): This states that the Künneth components for the diagonal of a product variety are algebraic cycles. This would imply that the Künneth formula for cohomology holds at the level of motives.
These conjectures, if proven, would imply the semi-simplicity of the category of motives and provide a powerful framework for understanding the structure of cohomology groups. Deligne's proof of the Weil Conjectures for varieties over finite fields can be seen as a major step towards the Standard Conjectures, as it established the purity and existence of weights, which are consistent with the motivic philosophy. However, the Standard Conjectures remain largely open, representing some of the deepest challenges in algebraic geometry and number theory. Étale cohomology provides one of the most important "realizations" of these hypothetical motives, allowing mathematicians to study their properties through concrete cohomology groups.

Application of Motivic Thinking to a Problem
Consider a smooth projective variety X over a finite field k. The Weil Conjectures establish the rationality of the zeta function Z(X, t) and provide bounds on the eigenvalues of Frobenius. How does the motivic perspective, particularly the Standard Conjectures, deepen our understanding of the coefficients of the polynomial Pi(t) appearing in the numerator of Z(X, t)?
The zeta function Z(X, t) is given by a product of polynomials: Z(X, t) = Πi=02dim(X) Pi(t)(-1)i+1, where Pi(t) = det(1 - t Frob | Hiét(Xk̄, ℚℓ)). The roots of Pi(t) are the reciprocals of the eigenvalues of Frobenius acting on the i-th ℓ-adic cohomology group. The Weil Conjectures state that these eigenvalues are algebraic integers whose absolute values are (√|k|)i.

From a motivic perspective, if the category of motives were semi-simple and the Standard Conjectures held, each cohomology group Hiét(Xk̄, ℚℓ) would be the ℓ-adic realization of a pure motive Mi of weight i. The coefficients of Pi(t) would then reflect the structure of this motive. Specifically:
  1. Lefschetz Standard Conjecture (B(X)): This would imply that the action of Frobenius on Hiét(Xk̄, ℚℓ) is related to the action on H2dim(X)-iét(Xk̄, ℚℓ) via Poincaré duality and the Lefschetz operator. This is crucial for the functional equation of the zeta function, which relates Pi(t) to P2dim(X)-i(t).
  2. Hodge Standard Conjecture (C(X)): This would imply that the "primitive part" of the cohomology group Hiét(Xk̄, ℚℓ) (obtained by removing the part generated by hyperplane sections) corresponds to a "primitive motive." The eigenvalues of Frobenius on this primitive part would carry specific arithmetic information not reducible to lower-dimensional cycles.
  3. Künneth Standard Conjecture (D(X)): This would ensure that if X is a product of two varieties, say Y × Z, then the cohomology of X decomposes as a tensor product of the cohomology of Y and Z at the motivic level. This means the zeta function of X would be the product of the zeta functions of Y and Z, and the polynomials Pi(t) for X would be directly related to those of Y and Z.
In essence, the Standard Conjectures provide a structural explanation for the properties observed in the ℓ-adic cohomology groups and the zeta function, suggesting that these properties arise from a deeper, underlying motivic structure. They would imply that the coefficients of Pi(t) are not just arbitrary numbers but are constrained by the algebraic cycle structure of the variety.
Connecting Abstract Theory to Concrete Problems
When encountering highly abstract concepts like "motives" or "standard conjectures," always try to link them back to concrete examples or previously learned theorems. For instance, think about how the Weil Conjectures (which are proven) fit into the motivic framework as "realizations." Consider how the functional equation of the zeta function for a variety over a finite field is a consequence of Poincaré duality, which itself is a "shadow" of the Lefschetz Standard Conjecture. This helps in understanding the *purpose* and *implications* of the abstract theory, rather than just memorizing definitions.

Iwasawa Theory: Étale Cohomology and p-adic L-functions

Iwasawa theory, initiated by Kenkichi Iwasawa in the 1950s, studies the behavior of arithmetic invariants (like class groups and Galois groups) in towers of number fields. These towers are typically constructed by adjoining p-power roots of unity, forming a ℤp-extension. Étale cohomology, particularly Galois cohomology, plays a crucial role in this theory, providing the algebraic machinery to analyze these invariants in the infinite extensions involved.

A central object in Iwasawa theory is the p-adic L-function, which interpolates the values of classical L-functions at negative integers. These p-adic L-functions are conjectured to be related to the characteristic polynomials of certain modules over the Iwasawa algebra, which is the completed group ring ℤp[[Gal(K∞/K)]] for a ℤp-extension K∞/K. The "Main Conjecture of Iwasawa Theory" (now a theorem in many cases, notably for cyclotomic ℤp-extensions of ℚ by Mazur and Wiles) states that these characteristic polynomials are equal to the ideal generated by the p-adic L-function.

The connection to étale cohomology arises because the relevant modules in Iwasawa theory are often constructed from ideal class groups or Selmer groups, which can be interpreted as Galois cohomology groups. For example, the p-part of the ideal class group of a number field Kn in a ℤp-extension K∞/K can be studied via H1(Gal(Kn/K), ℤ/pmℤ). Taking inverse limits as n and m vary leads to modules over the Iwasawa algebra, which are then analyzed using techniques from commutative algebra and homological algebra.

More specifically, the Selmer group of an elliptic curve E over a number field K, denoted Selp(E/K), measures the failure of the local-global principle for rational points. It is defined as a subgroup of H1(Gal(KS/K), E[p]), where KS is a suitable extension of K and E[p] is the group of p-torsion points of E. In a ℤp-extension K∞/K, one studies the Iwasawa module of Selmer groups, which is the inverse limit of Selpn(E/Km) as n, m → ∞. This module is a torsion module over the Iwasawa algebra, and its characteristic polynomial is conjectured to be related to the p-adic L-function associated with E. This is the "Main Conjecture for Elliptic Curves," a deep generalization of the classical Main Conjecture.

The techniques involve intricate computations with Galois cohomology groups, often using local-global arguments and explicit reciprocity laws. The theory of p-adic Galois representations, as developed by Fontaine and Mazur, provides the framework for understanding the Galois action on these cohomology groups. Étale cohomology, particularly its application to schemes over ℤp or finite fields, allows for the construction and study of the modules that are central to Iwasawa theory, bridging the gap between algebraic number theory and arithmetic geometry. The profound connections established by Iwasawa theory between p-adic L-functions and the arithmetic of number fields continue to be a vibrant area of research, with étale cohomology serving as an indispensable tool.

Weights on Singular Varieties: Constructible Sheaves and Intersection Cohomology

The theory of weights, a cornerstone of the Weil Conjectures, describes the purity of Frobenius eigenvalues on the ℓ-adic cohomology of smooth projective varieties over finite fields. For a smooth variety X of dimension d, the eigenvalues on Hiét(Xk̄, ℚℓ) have absolute value |k|i/2. However, when dealing with singular varieties, the situation becomes significantly more complex. The standard ℓ-adic cohomology of a singular variety X is generally "mixed," meaning its Frobenius eigenvalues do not all have the same absolute value, and the purity statement no longer holds directly. To address this, the theory of mixed sheaves and intersection cohomology becomes essential.

A key concept is that of a constructible sheaf. An ℓ-adic sheaf ℱ on a scheme X is constructible if X can be stratified into a finite number of locally closed subschemes Zα such that the restriction of ℱ to each Zα is a locally constant sheaf of finite rank. This allows for a precise definition of sheaves on singular spaces by building them up from locally constant sheaves on smooth strata. The derived category of constructible ℓ-adic sheaves, Dbc(X, ℚℓ), is the natural setting for studying cohomology on singular varieties.

For a singular variety X, Deligne's theory of weights for mixed sheaves provides a filtration (the weight filtration) on the cohomology groups Hiét(Xk̄, ℚℓ), such that the graded pieces are pure of specific weights. This generalizes the purity statement for smooth varieties. However, this filtration is not canonical and depends on choices. A more robust approach for singular varieties is intersection cohomology, denoted IHi(X, ℚℓ). Intersection cohomology groups are defined using perverse sheaves, which are special objects in the derived category of constructible sheaves. Specifically, for a singular variety X, the intersection cohomology groups IHi(X, ℚℓ) are the cohomology groups of the intersection complex ICX, which is a particular perverse sheaf on X.

A crucial property of intersection cohomology is that it satisfies a form of Poincaré duality and, more importantly for singular varieties over finite fields, it satisfies the Weil Conjectures. That is, for a singular projective variety X over a finite field k, the Frobenius eigenvalues on IHi(Xk̄, ℚℓ) are pure of weight i.
