hand/geometric-analysis.html:
Regularity Theory for Minimal Surfaces

Regularity theory addresses the question of whether a weak solution of the minimal surface equation — or more generally a stationary varifold — is smooth. The foundational result is Allard's regularity theorem (1972): if an integral varifold V in a Riemannian manifold has bounded first variation and its density is close to 1 at a point, then V is a smooth embedded minimal hypersurface near that point. The proof uses a blow‑up argument and the monotonicity formula for the area ratio Θ(r)=r−nμ(B_r(x)). For codimension one, De Giorgi (1961) proved that any bounded solution of the minimal graph equation in ℝⁿ is analytic when n≤7, while Simons (1968) showed that the Simons cone {x∈ℝ⁸ : x₁²+…+x₄² = x₅²+…+x₈²} is a stable minimal cone that is singular at the origin, establishing the optimal dimension threshold. In higher codimension, Almgren's big regularity paper (2000) proved that area‑minimizing integral currents are smooth except on a singular set of Hausdorff dimension at most m−2, where m is the dimension of the current. The proof introduces the frequency function and a sophisticated center‑manifold construction. Later, De Lellis and Spadaro (2014) gave a more streamlined proof using multiple‑valued functions. These results are the analytic backbone for the existence theory of minimal surfaces via geometric measure theory and for the min‑max constructions of closed minimal hypersurfaces.

The Willmore Functional and the Willmore Conjecture

The Willmore functional W(Σ)=∫_Σ H² dA assigns to an immersed closed surface Σ in ℝ³ the integral of the square of its mean curvature H. It is invariant under conformal transformations of ℝ³∪{∞}, a property discovered by Willmore (1965) and later explained by the fact that the functional equals the L²‑norm of the trace‑free second fundamental form plus a topological term 4πχ(Σ). The Euler–Lagrange equation for critical points is the Willmore equation ΔH + 2H(H²−K)=0, where Δ is the Laplace–Beltrami operator on Σ and K is the Gauss curvature. The Willmore conjecture, posed in 1965, asserted that for any immersed torus Σ⊂ℝ³ one has W(Σ)≥2π², with equality only for the Clifford torus S¹(1/√2)×S¹(1/√2)⊂S³⊂ℝ⁴ after stereographic projection. The conjecture resisted attack for decades; partial results included the lower bound W(Σ)≥π² for embedded tori (Li–Yau 1982) and the proof for tori of revolution (Weiner 1978). The full conjecture was finally proved by Marques and Neves (2014) using Almgren–Pitts min‑max theory in the 3‑sphere. They constructed a 5‑parameter sweepout of S³ by Clifford tori, showed that the min‑max width equals 2π², and identified the Clifford torus as the unique minimizer. The proof also established the multiplicity‑one conjecture for this setting, a key technical step. The Willmore functional appears in physics as the bending energy of fluid membranes and in conformal geometry as the critical functional for the conformal invariant Q‑curvature in dimension four.

Technique: Variational Derivation of the Willmore Equation
Derive the Euler–Lagrange equation for the Willmore functional W(Σ)=∫_Σ H² dA on a closed surface Σ in ℝ³.
Let Σ_t be a normal variation with variation vector field V = φ ν, where ν is the unit normal and φ∈C^∞(Σ). The first variation of area is δA = −∫_Σ H φ dA. The first variation of mean curvature is δH = Δφ + (|A|²) φ, where |A|² = 4H²−2K. Then δW = ∫_Σ 2H δH dA + ∫_Σ H² δ(dA) = ∫_Σ 2H(Δφ + |A|² φ) dA − ∫_Σ H³ φ dA. Integrate the Laplacian term by parts: ∫_Σ 2H Δφ dA = ∫_Σ φ Δ(2H) dA. Collecting terms gives δW = ∫_Σ φ (Δ(2H) + 2H|A|² − H³) dA. Using |A|² = 4H²−2K, the bracket simplifies to 2ΔH + 2H(4H²−2K) − H³ = 2ΔH + 8H³−4HK − H³ = 2ΔH + 7H³−4HK. Dividing by 2 and noting that the critical condition δW=0 for all φ yields ΔH + 2H(H²−K)=0, which is the Willmore equation.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the Euler–Lagrange equation of a geometric functional, first write the functional in local coordinates, compute the first variation using the normal variation vector field, and integrate by parts. Remember that the Willmore equation is ΔH + 2H(H²−K)=0, where H is mean curvature and K is Gauss curvature. Memorise this form; it appears in multiple choice and short‑answer items.

Geometric Measure Theory and the Almgren–Pitts Min–Max Theory

Geometric measure theory provides a compactness framework for sequences of surfaces with bounded area. The basic objects are integral currents (Federer–Fleming 1960) and integral varifolds (Almgren 1965). A varifold is a Radon measure on the Grassmannian bundle of tangent planes; its first variation δV measures how area changes under diffeomorphisms. Stationary varifolds satisfy δV=0 and correspond to weak minimal surfaces. Almgren's Pitts min‑max theory (Pitts 1981, building on Almgren's unpublished work) constructs closed minimal hypersurfaces in a closed Riemannian manifold (Mn+1,g) by considering sweepouts — continuous maps from a cubical complex into the space of mod‑2 cycles — and defining the width as the infimum over all sweepouts of the maximal area. The min‑max theorem guarantees the existence of a stationary integral varifold whose area equals the width. Regularity of the min‑max limit was a major open problem until Marques and Neves (2017) proved that for 3≤n≤6 the min‑max minimal hypersurface is smooth and embedded, with singular set of dimension at most n−7. Their proof combines the Almgren–Pitts construction with the regularity theory of Schoen–Simon (1981) and the generic metrics program. The theory has produced infinitely many distinct closed minimal hypersurfaces in any closed manifold of dimension 3≤n+1≤7 (Irie–Marques–Neves 2018) and has been extended to free boundary problems and to the construction of minimal submanifolds of higher codimension via the Almgren–Pitts–Schoen–Simon framework.

The Positive Mass Theorem and its Role in the Yamabe Problem

The positive mass theorem (Schoen–Yau 1979, Witten 1981) states that an asymptotically flat 3‑manifold with nonnegative scalar curvature has nonnegative ADM mass, with equality only for Euclidean space. Schoen and Yau's proof uses minimal hypersurface techniques: they construct a stable minimal surface asymptotic to a coordinate plane and apply the stability inequality together with the Gauss–Bonnet theorem to obtain a mass integral that is nonnegative. Witten's proof uses a spinor field satisfying the Dirac equation and integrates a Bochner‑type identity. In the Yamabe problem, the positive mass theorem enters at the final step of Schoen's 1984 solution. After Trudinger (1968) and Aubin (1976) reduced the problem to showing that the Yamabe constant Y(M,[g]) is strictly less than the Yamabe constant of the sphere Y(Sⁿ)=n(n−1)ω_n2/n, Schoen considered the Green's function G_p of the conformal Laplacian L_g at a point p. The conformally related metric ̃g = G_p4/(n−2) g is asymptotically flat near p, and its scalar curvature is zero. The ADM mass of this asymptotically flat end is proportional to the coefficient of the next term in the expansion of G_p. The positive mass theorem forces this mass to be positive unless (M,g) is conformally equivalent to the sphere, yielding the strict inequality Y(M,[g]) < Y(Sⁿ) for non‑spherical manifolds. This strict inequality guarantees that the minimizing sequence for the Yamabe functional does not lose mass to a bubble, and a minimizer exists, giving a constant scalar curvature metric in the conformal class.

The Calabi Conjecture and Yau's Solution

The Calabi conjecture (1954) asserts that on a compact Kähler manifold (M,ω) with first Chern class c₁(M) ≤ 0 (in the sense of forms), any Kähler form ω' in the same cohomology class as ω is the Ricci form of a unique Kähler metric. Equivalently, given a smooth function f with ∫_M e^f ωⁿ = ∫_M ωⁿ, there exists a unique Kähler metric ω_φ = ω + i∂∂̄φ whose Ricci form satisfies Ric(ω_φ) = −i∂∂̄f. The equation reduces to the complex Monge–Ampère equation (ω + i∂∂̄φ)ⁿ = e^f ωⁿ. Yau (1978) solved the conjecture by establishing a priori C⁰, C², and higher estimates for φ using the maximum principle and the Calabi‑Yau inequality Δ log tr_ω ω_φ ≥ −C tr_ω ω_φ. The C⁰ estimate uses the Moser iteration on the equation; the C² estimate relies on the Chern–Lu inequality and the fact that the bisectional curvature of the background metric is nonpositive when c₁ ≤ 0. Once uniform bounds are obtained, the continuity method yields a smooth solution. The Calabi–Yau theorem has profound consequences: it provides Ricci‑flat Kähler metrics on Calabi–Yau manifolds (c₁=0), Kähler–Einstein metrics with negative Ricci curvature on manifolds of general type (c₁<0), and underpins the SYZ conjecture for mirror symmetry. It also implies the Bogomolov–Miyaoka–Yau inequality c₁² ≤ 3c₂ for surfaces of general type.

  • Confusing the Willmore functional with the bending energy of curves; the Willmore functional integrates H², not κ².
  • Assuming the Almgren–Pitts min‑max width always produces an embedded hypersurface without the dimension restriction n≤6.
  • Misstating the positive mass theorem as applying to any manifold with nonnegative scalar curvature, ignoring the asymptotic flatness hypothesis.
  • Thinking the Calabi conjecture covers the case c₁>0; the Fano case requires the continuity method with a different twist and was solved later by the work of Aubin and Yau on the existence of Kähler–Einstein metrics under stability conditions.
  • Overlooking the role of the conformal Laplacian's Green's function in Schoen's proof of the Yamabe problem; the positive mass theorem is applied to the asymptotically flat metric derived from that Green's function.
  • Believing that the Willmore conjecture was proved by a direct variational method on ℝ³; the Marques–Neves proof uses min‑max in S³ and stereographic projection.
  • Neglecting the singular set dimension bound n−7 in the regularity theory of area‑minimizing currents; this bound is sharp, as shown by the Simons cone in dimension 8.

The advanced topics above illustrate how geometric analysis intertwines PDE techniques, variational methods, and topological constraints to solve deep problems in differential geometry.

hand/game-theory.html:
Bayesian Games and Incomplete Information

In many strategic situations players do not know the exact payoff functions of their opponents. A Bayesian game models this by introducing a set of types for each player, a common prior probability distribution over type profiles, and payoff functions that depend on both actions and types. Each player observes his own type but not the types of others, and chooses a strategy that maps his type to an action. A Bayesian Nash equilibrium is a profile of type‑contingent strategies such that each player's strategy maximizes his expected payoff given the strategies of the others and the prior distribution.

The classic example is a first‑price sealed‑bid auction with private values. Each bidder’s valuation is his type, drawn independently from a known distribution. Bidders submit bids as a function of their valuation. In equilibrium, each bidder shades his bid below his true valuation; the shading factor depends on the number of bidders and the distribution. The revenue equivalence theorem extends to Bayesian settings: any standard auction format that allocates the object to the highest type and gives zero payoff to the lowest type yields the same expected revenue.

Mechanism design with incomplete information uses the revelation principle: any Bayesian Nash equilibrium outcome can be implemented by a direct mechanism where players truthfully report their types. The Vickrey–Clarke–Groves (VCG) mechanism is a dominant‑strategy implementation for efficient allocation, but it requires quasi‑linear utilities and may run a budget deficit. The Myerson optimal auction characterizes the revenue‑maximizing mechanism for a single item with independent private values, introducing virtual valuations and ironing to handle non‑monotonic hazard rates.

Key technical tools include the envelope theorem for deriving expected payoff functions, the monotonicity condition for implementability, and the use of interim individual rationality constraints. Understanding these concepts is essential for analyzing auctions, voting rules, and any setting where private information shapes strategic interaction.

Correlated Equilibrium and Communication

A correlated equilibrium generalizes Nash equilibrium by allowing players to condition their actions on a public signal drawn from a known distribution. The signal can be thought of as a recommendation from a trusted mediator. Each player receives a private recommendation and decides whether to follow it. A distribution over action profiles is a correlated equilibrium if, for every player and every possible recommendation, the expected payoff from obeying the recommendation is at least as high as the expected payoff from any unilateral deviation, given the conditional distribution over opponents’ actions.

Correlated equilibria can achieve outcomes that are not attainable in any Nash equilibrium. In the game of Chicken, the mixed‑strategy Nash equilibrium gives each player an expected payoff of 2.5, while a correlated equilibrium that recommends (Swerve, Straight) with probability ½ and (Straight, Swerve) with probability ½ yields an expected payoff of 3 for each player. The set of correlated equilibria is a convex polytope defined by linear inequalities, making it computationally tractable to find via linear programming.

Communication protocols can implement correlated equilibria without a mediator. Cheap talk — costless, non‑binding messages — can sometimes coordinate players on a correlated equilibrium if the game has a suitable structure. In games with common interest, a simple announcement of intended actions can be self‑enforcing. In games with conflict, more elaborate protocols such as the “mediated talk” of Forges (1986) or the “correlated equilibrium via cryptographic protocols” of Dodis, Halevi, and Rabin (2000) are required.

The concept of correlated equilibrium is central to the study of learning in games. No‑regret learning dynamics, such as multiplicative weights update, converge to the set of correlated equilibria in repeated play. This provides a behavioral foundation: rational players who adapt their strategies based on past payoffs will eventually play according to a correlated equilibrium, even without explicit coordination.

Worked Example: Correlated Equilibrium in a Coordination Game
Consider the following payoff matrix for a two‑player coordination game. Player 1 chooses rows (U, D); Player 2 chooses columns (L, R). Payoffs are (Player1, Player2).
U,L → (4,4) U,R → (0,0)
D,L → (0,0) D,R → (2,2)
The game has two pure Nash equilibria: (U,L) and (D,R). The mixed‑strategy Nash equilibrium puts probability 2/3 on U for Player 1 and 2/3 on L for Player 2, yielding expected payoff 8/3 ≈ 2.67 for each. A correlated equilibrium can do better. Let the mediator recommend (U,L) with probability ½ and (D,R) with probability ½. If a player receives recommendation U, he knows the opponent received L, so deviating to D yields 0 < 4. If he receives D, he knows the opponent received R, so deviating to U yields 0 < 2. Both recommendations are incentive compatible. Expected payoff = ½·4 + ½·2 = 3, which strictly exceeds the mixed Nash payoff. Hence the correlated equilibrium Pareto‑dominates the mixed Nash equilibrium.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for a correlated equilibrium, first write down the linear incentive constraints for each player and each recommendation. Check whether a simple public randomization over pure Nash equilibria satisfies them. If it does, you have found a correlated equilibrium without solving a full linear program. Remember that any convex combination of Nash equilibria is a correlated equilibrium, but not every correlated equilibrium is a convex combination of Nash equilibria.

Stochastic Games and Markov Perfect Equilibrium

Stochastic games extend repeated games by allowing the state of the world to evolve according to a Markov process that depends on the current state and the players’ actions. At each stage, players observe the current state, choose actions, receive stage payoffs, and the state transitions to a new state according to a known probability kernel. A strategy specifies an action for every possible history of states and actions. A Markov strategy conditions only on the current state, ignoring the full history. A Markov perfect equilibrium (MPE) is a profile of Markov strategies that constitutes a subgame‑perfect equilibrium in every state.

The existence of MPE in finite‑state, finite‑action stochastic games with discounted payoffs was proved by Maskin and Tirole (2001) using a fixed‑point argument on the space of value functions. The Bellman optimality equations characterize the value function for each player: V_i(s) = maxa_i [ u_i(s, a_i, a-i) + δ ∑s' P(s'|s, a_i, a-i) V_i(s') ], where δ is the discount factor. In an MPE, each player’s action maximizes the right‑hand side given the opponents’ Markov strategies.

Applications include dynamic oligopoly (Ericson‑Pakes model), investment games, and environmental resource management. In a duopoly with capacity investment, the state is the vector of capacities. Firms choose investment levels; capacities depreciate and evolve stochastically. The MPE captures the strategic incentive to over‑invest to deter entry or to under‑invest to soften competition. Computation of MPE often requires numerical methods such as value iteration or policy iteration, because analytical solutions are rare.

A key distinction from repeated games is that the state variable creates a natural link across periods that cannot be replicated by simple trigger strategies. The folk theorem for stochastic games (Dutta, 1995) shows that any feasible, individually rational payoff vector can be approximated by an MPE if players are sufficiently patient and the state space is rich enough. However, the set of MPE payoffs can be a strict subset of the set of subgame‑perfect equilibrium payoffs when players are restricted to Markov strategies.

Bargaining Theory and the Nash Bargaining Solution

Bargaining theory studies how two or more parties divide a surplus when they have conflicting interests. The Nash bargaining solution (NBS) is the unique outcome satisfying four axioms: Pareto efficiency, symmetry, invariance to affine transformations of utility, and independence of irrelevant alternatives. Given a feasible set S ⊂ ℝ² of utility pairs and a disagreement point d = (d₁, d₂), the NBS maximizes the product (u₁ − d₁)(u₂ − d₂) over (u₁, u₂) ∈ S with u_i ≥ d_i.

The alternating‑offers model of Rubinstein (1982) provides a non‑cooperative foundation. Two players alternate proposing divisions of a pie of size 1. If a proposal is accepted, the game ends; otherwise the game continues to the next period with discount factors δ₁, δ₂. The unique subgame‑perfect equilibrium gives the first proposer a share (1 − δ₂) / (1 − δ₁δ₂). As the time between offers shrinks to zero, the equilibrium converges to the NBS with disagreement point (0,0) and equal bargaining power when δ₁ = δ₂.

Extensions incorporate incomplete information (Myerson‑Satterthwaite impossibility theorem), multiple issues, and outside options. The Kalai‑Smorodinsky solution replaces independence of irrelevant alternatives with monotonicity, yielding a different prediction when the feasible set is not symmetric. In practice, bargaining outcomes depend on institutional details such as commitment power, deadline effects, and the ability to make side payments.

Understanding the axioms and the strategic foundations helps in analyzing labor negotiations, international trade agreements, and merger settlements. The NBS is often used as a benchmark in mechanism design to evaluate the fairness and efficiency of allocation rules.

Network Games and Strategic Complementarities

Network games model situations where each player’s payoff depends on his own action and the actions of his neighbors in a graph. A common specification is the linear‑quadratic utility: u_i = a_i − ½ a_i² + φ ∑j∈N(i) a_i a_j, where φ > 0 captures strategic complementarities (higher neighbor actions increase marginal return to own action). The Nash equilibrium satisfies a_i = 1 + φ ∑j∈N(i) a_j. In matrix form, a* = (I − φ G)⁻¹ 1, where G is the adjacency matrix. The equilibrium exists and is unique if φ λ_max(G) < 1, where λ_max is the largest eigenvalue of G.

Key results link network centrality to equilibrium actions. Bonacich centrality b = (I − φ G)⁻¹ 1 gives the vector of equilibrium actions; players with higher centrality exert higher effort. This explains peer effects in education, crime, and technology adoption. Policy interventions that target “key players” — those whose removal most reduces total activity — can be identified by solving a combinatorial optimization problem (Ballester, Calvó‑Armengol, Zenou, 2006).

When φ < 0 (strategic substitutes), the best‑response dynamics may cycle, and multiple equilibria can arise. The potential function approach (Monderer & Shapley, 1996) shows that any finite game with strategic complements or substitutes on a network is a potential game, guaranteeing convergence of best‑response dynamics to a pure Nash equilibrium. For general payoff functions, the concept of pairwise stability (Jackson & Wolinsky, 1996) analyzes network formation where links require mutual consent.

Empirical estimation of network games uses spatial econometric techniques (Bramoullé, Djebbari, Fortin, 2009) to address the reflection problem. Instrumental variables based on the network structure (e.g., friends‑of‑friends) identify the peer effect parameter φ. These methods are now standard in applied microeconomics and development economics.

Common Traps

  • Confusing Bayesian Nash equilibrium with perfect Bayesian equilibrium; the latter requires sequential rationality and consistent beliefs at every information set.
  • Assuming every correlated equilibrium can be implemented by cheap talk; many require a mediator or cryptographic protocol.
  • Treating Markov perfect equilibrium as the only subgame‑perfect equilibrium in stochastic games; history‑dependent strategies can support a larger payoff set.
  • Applying the Nash bargaining solution without verifying the disagreement point is correctly specified; an incorrect d shifts the entire solution.
  • Ignoring the spectral radius condition φ λ_max(G) < 1 when solving linear‑quadratic network games; violation leads to non‑existence or unbounded actions.
  • Believing the revenue equivalence theorem holds for all auction formats; it fails with risk‑averse bidders, correlated values, or budget constraints.
  • Overlooking that the folk theorem for repeated games requires perfect monitoring; with imperfect public monitoring the set of equilibrium payoffs shrinks.

hand/calc-variations.html:
Second Variation and Sufficient Conditions for Minima

The Euler–Lagrange equation provides a necessary condition for a stationary point of a functional, but it does not distinguish minima, maxima, or saddle points. The second variation δ²J[y;h] = ∫ₐᵇ (Lyy h² + 2Lyy' h h' + Ly'y' h'²) dx, where h is an admissible variation vanishing at the endpoints, supplies the decisive test. If δ²J > 0 for all non‑zero h, the stationary function is a strict local minimiser; if δ²J < 0 for some h, it is not a minimum. The Legendre condition Ly'y' ≥ 0 along the extremal is the pointwise necessary condition for a minimum. The strengthened Legendre condition Ly'y' > 0 is required for the Jacobi accessory equation to be non‑singular. Jacobi’s conjugate point theory states that a minimiser exists on [a,b] iff the interval contains no point conjugate to a. The accessory equation is a linear second‑order ODE derived from the second variation; its solutions describe the behaviour of nearby extremals. If a conjugate point appears before b, the second variation can be made negative by a suitable variation, violating minimality. The Weierstrass excess function E(x,y,y',p) = L(x,y,p) − L(x,y,y') − (p−y')Ly'(x,y,y') provides a stronger, global sufficient condition: if E ≥ 0 for all admissible p and the strengthened Legendre condition holds, the extremal yields a strong minimum. These criteria together form the classical sufficient framework used in rigorous calculus of variations and in the analysis of stability for mechanical systems.

Corner Conditions and Weierstrass‑Erdmann Theory

Classical derivations of the Euler–Lagrange equation assume the extremal y(x) is continuously differentiable. In many physical problems — refraction of light, elastic strings with point loads, or optimal control with bang‑bang arcs — the optimal curve may have corners where y' jumps. Weierstrass and Erdmann showed that at a corner point c the following quantities must be continuous: the momentum p = ∂L/∂y' and the Hamiltonian H = y'∂L/∂y' − L. These are the Weierstrass‑Erdmann corner conditions. They follow from requiring the first variation to vanish for variations that shift the corner location. If L does not depend explicitly on x, the Hamiltonian continuity reduces to the Beltrami identity holding on both sides of the corner. The conditions are necessary for any piecewise C¹ extremal. In the brachistochrone with a medium change, Snell’s law emerges precisely from the continuity of ∂L/∂y'. In optimal control, the corner conditions become the continuity of the costate and the Hamiltonian across switching times, a cornerstone of the Pontryagin maximum principle. The theory also yields the Weierstrass necessary condition for a strong minimum: the excess function E must be non‑negative for all admissible slopes p at every point of the extremal, including corners. This condition rules out pathological minimisers that satisfy the Euler–Lagrange equation but fail to be true minima.

Worked Example: Corner Conditions in a Refraction Problem
A light ray travels from point A(0,0) in medium 1 (refractive index n₁) to point B(d, h) in medium 2 (refractive index n₂) with a planar interface at x = c. The travel time functional is T[y] = ∫₀ᶜ n₁√(1+y'²) dx + ∫_c^d n₂√(1+y'²) dx. Find the condition at the interface.
The Lagrangians are L₁ = n₁√(1+y'²), L₂ = n₂√(1+y'²). The momentum p = ∂L/∂y' = n y'/√(1+y'²) = n sinθ, where θ is the angle with the normal. The Weierstrass‑Erdmann condition requires p continuous at x = c, giving n₁ sinθ₁ = n₂ sinθ₂, which is Snell’s law. The Hamiltonian H = y'p − L = −n/√(1+y'²) = −n cosθ is also continuous, yielding the same relation. Thus the corner conditions reproduce the physical law of refraction.
Exam Strategy
When a problem involves piecewise smooth extremals, always write down the Weierstrass‑Erdmann conditions explicitly. Examiners often award marks for stating the continuity of ∂L/∂y' and H even if the full solution is not completed. Remember that the excess function test is a strong minimum check; if a question asks “show the extremal is a minimiser”, verify Legendre, Jacobi, and Weierstrass conditions in that order.

Variational Problems with Constraints — Lagrange Multipliers and Isoperimetric Problems

Many optimisation problems involve integral constraints, e.g. finding the curve of given length that encloses maximal area (Dido’s problem) or the shape of a hanging chain with fixed length. The method of Lagrange multipliers extends to functionals: introduce a constant multiplier λ and consider the augmented functional J̃[y] = ∫ₐᵇ (L(x,y,y') + λ M(x,y,y')) dx, where the constraint is ∫ₐᵇ M(x,y,y') dx = C. The Euler–Lagrange equation for J̃ yields the necessary condition for a constrained extremum. The multiplier λ is determined by the constraint itself. For holonomic constraints g(x,y) = 0, the multiplier becomes a function λ(x) and the augmented Lagrangian is L + λ(x)g(x,y). The resulting system couples the Euler–Lagrange equation with the constraint. In isoperimetric problems, the constraint is an integral; the multiplier is constant. Classic examples: the catenary of given length minimises potential energy subject to ∫√(1+y'²) dx = L; the solution is y = a cosh((x−b)/a) + c with parameters fixed by endpoints and length. The Sturm–Liouville eigenvalue problem arises from the Rayleigh quotient R[y] = ∫(p y'² + q y²) dx / ∫ w y² dx; minimising R yields the principal eigenvalue and eigenfunction, with the constraint ∫ w y² dx = 1 providing the multiplier. In optimal control, integral constraints lead to additional costate equations and constant multipliers that appear in the Hamiltonian. The theory of constrained variations underpins the calculus of variations on manifolds and the derivation of field equations from action principles with gauge constraints.

Field Theory and the Carathéodory Complete Figure

Field theory provides a geometric construction that yields global minimisers without solving the Euler–Lagrange equation pointwise. A field is a one‑parameter family of extremals that covers a domain without intersections. Carathéodory’s complete figure consists of a field together with a transversal curve (the “base”) such that every point in the domain lies on exactly one extremal of the field. If a field exists, the Hilbert invariant integral I = ∫ (L dx + p dy) is path‑independent, and any curve in the domain has action greater than or equal to the action of the field extremal connecting the same endpoints. This gives a sufficient condition for a strong absolute minimum. The construction is equivalent to finding a complete solution of the Hamilton–Jacobi equation; the generating function S(x,y) of the field satisfies ∂S/∂x + H(x,y,∂S/∂y) = 0. The classical example is the central field for the geodesics on a surface of revolution: the Clairaut integral r sinφ = constant generates a field of geodesics, and the complete figure proves that the meridian is the unique shortest path between two points on the same meridian. In optimal control, the synthesis of optimal trajectories (the “field of extremals”) is the analogue of Carathéodory’s construction; the value function solves the Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman equation and its level sets form the complete figure. The method also underlies the verification theorem in dynamic programming: if a smooth solution of the HJB equation exists, it certifies optimality of the associated feedback law.

Applications to Optimal Control — Pontryagin Maximum Principle

The Pontryagin maximum principle (PMP) extends the calculus of variations to systems with control variables u(t) appearing nonlinearly and subject to inequality constraints u ∈ U. The state equation is ẋ = f(x,u,t), the cost functional is J = ∫₀ᵀ L(x,u,t) dt + φ(x(T)). Introduce the costate p(t) and the Hamiltonian H(x,u,p,t) = p·f(x,u,t) − L(x,u,t). The PMP states that for an optimal pair (x*,u*) there exists a non‑zero absolutely continuous costate p(t) such that: (1) ẋ* = ∂H/∂p, ṗ = −∂H/∂x; (2) u*(t) maximises H(x*(t),u,p(t),t) over u ∈ U for almost every t; (3) transversality conditions hold at the terminal time. The maximisation condition replaces the stationary condition ∂H/∂u = 0 when U has interior; if the maximum occurs on the boundary, the optimal control is of bang‑bang type. The principle also handles state constraints via additional multipliers and jump conditions for the costate. The PMP reduces to the Euler–Lagrange equation when f = u and U = ℝⁿ. Landmark applications: time‑optimal control of a double integrator (bang‑bang with at most one switch), the Goddard rocket problem (singular arcs), and the Zermelo navigation problem. The PMP is the cornerstone of modern optimal control theory and provides the necessary conditions used in numerical shooting methods and indirect optimisation algorithms.

  • Confusing the Legendre condition (pointwise) with the Jacobi condition (interval) — both are necessary but only together with Weierstrass give sufficiency.
  • Forgetting that the Weierstrass‑Erdmann corner conditions apply only to piecewise C¹ extremals; they are not needed for smooth solutions.
  • Treating the Lagrange multiplier in isoperimetric problems as a function of x instead of a constant.
  • Assuming a field exists for every variational problem; many problems have no global field, so the Hilbert invariant integral cannot be used.
  • Applying the Pontryagin maximum principle without checking the non‑triviality condition (p,λ) ≠ (0,0).
  • Neglecting transversality conditions at free endpoints or free terminal time, which often determine the multiplier values.
  • Misidentifying singular arcs in optimal control as regular bang‑bang switches; singular arcs require the generalised Legendre‑Clebsch condition.

hand/thin-groups.html:
Helfgott's Growth Theorem and the Bourgain–Gamburd Machine

Helfgott's 2008 product theorem for SL₂(𝔽ₚ) states that any symmetric generating set A ⊂ SL₂(𝔽ₚ) which is not contained in a proper subgroup satisfies |A³| ≥ |A|1+δ for an absolute δ > 0. This uniform growth statement is the engine behind the Bourgain–Gamburd machine: starting from a Zariski‑dense subgroup Γ = ⟨S⟩ ⊂ SLₙ(ℤ), one reduces modulo a square‑free integer q and studies the random walk on the finite quotients Γq. The machine requires three ingredients — a non‑concentration estimate (the random walk does not concentrate on proper subgroups), a flattening lemma (convolution powers of the step distribution become nearly uniform), and the product theorem to bootstrap small doubling into expansion. In the original Bourgain–Gamburd paper the eigenvalues of the generators were assumed real; later work of Varjú, Pyber–Szabó and Breuillard–Green–Tao removed this hypothesis by proving a uniform product theorem for all finite simple groups of Lie type. The consequence is that for any Zariski‑dense Γ ⊂ SLₙ(ℤ) the family of Cayley graphs Cay(Γq, Sq) forms an expander family as q runs over square‑free integers. This result is the precise formulation of superstrong approximation.

Key steps in the machine

  1. Non‑concentration: Using the Zariski density of Γ one shows that the probability of the random walk landing in any proper algebraic subgroup of SLₙ(𝔽ₚ) decays exponentially in the walk length.
  2. Flattening lemma: If a probability measure μ on a finite group has ‖μ‖₂ not too small, then μ * μ has significantly smaller ℓ²‑norm unless μ is already close to uniform.
  3. Product theorem: Helfgott's growth (or its higher‑rank analogues) forces any set with small tripling to be essentially a subgroup; combined with non‑concentration this yields a uniform spectral gap.

The machine has been adapted to other algebraic groups (e.g. Sp₂ₙ, SOₙ) and to thin subgroups of higher rank, where the product theorem is replaced by the Breuillard–Green–Tao structure theorem for approximate groups.

Spectral Gap Estimates for Thin Subgroups via the Flattening Lemma

For a thin subgroup Γ ⊂ SL₂(ℤ) the critical exponent δ(Γ) (the Hausdorff dimension of the limit set) governs the base eigenvalue λ₀ = δ(1−δ) of the Laplacian on the hyperbolic surface ℍ²/Γ. Superstrong approximation provides a uniform spectral gap for the congruence quotients Γ(q) ℍ², i.e. there exists ε > 0 such that the first non‑zero eigenvalue λ₁(Γ(q)) ≥ λ₀ + ε for all square‑free q. The proof proceeds by lifting the expander property of the Cayley graphs to the continuous spectrum via the Selberg trace formula. The flattening lemma, originally due to Bourgain and Gamburd, asserts that if a symmetric probability measure μ on a finite group G satisfies ‖μ‖₂ ≤ |G|−1/2+η then either μ is already close to uniform or μ * μ has strictly smaller ℓ²‑norm. Iterating this lemma yields rapid mixing of the random walk on Γ(q) and, by a standard comparison argument, a uniform lower bound on the spectral gap of the Laplacian on the associated hyperbolic orbifolds. In the thin setting the initial measure is supported on the image of a fixed generating set S; the non‑concentration estimate uses the fact that Γ is not virtually solvable, so its projections modulo p are not contained in proper subgroups for a density‑one set of primes. The resulting spectral gap is effective: one can compute explicit ε in terms of the generating set and the rank of the ambient algebraic group. This quantitative gap feeds directly into the affine sieve, where the level of distribution of the sifted set depends on the size of the spectral gap.

Worked Example: Verifying the Flattening Condition
Let Γ = ⟨S⟩ ⊂ SL₂(ℤ) be a Zariski‑dense subgroup with S = { (1 2; 0 1), (1 0; 2 1) }. For a prime p ≥ 5, let μₚ be the uniform probability measure on the image Sₚ ⊂ SL₂(𝔽ₚ). Show that ‖μₚ * μₚ‖₂ ≤ p−1/2+o(1) for all sufficiently large p.

Step 1: Compute the support size. The two matrices generate a free subgroup of rank 2, so their images in SL₂(𝔽ₚ) are distinct for all p ≥ 5. Hence |Sₚ| = 4 and μₚ is uniform on a set of size 4.

Step 2: The ℓ²‑norm of μₚ is ‖μₚ‖₂ = (4 · (1/4)²)1/2 = 1/2.

Step 3: Convolution μₚ * μₚ is supported on the set of products of two generators. By the product theorem in SL₂(𝔽ₚ) (Helfgott 2008), any subset A with |A| ≤ p2−δ satisfies |A³| ≥ |A|1+δ. Since |Sₚ| = 4 is constant, repeated multiplication rapidly expands the support until it reaches size ≫ p2−δ. After O(log p) steps the support is a positive proportion of SL₂(𝔽ₚ), whose order is p(p²−1) ≈ p³.

Step 4: At the second convolution step the support size is at most 16, still far below p2−δ. However the flattening lemma does not require the support to be large; it only needs that the measure is not concentrated on a proper subgroup. Because Γ is Zariski‑dense, the image of Γ in SL₂(𝔽ₚ) is the whole group for all but finitely many p (strong approximation). Hence the random walk equidistributes, and standard Fourier analysis on SL₂(𝔽ₚ) gives ‖μₚ * μₚ‖₂ ≤ C p−3/2 for some absolute C. Since p−3/2 = p−1/2·p−1, the bound p−1/2+o(1) holds.

Thus the flattening condition is satisfied for all large primes.

Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the spectral gap of a thin subgroup, first identify whether the subgroup is Zariski‑dense in a higher‑rank group or in SL₂. For higher rank, cite the Breuillard–Green–Tao approximate group theorem; for SL₂, invoke Helfgott's product theorem and the Bourgain–Gamburd flattening lemma. Always mention the role of the critical exponent δ and the base eigenvalue δ(1−δ). A concise answer listing the three pillars — non‑concentration, flattening, product theorem — earns full marks.

Integral Apollonian Circle Packings and the Local–Global Conjecture

An integral Apollonian circle packing is generated by four mutually tangent circles with integer curvatures (bend numbers). The Descartes quadratic form Q(a,b,c,d) = a²+b²+c²+d² − ½(a+b+c+d)² = 0 encodes the tangency relations. The Apollonian group 𝒜 ⊂ OQ(ℤ) ≅ O(3,1;ℤ) is a thin subgroup generated by four reflections in the coordinate hyperplanes. Its orbit on a primitive integer solution of Q = 0 yields all curvatures in the packing. The local–global conjecture (proved by Bourgain–Kontorovich 2010 for a density‑one set of packings) asserts that every sufficiently large integer satisfying the obvious congruence obstructions modulo 24 appears as a curvature. The proof combines the affine sieve with the spectral gap for the congruence quotients 𝒜(q). The critical exponent δ(𝒜) ≈ 1.30568 is the Hausdorff dimension of the residual set of the packing; the base eigenvalue λ₀ = δ(1−δ) ≈ 0.396. Superstrong approximation gives a uniform gap ε > 0, so the level of distribution in the sieve reaches X1−η for some η > 0, sufficient to detect almost‑primes of bounded order. The positive density of prime curvatures (Sarnak–Kontorovich 2011) follows by showing that the sifted set has the expected asymptotic with a main term of order X/(log X). Recent work of Zhang (2022) extended the local–global principle to all integral Apollonian packings, removing the density‑one restriction.

Congruence obstructions

The Descartes equation forces each curvature to be congruent to 0, 4, 12, or 16 modulo 24. These four residue classes are the only local obstructions; the local–global conjecture states they are also the only global obstructions. The proof uses the fact that the Apollonian group surjects onto OQ(ℤ/qℤ) for all square‑free q, a consequence of strong approximation for the orthogonal group O(3,1). The expander property of the Cayley graphs of these finite quotients provides the necessary equidistribution of the orbit modulo q, which is the analytic input for the affine sieve.

Higher Rank Affine Sieve and the Saturation Problem

The original affine sieve of Bourgain–Gamburd–Sarnak was developed for thin subgroups of SL₂(ℤ) acting on ℤ². In higher rank, say Γ ⊂ SLₙ(ℤ) with n ≥ 3, the orbit Γ·x₀ lives in ℤⁿ and the polynomial f may be a product of linear forms. The saturation problem asks whether the set of values f(Γ·x₀) contains integers with an arbitrarily large number of prime factors, and whether the local–global principle holds for the primitive values. The main new difficulty is that the critical exponent δ(Γ) can be strictly smaller than the dimension of the ambient symmetric space, so the base eigenvalue λ₀ = δ(1−δ) may be far from the tempered spectrum. However, property (τ) for the congruence quotients Γ(q) (which follows from superstrong approximation for Zariski‑dense subgroups of higher rank by the work of Salehi‑Golsefidy–Varjú) still provides a uniform spectral gap. This gap yields a level of distribution X1−η in the sieve, where η depends on the spectral gap and the degree of f. Recent results of Bourgain–Kontorovich–Magee (2020) and of Oh–Winter (2021) show that for any Zariski‑dense Γ ⊂ SLₙ(ℤ) and any non‑constant polynomial f which is not identically zero on the orbit, the set of almost‑prime values has the expected asymptotic density. The local–global conjecture in higher rank remains open in general, but it is known for certain symmetric spaces (e.g. integral orthogonal groups acting on quadratic forms) where the orbit is a single adelic orbit.

Key technical tools

  • Uniform exponential mixing of the geodesic flow on ΓG/K (Mohammadi–Oh 2015).
  • Effective equidistribution of expanding horospheres (Einsiedler–Lindenstrauss 2010).
  • The affine linear sieve framework of Bourgain–Gamburd–Sarnak adapted to the higher‑rank setting via the spectral gap for the Laplacian on Γ(q)G/K.

Property (τ) versus Property (T) in Arithmetic and Thin Groups

Property (T) (Kazhdan) means that the trivial representation is isolated in the unitary dual of the whole group G; it implies a uniform spectral gap for all families of finite‑index subgroups. Property (τ) is a relative version: a group Γ has property (τ) with respect to a family of finite‑index subgroups {Γᵢ} if the trivial representation is isolated in the unitary dual of Γ when restricted to representations that factor through some Γᵢ. All higher‑rank arithmetic lattices (e.g. SLₙ(ℤ), n ≥ 3) have property (T), hence property (τ) for any family of congruence subgroups. Thin subgroups of SL₂(ℤ) never have property (T) because they are free or virtually free, but they can have property (τ) with respect to their congruence quotients — this is exactly the content of Selberg's 3/16 theorem for congruence subgroups and its extension to thin groups via superstrong approximation. The distinction is crucial for the affine sieve: property (τ) provides the spectral gap needed for level of distribution, while property (T) would give a stronger, uniform gap independent of the family. In rank one, the optimal spectral gap is the Ramanujan bound λ₁ ≥ 1/4 (Selberg's eigenvalue conjecture), which is known for congruence subgroups of SL₂(ℤ) by the work of Deligne (via the Ramanujan–Petersson conjecture) but remains open for thin subgroups. The best known bound for thin subgroups is λ₁ ≥ λ₀ + ε, where λ₀ = δ(1−δ) and ε comes from the expander constant. Understanding whether thin subgroups can achieve the Ramanujan bound is an active research area; recent numerical experiments suggest that many thin groups do attain λ₁ = 1/4, but a proof would require new ideas beyond the Bourgain–Gamburd machine.

  • Trap 1: Confusing property (τ) with property (T); thin subgroups of SL₂ never have property (T) but often have property (τ) for congruence quotients.
  • Trap 2: Assuming the Ramanujan bound λ₁ ≥ 1/4 holds for all thin subgroups; it is only known for arithmetic lattices and remains conjectural for thin groups.
  • Trap 3: Overlooking the requirement that the generating set be symmetric and not contained in a proper algebraic subgroup when applying Helfgott's product theorem.
  • Trap 4: Treating the critical exponent δ as the Hausdorff dimension of the limit set without noting that δ < 1 for thin subgroups of SL₂(ℤ) and δ = 1 only for lattices.
  • Trap 5: Ignoring the congruence obstructions modulo 24 in Apollonian packings; the local–global principle only concerns integers satisfying these necessary local conditions.
  • Trap 6: Confusing the affine sieve's level of distribution X1−η with the full range X; the sieve only detects almost‑primes, not primes, unless additional bilinear forms estimates are available.
  • Trap 7: Assuming superstrong approximation holds for all Zariski‑dense subgroups without the square‑free modulus condition; the expander family is proved for square‑free q, and the general case requires additional work.

These advanced topics illustrate how the interplay of group theory, spectral geometry, and analytic number theory drives modern progress on thin groups and their arithmetic applications.

hand/ordered-algebra.html:
Hahn Embedding Theorem for Ordered Abelian Groups

The Hahn embedding theorem provides a concrete representation of any ordered abelian group as a lexicographically ordered subgroup of a Hahn group — a group of functions from a totally ordered index set to the real numbers with well‑ordered support. Let (G,+,≤) be an ordered abelian group. Its set of convex subgroups forms a chain under inclusion; this chain is order‑isomorphic to a totally ordered set Λ. For each λ∈Λ let G_λ be the corresponding convex subgroup and define the factor group G_λ/G<λ. Each factor is an Archimedean ordered group, hence embeds into (ℝ,+,≤) by Hölder’s theorem. Choosing an embedding for each factor yields a homomorphism φ:G→ℝ^Λ where φ(g)(λ) is the image of the coset of g in the factor. The image of φ lies in the Hahn group H(Λ,ℝ) = {f:Λ→ℝ | supp(f) is well‑ordered}. The order on H is lexicographic: f>0 iff the first non‑zero value of f on the well‑ordered support is positive. The theorem states that φ is an order‑preserving group embedding. Consequently every ordered abelian group is isomorphic to a lexicographically ordered subgroup of a Hahn group. This representation is unique up to order‑isomorphism of the index set and the chosen Archimedean embeddings. The Hahn embedding is a powerful tool for transferring problems about ordered groups to the setting of generalized power series, where valuation‑theoretic techniques apply.

Applications include the classification of ordered groups of finite rank, the study of valuations on fields via their value groups, and the construction of non‑Archimedean ordered fields such as the field of Hahn series ℝ((t^Γ)). The theorem also underlies the proof that the class of ordered abelian groups is an elementary class in the language of ordered groups, because the Hahn group construction can be described by a first‑order scheme.

Model Completeness and Quantifier Elimination in Real Closed Fields

A real closed field (RCF) is an ordered field in which every positive element has a square root and every polynomial of odd degree has a root. Tarski proved that the first‑order theory of real closed fields in the language {+,·,≤,0,1} admits quantifier elimination. This means that for any formula φ(x₁,…,xₙ) there exists a quantifier‑free formula ψ(x₁,…,xₙ) such that RCF ⊨ φψ. The quantifier‑free formulas are Boolean combinations of polynomial equalities and inequalities. As a corollary, the theory is model complete: every embedding of real closed fields is elementary. The Tarski–Seidenberg theorem, which states that the projection of a semialgebraic set is semialgebraic, is the geometric counterpart of quantifier elimination. It implies that the class of semialgebraic subsets of ℝⁿ is closed under projection, finite unions, intersections, and complements. Model completeness yields the transfer principle: any first‑order sentence true in ℝ holds in every real closed field, for example in the field of real algebraic numbers ℝ_alg or in the field of Puiseux series ℝ((t^ℚ)). This principle is the foundation of real algebraic geometry and of algorithms for deciding the truth of sentences in the theory of real closed fields, such as cylindrical algebraic decomposition (CAD). The complexity of quantifier elimination is doubly exponential in the number of quantifier alternations, a bound that is essentially optimal. Nevertheless, for many practical problems the CAD algorithm and its modern variants (e.g., virtual substitution, critical point methods) perform well.

Worked Example: Deciding a Sentence in RCF
Determine whether the sentence ∃x (x² + 1 = 0) is true in every real closed field.
In any ordered field, squares are non‑negative, so x² + 1 ≥ 1 > 0. Hence the equation x² + 1 = 0 has no solution. The sentence is false in ℝ, and by the transfer principle it is false in every real closed field. Quantifier elimination would replace the existential formula with the quantifier‑free false statement 0=1, confirming the result.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the truth of a first‑order statement in all real closed fields, first test it in ℝ. If it fails in ℝ, it fails everywhere by the transfer principle. If it holds in ℝ, check whether the statement is purely universal; universal sentences true in ℝ are true in all real closed fields. For existential statements, use quantifier elimination conceptually: replace the existential block by a quantifier‑free condition on the coefficients.

Archimedean and Non‑Archimedean Ordered Vector Lattices

An ordered vector lattice (or Riesz space) is a real vector space equipped with a lattice order that is compatible with addition and scalar multiplication by non‑negative scalars. The Archimedean property for a vector lattice E states that for any x,y∈E with nx ≤ y for all n∈ℕ, we must have x ≤ 0. Equivalently, the order is Archimedean iff the natural embedding of E into its order completion (the Dedekind completion) is injective. Every Archimedean vector lattice can be represented as a space of real‑valued functions on a compact Hausdorff space via the Yosida representation: there exists a compact Hausdorff space X such that E is lattice‑isomorphic to a dense sublattice of C(X) containing the constant functions. The representation is unique up to homeomorphism of X. Non‑Archimedean vector lattices contain infinitesimal elements: there exist x>0 such that nx ≤ y for all n but x≰0. The classic example is the space of formal power series ℝ[[t]] with the lexicographic order, where t is a positive infinitesimal. The theory of bands and projection bands extends to the non‑Archimedean setting, but the spectral theorem for order‑bounded operators requires Archimedeanity. In functional analysis, the Kakutani–Krein theorem characterizes the order dual of an Archimedean vector lattice as a band in the space of order‑bounded linear functionals. For non‑Archimedean lattices, the order dual may fail to separate points, leading to a richer structure of order‑continuous functionals.

Applications appear in the study of ordered algebras of operators, in the theory of vector measures, and in the construction of non‑standard models of analysis via ultrapowers of Archimedean lattices. The distinction between Archimedean and non‑Archimedean also governs the validity of the Hahn–Banach extension theorem for positive linear functionals: it holds in Archimedean lattices but may fail otherwise.

Spectral Theory of f‑Rings and the Yosida Representation

An f‑ring is a lattice‑ordered ring (A,∧,∨,+,·) satisfying the condition that a∧b=0 and c≥0 imply ca∧b=0 and ac∧b=0. This condition ensures that multiplication by a positive element is a lattice homomorphism. The Birkhoff–Pierce theorem states that every Archimedean f‑ring with identity is isomorphic to a sub‑f‑ring of C(X) for some compact Hausdorff space X, with pointwise operations and order. The space X can be taken as the maximal spectrum of the f‑ring, i.e., the set of maximal ℓ‑ideals equipped with the hull‑kernel topology. The Yosida representation extends this to Archimedean f‑rings without identity by adjoining a unit and representing the resulting unital f‑ring. The representation is functorial: ℓ‑homomorphisms correspond to continuous maps between the representing spaces. For a general f‑ring, the structure space of minimal prime ℓ‑ideals (the Pierce spectrum) carries a spectral topology and the f‑ring embeds into a sheaf of totally ordered rings over this space. The stalks are the quotients by minimal prime ℓ‑ideals, which are totally ordered integral domains. This sheaf representation is the analogue of the structure sheaf in algebraic geometry and provides a bridge between the algebraic theory of f‑rings and the topological theory of rings of continuous functions. Important consequences include the characterization of projective f‑rings, the description of the lattice of ℓ‑ideals as the lattice of open sets of the spectrum, and the fact that the class of Archimedean f‑rings is a variety generated by C([0,1]).

O‑Minimal Expansions beyond the Real Exponential Field

An o‑minimal structure on a dense linear order (R,<,+) is a sequence of Boolean algebras of definable subsets of Rⁿ closed under Cartesian products, permutations of coordinates, and projections, such that the definable subsets of R are exactly finite unions of intervals and points. The real field (ℝ,+,·,<) is o‑minimal. Wilkie proved that adding the real exponential function exp yields an o‑minimal structure ℝ_exp. Further expansions include ℝ_an, the structure generated by restricted analytic functions (functions analytic on a neighbourhood of [0,1]ⁿ and extended by zero outside), and ℝ_an,exp, the combination of both. Van den Dries, Macintyre, and Marker showed that ℝ_an,exp is o‑minimal and admits quantifier elimination in an expanded language. Another important class is the Pfaffian closure of an o‑minimal structure, obtained by adding solutions of Pfaffian differential equations; Khovanskii’s theory of fewnomials implies that Pfaffian closures remain o‑minimal. The Pila–Wilkie counting theorem applies to any o‑minimal structure: for a definable set X⊆ℝⁿ, the number of rational points of height ≤T lying outside the algebraic part of X grows slower than any power of T. This theorem has been instrumental in the proof of the André–Oort conjecture by Pila and Tsimerman, and in the Manin–Mumford conjecture for abelian varieties. Recent work by Binyamini and Novikov extends the counting theorem to definable families in ℝ_an,exp, opening the way to effective bounds in diophantine geometry. The classification of all o‑minimal expansions of the real field remains an open problem; it is known that any such expansion is either polynomially bounded (like ℝ_an) or defines the exponential function (like ℝ_exp).

  • Confusing the Hahn embedding with the Hölder embedding; the former works for arbitrary ordered abelian groups, the latter only for Archimedean ones.
  • Assuming quantifier elimination holds in the language of ordered rings without the order symbol; the order is essential for the Tarski–Seidenberg theorem.
  • Treating every vector lattice as Archimedean; non‑Archimedean examples such as ℝ[[t]] are standard counterexamples.
  • Believing the Birkhoff–Pierce representation applies to all f‑rings; it requires the Archimedean property and a unit.
  • Thinking o‑minimality is preserved under arbitrary expansions; adding the unrestricted sine function destroys o‑minimality.
  • Misapplying the Pila–Wilkie theorem to sets that are not definable in an o‑minimal structure; the theorem requires a fixed o‑minimal structure.
  • Overlooking that the transfer principle for real closed fields only covers first‑order sentences; second‑order properties like completeness do not transfer.

hand/quantum-cohomology.html:
Higher Genus Gromov–Witten Theory and the Holomorphic Anomaly Equation

Genus‑zero Gromov–Witten invariants are governed by the WDVV equations and the Frobenius manifold structure. For higher genus the picture is richer: the generating functions F_g(t) for g ≥ 1 satisfy the Bershadsky–Cecotti–Ooguri–Vafa (BCOV) holomorphic anomaly equations. These equations express the anti‑holomorphic derivative of F_g with respect to the complex structure moduli of the mirror Calabi–Yau threefold in terms of lower‑genus data and the genus‑zero Yukawa couplings. Concretely, ∂bar i F_g = ½ Cbar ijk ( D_j D_k Fg-1 + ∑h=1g-1 D_j F_h D_k Fg-h ), where Cbar ijk is the conjugate of the Yukawa coupling and D_j denotes the covariant derivative with respect to the Weil–Petersson metric. The anomaly arises because the path integral measure on the moduli space of stable maps fails to be holomorphic; the equation restores modularity when combined with the holomorphic ambiguity, a polynomial in the generators of the ring of modular forms. Solving the holomorphic anomaly recursively, together with boundary conditions at the large‑radius limit and the conifold point, determines all higher‑genus invariants for many Calabi–Yau threefolds, notably the quintic. The BCOV formalism also predicts the gap condition at the conifold, which fixes the holomorphic ambiguity uniquely. This recursive structure underlies the celebrated computation of genus‑one and genus‑two invariants for the quintic and for local Calabi–Yau geometries.

The holomorphic anomaly equation is deeply connected to the theory of topological string amplitudes on the B‑model side. The genus‑g free energy F_g can be interpreted as a section of a line bundle over the moduli space, and the anomaly reflects the failure of the B‑model topological string to be independent of the choice of polarization on the phase space of the Kodaira–Spencer theory. In the A‑model language, the same recursion appears in the Givental quantization formalism: the total descendant potential is obtained by applying a quantized symplectic transformation to the genus‑zero data. The equivalence of the two approaches is a non‑trivial theorem, proved in various settings by Givental, Coates–Givental, and others. For practical enumerative geometry, the holomorphic anomaly provides an algorithmic way to compute higher‑genus Gromov–Witten invariants without directly integrating over the compactified moduli spaces of stable maps, which are notoriously singular and high‑dimensional.

Givental's Quantization and the Topological Vertex

Givental’s quantization formalism gives a universal construction of the total Gromov–Witten potential from the genus‑zero Frobenius manifold. One starts with the symplectic vector space H = H^*(X)((z-1)) equipped with the symplectic form Ω(f,g) = Resz=0 (f(-z), g(z)) dz. The genus‑zero data determine a Lagrangian cone L ⊂ H, and the quantization of a symplectic transformation R(z) acting on H produces an operator R on the Fock space of formal power series in the variables q_k^α. The total descendant potential Z_X = R S Psi (τpt) is then expressed as the action of three quantized operators on the trivial theory τpt. Here S encodes the fundamental solution of the quantum differential equation, Psi implements the change of basis from flat coordinates to the canonical basis, and R is the asymptotic expansion of the fundamental solution at z = ∞. This factorization is the mathematical incarnation of the B‑model topological string partition function on the mirror.

The topological vertex, introduced by Aganagic, Klemm, Marino, and Vafa, provides a combinatorial rule for computing the open and closed topological string amplitudes on toric Calabi–Yau threefolds. It assigns a weight to each trivalent vertex of the toric diagram, expressed in terms of Schur functions and the framing factor. Gluing vertices along edges corresponds to summing over representations, yielding the full partition function. The topological vertex is equivalent to the Givental quantization for toric varieties: the quantized operator R can be identified with the product of vertex operators, and the gluing rules reproduce the symplectic transformation that relates the A‑model and B‑model potentials. This equivalence has been proved by Liu, Liu, and Zhou using the Eynard–Orantin topological recursion on the mirror curve. The vertex formalism also extends to open Gromov–Witten invariants with Lagrangian branes, giving a powerful tool for computing disk and annulus amplitudes. In the context of the Donaldson–Thomas/Gromov–Witten correspondence, the topological vertex computes the DT partition function via the non‑commutative Donaldson–Thomas theory of Szendrői, providing a bridge between curve counting and ideal sheaf counting.

Worked Example: Genus‑One Quintic Invariant via Holomorphic Anomaly
Using the BCOV holomorphic anomaly equation, compute the genus‑one Gromov–Witten invariant N1 for the quintic threefold X ⊂ ℙ4. The genus‑zero Yukawa coupling is Cttt = 5 / (1 - 55 q) where q = e^t. The genus‑one free energy satisfies ∂bar t F1 = ½ Cbar ttt D_t D_t F0. The holomorphic ambiguity is fixed by the boundary condition F1 ∼ -½ log Δ at the conifold, where Δ = 1 - 55 q.
The genus‑zero prepotential is F0 = 5/6 t3 + ∑d≥1 N_d edt with N1 = 2875. The covariant derivative D_t F0 = ∂_t F0 - 2 ∂_t K F0, where K is the Kähler potential. At large radius, the Weil–Petersson metric gives Cbar ttt = (Cttt)-1 gtbar t gtbar t. Using the known expression for the genus‑one potential on the quintic, F1 = -½ log( (1 - 55 q) q-5/2 ) + constant. Expanding F1 = ∑d≥1 N1(1) edt yields N1(1) = -200/3? Actually the integer invariant after Gopakumar–Vafa transformation is n1 = 0 for genus one? Wait, the genus‑one Gromov–Witten invariant for the quintic is N1 = 0? The correct genus‑one invariant is N1 = 0 because there are no genus‑one curves in the quintic? The BCOV computation gives F1 = -½ log(1 - 55 q) + 5/2 log q + const. The coefficient of q is 0, so N1 = 0. The first non‑zero higher‑genus invariant appears at genus two. Thus the holomorphic anomaly correctly predicts the vanishing of the genus‑one invariant.
Exam Strategy
When a question asks for the structure of higher‑genus invariants, recall that the BCOV equation is recursive and requires the genus‑zero Yukawa coupling and the Weil–Petersson metric. The holomorphic ambiguity is fixed by boundary conditions at large radius and the conifold. For toric Calabi–Yau threefolds, the topological vertex gives a purely combinatorial alternative. Know the distinction: BCOV works for any Calabi–Yau threefold with a mirror, while the vertex is specific to toric geometries. In multiple‑choice items, the phrase “holomorphic anomaly” almost always signals the BCOV recursion, not the WDVV equations.

Orbifold Quantum Cohomology and the Crepant Resolution Conjecture

Orbifold Gromov–Witten theory extends the standard theory to target spaces that are Deligne–Mumford stacks, notably global quotient stacks [X/G] where G is a finite group acting on a smooth variety X. The state space is the Chen–Ruan orbifold cohomology H^*CR([X/G]), which includes twisted sectors indexed by conjugacy classes of G. The orbifold quantum product deforms the Chen–Ruan cup product by genus‑zero orbifold Gromov–Witten invariants, which count stable maps from orbifold curves to the stack. The Crepant Resolution Conjecture (CRC), formulated by Ruan and refined by Bryan–Graber, asserts that if Y → X is a crepant resolution of an orbifold X (i.e., the canonical bundles match), then the quantum cohomology of Y and the orbifold quantum cohomology of X become isomorphic after an analytic continuation in the quantum parameters and a suitable change of variables (the “crepant transformation”). For example, the orbifold ℂ3/ℤ3 has crepant resolution the total space of Oℙ2(-3); their quantum cohomology rings match after identifying the quantum parameter q_Y with -q_X and analytically continuing across the wall q = -1. The conjecture has been proved in many toric cases by Coates, Iritani, Jiang, and others using the Givental formalism and the theory of I‑functions. The CRC also predicts a correspondence between the Gromov–Witten invariants of Y and the orbifold invariants of X, which has been verified for local ℙ2 and for the Hilbert scheme of points on ℂ2 versus the symmetric product.

The orbifold quantum product is encoded in the orbifold J‑function, a generating function of one‑point descendant invariants with a twisted sector insertion. The J‑function satisfies a quantum differential equation (the orbifold Picard–Fuchs equation) whose solutions provide the mirror map for the stack. In the Givental framework, the orbifold theory is obtained by quantizing a symplectic transformation that relates the orbifold cone to the trivial cone. The crepant transformation corresponds to a symplectic transformation between the cones of Y and X, which is induced by the Fourier–Mukai kernel of the derived equivalence between D^b(Y) and D^b([X/G]). This derived equivalence is the categorical shadow of the CRC, and it underlies the homological mirror symmetry statement for stacks. The CRC has profound implications for the McKay correspondence: it identifies the quantum cohomology of the minimal resolution of a Kleinian singularity ℂ2/Γ with the orbifold quantum cohomology of the quotient stack, and the quantum parameters correspond to the exceptional divisors.

Quantum Lefschetz Hyperplane Theorem and Applications

The Quantum Lefschetz Hyperplane Theorem, proved by Coates and Givental, relates the genus‑zero Gromov–Witten invariants of a smooth hypersurface X ⊂ Y to those of the ambient variety Y. Let Y be a smooth projective variety with a convex vector bundle E (i.e., H1(C, f^*E) = 0 for all stable maps f: C → Y). If X is the zero locus of a regular section of E, then the genus‑zero Gromov–Witten invariants of X can be expressed in terms of the twisted Gromov–Witten invariants of Y, where the twist is given by the Euler class of the obstruction bundle R1π_*ev^*E on the moduli space of stable maps to Y. In the language of the quantum D‑module, the J‑function of X is obtained from the twisted J‑function of Y by applying the “quantum Lefschetz” operator, which is a certain hypergeometric modification of the fundamental solution. Concretely, if Y = ℙ^n and E = O(d), then the I‑function of the degree‑d hypersurface X_d is I_X(q,z) = ∑k≥0 q^k ∏m=1dk (dH + mz) / ∏m=1^k (H + mz)n+1, where H is the hyperplane class. The mirror map is extracted from the coefficient of 1/z, and the genus‑zero potential follows by the usual reconstruction. This theorem is the engine behind the mirror theorem for complete intersections in toric varieties: one first computes the twisted I‑function of the ambient toric variety using the toric mirror theorem, then applies the quantum Lefschetz operator for each defining equation.

Applications of the Quantum Lefschetz theorem are numerous. It gives a uniform proof of the mirror formula for Calabi–Yau complete intersections in toric varieties, including the famous quintic threefold. It also yields the quantum cohomology of Fano complete intersections, such as cubic threefolds and intersections of quadrics. In the Fano case, the quantum product is semisimple, and the quantum Lefschetz theorem provides the initial data for the Dubrovin reconstruction of the Frobenius manifold. The theorem extends to orbifold targets: if Y is a smooth Deligne–Mumford stack and E a convex orbibundle, the same formula holds for the orbifold quantum cohomology of the zero locus. This orbifold version is crucial for the proof of the Crepant Resolution Conjecture for toric Calabi–Yau threefolds, where the ambient space is a toric stack and the hypersurface is a crepant resolution. Moreover, the quantum Lefschetz theorem has a K‑theoretic analogue, the Quantum K‑theoretic Lefschetz theorem, which relates the quantum K‑theory of a hypersurface to the twisted quantum K‑theory of the ambient space, opening the way to mirror symmetry in quantum K‑theory.

  • Confusing the holomorphic anomaly equation (higher genus) with the WDVV equations (genus zero).
  • Assuming the topological vertex works for arbitrary Calabi–Yau threefolds; it is restricted to toric geometries.
  • Neglecting the analytic continuation in the Crepant Resolution Conjecture; the isomorphism of quantum rings holds only after continuation across a wall.
  • Forgetting the convexity hypothesis in the Quantum Lefschetz theorem; without it the obstruction bundle does not vanish and the formula fails.
  • Mixing up the orbifold Chen–Ruan cohomology grading (age shift) with the ordinary cohomology grading when computing orbifold quantum products.
  • Treating the Givental quantization as a formal power series trick without recognizing its geometric origin in the symplectic structure of the loop space.
  • Overlooking the role of the framing factor in the topological vertex; different framings give different open invariants and must be matched to the A‑model boundary conditions.

These advanced topics form the core of modern research in Gromov–Witten theory and mirror symmetry and are essential for a deep understanding of the subject.
