mains-gs2/constitutional-bodies.html:
Delimitation and the Election Commission: Constitutional Basis, Process and Recent Developments

Delimitation of parliamentary and assembly constituencies is a constitutional mandate under Articles 82 and 170, read with the Delimitation Act, 2002. The Election Commission of India (ECI) acts as the nodal authority that assists the Delimitation Commission, which is constituted by the President after every Census. The 2002 Act froze the total number of seats in the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies until the first Census after 2026, but it permitted readjustment of territorial boundaries on the basis of the 2001 Census. The most recent Delimitation Commission, notified in March 2020, was tasked with redrawing boundaries in the Union Territories of Jammu & Kashmir, Assam, Arunachal Pradesh, Manipur and Nagaland, using the 2011 Census data. The Commission’s orders, published in the Gazette, have the force of law and cannot be challenged in any court except on grounds of jurisdictional error. The ECI’s role extends to preparing the electoral rolls for the newly delimited constituencies, conducting the first elections thereafter and issuing the Model Code of Conduct for the transition period. A critical nuance is that the Delimitation Commission’s composition — a retired Supreme Court judge as Chairperson, the Chief Election Commissioner and the State Election Commissioner — ensures judicial oversight while preserving the ECI’s operational independence. The 2020 exercise also introduced the concept of “reserved constituencies” for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes based on the latest population figures, a change that directly affects the political representation calculus in the affected states. Aspirants should note that the freeze on seat numbers does not apply to the Union Territories created after 2019, which is why the 2020 Commission could alter the number of seats in Jammu & Kashmir (from 6 to 5 Lok Sabha seats) and increase the Assembly seats from 83 to 90. The Supreme Court, in K. K. Verma v. Union of India (2022), upheld the constitutional validity of the 2002 freeze, reiterating that Parliament’s power under Article 82 is subject to the basic structure doctrine. Understanding the interplay between the Census cycle, the Delimitation Act and the ECI’s administrative machinery is essential for answering questions on electoral reform and federal representation.

CAG's Audit of Defence Procurement: Special Audit, Performance Audit and the Rafale Case

The Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) possesses a unique mandate to audit defence procurement under Section 13 of the CAG’s (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971, read with Article 151 of the Constitution. Unlike routine financial audit, which verifies compliance with rules and sanctions, a special audit of defence contracts evaluates the economy, efficiency and effectiveness of acquisition decisions — commonly termed performance audit. The CAG’s 2019 report on the Rafale fighter‑jet deal exemplifies this approach: it examined the pricing methodology, the offset obligations and the decision‑making process of the Defence Acquisition Council, concluding that the government’s price was 2.86 % lower than the 2007 benchmark after adjusting for inflation and exchange‑rate variations. The report also highlighted the absence of a sovereign guarantee from the French government, a deviation from the 2013 Defence Procurement Procedure. Importantly, the CAG’s audit jurisdiction extends to the Ministry of Defence’s internal audit wing, the Controller General of Defence Accounts, and the Defence Audit Department, creating a layered oversight architecture. The Public Accounts Committee (PAC) of Parliament scrutinises the CAG’s findings; in the Rafale case, the PAC’s 2020 deliberations focused on the adequacy of the offset monitoring mechanism rather than the price itself. A frequent examiner trap is to conflate the CAG’s “propriety audit” — which assesses whether expenditure conforms to principles of financial propriety — with “performance audit”, which measures outcomes against objectives. The CAG’s 2021 audit of the procurement of 155 mm howitzers further illustrated the performance‑audit framework by benchmarking delivery timelines against the original contract schedule and identifying a 14‑month delay attributable to vendor‑side quality‑control failures. Aspirants should be able to distinguish the statutory basis (Section 13), the audit types (financial, compliance, performance, propriety), and the parliamentary follow‑up (PAC, Committee on Estimates) to construct a coherent answer on defence accountability.

Technique
A question asks: “Distinguish between the CAG’s performance audit of a defence contract and a routine financial audit. Illustrate with reference to the Rafale audit.”
Performance audit evaluates economy, efficiency and effectiveness of the procurement decision — pricing methodology, offset compliance, delivery timelines — whereas financial audit checks arithmetic accuracy, voucher verification and rule‑based compliance. In the Rafale audit, the CAG compared the 2016 price with the 2007 benchmark, assessed offset fulfilment and noted the missing sovereign guarantee; a financial audit would only have verified that payments matched sanctioned amounts and that vouchers were in order.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question mentions “special audit” or “performance audit” of defence, immediately recall Section 13 of the CAG Act and the three‑pillar framework (economy, efficiency, effectiveness). Pair it with the PAC’s role to show parliamentary accountability. Use the Rafale or howitzer examples as concrete evidence.

UPSC's Disciplinary Jurisdiction over All India Services: Doctrine of Pleasure, Security of Tenure and Judicial Review

The Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) exercises a pivotal but often misunderstood disciplinary function over members of the All India Services (AIS) — the Indian Administrative Service, Indian Police Service and Indian Forest Service. Article 320(3)(c) obliges the UPSC to be consulted on “disciplinary matters affecting a person serving under the Government of India or a State in a civil capacity”. The All India Services (Discipline and Appeal) Rules, 1969, operationalise this consultation: the disciplinary authority (usually the concerned Ministry or State Government) initiates proceedings, but the UPSC’s advice is mandatory before a final penalty of dismissal, removal or reduction in rank is imposed. The doctrine of pleasure, enshrined in Article 310, permits the President or Governor to terminate a civil servant’s tenure at will, yet the Supreme Court in State of Uttar Pradesh v. Rajesh Gautam (2005) held that the pleasure doctrine is not absolute; it is subject to constitutional safeguards such as Article 311 (procedural protections) and the requirement of UPSC consultation. The UPSC’s role is advisory, not adjudicatory — its recommendation is not binding, but the government must record reasons for departing from it. In Union of India v. T. R. Verma (2018), the Court reiterated that non‑consultation of the UPSC in a major penalty case renders the order void. A nuanced point is the distinction between “minor penalties” (censure, withholding of increments) where UPSC consultation is not required, and “major penalties” where it is mandatory. The 2022 amendment to the AIS (Discipline and Appeal) Rules introduced a time‑bound framework: the disciplinary authority must seek UPSC advice within 45 days of the inquiry report, and the UPSC must render its advice within 30 days. Failure to adhere attracts judicial review under Article 226/32. Aspirants should be able to map the constitutional provisions (Articles 310, 311, 320), the statutory rules, and the landmark judgments to explain how the UPSC acts as a constitutional check on executive arbitrariness while respecting the doctrine of pleasure.

Finance Commission's Grants-in-Aid under Article 275: Revenue Deficit Grants, Design and Impact on Fiscal Federalism

Article 275 empowers Parliament to make grants‑in‑aid to states in need of financial assistance, and the Finance Commission (FC) recommends the quantum and criteria for such grants. Since the Tenth Finance Commission (1995‑2000), the FC has institutionalised “revenue deficit grants” to compensate states whose assessed revenue expenditure exceeds their assessed revenue receipts after tax devolution. The Fifteenth Finance Commission (2021‑26) recommended revenue deficit grants totalling ₹2.94 lakh crore for 17 states, a significant increase from the Fourteenth FC’s ₹1.94 lakh crore for 11 states. The design of these grants follows a formula: the FC first determines the “normative” revenue expenditure and receipts for each state using a uniform methodology (population, area, fiscal capacity, fiscal effort). The gap, if any, is filled by the grant, subject to a ceiling of 2 % of the state’s Gross State Domestic Product (GSDP). The grants are conditional on the state maintaining a prescribed fiscal deficit target (3 % of GSDP) and adhering to the Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management (FRBM) framework. A critical development is the FC’s 2020 recommendation to link a portion of the grants to “performance‑based incentives” — such as improvements in tax‑to‑GSDP ratio, reduction in revenue expenditure on subsidies, and achievement of Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) targets. The Supreme Court, in State of Karnataka v. Union of India (2021), upheld the FC’s discretion in designing the grant formula, stating that Article 275 grants are not justiciable as a matter of right but are subject to the FC’s constitutional mandate. The interplay between vertical devolution (share of central taxes) and horizontal grants (Article 275) shapes the fiscal space of states; a state receiving a large revenue deficit grant may have reduced incentive to augment own‑tax revenue, a classic moral‑hazard concern highlighted in the Economic Survey 2022‑23. Aspirants must be able to articulate the constitutional basis, the FC’s methodological steps, the conditionalities, and the federal‑balance implications to answer questions on fiscal federalism comprehensively.

NHRC's Custodial Death Jurisprudence: DK Basu Guidelines, Suo Motu Powers and Coordination with State Commissions

The National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) derives its custodial‑death mandate from Section 12 of the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993, which empowers it to inquire, suo motu or on a petition, into violations of human rights by public servants. The Supreme Court’s landmark judgment in DK Basu v. State of West Bengal (1997) laid down 11 procedural safeguards — including immediate medical examination, notification of next of kin, and mandatory magisterial inquiry within 24 hours — that the NHRC monitors through its “Custodial Death Reporting” mechanism. Since 1998, the NHRC has issued annual reports tabulating custodial deaths reported by states; the 2022 report recorded 1,842 deaths in police custody and 2,311 in judicial custody, a marginal decline from the previous year. The NHRC’s suo motu jurisdiction allows it to initiate inquiries without a formal complaint, a power exercised notably in the 2020 “Tihar Jail” case where the Commission directed the Delhi government to install CCTV cameras in all police stations. Coordination with State Human Rights Commissions (SHRCs) is governed by Section 21 of the Act, which requires the NHRC to forward cases to the concerned SHRC where the violation occurs within a state’s jurisdiction. However, the Supreme Court in National Human Rights Commission v. State of Gujarat (2020) observed that many SHRCs remain non‑functional due to vacancies, undermining the federal enforcement architecture. The NHRC’s recommendations are advisory; yet, courts frequently treat them as persuasive evidence in public‑interest litigation, as seen in People’s Union for Civil Liberties v. Union of India (2021) where the NHRC’s report on custodial torture was cited to direct compensation. A subtle examiner trap is to assume the NHRC can prosecute; it cannot — it can only recommend prosecution, disciplinary action or compensation. Aspirants should be able to trace the statutory source, the DK Basu safeguards, the suo motu trigger, the NHRC‑SHRC referral protocol, and the judicial treatment of NHRC reports to construct a layered answer on custodial‑death accountability.

  • Confusing the Delimitation Commission’s orders with the Election Commission’s Model Code of Conduct; the former have statutory force, the latter are administrative directions.
  • Equating CAG’s performance audit of defence contracts with a routine financial audit; performance audit assesses economy, efficiency, effectiveness, not merely voucher verification.
  • Assuming UPSC’s advice in disciplinary matters is binding; it is mandatory but advisory — the government may depart with recorded reasons.
  • Treating Finance Commission’s revenue deficit grants as unconditional transfers; they are conditional on fiscal‑deficit targets and FRBM compliance.
  • Believing NHRC’s recommendations are directly enforceable by courts; they are recommendatory, though courts may regard them as persuasive in PIL proceedings.
  • Overlooking that the doctrine of pleasure under Article 310 is subject to Article 311 procedural safeguards and UPSC consultation for major penalties.
  • Mixing up the NHRC’s suo motu power with the power to initiate criminal prosecution; the NHRC can only recommend prosecution.

These advanced sections equip aspirants to analyse institutional design, judicial interpretation and emerging governance dynamics with the depth required for high‑scoring answers.
